concept_text: A company's Flight Deals website (on-premises) hosts high-resolution photos and uses third-party payments. Heavy marketing campaign = massive traffic increase expected . Tight deadline = no time for full AWS migration . Need security rules blocking SQL injection and XSS attacks. Which option maintains functionality despite massive incoming traffic? A. Generate AMI, launch EC2 fleet with Auto Scaling behind ALB balancing on-premises and AWS servers B. Use CloudFront to cache high-resolution images/static assets. Deploy AWS WAF on CloudFront distribution C. Use AWS Application Migration Service to migrate website to VPC. Create Auto Scaling group and deploy WAF on CloudFront D. Create S3 static website hosting, move domain to Route 53, enable S3 encryption with KMS ✅ B. CloudFront + WAF 🎯 CloudFront provides immediate scalability for high-resolution images without migration time, while WAF blocks attacks. Perfect for tight deadline constraint. ⚠️ A — Requires Direct Connect/VPN connection between on-premises and AWS (not mentioned) ⚠️ C — Migration takes time, violates "tight deadline" constraint ⚠️ D — Dynamic website with payments can't use static S3 hosting 📖 Full Explanation Amazon CloudFront is a web service that speeds up distribution of your static and dynamic web content, such as .html, .css, .js, and image files, to your users. CloudFront delivers your content through a worldwide network of data centers called edge locations. When a user requests content that you're serving with CloudFront, the user is routed to the edge location that provides the lowest latency (time delay), so that content is delivered with the best possible performance. AWS WAF is a web application firewall that helps protect your web applications or APIs against common web exploits that may affect availability, compromise security, or consume excessive resources. AWS WAF gives you control over how traffic reaches your applications by enabling you to create security rules that block common attack patterns, such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting, and rules that filter out specific traffic patterns you define. You can get started quickly using Managed Rules for AWS WAF, a pre-configured set of rules managed by AWS or AWS Marketplace Sellers. The Managed Rules for WAF address issues like the OWASP Top 10 security risks. These rules are regularly updated as new issues emerge. AWS WAF includes a full-featured API that you can use to automate the creation, deployment, and maintenance of security rules. AWS WAF is easy to deploy and protect applications deployed on either Amazon CloudFront as part of your CDN solution, the Application Load Balancer that fronts all your origin servers, or Amazon API Gateway for your APIs. There is no additional software to deploy, DNS configuration, SSL/TLS certificate to manage, or need for a reverse proxy setup. With AWS Firewall Manager integration, you can centrally define and manage your rules, and reuse them across all the web applications that you need to protect. Hence, the option that says: Use CloudFront to cache and distribute the high resolution images and other static assets of the website. Deploy AWS WAF on the Amazon CloudFront distribution to protect the website from common web attacks is correct because CloudFront will provide the scalability the website needs without doing major infrastructure changes. You can create a CloudFront distribution using a custom origin. Each distribution will can point to an S3 or to a custom origin. A custom origin is an HTTP server, for example, a web server. The HTTP server can be an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance or an HTTP server that you manage privately (like an on-premises web server). Take note that the website has a lot of high-resolution images which can easily be cached using CloudFront to alleviate the massive incoming traffic going to the on-premises web server and also provide a faster page load time for the web visitors. The option that says: Use the AWS Application Migration Service to easily migrate the website from your on-premises data center to your VPC. Create an Auto Scaling group to automatically scale the web tier based on the incoming traffic. Deploy AWS WAF on the Amazon CloudFront distribution to protect the website from common web attacks is incorrect as migrating to AWS would be time-consuming compared with simply using CloudFront. Although this option can provide a more scalable solution, the scenario says that the company does not have ample time to do the migration. The option that says: Create and configure an S3 bucket as a static website hosting. Move the web domain of the website from your on-premises data center to Route53 then route the newly created S3 bucket as the origin. Enable Amazon S3 server-side encryption with AWS Key Management Service managed keys is incorrect because the website is a dynamic website that accepts payments and bookings. Migrating your web domain to Route 53 may also take some time. The option that says: Generate an AMI based on the existing Flight Deals website. Launch the AMI to a fleet of EC2 instances with Auto Scaling group enabled, for it to automatically scale up or scale down based on the incoming traffic. Place these EC2 instances behind an ALB which can balance traffic between the web servers in the on-premises data center and the web servers hosted in AWS is incorrect because it didn't mention any existing AWS Direct Connect or VPN connection. Although an Application Load Balancer can load balance the traffic between the EC2 instances in AWS Cloud and web servers located in the on-premises data center, your systems should be connected via Direct Connect or VPN connection first. In addition, the application seems to be used around the world because the company launched a global marketing campaign. Hence, CloudFront is a more suitable option for this scenario.

A company uses AWS Organizations for multi-account infrastructure. They need to automate sharing AWS resources between accounts using AWS RAM. A service needs to perform tasks on organization accounts on behalf of a previous account moderator who maintained specific configurations. What is the simplest solution to allow the service to perform tasks on organization accounts on the moderator's behalf? A. Enable cross-account access with AWS Organizations in the Resource Access Manager Console. Mirror the configuration changes that was performed by the account that previously managed this service. B. Configure a service-linked role for AWS RAM and modify the permissions policy to specify what the role can and cannot do. Lastly, modify the trust policy of the role so that other processes can utilize AWS RAM. C. Use trusted access by running the enable-sharing-with-aws-organization command in the AWS RAM CLI. Mirror the configuration changes that was performed by the account that previously managed this service. D. Attach an IAM role on the service detailing all the allowed actions that it will be able to perform. Install an SSM agent in each of the worker VMs. Use AWS Systems Manager to build automation workflows that involve the daily key processes. ✅ C. Use trusted access by running the enable-sharing-with-aws-organization command 🎯 Trusted access allows AWS RAM to create service-linked roles across all organization accounts automatically, enabling centralized resource sharing management. ⚠️ A. Cross-account access — Should enable trusted access, not cross-account access ⚠️ B. Manual service-linked role — Trust policies of service-linked roles cannot be modified ⚠️ D. SSM automation — Overly complex solution that doesn't address RAM-Organizations integration 📖 Full Explanation AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) enables you to share specified AWS resources that you own with other AWS accounts. To enable trusted access with AWS Organizations: From the AWS RAM CLI, use the enable-sharing-with-aws-organizations command. Name of the IAM service-linked role that can be created in accounts when trusted access is enabled: AWSResourceAccessManagerServiceRolePolicy. You can use trusted access to enable an AWS service that you specify, called the trusted service, to perform tasks in your organization and its accounts on your behalf. This involves granting permissions to the trusted service but does not otherwise affect the permissions for IAM users or roles. When you enable access, the trusted service can create an IAM role called a service-linked role in every account in the organization. That role has a permissions policy that allows the trusted service to do the tasks that are described in that service's documentation.

An IT consultancy uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple regional AWS accounts. A new account was added to an OU for systems administration. The account uses a root-created ECS Cluster with service-linked role . A solutions architect created a custom SCP to deny certain ECS actions but the account can still perform the restricted actions. Which is the most likely reason for this problem? A. The default SCP grants all permissions attached to every root, OU, and account. To apply stricter permissions, this policy is required to be modified. B. There is an SCP attached to a higher-level OU that permits the actions of the service-linked role. This permission would therefore be inherited by the current OU, and override the SCP placed by the administrator. C. SCPs do not affect any service-linked role. Service-linked roles enable other AWS services to integrate with AWS Organizations and can't be restricted by SCPs. D. The ECS service is being run outside the jurisdiction of the organization. SCPs affect only the principals that are managed by accounts that are part of the organization. ✅ C. SCPs do not affect any service-linked role 🎯 Service-linked roles are AWS-managed roles that enable service integration with Organizations and are explicitly exempt from SCP restrictions. ⚠️ A. Default SCP — scenario states custom deny policy was already created ⚠️ B. Higher-level OU permissions — deny policies override any allow policies in SCP hierarchy ⚠️ D. Service outside organization — service-linked role exists within the organization account 📖 Full Explanation Users and roles must still be granted permissions using IAM permission policies attached to them or to groups. The SCPs filter the permissions granted by such policies, and the user can't perform any actions that the applicable SCPs don't allow. Actions allowed by the SCPs can be used if they are granted to the user or role by one or more IAM permission policies. When you attach SCPs to the root, OUs, or directly to accounts, all policies that affect a given account are evaluated together using the same rules that govern IAM permission policies: – Any action that has an explicit Deny in an SCP can't be delegated to users or roles in the affected accounts. An explicit Deny statement overrides any Allow that other SCPs might grant. – Any action that has an explicit Allow in an SCP (such as the default "*" SCP or by any other SCP that calls out a specific service or action) can be delegated to users and roles in the affected accounts. – Any action that isn't explicitly allowed by an SCP is implicitly denied and can't be delegated to users or roles in the affected accounts. By default, an SCP named FullAWSAccess is attached to every root, OU, and account. This default SCP allows all actions and all services. So in a new organization, until you start creating or manipulating the SCPs, all of your existing IAM permissions continue to operate as they did. As soon as you apply a new or modified SCP to a root or OU that contains an account, the permissions that your users have in that account become filtered by the SCP. Permissions that used to work might now be denied if they're not allowed by the SCP at every level of the hierarchy down to the specified account. As stated in the documentation of AWS Organizations, SCPs DO NOT affect any service-linked role. Service-linked roles enable other AWS services to integrate with AWS Organizations and can't be restricted by SCPs.

A print media company has a web application for searching newspaper archives. They scanned old newspapers to PNG images and used OCR software to convert to text. The OCR license expires soon and they want to move to AWS with a scalable, durable, highly available architecture. Which is the best option to achieve this requirement? A. Store images in S3, use Amazon Kendra for search, lifecycle policy to Glacier after 3 months with Glacier Select B. CloudFormation with EBS-backed EC2 instances, ALB, NGINX web server, open source search, EBS volumes with Data Lifecycle Manager C. S3 bucket with CloudFront, Elastic Beanstalk multi-AZ website, Amazon OpenSearch Service for queries, Amazon Textract for OCR D. S3 Intelligent-Tiering, migrate existing OCR software to Auto Scaling Spot instances with ALB, use Amazon Rekognition for text ✅ C. S3 + CloudFront + Elastic Beanstalk + OpenSearch + Textract 🎯 Amazon Textract replaces expiring OCR software, OpenSearch provides scalable search, multi-AZ ensures high availability. ⚠️ A. Kendra can't extract text from scanned images, Glacier affects retrieval performance ⚠️ B. EBS volumes less scalable/durable than S3, more maintenance overhead ⚠️ D. Still uses expiring OCR software, Rekognition not optimized for document text extraction 📖 Full Explanation Amazon OpenSearch Service simplifies deployment and scaling of search capabilities without hardware management. Amazon Textract is specifically designed for OCR from documents, going beyond simple text recognition to extract structured data. S3 provides durable storage, CloudFront improves global performance, and Elastic Beanstalk offers managed multi-AZ hosting. Option A fails because Kendra doesn't perform OCR and Glacier impacts performance. Option B uses less scalable EBS storage with maintenance overhead. Option D keeps the expiring OCR software and uses Rekognition incorrectly for document text extraction.

A multi-tiered web application uses Auto Scaling EC2 instances in private subnets across two AZs . The "find nearby store" function (third-party API call) works only 50% of the time when refreshed. The application uses EC2 NAT instances for outbound calls. Which is the MOST likely reason and recommended solution? A. Failed NAT instance in public subnet. Use NAT Gateways instead of EC2 NAT instances. B. AZ failure at third-party provider. Contact provider support. C. Overloaded NAT instance. Scale to larger EC2 instances. D. Misconfigured Network ACL blocking outbound traffic. Update ACL rules. ✅ A: Failed NAT instance - Use NAT Gateways 🎯 50% failure rate with 2 AZs suggests one NAT instance failed. NAT instances aren't automatically recovered by AWS. ⚠️ B: Third-party AZ failure would affect all requests, not 50% ⚠️ C: Overload would cause timeouts/slowness, not intermittent 50% failures ⚠️ D: NACLs would block all traffic, not create intermittent failures 📖 Full Explanation You can use a NAT device to enable instances in a private subnet to connect to the Internet or other AWS services, but prevent the Internet from initiating connections with the instances. AWS recommends NAT gateways because they provide better availability and bandwidth over NAT instances. NAT instances are managed by the customer, so if the instance goes down, there could be impact on availability. NAT Gateways are highly available with redundancy in each AZ and are managed by AWS, automatically scaling bandwidth without choosing instance types.

A media streaming startup runs hundreds of containerized microservices on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate . They need to be alerted when Fargate vCPUs exceed 75% of service quota limits to prevent disruptions. The company plans to use ECS Anywhere for on-premises workloads. Which solution is MOST operationally efficient? A. Use CloudWatch to monitor AWS/Usage metrics. Set alarm when metricId/SERVICE_QUOTA(metricId)*100 > 75. Use SNS for notifications. B. Monitor sample count metric for each ECS service. Create alarm based on sample count/SERVICE_QUOTA(service)*100 > 75. Use SNS. C. Use Service Quotas to increase Fargate limit to 200%. Configure Health Dashboard and EventBridge/Lambda/SNS for 75% alerts. D. Use Container Insights to monitor clusters. Create custom dashboard and alarm based on custom metric for task percentage. ✅ A. CloudWatch AWS/Usage metrics with SERVICE_QUOTA() function 🎯 AWS/Usage namespace provides built-in service quota monitoring, and SERVICE_QUOTA() function automatically retrieves current limits for efficient threshold calculations. ⚠️ B — Sample count tracks requests/invocations, not actual vCPU quota usage ⚠️ C — Focuses on increasing quotas rather than monitoring; Health Dashboard is reactive, not proactive ⚠️ D — Requires custom metrics and manual configuration when native AWS/Usage metrics already exist 📖 Full Explanation Amazon CloudWatch provides metrics on service quota usage through the AWS/Usage namespace, including Fargate vCPU utilization. A CloudWatch alarm can be created using metricid/SERVICE_QUOTA(metricid)*100, where SERVICE_QUOTA() is a built-in function that retrieves the service quota for specific resources. This enables proactive monitoring when usage exceeds 75%, triggering SNS notifications to the operations team. This solution is operationally efficient as it uses native AWS services without requiring custom metrics or complex configurations.

A tech startup is launching a global mobile marketplace using AWS Amplify. Backend APIs will be deployed to multiple AWS regions for low latency . The system must ensure transactions made in one region are automatically replicated to other regions . Expected to have millions of users across North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. Which is the most scalable, cost-effective, and highly available architecture? A. Create a Global DynamoDB table with replica tables across several AWS regions. Store transactions to DynamoDB replica table in same region. Changes automatically replicated across all tables. B. Use AWS Control Tower and Amazon Connect to launch and manage multiple DynamoDB tables in various regions. Store transactions to DynamoDB replica table in same region. C. Store transactions to DynamoDB table in each region. Set up Lambda function to read recent writes and replay data to DynamoDB tables in all other regions. D. Create S3 buckets in all regions. Store transactions in local S3 bucket. Replicate using S3 Cross-Region Replication. ✅ A. Global DynamoDB table with automatic cross-region replication 🎯 DynamoDB Global Tables provide fully managed, multi-region, multi-master replication with automatic conflict resolution for massive scale. ⚠️ B. Control Tower/Connect — These services don't create Global Tables ⚠️ C. Lambda replication — Not scalable for millions of transactions ⚠️ D. S3 Cross-Region Replication — S3 isn't designed for transactional workloads 📖 Full Explanation Global Tables builds upon DynamoDB's global footprint to provide you with a fully managed, multi-region, and multi-master database that provides fast, local, read and write performance for massively scaled, global applications. Global Tables replicates your Amazon DynamoDB tables automatically across your choice of AWS regions. Global Tables eliminates the difficult work of replicating data between regions and resolving update conflicts, enabling you to focus on your application's business logic. In addition, Global Tables enables your applications to stay highly available even in the unlikely event of isolation or degradation of an entire region. Using Lambda for replication is not scalable for millions of customers. Control Tower and Connect don't create Global Tables. S3 Cross-Region Replication isn't suitable for real-time transactional data.

Company building containerized microservices CRM portal on Amazon ECS. Must follow least privilege security , support security groups and network monitoring at container level per strict IT policies. Which provides the MOST secure configuration? A. Use bridge network mode. Attach security groups to EC2 instances, use IAM roles for EC2 instances. B. Use AWS App Runner instead. Select VPC and security groups for deployment. Add IAM credentials to environment variables. C. Use awsvpc network mode. Attach security groups to ECS tasks, use IAM roles for tasks. D. Use awsvpc network mode. Attach security groups to ECS tasks, pass IAM credentials into container at launch. ✅ C: Use awsvpc network mode with security groups on tasks and IAM roles for tasks 🎯 Only awsvpc mode allows security groups and network monitoring at container level. IAM roles for tasks follow least privilege vs passing credentials. ⚠️ A: Bridge mode doesn't support security groups at container level, only at EC2 instance level ⚠️ B: Environment variables with IAM credentials violate security best practices ⚠️ D: Passing IAM credentials into containers creates security risk and credential exposure 📖 Full Explanation Task definitions are split into separate parts: the task family, the IAM task role, the network mode, container definitions, volumes, task placement constraints, and launch types. The family and container definitions are required in a task definition, while task role, network mode, volumes, task placement constraints, and launch type are optional. You can configure various Docker networking modes that will be used by containers in your ECS task. The valid values are none, bridge, awsvpc, and host. The default Docker network mode is bridge. With IAM roles for Amazon ECS tasks, you can specify an IAM role that can be used by the containers in a task. Applications must sign their AWS API requests with AWS credentials, and this feature provides a strategy for managing credentials for your applications to use, similar to the way that Amazon EC2 instance profiles provide credentials to EC2 instances. Instead of creating and distributing your AWS credentials to the containers or using the EC2 instance's role, you can associate an IAM role with an ECS task definition or RunTask API operation. The applications in the task's containers can then use the AWS SDK or CLI to make API requests to authorized AWS services. If the network mode is set to none, the task's containers do not have external connectivity, and port mappings can't be specified in the container definition. If the network mode is bridge, the task utilizes Docker's built-in virtual network which runs inside each container instance. If the network mode is host, the task bypasses Docker's built-in virtual network and maps container ports directly to the EC2 instance's network interface directly. In this mode, you can't run multiple instantiations of the same task on a single container instance when port mappings are used. If the network mode is awsvpc, the task is allocated an elastic network interface, and you must specify a NetworkConfiguration when you create a service or run a task with the task definition. When you use this network mode in your task definitions, every task that is launched from that task definition gets its own elastic network interface (ENI) and a primary private IP address. The task networking feature simplifies container networking and gives you more control over how containerized applications communicate with each other and other services within your VPCs. Task networking also provides greater security for your containers by allowing you to use security groups and network monitoring tools at a more granular level within your tasks. Because each task gets its own ENI, you can also take advantage of other Amazon EC2 networking features like VPC Flow Logs so that you can monitor traffic to and from your tasks. Additionally, containers that belong to the same task can communicate over the localhost interface. A task can only have one ENI associated with it at a given time.

A media company processes videos using EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that scales based on SQS queue messages. Videos take 20-40 minutes to process. Visibility timeout: 1 hour, maxReceiveCount: 1 . Several videos appear in the dead-letter queue despite no operational errors or processing time exceeded. CloudTrail shows repeated ReceiveMessage API calls for specific videos. Which solution should the architect implement? A. Set minimum EC2 instances on Auto Scaling group B. Set maxReceiveCount to 10 to allow retry attempts C. Update visibility timeout to 2 hours D. Configure higher delivery delay on SQS queue ✅ B. Set maxReceiveCount to 10 to allow retry attempts 🎯 maxReceiveCount of 1 means any receive failure (network errors, client issues) immediately sends messages to DLQ. Higher value allows legitimate retries before DLQ. ⚠️ A. Minimum instances — doesn't address the maxReceiveCount issue causing premature DLQ moves ⚠️ C. Longer visibility timeout — videos process in 20-40 min, 1 hour is already sufficient ⚠️ D. Delivery delay — only affects new messages, not processing failures of existing messages 📖 Full Explanation The maxReceiveCount determines when messages move to DLQ. With maxReceiveCount=1, any receive failure (network issues, client dependency errors) immediately sends messages to DLQ, even if processing would succeed on retry. Setting it to 10 allows legitimate retry attempts before DLQ movement. The visibility timeout of 1 hour is sufficient for 20-40 minute processing. Auto Scaling responds to queue depth, so minimum instances aren't needed. Delivery delay only affects new message delivery, not processing failures.

A company needs a deployment solution with these requirements: • 500GB static dataset accessible at boot • Auto scaling capability • Multiple daily code deployments • OS patches within 48 hours • Cost-effective Which solution should the Solutions Architect implement? A. Install OS patches and create new AMI using Systems Manager. Use new AMI for Auto Scaling group and replace instances. Create scheduled batch job to deploy application and install patches nightly. Mount EFS volume with static dataset. B. Install OS patches and create new AMI using Systems Manager. Use new AMI for Auto Scaling group and replace instances. Deploy application using CodeDeploy. Mount EFS volume with static dataset. C. Create Auto Scaling group with Amazon Linux AMI. Install application on instances. Replace instances when new Amazon Linux AMI releases. User data script downloads 500GB from S3. Deploy using CodeDeploy. D. Create Auto Scaling group with Amazon Linux AMI. Install application on instances. User data script downloads 500GB from S3. Use Systems Manager for OS patches. Deploy using CodeDeploy. ✅ B) Systems Manager patches → AMI, CodeDeploy for apps, EFS for dataset 🎯 EFS shared storage is cost-effective vs individual EBS volumes. CodeDeploy enables multiple daily deployments vs batch jobs. ⚠️ A) Batch jobs run nightly, not suitable for multiple daily deployments ⚠️ C) Amazon Linux AMI updates take weeks/months, not 48 hours ⚠️ D) S3 download to local EBS storage costs more than shared EFS 📖 Full Explanation AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager automates the process of patching managed instances with both security-related and other types of updates. You can use Patch Manager to apply patches for both operating systems and applications. You can use Patch Manager to install Service Packs on Windows instances and perform minor version upgrades on Linux instances. Patch Manager uses patch baselines, which include rules for auto-approving patches within days of their release, as well as a list of approved and rejected patches. You can install patches on a regular basis by scheduling patching to run as a Systems Manager maintenance window task. AWS Systems Manager Automation simplifies common maintenance and deployment tasks of Amazon EC2 instances and other AWS resources. Automation enables you to do the following: – Build automations to configure and manage instances and AWS resources. – Create custom runbooks or use pre-defined runbooks maintained by AWS. – Receive notifications about Automation tasks and runbooks by using Amazon EventBridge. – Monitor Automation progress and details by using the AWS Systems Manager console. AWS Systems Manager Automation provides several runbooks with pre-defined steps that you can use to perform common tasks like restarting one or more EC2 instances or creating an Amazon Machine Image (AMI). A Systems Manager Automation runbook defines the actions that Systems Manager performs on your managed instances and other AWS resources when an automation runs. A runbook contains one or more steps that run in sequential order. Each step is built around a single action. Output from one step can be used as input in a later step. Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) provides a simple, scalable, fully managed elastic NFS file system for use with AWS Cloud services and on-premises resources. Amazon EFS has a simple web services interface that allows you to create and configure file systems quickly and easily. With Amazon EFS, you pay only for the storage used by your file system and there is no minimum fee or setup cost. Amazon EFS oﬀers two storage classes, Standard and Infrequent Access. The Standard storage class is used to store frequently accessed files. The Infrequent Access (IA) storage class is a lower-cost storage class that's designed for storing long-lived, infrequently accessed ﬁles cost-eﬀectively. Amazon Elastic File System presents a standard file-system interface that supports full file-system access semantics. Using Network File System (NFS) version 4.1 (NFSv4.1), you can mount your Amazon EFS file system on any Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Linux-based instance. After your system is mounted, you can work with the files and directories just as you do with a local file system.

A company wants to host an internal web application with Docker containers connecting to MySQL backend . Documents are accessed frequently for 3 months, then rarely , but must be retained for 5 years . The company wants AWS-managed container services and the lowest possible cost . Which implementation is the most cost-effective solution? A. ECS with On-Demand EC2, RDS On-Demand, EFS storage, cron job to Glacier B. ECS with Spot EC2, Aurora Serverless v2, EBS storage, cron job deletion C. ECS with Spot EC2 (draining enabled), RDS Reserved, S3 with lifecycle to Glacier D. EKS with Spot EC2, RDS On-Demand, S3 with lifecycle to Glacier ✅ C. ECS with Spot EC2 (draining enabled), RDS Reserved, S3 with lifecycle to Glacier 🎯 Combines cheapest compute (Spot), predictable DB pricing (Reserved), and automated storage lifecycle management for cost optimization. ⚠️ A — On-Demand instances are more expensive than Spot/Reserved, EFS costs more than S3 ⚠️ B — Aurora Serverless v2 expensive for predictable workloads, EBS storage costlier than S3 ⚠️ D — RDS On-Demand more expensive than Reserved instances for continuous workloads 📖 Full Explanation Spot Instances provide up to 90% cost savings vs On-Demand. ECS Spot draining (ECS_ENABLE_SPOT_INSTANCE_DRAINING=true) gracefully handles interruptions by placing instances in DRAINING status and moving tasks to available instances. Reserved instances offer significant savings for predictable RDS workloads vs On-Demand pricing. S3 lifecycle policies automatically transition objects to Glacier after 3 months and delete after 5 years, eliminating manual intervention and providing durable, cost-effective storage. This combination minimizes compute, database, and storage costs while meeting all requirements.

Company runs weather simulations generating terabytes of data stored in MySQL 8.0 on EC2. Ruby on Rails app on separate EC2 processes data. Current DB: 16 TiB, growing continuously . Need highly scalable, highly available, 24x7 reliability, cost-effective solution. Which is the MOST cost-effective solution? A. Auto Scaling EC2 + ALB + Reserved instances + Aurora + read-replica in another AZ B. Lambda@Edge functions + RDS MySQL Multi-AZ + storage autoscaling C. Auto Scaling EC2 + ALB + Reserved instances + RDS MySQL Multi-AZ + manual storage adjustment D. Reserved EC2 for app/DB + Auto Scaling Multi-AZ + source-replica setup + LVM for storage ✅ A. Auto Scaling EC2 + ALB + Reserved instances + Aurora + read-replica 🎯 Aurora auto-scales storage to 128 TiB (vs RDS 64 TiB limit) and offers better performance/cost for large datasets. Read replica provides HA across AZs. ⚠️ B. Lambda@Edge — designed for CloudFront edge computing, not heavy data processing applications ⚠️ C. RDS MySQL — limited to 64 TiB max storage, manual adjustment unnecessary when autoscaling available ⚠️ D. Self-managed MySQL — high operational overhead, manual scaling, not cost-effective vs managed Aurora 📖 Full Explanation You can launch and automatically scale a fleet of On-Demand Instances and Spot Instances within a single Auto Scaling group. In addition to receiving discounts for using Spot Instances, you can use Reserved Instances or a Savings Plan to receive discounted rates of the regular On-Demand Instance pricing. All of these factors combined help you to optimize your cost savings for Amazon EC2 instances, while making sure that you obtain the desired scale and performance for your application. Amazon Aurora storage automatically scales with the data in your cluster volume. As your data grows, your cluster volume storage expands up to a maximum of 128 tebibytes (TiB). Even though an Aurora cluster volume can scale up in size to many tebibytes, you are only charged for the space that you use in the volume. The mechanism for determining billed storage space depends on the version of your Aurora cluster. Aurora stores copies of the data in a DB cluster across multiple Availability Zones in a single AWS Region. Aurora stores these copies regardless of whether the instances in the DB cluster span multiple Availability Zones. However, you still need to create a read-replica for the high availability of the Aurora DB instance. A single read-replica is enough to quickly recover the database in case the primary instance fails.

A company is launching an e-commerce website on AWS Fargate with ALB and CloudFront. They need protection against man-in-the-middle attacks including DNS spoofing, HTTPS spoofing, and SSL hijacking . Which configuration provides the MOST secure access? A. Route 53 registration + EC2 BIND servers for DNSSEC + ACM certificate + ALB HTTPS + CloudFront SNI/redirect B. Route 53 registration + 3rd party DNS with DNSSEC + imported 3rd party SSL to ACM + ALB HTTPS + CloudFront SNI/redirect C. Route 53 registration + 3rd party DNS with DNSSEC + ACM certificate + ALB HTTPS + CloudFront SNI/redirect D. Route 53 registration + enable DNSSEC validation on hosted zones + ACM certificate + ALB HTTPS + CloudFront SNI/redirect ✅ D. Route 53 registration + enable DNSSEC validation on hosted zones + ACM certificate + ALB HTTPS + CloudFront SNI/redirect 🎯 Route 53 now natively supports DNSSEC signing for hosted zones, eliminating need for third-party DNS or custom EC2 solutions. ⚠️ A. EC2 BIND servers — outdated workaround, Route 53 supports DNSSEC natively ⚠️ B. 3rd party DNS + imported SSL — unnecessary complexity, Route 53 + ACM are sufficient ⚠️ C. 3rd party DNS — unnecessary when Route 53 supports DNSSEC signing 📖 Full Explanation Amazon now allows you to enable Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) signing for all existing and new public hosted zones, and enable DNSSEC validation for Amazon Route 53 Resolver. Amazon Route 53 DNSSEC provides data origin authentication and data integrity verification for DNS and can help customers meet compliance mandates, such as FedRAMP. When you enable DNSSEC signing on a hosted zone, Route 53 cryptographically signs each record in that hosted zone. Route 53 manages the zone-signing key, and you can manage the key-signing key in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Amazon's domain name registrar, Route 53 Domains, already supports DNSSEC, and customers can now register domains and host their DNS on Route 53 with DNSSEC signing enabled. When you enable DNSSEC validation on the Route 53 Resolver in your VPC, it ensures that DNS responses have not been tampered with in transit. This can prevent DNS Spoofing. AWS Certificate Manager is a service that lets you easily provision, manage, and deploy public and private Secure Sockets Layer/Transport Layer Security (SSL/TLS) certificates for use with AWS services and your internal connected resources. SSL/TLS certificates are used to secure network communications and establish the identity of websites over the Internet as well as resources on private networks. AWS Certificate Manager removes the time-consuming manual process of purchasing, uploading, and renewing SSL/TLS certificates. Using a valid SSL Certificate for your application load balancer ensures that all requests are encrypted on transit as well as protection against SSL hijacking. CloudFront supports Server Name Indication (SNI) for custom SSL certificates, along with the ability to take incoming HTTP requests and redirect them to secure HTTPS requests to ensure that clients are always directed to the secure version of your website.

A multi-national tech company has multiple VPCs with peering between departments. They need to launch a central database server accessible by other VPCs using database.tutorialsdojo.com domain name. The server should only be resolvable and accessible within associated VPCs for internal applications only. Which solution should the architect implement? A. Set up a public hosted zone with tutorialsdojo.com and associate VPCs. Create A record for database.tutorialsdojo.com mapping to EC2 IP. Set enableDnsHostNames=true, enableDnsSupport=true B. Set up a private hosted zone with tutorialsdojo.com and associate VPCs. Create A record for database.tutorialsdojo.com mapping to EC2 IP. Set enableDnsHostNames=true, enableDnsSupport=true C. Set up a public hosted zone with tutorialsdojo.com and associate VPCs. Create CNAME record for database.tutorialsdojo.com mapping to EC2 IP. Set enableDnsHostNames=false, enableDnsSupport=false D. Set up a private hosted zone with tutorialsdojo.com and associate VPCs. Create A record for database.tutorialsdojo.com mapping to Elastic IP . Set enableDnsHostNames=true, enableDnsSupport=false ✅ B. Private hosted zone with A record, both DNS attributes true 🎯 Private hosted zones route traffic within VPCs only (not internet), meeting the internal-only requirement. Both DNS attributes must be true for proper resolution. ⚠️ A — Public hosted zones route internet traffic, violating internal-only requirement ⚠️ C — Public zone + wrong record type + DNS attributes disabled ⚠️ D — Elastic IP is public/internet-reachable + enableDnsSupport must be true 📖 Full Explanation In AWS, there are two types of hosted zones: Public hosted zones contain records for internet traffic routing, while Private hosted zones contain records for traffic routing within Amazon VPCs only. Since the database should only be accessible within associated VPCs (internal applications only), a private hosted zone is required. enableDnsHostnames indicates whether instances get public DNS hostnames, while enableDnsSupport enables DNS resolution through Amazon DNS server. Both must be true for proper DNS resolution. Option A is incorrect because public hosted zones route internet traffic. Option C uses public zone with wrong record type and disabled DNS attributes. Option D uses Elastic IP (public IPv4) which violates internal-only requirement, plus enableDnsSupport must be true.

A company has multiple AWS accounts for different departments (finance, HR, engineering). Each account is managed by Systems Administrators with root access. Requirement: centrally manage policies across multiple AWS accounts to allow/deny specific AWS services for individual accounts or groups of accounts. Which is the most suitable solution with the LEAST complexity? A. Connect all departments by setting up cross-account access to each of the AWS accounts of the company. Create and attach IAM policies to your resources based on their respective departments to control access. B. Use AWS Organizations and Service Control Policies to control the list of AWS services that can be used by each member account. C. Set up AWS Organizations and Organizational Units (OU) to connect all AWS accounts of each department. Create a custom IAM Policy to allow or deny the use of certain AWS services for each account. D. Provide access to externally authenticated users via Identity Federation. Set up an IAM role to specify permissions for users from each department whose identity is federated from your organization or a third-party identity provider. ✅ B. Use AWS Organizations and Service Control Policies 🎯 SCPs centrally control AWS service access across multiple accounts and can restrict even root users, unlike IAM policies which only work within individual accounts. ⚠️ A. Cross-account access — Too complex for multiple accounts, more suited for 2-account scenarios ⚠️ C. Custom IAM Policy — IAM policies can't restrict services across accounts, need SCPs not IAM ⚠️ D. Identity Federation — Focuses on authentication, not service-level policy management across accounts 📖 Full Explanation AWS Organizations offers policy-based management for multiple AWS accounts. With Organizations, you can create groups of accounts, automate account creation, and apply and manage policies for those groups. Organizations enables you to centrally manage policies across multiple accounts, without requiring custom scripts and manual processes. It allows you to create Service Control Policies (SCPs) that centrally control AWS service use across multiple AWS accounts. Remember that AWS Organizations does not replace associating IAM policies with users, groups, and roles within an AWS account. Hence, you still need to set up appropriate IAM policies for your root and member accounts. IAM policies let you allow or deny access to AWS services (such as Amazon S3), individual AWS resources (such as a specific S3 bucket), or individual API actions (such as s3:CreateBucket). An IAM policy can be applied only to IAM users, groups, or roles, and it can never restrict the root identity of the AWS account. By contrast, AWS Organizations lets you use service control policies (SCPs) to allow or deny access to particular AWS services for individual AWS accounts, or for groups of accounts within an organizational unit (OU). The specified actions from an attached SCP affect all IAM users, groups, and roles for an account, including the root account identity.

A multinational financial company has web applications in multiple VPCs across AWS regions. They need a logging solution to track all changes to AWS resources (EC2, S3, CloudFront, IAM) in all regions with security, integrity, and durability for compliance. The solution must provide event history from console, SDKs, CLI, and API calls. Which option provides the best solution? A. AWS CloudTrail with --is-multi-region-trail and --include-global-service-events, KMS encryption, MFA Delete on S3 B. Amazon CloudWatch trail with --include-global-service-events, KMS encryption, MFA Delete on S3 C. AWS CloudTrail with --no-include-global-service-events and --is-multi-region-trail, KMS encryption, MFA Delete on S3 D. Amazon CloudWatch trail with --is-multi-region-trail and --include-global-service-events, KMS encryption, MFA Delete on S3 ✅ A. AWS CloudTrail with --is-multi-region-trail and --include-global-service-events 🎯 CloudTrail is the AWS service for API logging and auditing. Both parameters are required: --is-multi-region-trail covers all regions, --include-global-service-events captures IAM and CloudFront activities. ⚠️ B & D — CloudWatch is for metrics/monitoring, not API auditing trails ⚠️ C — --no-include-global-service-events excludes IAM/CloudFront events, missing compliance requirement 📖 Full Explanation The accounting firm requires a secure and durable logging solution that will track all of the activities of all AWS resources (such as EC2, S3, CloudFront, and IAM) on all regions. CloudTrail can be used for this case with multi-region trail enabled. However, CloudTrail will only cover the activities of the regional services (EC2, S3, RDS etc.) and not for global services such as IAM, CloudFront, AWS WAF, and Route 53. The correct option provides security, integrity, and durability to your log data. In addition, it has the -include-global-service-events parameter enabled which will also include activity from global services such as IAM, Route 53, AWS WAF, and CloudFront.

A telecommunications company hosts a WordPress website on ECS Fargate. Database credentials must be provided via environment variables but kept secure , not viewable on the cluster , stored in dedicated storage with lifecycle management and key rotation . Which solution requires the least effort? A. Store credentials in Systems Manager Parameter Store, encrypt with KMS, create IAM role for ECS task execution, specify secrets in container definition with Parameter Store ARN. B. Migrate to EKS, use Kubernetes Secrets objects, reference with secretKeyRef, configure automatic rotation. C. Store credentials in ECS task definition encrypted with KMS, store JSON in private S3 with HTTPS, use --cli-input-json parameter. D. Store credentials in Secrets Manager, encrypt with KMS, create IAM role for ECS task execution, specify secrets in container definition with Secrets Manager ARN. ✅ D. Secrets Manager with lifecycle management and key rotation 🎯 Secrets Manager provides dedicated secrets storage with built-in lifecycle management and automatic key rotation, unlike Parameter Store which lacks these features. ⚠️ A. Parameter Store — no lifecycle management or key rotation ⚠️ B. EKS migration — more effort, no native secret rotation ⚠️ C. S3 storage — not recommended for credentials, manual overhead 📖 Full Explanation Amazon ECS enables you to inject sensitive data into your containers by storing your sensitive data in either AWS Secrets Manager secrets or AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store parameters and then referencing them in your container definition. This feature is supported by tasks using both the EC2 and Fargate launch types. Within your container definition, specify secrets with the name of the environment variable to set in the container and the full ARN of either the Secrets Manager secret or Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter containing the sensitive data to present to the container. AWS Secrets Manager is a secrets management service that helps you protect access to your applications, services, and IT resources. This service enables you to easily rotate, manage, and retrieve database credentials, API keys, and other secrets throughout their lifecycle. If you want a single store for configuration and secrets, you can use Parameter Store. If you want a dedicated secrets store with lifecycle management, use Secrets Manager. The Systems Manager Parameter Store option is incorrect because although valid for securing sensitive data in ECS, this service doesn't provide dedicated storage with lifecycle management and key rotation, unlike Secrets Manager. The S3 option is incorrect because it's not recommended to store sensitive credentials in S3 and entails manual configuration overhead. The EKS option is incorrect because migration from ECS to EKS requires more effort, and Kubernetes doesn't natively support automatic rotation of secrets.

A media company has web applications in US West (N. California) with EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer using public SSL/TLS certificates for HTTPS traffic . They need to expand to multiple AWS regions (ap-southeast-2, ca-central-1, eu-west-3) while ensuring HTTPS services continue without interruption . Which approach should the Architect implement? A. In each new AWS Region, request SSL/TLS certificates using AWS KMS for each FQDN B. In each new AWS Region, request SSL/TLS certificates using AWS Certificate Manager for each FQDN C. Use AWS KMS in US West to request certificates for all regions D. Use AWS Certificate Manager in US West to request certificates for all regions ✅ B. Request ACM certificates in each new region for each FQDN 🎯 ALB requires ACM certificates from the same region. Cross-region certificate sharing only works with CloudFront (us-east-1). ⚠️ A. AWS KMS is for encryption keys, not SSL certificates ⚠️ C. Wrong service (KMS) and certificates can't be shared across regions for ALB ⚠️ D. ACM certificates can only be shared cross-region with CloudFront, not ALB 📖 Full Explanation AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) is the correct service for SSL/TLS certificates. For Application Load Balancers, you must request certificates in each region where the ALB is deployed - certificates cannot be shared across regions for ALB. Cross-region certificate sharing only works with CloudFront distributions (and requires certificates in us-east-1). AWS KMS is for encryption keys, not SSL certificates. Each new region needs its own ACM certificate for the same FQDN to work with ALBs in that region.

A company migrates to AWS using EKS clusters and RDS MySQL . System has predictable high usage during sales events and holidays . Need MOST cost-optimized pricing solution. What pricing options should the company consider? A. EC2 Instance Savings Plans + On-Demand scaling + 1-year Partial Upfront RDS RI B. Standard Reserved Instances + Dedicated Instance scaling + 1-year All Upfront RDS RI C. Compute Savings Plans + On-Demand Capacity Reservations + 1-year No Upfront RDS RI + read replicas D. Compute Savings Plans + Spot Instance scaling + 1-year All Upfront RDS RI + vertical scaling ✅ D. Compute Savings Plans + Spot instances + All Upfront RDS RI 🎯 Compute Savings Plans offer flexibility across instance types (66% savings), Spot instances provide cheapest peak scaling, All Upfront RDS RI maximizes database savings for predictable workloads. ⚠️ A. EC2 Instance Savings Plans lock to specific instance family, On-Demand more expensive than Spot ⚠️ B. Dedicated Instances are premium-priced for compliance, not cost optimization ⚠️ C. On-Demand Capacity Reservations provide no cost savings, No Upfront RI offers smaller discount 📖 Full Explanation AWS offers multiple purchasing options such as Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, and Spot Instances to allow customers optimize their workloads in terms of cost. There are also multiple services that can be used when monitoring usage and cost to help in this analysis, such as AWS Pricing Calculator, AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets. For EC2 usage, EC2 Instance Savings Plans offer the highest savings (up to 72%) and are applied to a specific instance within a chosen region. Compute Savings Plans offer slightly lower savings (up to 66%) but provide more flexibility as they apply to any instance family and can cover usage across different services like EC2, Fargate, and Lambda. For use cases when there is an increase in load during certain periods, Spot instances can be a cost-effective solution. These instances provide flexibility and allow using spare EC2 capacity at a significant discount. For the database instance, paying for an entire Reserve Instance term (1 year) with an upfront payment provides a large discount compared with other payment options. Since the usage is predictable, database sizing can also be planned beforehand. Vertical scaling or scaling up is adding to the resources of a server. This is an effective way to handle high traffic during sales events and holiday seasons. Scaling up the database can be scheduled to handle the increased load.

A clinic runs Windows EC2 instances for medical records. Requirements: latest security patches must be installed and system must check for approved AMIs . The solution should NOT impede developers from launching unapproved AMIs but must notify of non-compliant instances . Which TWO should be implemented? (Select TWO.) A. Set up a patch baseline using AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager B. Set up Amazon GuardDuty to monitor patches and AMIs with CloudWatch Alarms C. Use AWS Shield Advanced to patch instances and detect uncompliant AMIs D. Create IAM policy restricting developers from launching unapproved AMIs E. Use AWS Config Managed Rule to check approved AMIs with CloudWatch Alarms ✅ A & E: Systems Manager Patch Manager + AWS Config Managed Rule 🎯 Patch Manager handles automated patching with baselines. Config Managed Rules monitor AMI compliance without blocking deployment. ⚠️ B — GuardDuty detects threats, not patch compliance or AMI approval ⚠️ C — Shield Advanced prevents DDoS attacks, doesn't patch or check AMIs ⚠️ D — IAM restrictions would impede developers (violates requirement) 📖 Full Explanation AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager automates the process of patching managed instances with security-related updates. You can patch fleets of Amazon EC2 instances by operating system type and use patch baselines that include rules for auto-approving patches within days of their release. AWS Config provides managed rules that evaluate whether AWS resources comply with best practices. The AWS Config Managed Rule can automatically check whether running EC2 instances are using approved AMIs and notify via CloudWatch Alarms without preventing deployment. GuardDuty is a threat detection service for malicious activity, not compliance monitoring. Shield Advanced prevents DDoS attacks. IAM restrictions would block developers, violating the requirement to not impede their work.

Company needs multi-account strategy for 50 teams across research facilities . One DNS team manages all domains/subdomains for the organization. Solution must allow private DNS sharing among VPCs in different AWS accounts . Which solution has the LEAST complex DNS architecture and allows all VPCs to resolve needed domain names? A. VPC peering among all accounts. Set enableDnsHostnames/enableDnsSupport to TRUE. Create Route 53 private hosted zone in central account. Other accounts create private hosted zones with NS entries pointing to central DNS. B. AWS RAM shared services VPC in central account. VPC peering to other accounts. Route 53 private hosted zone in shared VPC. Programmatically associate other VPCs with hosted zone. C. AWS RAM shared services VPC in central account. VPC peering to other accounts. Route 53 private hosted zone in shared VPC. Other accounts create private hosted zones with NS entries pointing to central DNS. D. Direct Connect connections among VPCs with private virtual interfaces. Set enableDnsHostnames/enableDnsSupport to FALSE. Route 53 private hosted zone in central account. Programmatically associate other VPCs. ✅ B. AWS RAM shared services VPC with programmatic cross-account Route 53 association 🎯 Route 53 private hosted zones can be programmatically associated with VPCs across accounts, eliminating need for complex NS configurations. ⚠️ A — NS entries in private zones don't work for cross-account DNS resolution ⚠️ C — Same NS configuration issue as option A ⚠️ D — Direct Connect inappropriate for VPC-to-VPC, enableDns* should be TRUE 📖 Full Explanation When you create a VPC using Amazon VPC, Route 53 Resolver automatically answers DNS queries for local VPC domain names for EC2 instances (ec2-192-0-2-44.compute-1.amazonaws.com) and records in private hosted zones (acme.example.com). For all other domain names, Resolver performs recursive lookups against public name servers. You also can integrate DNS resolution between Resolver and DNS resolvers on your network by configuring forwarding rules. Your network can include any network that is reachable from your VPC, such as the following: – The VPC itself – Another peered VPC – An on-premises network that is connected to AWS with AWS Direct Connect, a VPN, or a network address translation (NAT) gateway VPC sharing allows customers to share subnets with other AWS accounts within the same AWS Organization. This is a very powerful concept that allows for a number of benefits: – Separation of duties: centrally controlled VPC structure, routing, IP address allocation. – Application owners continue to own resources, accounts, and security groups. – VPC sharing participants can reference security group IDs of each other. – Efficiencies: higher density in subnets, efficient use of VPNs and AWS Direct Connect. – Hard limits can be avoided, for example, 50 VIFs per AWS Direct Connect connection through simplified network architecture. – Costs can be optimized through reuse of NAT gateways, VPC interface endpoints, and intra-Availability Zone traffic. Essentially, we can decouple accounts and networks. In this model, the account that owns the VPC (owner) shares one or more subnets with other accounts (participants) that belong to the same organization from AWS Organizations. After a subnet is shared, the participants can view, create, modify, and delete their application resources in the subnets shared with them. Participants cannot view, modify, or delete resources that belong to other participants or the VPC owner. You can simplify network topologies by interconnecting shared Amazon VPCs using connectivity features, such as AWS PrivateLink, AWS Transit Gateway, and Amazon VPC peering.

A startup builds a ReactJS web app for users to post photos of neighborhood good deeds with 143-character captions. App needs DynamoDB access , runs on broad range of devices, and shows no large usage spikes . Need most cost-effective and scalable architecture. Which option provides the most cost-effective and scalable architecture? A. ReactJS client with STS temporary credentials via Token Vending Machine on EC2. IAM user with GET/PUT to DynamoDB and S3. Serve from S3 website. B. Web Identity Provider (Google/Facebook) with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API for temporary credentials. IAM role with GET/PUT to S3 and DynamoDB. Serve from S3 website. C. Web Identity Provider with IAM role for DynamoDB GET/PUT. Serve from NGINX on load-balanced, auto-scaled EC2 fleet with IAM role. D. ReactJS client with STS via Token Vending Machine for DynamoDB credentials. Serve from NGINX on load-balanced, auto-scaled EC2 fleet with IAM role. ✅ B. Web Identity Provider with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity + S3 website hosting 🎯 ReactJS is static files that render dynamically in browser - perfect for S3 website hosting. Web Identity Provider gives secure, scalable authentication without infrastructure costs. ⚠️ A. Token Vending Machine on single EC2 creates single point of failure ⚠️ C. EC2 infrastructure unnecessary and more expensive than S3 hosting ⚠️ D. Combines TVM single point of failure with expensive EC2 infrastructure 📖 Full Explanation ReactJS is a modern framework for creating front-ends for your web applications. From the users perspective, this website is dynamic since it asks for users to login and users can upload images to it. But since it is written on ReactJS framework, it is basically just a bunch of static files and the web browser renders the page dynamically. We can have full-blown web pages like this and be hosted on Amazon S3 (with enabling static website hosting) with no problems. From Amazon S3's perspective, it is hosting a static website, since all files that are on the bucket are static files only. But ReactJS allows the client's web browser to interpret these static files and render the webpage dynamically for the user. Amazon Cognito follows the OIDC specification to authenticate users of web and mobile apps. Users can sign in directly through the Amazon Cognito hosted UI or through a federated identity provider, such as Amazon, Facebook, Apple, or Google. The hosted UI workflows include sign-in and sign-up, password reset, and MFA. Since not all customer workflows are the same, you can customize Amazon Cognito workflows at key points with AWS Lambda functions, allowing you to run code without provisioning or managing servers. After a user authenticates, Amazon Cognito returns standard OIDC tokens. You can use the user profile information in the ID token to grant your users access to your own resources or you can use the tokens to grant access to APIs hosted by Amazon API Gateway. You can also exchange the tokens for temporary AWS credentials to access other AWS services. If you don't use Amazon Cognito, then you choose to write a custom code or app that interacts with a web IdP (Login with Amazon, Facebook, Google, or any other OIDC-compatible IdP) and then call the AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API to trade the authentication token you get from those IdPs for AWS temporary security credentials. If you have already used this approach for existing apps, you can continue to use it. You can also deploy your app in the S3 bucket. The option that says: Register the web application with a Web Identity Provider such as Google, Facebook, Amazon, or any other popular social sites and use the AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API of STS to generate temporary credentials. Create an IAM role for that web provider and set up permissions for the IAM role to allow GET and PUT operations in Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. Serve your web app out of an S3 bucket enabled as a website is correct because it authenticates the application via a federated identity provider such as Google, Facebook, Amazon, or other social sites. It sets up proper permission for DynamoDB access and hosts the website in S3. Plus, it also uses STS and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API which provides a better authentication. The option that says: Configure the ReactJS client with temporary credentials from the Security Token Service using a Token Vending Machine (TVM) on an EC2 instance. This will provide signed credentials to an IAM user allowing GET and PUT operations in the DynamoDB table and the S3 bucket. You serve your mobile application out of an S3 bucket enabled as a website is incorrect. The Token Vending Machine (STS Service) is implemented on just a single EC2 instance. This poses a single point of failure which means that the architecture is not highly available and not fault-tolerant. This is not a scalable solution either as the instance can become the performance bottleneck. The option that says: Configure the ReactJS client with temporary credentials from the Security Token Service using a Token Vending Machine (TVM) to provide signed credentials to an IAM user. This will allow GET and PUT operations to DynamoDB. Serve your web application from an NGINX server hosted in a fleet of EC2 instances that are load-balanced and auto-scaled. Your EC2 instances are configured with an IAM role that allows GET and PUT operations in DynamoDB is incorrect. Although this solution is highly-available and scalable, deploying EC2 instances in an auto-scaled environment is not as a cost-effective solution as the S3 website. The option that says: Register the web application with a Web Identity Provider such as Google, Facebook, Amazon, or from any other popular social site. Create an IAM role for that web provider and set up permissions for the IAM role to allow GET and PUT operations in DynamoDB. Serve your web application from an NGINX server hosted on a fleet of EC2 instances, with a load balancer and auto-scaling. Add an IAM role to the EC2 instance to allow GET and PUT operations to DynamoDB tables is incorrect because it does not mention any security token service that generates temporary credentials. Furthermore, deploying EC2 instances in an auto-scaled environment, albeit scalable, is not as cost-effective as the S3 website.

A company migrating from on-premises Oracle to PostgreSQL on AWS requires heterogeneous database migration with schema and code transformation prior to data migration. Which approach is most suitable? A. Use AWS SAM with Lambda functions to transform database to PostgreSQL. Migrate using DMS to RDS. B. Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to convert source schema. Migrate data using DMS to RDS for PostgreSQL. C. Migrate using AWS Application Migration Service, then use DMS to convert and migrate to RDS PostgreSQL. D. Use AWS Glue to convert schema/code. Use AWS Batch with Spot instances to migrate data. ✅ B. Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to convert source schema. Migrate data using DMS to RDS for PostgreSQL. 🎯 Heterogeneous migrations require SCT for schema conversion first, then DMS for data migration. This is the standard two-step AWS process. ⚠️ A. SAM — Framework for serverless apps, not database migration ⚠️ C. Application Migration Service — For entire applications, not database schema conversion ⚠️ D. Glue — ETL service, not designed for Oracle to PostgreSQL schema conversion 📖 Full Explanation AWS Database Migration Service helps you migrate databases to AWS quickly and securely. The source database remains fully operational during the migration, minimizing downtime to applications that rely on the database. The AWS Database Migration Service can migrate your data to and from the most widely used commercial and open-source databases. AWS Database Migration Service can migrate your data to and from most of the widely used commercial and open-source databases. It supports homogeneous migrations, such as Oracle to Oracle, as well as heterogeneous migrations between different database platforms, such as Oracle to Amazon Aurora. Migrations can be from on-premises databases to Amazon RDS or Amazon EC2, databases running on EC2 to RDS, or vice versa, as well as from one RDS database to another RDS database. It can also move data between SQL, NoSQL, and text-based targets. In heterogeneous database migrations, the source and target databases engines are different, like in the case of Oracle to Amazon Aurora, Oracle to PostgreSQL, or Microsoft SQL Server to MySQL migrations. In this case, the schema structure, data types, and database code of source and target databases can be quite different, requiring a schema and code transformation before the data migration starts. That makes heterogeneous migrations a two-step process. Hence, the correct answer is: Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool to convert the source schema and code to match that of the target database, and then use the AWS Database Migration Service to migrate data from the source database to the target database. All the required data type conversions will automatically be done by the AWS Database Migration Service during the migration. The source database can be located in your own premises outside of AWS, running on an Amazon EC2 instance, or it can be an Amazon RDS database. The target can be a database in Amazon EC2 or Amazon RDS.

A smartwatch company will ingest millions of records per minute globally. Requirements: records 4KB , durable storage , 120-day retention , low latency retrieval . Estimated 10-15TB annually . Need most cost-effective solution. Which storage solution is recommended? A. Use Amazon MSK to ingest/store records with 120-day retention, send to S3 for durability B. Store each record as S3 object with unique filename, use lifecycle policy for 120-day expiration C. Use DynamoDB table with proper scaling and TTL for 120-day deletion D. Use Aurora Serverless with Lambda function to delete records older than 120 days nightly ✅ C. DynamoDB with TTL for automatic 120-day deletion 🎯 DynamoDB TTL automatically deletes expired items without consuming write throughput, making it most cost-effective for high-volume ingestion with time-based expiration. ⚠️ A. MSK — not optimized for low-latency retrieval, unnecessary S3 duplication adds cost ⚠️ B. S3 — doesn't meet low-latency retrieval requirement for real-time access ⚠️ D. Aurora Serverless — continuous ingestion negates serverless cost benefits, Lambda deletion adds complexity 📖 Full Explanation Amazon DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL) allows you to define a per-item timestamp to determine when an item is no longer needed. Shortly after the date and time of the specified timestamp, DynamoDB deletes the item from your table without consuming any write throughput. TTL is provided at no extra cost as a means to reduce stored data volumes by retaining only the items that remain current for your workload's needs. TTL is useful if you store items that lose relevance after a specific time. When enabling TTL on a DynamoDB table, you must identify a specific attribute name that the service will look for when determining if an item is eligible for expiration. The scanner background process compares the current time, in Unix epoch time format in seconds, to the value stored in the user-defined attribute of an item.

A private bank hosts a secure web application for agents to view sensitive client information. Traffic is predictable . The CISO requires the SSL private key cannot be moved outside AWS . Application logs contain sensitive data and must be stored durably and securely, decryptable only by authorized employees . EBS volumes are encrypted. Which architecture meets ALL requirements with high availability? A. ELB with TCP load balancing. AWS CloudHSM for SSL. Store logs in private S3 with server-side encryption. B. ELB with TCP load balancing. Web servers retrieve SSL key from S3 on boot. Store logs in S3 with server-side encryption. C. ELB with SSL offloading. Store logs on encrypted instance store with random AES key. D. ELB with TCP load balancing. CloudHSM in two AZs for SSL. Store logs in private S3 with server-side encryption. ✅ D. CloudHSM in two AZs + S3 server-side encryption 🎯 CloudHSM keeps SSL keys secure in AWS hardware. Two AZs ensures high availability. SSE-C allows customer-managed keys for authorized-only decryption. ⚠️ A — Single AZ CloudHSM lacks high availability ⚠️ B — SSL key in S3 can be moved outside AWS environment ⚠️ C — Instance store is ephemeral, not durable for logs 📖 Full Explanation AWS CloudHSM is a cloud-based hardware security module (HSM) that enables you to easily generate and use your own encryption keys on the AWS Cloud. With CloudHSM, you can manage your own encryption keys and automate time-consuming administrative tasks for you, such as hardware provisioning, software patching, high-availability, and backups. The correct answer uses CloudHSM deployed to two Availability Zones to perform the SSL transactions and deliver application logs to a private Amazon S3 bucket using server-side encryption. It uses CloudHSM for performing the SSL transaction without requiring any additional way of storing or managing the SSL private key. This is the most secure way of ensuring that the key will not be moved outside of the AWS environment. Also, it uses the highly available and durable S3 service for storing the logs. Option B is incorrect because it does not use a secure way of managing the SSL private key - storing it in S3 allows it to be moved outside the AWS environment. Option C is incorrect because application logs are written to an ephemeral instance store volume, which means data will be lost when the EC2 instance is terminated. This solution is neither durable nor secure. Option A is incorrect because the architecture did not explicitly say that the CloudHSM is deployed to multiple Availability Zones, making it not highly available compared to option D. Note: The correct option implies using SSE-C (Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys) rather than SSE-S3, as this allows only authorized employees to decrypt the logs by managing their own encryption keys.

A company hosts a multi-tier web application with ALB and EC2 instances across 3 AZs. During peak load, stateless web servers operate at 95% utilization . Current setup: Reserved Instances for steady-state, On-Demand for peak load. Need cost-effective architecture for quick AZ failure recovery during peak load . Which provides the most cost-effective architecture for quick recovery if an AZ becomes unavailable during peak load? A. Use Spot and On-Demand instances on each AZ for both steady state and peak load B. Use Reserved and On-Demand instances on each AZ for both steady state and peak load C. Launch Auto Scaling group of Reserved instances on each AZ for peak load. Retain current setup for steady state D. Launch Spot Fleet with diversified allocation strategy and Auto Scaling on each AZ for peak load. Retain current setup for steady state ✅ D. Spot Fleet with diversified allocation + Auto Scaling 🎯 Spot instances are most cost-effective for temporary peak loads. Diversified allocation across AZs ensures capacity availability during outages. ⚠️ A. No Auto Scaling mentioned - required for quick recovery ⚠️ B. No Auto Scaling mentioned - required for quick recovery ⚠️ C. Reserved instances cost more than Spot for peak loads 📖 Full Explanation The scenario requires a cost-effective architecture to allow the application to recover quickly, hence, using an Auto Scaling group is a must to handle the peak load and improve both the availability and scalability of the application. Setting up a diversified allocation strategy for your Spot Fleet is a best practice to increase the chances that a spot request can be fulfilled by EC2 capacity in the event of an outage in one of the Availability Zones. You can include each AZ available to you in the launch specification. And instead of using the same subnet each time, use three unique subnets (each mapping to a different AZ). The Spot instances are the most cost-effective for handling the temporary peak loads of the application.

Enterprise CMS runs on Auto Scaling group with ALB. New instances marked unhealthy and terminated. CloudWatch logs show no clear errors. Need to troubleshoot before instances terminate. Quickest way to troubleshoot the unhealthy instances? A. Update application log settings for verbose logging and ensure CloudWatch agent is running B. Enable EC2 instance termination protection on one instance and use Session Manager C. Create temporary EC2 instance, deploy app version, add to ALB for real-time inspection D. Suspend "Terminate" process in ASG and login via Session Manager ✅ D. Suspend "Terminate" process in ASG and login via Session Manager 🎯 Suspending ASG terminate process prevents instance replacement, giving time to troubleshoot via Session Manager. ⚠️ A. Verbose logging — Won't prevent termination during troubleshooting ⚠️ B. Instance termination protection — ASG can still terminate instances it created ⚠️ C. Temporary instance — Takes longer, not the quickest solution 📖 Full Explanation Auto Scaling groups maintain desired capacity by performing health checks and replacing unhealthy instances. You can suspend specific processes like "Terminate" to prevent instance replacement during troubleshooting. Session Manager provides secure access without SSH keys or bastion hosts. Instance termination protection doesn't prevent ASG from terminating instances it created. Creating temporary instances adds unnecessary complexity and time.

Company hosts production on AWS Fargate . CIO wants development workloads on on-premises servers to leverage existing investments. Solution must: manage both on-premises and Fargate in same cluster , easily migrate dev to prod , and ensure consistent tooling/API experience . Which is the MOST operationally efficient solution? A. Use Amazon EKS Anywhere to simplify on-premises Kubernetes management with default component configurations and automated cluster management tools. This makes it easy to migrate the development workloads running on-premises to EKS in an AWS region on Fargate. B. Install and configure AWS Outposts in your on-premises data center. Run Amazon ECS on Outposts to launch the development environment workloads. Migrate development workloads to production that is running on AWS Fargate. C. Install and configure AWS Outposts in your on-premises data center. Run Amazon EKS Anywhere on Outposts to launch container-based workloads. Migrate development workloads to production that is running on AWS Fargate. D. Utilize Amazon ECS Anywhere to streamline software management on-premises and on AWS with a standardized container orchestrator. This makes it easy to migrate the development workloads running on-premises to ECS in an AWS region on Fargate. ✅ D. Amazon ECS Anywhere 🎯 ECS Anywhere allows on-premises compute, EC2 instances, and Fargate in the same ECS cluster with consistent tooling. ⚠️ A. EKS Anywhere — doesn't integrate with AWS Fargate or cloud-managed Kubernetes ⚠️ B. ECS on Outposts — Fargate is not supported on AWS Outposts ⚠️ C. EKS Anywhere on Outposts — EKS Anywhere not designed for Outposts infrastructure 📖 Full Explanation Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) Anywhere is a feature of Amazon ECS that lets you run and manage container workloads on your infrastructure. This feature helps you meet compliance requirements and scale your business without sacrificing your on-premises investments. It ensures consistency with the same on-premises Amazon ECS tools when you migrate to AWS. ECS Anywhere extends the reach of Amazon ECS to provide you with a single management interface for all of your container-based applications, irrespective of the environment they're running in. As a result, you have a simple, consistent experience when it comes to cluster management, workload scheduling, and monitoring for both the cloud and on-premises. With ECS Anywhere, you do not need to install and maintain any container orchestration software, thus removing the need for your team to learn specialized knowledge domains and skillsets for disparate tooling. ECS Anywhere makes it easy for you to run your applications in on-premises environments as long as desired and then migrate to the cloud with a single click at any time.

A tech company creates S3 bucket "www.tutorialsdojo.com" in us-west-2, enables static website hosting, uploads content including index.html. Route 53 domain registered and Alias record created pointing to S3 website endpoint. Users cannot see any content - both tutorialsdojo.com and www.tutorialsdojo.com don't work. Which is the MOST likely cause the Architect should fix? A. URL needs file name: www.tutorialsdojo.com/index.html B. Missing required error.html file configuration C. Route 53 still propagating changes (wait 12 hours) D. S3 bucket lacks public read access blocking visitors ✅ D. S3 bucket lacks public read access blocking visitors 🎯 S3 static websites require public read access for visitors to view content. Without it, all requests are blocked regardless of proper setup. ⚠️ A. S3 static hosting automatically serves index.html as default document ⚠️ B. error.html is optional, not required for basic functionality ⚠️ C. Route 53 propagation completes within 60 seconds, not 12 hours 📖 Full Explanation You can host a static website on Amazon S3 by configuring a bucket for website hosting and uploading content. This bucket must have public read access - it's intentional that everyone will have read access. The bucket name must exactly match the record name (tutorialsdojo.com or www.tutorialsdojo.com). In this scenario, the static S3 website doesn't work because the bucket lacks public read access. Error.html is not required. S3 automatically serves index.html without needing the filename in URL. Route 53 propagation takes ~60 seconds, not 12 hours.

A company is decommissioning its legacy web application (EC2 Auto Scaling + ALB) and building a new serverless architecture with Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB . Requirements: CI/CD pipeline for automated builds and gradual deployments . Which is the most suitable way to build, test, and deploy the new architecture? A.
