Use AWS Serverless Application Repository to organize components and deploy as single versioned entity B. Use AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM) with CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline C. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to deploy the application D. Use CodeBuild/CodeDeploy/CodePipeline with Systems Manager Automation ✅ B. AWS SAM with CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline 🎯 AWS SAM is specifically designed for serverless applications and integrates perfectly with AWS CI/CD tools for gradual deployments. ⚠️ A. Serverless Application Repository — Just a managed repository, not a build/deploy tool ⚠️ C. Elastic Beanstalk — Designed for EC2 applications, not serverless Lambda functions ⚠️ D. Systems Manager Automation — Used for instance management, not serverless application deployment 📖 Full Explanation The AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) is an open-source framework that you can use to build serverless applications on AWS. It consists of the AWS SAM template specification that you use to define your serverless applications, and the AWS SAM command line interface (AWS SAM CLI) that you use to build, test, and deploy your serverless applications. Because AWS SAM is an extension of AWS CloudFormation, you get the reliable deployment capabilities of AWS CloudFormation. You can define resources by using AWS CloudFormation in your AWS SAM template. Also, you can use the full suite of resources, intrinsic functions, and other template features that are available in AWS CloudFormation. You can use AWS SAM with a suite of AWS tools for building serverless applications. To build a deployment pipeline for your serverless applications, you can use CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline. To deploy your serverless application, you can use the Jenkins plugin, and you can use Stackery.io's toolkit to build production-ready applications.

A global financial company launches a cryptocurrency trading platform on AWS. For AML/CFT compliance , all report files must be blocked from FATF blacklisted countries while maintaining low latency for global users . What is the best way to satisfy this security requirement while delivering content globally with lower latency? A. Create a CloudFront distribution with Geo-Restriction enabled to block all of the blacklisted countries from accessing the trading platform. B. Deploy the trading platform using Elastic Beanstalk and deny all incoming traffic from the IP addresses of the blacklisted countries in the Network Access Control List (ACL) of the VPC. C. Use Route 53 with a Geolocation routing policy that blocks all traffic from the blacklisted countries. D. Use Route 53 with a Geoproximity routing policy that blocks all traffic from the blacklisted countries. ✅ A. CloudFront with Geo-Restriction 🎯 CloudFront provides both geo-blocking at country level AND global low-latency content delivery through edge locations. ⚠️ B. Elastic Beanstalk + NACL — Managing country IP ranges manually is impractical and doesn't provide global CDN benefits ⚠️ C. Route 53 Geolocation — Only DNS routing, no content delivery or caching for low latency ⚠️ D. Route 53 Geoproximity — Only DNS routing based on resource location, no blocking or CDN capabilities 📖 Full Explanation You can use geo restriction – also known as geoblocking – to prevent users in specific geographic locations from accessing content that you're distributing through a CloudFront web distribution. To use geo restriction, you have two options: Use the CloudFront geo restriction feature. Use this option to restrict access to all of the files that are associated with a distribution and to restrict access at the country level. Use a third-party geolocation service. Use this option to restrict access to a subset of the files that are associated with a distribution or to restrict access at a finer granularity than the country level. When a user requests your content, CloudFront typically serves the requested content regardless of where the user is located. If you need to prevent users in specific countries from accessing your content, you can use the CloudFront geo restriction feature to do one of the following: Allow your users to access your content only if they're in one of the countries on a whitelist of approved countries. Prevent your users from accessing your content if they're in one of the countries on a blacklist of banned countries. For example, if a request comes from a country where, for copyright reasons, you are not authorized to distribute your content, you can use CloudFront geo restriction to block the request. Hence, the option that says: Create a CloudFront distribution with Geo-Restriction enabled to block all of the blacklisted countries from accessing the trading platform is correct. CloudFront can provide the users low-latency access to the files as well as block certain countries on the FTAF list. The option that says: Deploy the trading platform using Elastic Beanstalk and deny all incoming traffic from the IP addresses of the blacklisted countries in the Network Access Control List (ACL) of the VPC is incorrect. Blocking all of the IP addresses of each blacklisted country in the Network Access Control List entails a lot of work and is not a recommended way to accomplish the task. Using CloudFront geo restriction feature is a better solution for this. The following options are incorrect because Route 53 only provides Domain Name Resolution and sends the requests based on the configured entries. It does not provide low-latency access to users around the globe, unlike CloudFront. Use Route 53 with a Geolocation routing policy that blocks all traffic from the blacklisted countries. Use Route 53 with a Geoproximity routing policy that blocks all traffic from the blacklisted countries. Geolocation routing policy is used when you want to route traffic based on the location of your users while Geoproximity routing policy is for scenarios where you want to route traffic based on the location of your resources and, optionally, shift traffic from resources on one location to resources in another.

A company uses LDAP for employee authentication . They're releasing a mobile app for employees to access AWS resources with federated access . Requirements: custom-built authentication solution and IAM roles for permissions . Which options should the Solutions Architect implement for authentication and authorization? (Select TWO.) A. Build custom SAML-compatible solution using LDAP for authentication and SAML assertion for IAM identity provider authorization B. Build custom LDAP connector with API Gateway/Lambda for authentication, use DynamoDB for authorization tokens C. Build custom OpenID Connect-compatible solution, use Amazon Cognito Identity Pools for AWS resource authorization D. Build custom SAML-compatible solution for authentication, leverage AWS IAM Identity Center for authorization E. Build custom OpenID Connect-compatible solution with AWS IAM Identity Center ✅ A & C: SAML with LDAP + OpenID Connect with Cognito 🎯 Mobile federation requires either SAML assertions to IAM or OpenID Connect to Cognito Identity Pools for temporary AWS credentials. ⚠️ B — Storing auth tokens in DynamoDB is not recommended security practice ⚠️ D — IAM Identity Center only supports web browsers, not mobile apps ⚠️ E — IAM Identity Center only supports SAML 2.0, not OpenID Connect 📖 Full Explanation AWS supports identity federation with SAML 2.0 (Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0), an open standard that many identity providers (IdPs) use. This feature enables federated single sign-on (SSO), so users can log in to the AWS Management Console or call the AWS API operations without having to create an IAM user for everyone in your organization. By using SAML, you can simplify the process of configuring federation with AWS because you can use the IdP's service instead of writing custom identity proxy code. You can use a role to configure your SAML 2.0-compliant identity provider (IdP) and AWS to permit your federated users to access the AWS Management Console. The role grants the user permissions to carry out tasks in the console. Amazon Cognito provides authentication, authorization, and user management for your web and mobile apps. Your users can sign in directly with a username and password or through a third party such as Facebook, Amazon, Google, or Apple. The two main components of Amazon Cognito are user pools and identity pools. User pools are user directories that provide sign-up and sign-in options for your app users. Identity pools enable you to grant your users access to other AWS services. Amazon Cognito identity pools provide temporary AWS credentials for users who are guests (unauthenticated) and for users who have been authenticated and have received a token. OpenID Connect is an open standard for authentication that is supported by a number of login providers. Amazon Cognito supports the linking of identities with OpenID Connect providers that are configured through AWS Identity and Access Management. The SAML solution allows using company LDAP for authentication with SAML assertions for IAM authorization. The OpenID Connect solution provides SSO functionality for mobile apps with Cognito Identity Pools providing temporary AWS credentials. AWS IAM Identity Center supports single sign-on to business applications through web browsers only, making it unsuitable for mobile applications. Storing authorization tokens permanently in DynamoDB is not recommended - tokens should be temporary with fixed session lengths.

An accounting firm has 200+ mixed Windows/Linux EC2 instances in production. Need to conduct monthly performance checks collecting system details like memory usage, disk space, and metrics . Logs will be analyzed using AWS Analytics tools and stored in S3. Must implement with minimal effort . Which is the most efficient way to collect and analyze logs from instances with minimal effort? A. Set up and configure a unified CloudWatch Logs agent in each On-Demand EC2 instance which will automatically collect and push data to CloudWatch Logs. Analyze the log data with CloudWatch Logs Insights. B. Enable Traffic Mirroring and install AWS CDK on each instance. Create custom daemon script to collect data to CloudWatch Logs. Use CloudWatch detailed monitoring and Logs Insights. C. Set up and install AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) on each instance to collect and push data to CloudWatch Logs. Analyze with CloudWatch Logs Insights. D. Set up AWS Inspector Agent on each instance to collect data to CloudWatch Logs. Use CloudWatch dashboard to analyze log data. ✅ A. Unified CloudWatch Logs agent + CloudWatch Logs Insights 🎯 Unified CloudWatch agent is AWS's recommended solution - works on both Windows/Linux, collects logs AND metrics with one agent, provides better performance than alternatives. ⚠️ B. Traffic Mirroring + CDK — Overcomplicated custom solution, Traffic Mirroring is for network traffic not system logs ⚠️ C. SSM Agent — Not designed for log collection, requires manual connection to instances ⚠️ D. Inspector Agent — Security assessment tool only, not for performance monitoring 📖 Full Explanation To collect logs from your Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises servers into CloudWatch Logs, AWS offers both a new unified CloudWatch agent, and an older CloudWatch Logs agent. It is recommended to use the unified CloudWatch agent which has the following advantages: – You can collect both logs and advanced metrics with the installation and configuration of just one agent. – The unified agent enables the collection of logs from servers running Windows Server. – If you are using the agent to collect CloudWatch metrics, the unified agent also enables the collection of additional system metrics, for in-guest visibility. – The unified agent provides better performance. CloudWatch Logs Insights enables you to interactively search and analyze your log data in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. You can perform queries to help you quickly and effectively respond to operational issues. If an issue occurs, you can use CloudWatch Logs Insights to identify potential causes and validate deployed fixes.

A company launched a central employee registry application with microservices architecture in Docker. Management teams in different VPCs need access . Requirements: traffic must NOT traverse public Internet and IT Security must be notified of denied requests with source IPs . How should the Solutions Architect implement this architecture? A. Set up Transit VPC with third-party VPN appliances on EC2, AWS Config rules for rejected traffic to CloudWatch Logs with subscription to IT Security B. Set up IPSec Tunnel between central VPC and teams' VPCs, VPC Flow Logs for rejected traffic to CloudWatch Logs with subscription to IT Security C. Link teams' VPCs to central VPC using VPC Peering, VPC Flow Logs for rejected traffic to CloudWatch Logs with subscription to IT Security D. Use Direct Connect between central VPC and teams' VPCs, VPC Flow Logs for rejected traffic to CloudWatch Logs with subscription to IT Security ✅ C. VPC Peering + VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch 🎯 VPC Peering enables private routing between VPCs without internet traversal. VPC Flow Logs capture rejected traffic with source IPs. ⚠️ A. VPN appliances use public internet, AWS Config can't capture source IPs ⚠️ B. IPSec tunnels traverse public internet ⚠️ D. Direct Connect connects on-premises to VPC, not VPC-to-VPC 📖 Full Explanation A VPC peering connection is a networking connection between two VPCs that enables you to route traffic between them privately. Instances in either VPC can communicate with each other as if they are within the same network. You can create a VPC peering connection between your own VPCs, with a VPC in another AWS account, or with a VPC in a different AWS Region. VPC Flow Logs is a feature that enables you to capture information about the IP traffic going to and from network interfaces in your VPC. Flow log data can be published to Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3. After you've created a flow log, you can retrieve and view its data in the chosen destination. Flow logs can help you with a number of tasks, such as: – Diagnosing overly restrictive security group rules – Monitoring the traffic that is reaching your instance – Determining the direction of the traffic to and from the network interfaces Flow log data is collected outside of the path of your network traffic, and therefore does not affect network throughput or latency. You can create or delete flow logs without any risk of impact to network performance. The IPSec tunnel option is incorrect because it uses the Internet to transfer data, violating the requirement. Direct Connect is for on-premises to VPC connections, not VPC-to-VPC. Transit VPC with VPN appliances also uses public internet and AWS Config cannot capture source IPs of rejected requests.

A company's flagship product page (3-tier .NET/MySQL app) experienced downtime during a traffic surge. Management wants to move to AWS with highly available, scalable infrastructure for 300,000 peak users while being cost-effective . Which design option satisfies these requirements? A. Elastic Beanstalk with EC2 Auto Scaling Group behind Network Load Balancer + RDS MySQL Multi-AZ + Route 53 Alias to NLB B. CloudFormation with EC2 Auto Scaling Group behind Application Load Balancer + Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ with "retain" deletion policy + Route 53 Alias to ALB C. CloudFormation with ECS cluster using Spot Instances behind Application Load Balancer + RDS MySQL Multi-AZ with "snapshot" deletion policy + Route 53 Alias to ALB D. Elastic Beanstalk with EC2 Auto Scaling across two regions behind ALBs + Aurora MySQL with cross-region read replica + Route 53 geoproximity routing ✅ B) CloudFormation with EC2 Auto Scaling + ALB + Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ 🎯 ALB handles HTTP/HTTPS traffic with path-based routing. Aurora provides better performance than RDS MySQL for high traffic. ⚠️ A) NLB operates at Layer 4 (TCP) and lacks HTTP routing features needed for web applications ⚠️ C) Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS, reducing reliability for flagship product ⚠️ D) Multi-region setup is unnecessarily complex and expensive; cross-AZ is sufficient 📖 Full Explanation AWS CloudFormation gives you an easy way to model a collection of related AWS resources, provision them quickly and consistently, and manage them throughout their lifecycles, by treating infrastructure as code. A CloudFormation template describes your desired resources and their dependencies so you can launch and configure them together as a stack. In CloudFormation, the AWS::AutoScaling::AutoScalingGroup resource defines an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group, which is a collection of Amazon EC2 instances that are treated as a logical grouping for the purposes of automatic scaling and management. Elastic Load Balancing is used to automatically distribute your incoming application traffic across all the EC2 instances that you are running. You can use Elastic Load Balancing to manage incoming requests by optimally routing traffic so that no one instance is overwhelmed. To use Elastic Load Balancing with your Auto Scaling group, you attach the load balancer to your Auto Scaling group to register the group with the load balancer. Your load balancer acts as a single point of contact for all incoming web traffic to your Auto Scaling group. An Application Load Balancer is ideal for this scenario as routes and load balances at the application layer (HTTP/HTTPS) and supports path-based routing. On CloudFormation you can set the RDS DeletionPolicy as "Retain" which keeps the resource without deleting it or its contents when its stack is deleted. This is helpful in the event that the stack is deleted and you need to quickly provision a new stack. You can quickly use the retained RDS instance from the old stack. Therefore, the correct answer is: Launch a CloudFormation stack that contains an Auto Scaling Group of Amazon EC2 instances spanning multiple Availability Zones that are behind an Application Load Balancer. Use the stack to launch an Amazon Aurora MySQL database cluster in a Multi-AZ configuration with a "retain" deletion policy. Create a Route 53 zone entry for the company's domain name with an Alias-record pointed to the ALB.

Company migrating Docker containers to AWS Fargate. Task definition and service created. Cluster on private subnet with no direct internet connection . Error when launching Fargate task: CannotPullContainerError: API error (500): Get https://111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/v2/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection Which option fixes this issue? A. This is a limitation of "awsvpc" network mode. Update to use "bridge" network mode instead B. Set auto-assign public IP to DISABLED. Launch NAT gateway on private subnet and update route table C. Set auto-assign public IP to ENABLED. Create gateway VPC endpoint for ECR and update route table D. Set auto-assign public IP to DISABLED. Launch NAT gateway on public subnet and update route table ✅ D. Set auto-assign public IP to DISABLED. Launch NAT gateway on public subnet 🎯 Private subnet tasks need NAT gateway in public subnet for internet access to pull ECR images. NAT gateway requires public IP and route to IGW. ⚠️ A. Fargate only supports awsvpc network mode, not bridge ⚠️ B. NAT gateway must be in public subnet, not private subnet ⚠️ C. Private subnet tasks don't need public IPs; should use interface endpoint not gateway 📖 Full Explanation AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers that works with both Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS). Fargate removes the need to provision and manage servers, lets you specify and pay for resources per application, and improves security through application isolation by design. The CannotPullContainer error (500) is caused by the Connection timed out when connecting to Amazon ECR. This indicates that when creating a task, the container image specified could not be retrieved. When a Fargate task is launched, its elastic network interface requires a route to the Internet to pull container images. To resolve this issue, you can: – For tasks in public subnets, specify ENABLED for Auto-assign public IP when launching the task. – For tasks in private subnets, specify DISABLED for Auto-assign public IP when launching the task, and configure a NAT gateway in your VPC to route requests to the Internet. The NAT gateway must be placed in a public subnet because it needs a Public IP address and a direct route to the Internet Gateway (IGW). AWS Fargate only supports the "awsvpc" network mode, not bridge mode.

A company hosts its immigration system on one large EC2 instance with EBS storage. The system accepts user documents/photos, performs automated verification, but becomes unavailable during surges. Processing takes too long and EBS volumes can't handle growing data uploads. Which option achieves high availability and scalable data storage ? A. Upgrade to EBS with Provisioned IOPS as main storage and use SQS queue to distribute tasks to Auto Scaling EC2 instances. B. Use SNS to distribute tasks to Auto Scaling EC2 instances based on SQS queue length. C. Use EBS with Provisioned IOPS, SNS for task distribution, Auto Scaling based on SNS notifications, CloudFormation for multi-region. D. Use S3 with cross-region replication for storage, SQS for task distribution to Auto Scaling EC2 instances, CloudFormation for multi-region. ✅ D. S3 with CRR + SQS + Auto Scaling + CloudFormation 🎯 S3 provides unlimited scalable storage unlike EBS volumes, while SQS properly distributes tasks for Auto Scaling processing. ⚠️ A. EBS volumes aren't scalable and syncing data across instances is complex ⚠️ B. SNS is for notifications, not task queuing—SQS handles task distribution ⚠️ C. EBS isn't scalable like S3, and SNS doesn't queue tasks like SQS 📖 Full Explanation In this scenario, you need to overhaul the existing immigration service to upgrade its storage and computing capacity. Since EBS Volumes can only provide limited storage capacity and are not scalable, you should use S3 instead. The system goes down at times when there is a surge of requests which indicates that the existing large EC2 instance could not handle the requests any longer. In this case, you should implement a highly-available architecture and a queueing system with SQS and Auto Scaling. The correct option provides high availability and scalable data storage with S3. Auto-scaling of EC2 instances reduces the overall processing time and SQS helps in distributing the tasks to a group of EC2 instances. The other options are incorrect because: EBS is not easily scalable compared to S3, SNS is for notifications not task queuing (SQS is better for distributing tasks to Auto Scaling groups), and having large EBS volumes on each instance is not economical and difficult to sync.

A company hosts production on-premises with Docker containers on self-managed VMs , web servers using commercial Oracle Java SE (high licensing costs), and MySQL source-replica setup . They want to migrate to AWS to gain flexibility/agility and use OpenJDK to save licensing costs without major application changes . Which migration strategy meets the above requirement? A. Re-factor/re-architect by converting Docker containers to AWS Lambda. Convert MySQL to DynamoDB using AWS SCT. B. Re-platform using AWS App Runner for Docker containers. Convert MySQL to DynamoDB using AWS SCT. C. Re-host by creating EC2 instances mirroring current servers. Host Docker on EC2, dump MySQL to S3, import to new EC2 MySQL instance. D. Re-platform using Amazon ECS for Docker containers. Upload OpenJDK containers to ECR. Migrate MySQL to RDS using DMS. ✅ D) Re-platform using ECS + RDS migration 🎯 Re-platforming provides cloud benefits (ECS managed containers, RDS managed database) while keeping core architecture intact, avoiding major application changes. ⚠️ A) Re-architecting requires major changes (Lambda functions, DynamoDB schema conversion) ⚠️ B) App Runner is valid but DynamoDB conversion requires major changes not requested ⚠️ C) Re-hosting mirrors on-premises setup, doesn't leverage cloud elasticity and agility 📖 Full Explanation The six most common application migration strategies are: Rehosting — Otherwise known as "lift-and-shift". Many early cloud projects gravitate toward net new development using cloud-native capabilities, but in a large legacy migration scenario where the organization is looking to scale its migration quickly to meet a business case, applications can be rehosted. Replatforming — Sometimes, this is called "lift-tinker-and-shift." Here you might make a few cloud (or other) optimizations in order to achieve some tangible benefit, but you aren't otherwise changing the core architecture of the application. You may be looking to reduce the amount of time you spend managing database instances by migrating to a database-as-a-service platform like Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) or migrating your application to a fully managed platform like Amazon Elastic Beanstalk. Repurchasing — Moving to a different product. Repurchasing is a move to a SaaS platform. Moving a CRM to Salesforce.com, an HR system to Workday, a CMS to Drupal, etc. Refactoring / Re-architecting — Re-imagining how the application is architected and developed, typically using cloud-native features. This is typically driven by a strong business need to add features, scale, or performance that would otherwise be difficult to achieve in the application's existing environment. For example, migrating from a monolithic architecture to a service-oriented (or server-less) architecture to boost agility. Retire — This strategy basically means: "Get rid of." Once you've discovered everything in your environment, you might ask each functional area who owns each application and see that some of the applications are no longer used. You can save costs by retiring these applications. Retain — Usually this means "revisit" or do nothing (for now). Maybe you aren't ready to prioritize an application that was recently upgraded or are otherwise not inclined to migrate some applications. You can retain these applications and revisit your migration strategy. Therefore, the correct answer is: Re-platform the environment on the AWS Cloud platform by running the Docker containers on Amazon ECS. Test the new OpenJDK Docker containers and upload them on Amazon Elastic Container Registry. Migrate the MySQL database to Amazon RDS using AWS Database Migration Service.

Company migrating 3-tier web app VMs from on-premises to AWS. Requirements: import VM images , sync changes until cutover , minimal downtime , migrate root + data volumes (TB scale) , minimal operational overhead . Which solution meets ALL requirements? A. AWS Discovery Service + Migration Hub + VM Import/Export with CLI scripts for sync B. AWS MGN for root volumes + CLI import-snapshot for data volumes C. AWS MGN with replication agents + automated sync + cutover D. VM Import/Export with scheduled CLI scripts for sync ✅ C. AWS MGN with replication agents + automated sync + cutover 🎯 MGN provides continuous replication with agents, handles both root/data volumes automatically, and supports automated cutover with minimal downtime. ⚠️ A. VM Import/Export cannot sync incremental changes - requires full re-import ⚠️ B. Manual data volume migration adds operational overhead when MGN handles all volumes ⚠️ D. VM Import/Export doesn't support continuous sync - only full imports 📖 Full Explanation AWS Application Migration Service minimizes time-intensive, error-prone manual processes by automatically converting your source servers to run natively on AWS. It also simplifies application modernization with built-in, post-launch optimization options. AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is a highly automated lift-and-shift (rehost) solution that simplifies, expedites, and reduces the cost of migrating applications to AWS. It enables companies to lift and shift a large number of physical, virtual, or cloud servers without compatibility issues, performance disruption, or long cutover windows. MGN replicates source servers into your AWS account. When you're ready, it automatically converts and launches your servers on AWS so you can quickly benefit from the cost savings, productivity, resilience, and agility of the Cloud. Once your applications are running on AWS, you can leverage AWS services and capabilities to quickly and easily re-platform or refactor those applications – which makes lift-and-shift a fast route to modernization. The first setup step for Application Migration Service is creating the Replication Settings template. Add source servers to Application Migration Service by installing the AWS Replication Agent (also referred to as "the Agent") on them. The Agent can be installed on both Linux and Windows servers. After you have added all of your source servers and configured their launch settings, you are ready to launch a Test instance. Once you have finalized the testing of all of your source servers, you are ready for cutover. The cutover will migrate your source servers to the Cutover instances on AWS. Therefore, the correct answer is: Create a job on AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) to migrate the virtual machines to AWS. Install the replication agent on each application tier to sync the changes from the on-premises environment to AWS. Launch Amazon EC2 instances based on the replicated VM from AWS MGN. After successful testing, perform a cutover and launch new instances based on the updated AMIs. The option that says: Write an AWS CLI script that uses VM Import/Export to migrate the virtual machines. Schedule the script to run at regular intervals to synchronize the changes from the on-premises environment to AWS. Launch Amazon EC2 instances based on the images created from VM Import/Export. After successful testing, re-run the script to perform a final replication before the cutover. Launch new instances based on the updated AMIs is incorrect. AWS VM Import/Export does not support synching incremental changes from the on-premises environment to AWS. You will need to import the VM again as a whole after you make changes to the on-premises environment. This requires a lot of time and adds more operational overhead. The option that says: Create a job on AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) to migrate the root volumes of the virtual machines to AWS. Import the data volumes using the AWS CLI import-snapshot command. Launch Amazon EC2 instances based on the images created from AWS MGN and attach the imported data volumes. After successful testing, perform a final replication before the cutover. Launch new instances based on the updated AMIs and attach the corresponding data volumes is incorrect. This may be possible but creating manual snapshots of the data volumes requires more operational overhead. AWS MGN supports syncing of attached volumes as well, so you don't have to migrate the data volumes manually. The option that says: Leverage both AWS Application Discovery Service and AWS Migration Hub to group the on-premises VMs as an application. Write an AWS CLI script that uses VM Import/Export to import the VMs as AMIs. Schedule the script to run at regular intervals to synchronize the changes from the on-premises environment to AWS. Launch Amazon EC2 instances based on the images created from VM Import/Export. After successful testing, perform a final virtual machine import before the cutover. Launch new instances based on the updated AMIs is incorrect. The AWS Application Discovery Service plans migration projects by gathering information about the on-premises data center, and all discovered data are stored in your AWS Migration Hub. This is similar to the other option for VM Import/Export, as you will need to import the VM again as a whole after you make changes on the on-premises environment.

A multinational investment bank uses a single 1 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection to connect 10 VPCs to their on-premises network. Recent IT audit identified a single point of failure that needs immediate cost-effective remediation. Which is the MOST cost-effective solution to improve connection redundancy? A. Establish a new point-to-point MPLS connection to all 10 VPCs with BGP active/passive routing B. Establish another 1 Gbps Direct Connect with private VIFs to all 10 VPCs and BGP peering C. Establish another 1 Gbps Direct Connect with public VIF and VPN tunnels to VGWs using BGP failover D. Establish VPN tunnels from on-premises to each of the 10 VPCs, terminate at VGWs, configure BGP ✅ D. VPN tunnels to each VPC with BGP 🎯 VPN provides cost-effective backup to Direct Connect while maintaining encryption and BGP routing capabilities. ⚠️ A. MPLS — Cannot directly connect MPLS to AWS VPCs ⚠️ B. Another Direct Connect — Not cost-effective for backup solution ⚠️ C. Direct Connect + VPN — Unnecessarily expensive using another Direct Connect 📖 Full Explanation With AWS Direct Connect plus VPN, you can combine one or more AWS Direct Connect dedicated network connections with the Amazon VPC VPN. This combination provides an IPsec-encrypted private connection that also reduces network costs, increases bandwidth throughput, and provides a more consistent network experience than Internet-based VPN connections. It costs a lot of money to establish a Direct Connect connection which you rarely use. For a more cost-effective solution, you can configure a backup VPN connection for failover with your AWS Direct Connect connection. If you want a short-term or lower-cost solution, you might consider configuring a hardware VPN as a failover option for a Direct Connect connection. VPN connections are not designed to provide the same level of bandwidth available to most Direct Connect connections. Ensure that your use case or application can tolerate a lower bandwidth if you are configuring a VPN as a backup to a Direct Connect connection.

A retail company's web application uses Auto Scaling EC2 instances behind an ALB. The target group health check queries a database page. During high database CPU usage, health checks timeout, causing Auto Scaling to continuously replace healthy instances, resulting in downtime. Which TWO solutions prevent this issue and improve future scalability? A. Create CloudWatch alarm to recover RDS instance during high load by rebooting database B. Change health check to simple HTML page; use Route 53 health check for database monitoring C. Create RDS read replicas and configure application to use reader endpoint for reads D. Change to TCP health check; use Route 53 health check for database monitoring E. Add ElastiCache cluster to cache frequent database queries ✅ B & E: Simple HTML health check + ElastiCache caching 🎯 Decouple health checks from database load (B) and reduce database queries with caching (E) ⚠️ A — Rebooting causes downtime, doesn't solve load issue ⚠️ C — Read replicas help but don't reduce repetitive health check queries ⚠️ D — ALB doesn't support TCP health checks, only HTTP/HTTPS 📖 Full Explanation The problem occurs because ALB health checks query the database repeatedly from multiple instances, overwhelming the database during high load periods. Option B solves this by using a simple HTML page for health checks while maintaining application monitoring through Route 53. Option E addresses the root cause by caching frequent queries with ElastiCache, reducing database load. Option A causes downtime through reboots. Option C helps performance but doesn't reduce health check database queries. Option D is technically impossible as ALB only supports HTTP/HTTPS health checks, not TCP.

A fintech startup's payment processing system (EC2, DynamoDB, S3, CloudFront) accepts credit cards and cryptocurrencies . Recent audit found credit card numbers not properly encrypted , failing PCI DSS compliance . You must protect sensitive card data AND improve CloudFront cache hit ratio . What is the best option to encrypt sensitive credit card information AND improve cache hit ratio? A. Add custom SSL in CloudFront. Configure origin to add User-Agent and Host headers to objects. B. Create origin access control (OAC) and add to CloudFront. Configure origin to add User-Agent and Host headers. C. Configure CloudFront to use Signed URLs. Configure origin to add Cache-Control max-age directive with longest practical value. D. Configure CloudFront to enforce HTTPS and field-level encryption. Configure origin to add Cache-Control max-age directive with longest practical value. ✅ D. HTTPS + field-level encryption + Cache-Control max-age 🎯 Field-level encryption protects specific data fields (like credit cards) throughout the entire application stack for PCI DSS compliance. Cache-Control max-age improves hit ratio by keeping content cached longer. ⚠️ A. Custom SSL — provides HTTPS but no field-level encryption for card data ⚠️ B. OAC — restricts S3 access but doesn't encrypt sensitive fields ⚠️ C. Signed URLs — controls private content access but doesn't encrypt card data 📖 Full Explanation Field-level encryption adds an additional layer of security, along with HTTPS, that lets you protect specific data throughout system processing so that only certain applications can see it. Field-level encryption allows you to securely upload user-submitted sensitive information to your web servers. The sensitive information provided by your clients is encrypted at the edge closer to the user and remains encrypted throughout your entire application stack, ensuring that only applications that need the data—and have the credentials to decrypt it—are able to do so. To use field-level encryption, you configure your CloudFront distribution to specify the set of fields in POST requests that you want to be encrypted, and the public key to use to encrypt them. You can encrypt up to 10 data fields in a request. You can improve performance by increasing the proportion of your viewer requests that are served from CloudFront edge caches instead of going to your origin servers for content; that is, by improving the cache hit ratio for your distribution. To increase your cache hit ratio, you can configure your origin to add a Cache-Control max-age directive to your objects, and specify the longest practical value for max-age. The shorter the cache duration, the more frequently CloudFront forwards another request to your origin to determine whether the object has changed and, if so, to get the latest version.

A university's serverless portal (Lambda + API Gateway) was compromised via SQL injection attack, causing complete data loss. Need cost-effective protection against SQL injection and track historical changes to firewall rules . Which solution provides the most suitable and cost-effective protection? A. AWS WAF web ACL in front of Lambda functions + AWS Firewall Manager for tracking B. Block attacker IP in NACL + CloudFront + AWS WAF web ACL + AWS Config for tracking C. Create ALB + AWS WAF on ALB + place API Gateway behind ALB + AWS Firewall Manager D. AWS WAF web ACL in front of API Gateway + AWS Config for tracking changes ✅ D) AWS WAF web ACL in front of API Gateway + AWS Config for tracking 🎯 WAF integrates directly with API Gateway (no extra components needed) and AWS Config tracks WAF rule changes effectively. ⚠️ A) WAF cannot be placed directly in front of Lambda functions ⚠️ B) CloudFront adds unnecessary cost when global distribution isn't required ⚠️ C) ALB adds unnecessary cost and Firewall Manager is for multi-account management 📖 Full Explanation AWS WAF is a web application firewall that helps protect web applications from common exploits like SQL injection. It can be deployed directly in front of API Gateway without additional infrastructure costs. AWS Config tracks changes to WAF web access control lists, including rule creation, deletion, and configuration updates. Option A is wrong because WAF cannot be placed directly in front of Lambda functions - it must be placed in front of API Gateway. Option B adds unnecessary CloudFront costs when global distribution isn't required. Option C adds unnecessary ALB costs, and AWS Firewall Manager is primarily for managing firewalls across multiple AWS accounts, not tracking WAF rule changes.

Company develops mobile apps needing cross-platform user customization data storage. 4KB per user , 3M customers , social login authentication . Need highly available, cost-effective, scalable, secure solution. How should the Solutions Architect design this solution? A. DynamoDB table with user preferences. Mobile app queries directly. Use STS, Web Identity Federation, DynamoDB Fine-Grained Access Control. B. RDS MySQL with read replicas in 2 AZs. Mobile app queries read replicas. Use MySQL user management for security. C. Store preferences in S3, DynamoDB table references S3 objects. Use STS, Web Identity Federation, S3 Access Points. D. RDS MySQL in 2 AZs with public-facing application server managing authentication. ✅ A. DynamoDB with Web Identity Federation 🎯 DynamoDB handles 3M users cost-effectively at scale. Web Identity Federation enables social login without managing credentials. ⚠️ B. RDS MySQL — Less scalable/cost-effective than DynamoDB, can't handle social logins ⚠️ C. S3 + DynamoDB — Unnecessary complexity for 4KB data, S3 Access Points not needed ⚠️ D. RDS + App Server — Not scalable, doesn't support social login requirements 📖 Full Explanation With web identity federation, users sign in using well-known identity providers (Amazon, Facebook, Google, OIDC-compatible IdPs), receive authentication tokens, then exchange for temporary AWS credentials mapped to IAM roles. This eliminates need for custom sign-in code or managing user identities while keeping AWS account secure without embedding long-term credentials. DynamoDB provides the scalability and cost-efficiency needed for 3M users with 4KB preference data per user. Fine-grained access control ensures proper authorization. RDS options are less scalable and cost-effective. S3 solution adds unnecessary complexity for small 4KB files that fit perfectly in DynamoDB.

A government agency has multiple VPCs across US regions that need private, dedicated network connectivity to an on-premises central office in Washington, D.C. Requirements: inter-region VPC access , enhanced security , predictable performance , and minimal management overhead . Which solution provides the most secure, highly available, and durable interconnectivity? A. AWS Direct Connect Gateway with virtual private gateways in each VPC and private virtual interfaces B. Inter-region VPC peering to keep traffic on AWS backbone C. Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke topology with Site-to-Site VPN D. Direct Connect Gateway with LAG and public virtual interfaces ✅ A. Direct Connect Gateway with private virtual interfaces 🎯 Direct Connect Gateway enables dedicated, private connectivity to multiple VPCs across regions with single BGP session management. ⚠️ B. VPC peering — requires extensive manual setup and lacks dedicated connectivity ⚠️ C. Transit Gateway + VPN — doesn't provide dedicated network or predictable performance ⚠️ D. Public virtual interfaces — incorrect for VPC connectivity (need private VIFs) 📖 Full Explanation AWS Direct Connect provides dedicated network connections from on-premises to AWS with higher privacy, bandwidth, and predictable performance. Direct Connect Gateway allows connecting to multiple VPCs across regions using private virtual interfaces, reducing administrative overhead by eliminating multiple BGP sessions. Option B (VPC peering) requires complex manual setup and lacks dedicated connectivity. Option C (Transit Gateway + VPN) doesn't provide dedicated network paths or predictable performance. Option D incorrectly uses public virtual interfaces (should be private for VPC connectivity) and unnecessarily includes LAG.

A company hosts an online delivery system on EC2 instances with ALB in ap-southeast-1. MySQL RDS stores deliveries/transactions. Requirements: RTO for disaster recovery, plus automatic PII/IP protection . Which disaster recovery strategy achieves the required RTO and RPO targets most cost-effectively? A. Schedule DB backup to AWS Storage Gateway hourly, transaction logs to S3 every 5 min. Use AWS Shield for PII/IP protection. B. Schedule 15-min DB backups to Glacier, transaction logs to S3 every 5 min. Use Amazon Macie for sensitive data protection. C. Schedule DB backup to S3 hourly, transaction logs to S3 every 5 min. Use Amazon Macie for sensitive data protection. D. Set up Multi-AZ with asynchronous replication. Use AWS Shield for PII/IP protection from RDS. ✅ C. Schedule DB backup to S3 hourly, transaction logs to S3 every 5 min. Use Amazon Macie 🎯 S3 enables fast backup retrieval for ⚠️ A. Storage Gateway is for hybrid environments (not needed here), Shield protects against DDoS not PII discovery ⚠️ B. Glacier standard retrieval takes 3-5 hours, violating RTO requirements ⚠️ D. Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication, doesn't help with regional outages, Shield doesn't discover PII 📖 Full Explanation Recovery time objective (RTO) is the time it takes after a disruption to restore a business process to its service level, as defined by the operational level agreement (OLA). For example, if a disaster occurs at 12:00 PM (noon) and the RTO is eight hours, the DR process should restore the business process to the acceptable service level by 8:00 PM. Recovery point objective (RPO) is the acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. For example, if a disaster occurs at 12:00 PM (noon) and the RPO is one hour, the system should recover all data that was in the system before 11:00 AM. Data loss will span only one hour, between 11:00 AM and 12:00 PM (noon). Amazon S3 is an ideal destination for backup data that might be needed quickly to perform a restore. Transferring data to and from Amazon S3 is typically done through the network, and is therefore accessible from any location. Amazon Macie is a security service that uses machine learning to automatically discover, classify, and protect sensitive data in AWS. Amazon Macie recognizes sensitive data such as personally identifiable information (PII) or intellectual property, and provides you with dashboards and alerts that give visibility into how this data is being accessed or moved. The fully managed service continuously monitors data access activity for anomalies, and generates detailed alerts when it detects risk of unauthorized access or inadvertent data leaks. Hence, the option that says: Schedule a database backup to an S3 bucket every hour and store transaction logs to a separate S3 bucket every 5 minutes. Use Amazon Macie to automatically discover, classify, and protect your sensitive data is correct because by using an S3 bucket, it makes data retrievals of the backups quicker. Since the transaction logs are stored in S3 every 5 minutes, this will help to restore the application to a state that is within the required RPO of 15 minutes.

A multinational corporation uses AWS Organizations with consolidated billing for multiple business units. The Baby products unit purchased 10 Reserved Instances but does not want RI discounts shared with other business units. Which solution prevents RI discount sharing? A. RI sharing cannot be disabled in AWS Organizations B. Remove the Baby products account from AWS Organizations C. Set RI sharing to private on the Baby products account D. Turn off RI sharing on the master account for Baby products members ✅ D. Turn off RI sharing on the master account for Baby products members 🎯 The master account can control RI sharing per member account via Billing Console preferences. ⚠️ A — RI sharing CAN be disabled by master account ⚠️ B — Removing from Organizations is unnecessary and loses consolidated billing benefits ⚠️ C — No "private" setting exists; member accounts cannot control their own RI sharing 📖 Full Explanation For billing purposes, the consolidated billing feature of AWS Organizations treats all the accounts in the organization as one account. This means that all accounts in the organization can receive the hourly cost-benefit of Reserved Instances that are purchased by any other account. In the payer account, you can turn off Reserved Instance discount sharing on the Preferences page on the Billing and Cost Management console. The master account of an organization can turn off Reserved Instance (RI) sharing for member accounts in that organization. This means that Reserved Instances are not shared between that member account and other member accounts. You can change this preference multiple times. Each estimated bill is computed using the last set of preferences. However, take note that turning off Reserved Instance sharing can result in a higher monthly bill.

A company processes petabytes of images monthly using an on-premises HPC cluster (5,000 cores, 10 PB capacity). Processing takes a week with thousands of parallel jobs. The data center is nearing capacity , forcing job spreading across the month. Need a scalable solution with least management overhead while maintaining current durability levels. Which solution meets requirements while being cost-effective? A. EMR cluster with Spark, On-demand/Reserved instances, DynamoDB job listing, S3 storage B. Docker images on ECR, run on EKS with auto scaling, EBS SC1 volumes, then S3 C. AWS Batch with Managed Compute Environments using Spot Instances, S3 storage, Job Queues D. SQS queue for jobs, Auto Scaling Group of Spot instances, EFS for data sharing, S3 storage ✅ C. AWS Batch with Managed Compute Environments using Spot Instances 🎯 AWS Batch automatically manages compute resources for batch jobs with no additional charges, ideal for HPC workloads requiring dynamic scaling. ⚠️ A. EMR — Adds management overhead with constantly running instances even during low job periods ⚠️ B. EKS — Requires significant application containerization changes; SC1 volumes aren't cost-effective for petabyte storage ⚠️ D. SQS+EFS — EFS more expensive than S3; SQS can cause duplicate job processing with Spot instance interruptions 📖 Full Explanation AWS Batch enables developers, scientists, and engineers to easily and efficiently run hundreds of thousands of batch computing jobs on AWS. AWS Batch dynamically provisions the optimal quantity and type of compute resources (e.g., CPU or memory optimized instances) based on the volume and specific resource requirements of the batch jobs submitted. With AWS Batch, there is no need to install and manage batch computing software or server clusters that you use to run your jobs, allowing you to focus on analyzing results and solving problems. There is no additional charge for AWS Batch. You only pay for the AWS resources (e.g. EC2 instances or Fargate jobs) you create to store and run your batch jobs. From the AWS Batch use cases page, we can see an example similar to this scenario wherein Digital Media and Entertainment companies require highly scalable batch computing resources to enable accelerated and automated processing of data as well as the compilation and processing of files, graphics, and visual effects for high-resolution video content. Use AWS Batch to accelerate content creation, dynamically scale media packaging, and automate asynchronous media supply chain workflows. In AWS Batch, job queues are mapped to one or more compute environments. Compute environments contain the Amazon ECS container instances that are used to run containerized batch jobs. A specific compute environment can also be mapped to one or many job queues. Within a job queue, the associated compute environments each have an order that's used by the scheduler to determine where jobs that are ready to be run should run.

A company's security team identified unusual API activity and port scanning from a specific IP address targeting EC2 instances in their VPC. The solutions architect needs to immediately block the offending IP address and protect against network/transport layer DDoS attacks . Which solution best satisfies these requirements? A. Change Windows Firewall settings to deny the IP. Use GuardDuty and Systems Manager Patch Manager. B. Block the IP using Route 53. Use Amazon Macie for DDoS protection. C. Deny access in Network ACL. Use AWS Shield Advanced. D. Add deny rule to Security Groups. Use AWS WAF and Config. ✅ C. Deny access in Network ACL. Use AWS Shield Advanced. 🎯 Network ACLs can deny specific IPs (stateless firewall at subnet level). Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS protection for network/transport layers. ⚠️ A — Windows Firewall only protects individual instances, not network-level blocking ⚠️ B — Route 53 cannot block IPs; Macie is for data classification, not DDoS ⚠️ D — Security Groups cannot deny (only allow); WAF/Config insufficient for DDoS 📖 Full Explanation AWS Shield is a managed Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS protection service that safeguards applications running on AWS. AWS Shield provides always-on detection and automatic inline mitigations that minimize application downtime and latency, so there is no need to engage AWS Support to benefit from DDoS protection. There are two tiers of AWS Shield – Standard and Advanced. All AWS customers benefit from the automatic protections of AWS Shield Standard, at no additional charge. AWS Shield Standard defends against most common, frequently occurring network and transport layer DDoS attacks that target your web site or applications. When you use AWS Shield Standard with Amazon CloudFront and Amazon Route 53, you receive comprehensive availability protection against all known infrastructure (Layer 3 and 4) attacks. A network access control list (ACL) is an optional layer of security for your VPC that acts as a firewall for controlling traffic in and out of one or more subnets. You might set up network ACLs with rules similar to your security groups in order to add an additional layer of security to your VPC. A network ACL has separate inbound and outbound rules, and each rule can either allow or deny traffic. Network ACLs are stateless; responses to allowed inbound traffic are subject to the rules for outbound traffic (and vice versa).

Fitness tracking app serves North American and Asian users . App is read-heavy with regular server pings. Requirements: fault-tolerant across regions , highly-available database writes in single region , multi-region database reads , resilient application tier per region , relational database semantics . Which TWO options meet these requirements? A. Auto Scaling EC2 + RDS MySQL per region + cross-region replication + S3 snapshots B. Route 53 geolocation routing + failover routing with health checks C. Auto Scaling EC2 active-active + Aurora Global Database + in-region endpoints + S3 snapshots D. Route 53 geoproximity routing + multivalue answer routing with health checks E. Auto Scaling EC2 + RDS MySQL + Multi-AZ + cross-region replication ✅ B + C: Route 53 geolocation/failover + Aurora Global Database 🎯 Aurora Global Database enables single-region writes with multi-region reads. Geolocation routing directs users to nearest region with failover capability. ⚠️ A — Can't sync two MySQL masters accepting writes ⚠️ D — Multivalue routing randomly distributes users, ignoring geography ⚠️ E — Multi-AZ doesn't protect from regional failures; MySQL master-master sync impossible 📖 Full Explanation Amazon Aurora Global Database spans multiple regions with one primary (write) region and up to five read-only secondary regions. Replication occurs with sub-second latency using dedicated infrastructure. This meets the requirement for highly-available writes in single region while enabling multi-region reads. Route 53 geolocation routing directs users based on geographic location (North America vs Asia), while failover routing with health checks provides automatic failover to healthy regions when primary fails. Options A and E fail because standard MySQL RDS cannot have multiple masters accepting writes across regions - this creates data conflicts. Option D uses multivalue routing which randomly distributes users rather than geographically optimizing traffic flow.

Company needs to migrate 60 TB Oracle data warehouse to Amazon Redshift . Database receives daily minor updates + monthly major updates . Migration must complete in 30 days . Only 50 Mbps internet available to avoid business impact. Keep costs low . Which action satisfies migration requirements while keeping costs low? A. Configure VPN + 1 Gbps Direct Connect, launch Oracle RAC on EC2, replicate data, use SCT+DMS to migrate to Redshift B. Create Oracle RDS, configure Site-to-Site VPN, replicate data, use SCT+DMS to migrate to Redshift C. Use Snowball Edge to export data, import to S3, create Oracle RDS, use SCT+DMS, copy daily updates over internet D. Use Snowball Edge with SCT, install extraction agent, migrate to S3 then Redshift, configure DMS for ongoing updates ✅ D. Snowball Edge + SCT + extraction agent 🎯 SCT with Snowball Edge handles large-scale migrations efficiently. Extraction agents enable ongoing replication for daily updates. ⚠️ A — Direct Connect expensive for one-time migration ⚠️ B — 60TB over 50Mbps takes too long, impacts business ⚠️ C — Unnecessary RDS step, no extraction agent configured 📖 Full Explanation You can use an AWS SCT agent to extract data from your on-premises data warehouse and migrate it to Amazon Redshift. The agent extracts your data and uploads the data to either Amazon S3 or, for large-scale migrations, an AWS Snowball Edge device. You can then use AWS SCT to copy the data to Amazon Redshift. Large-scale data migrations can include many terabytes of information and can be slowed by network performance and by the sheer amount of data that has to be moved. AWS Snowball Edge is an AWS service you can use to transfer data to the cloud at faster-than-network speeds using an AWS-owned appliance. An AWS Snowball Edge device can hold up to 100 TB of data. It uses 256-bit encryption and an industry-standard Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to ensure both security and full chain-of-custody for your data. AWS SCT works with AWS Snowball Edge devices. When you use AWS SCT and an AWS Snowball Edge device, you migrate your data in two stages. First, you use the AWS SCT to process the data locally and then move that data to the AWS Snowball Edge device. You then send the device to AWS using the AWS Snowball Edge process, and then AWS automatically loads the data into an Amazon S3 bucket. Next, when the data is available on Amazon S3, you use AWS SCT to migrate the data to Amazon Redshift. Data extraction agents can work in the background while AWS SCT is closed. You manage your extraction agents by using AWS SCT. The extraction agents act as listeners. When they receive instructions from AWS SCT, they extract data from your data warehouse.

A company runs a hybrid mobile app: on-premises 3TB MySQL (write-intensive) connected via VPN, AWS Lambda/API Gateway with DynamoDB for user preferences. Lambda execution averages 4.5 minutes (mostly wait time due to MySQL latency) , causing exponential cost increases with 20% monthly growth . Which solution should reduce overall Lambda costs? A. Provision AWS Direct Connect + mobile app caching + reduce Lambda timeout/memory + ElastiCache for DynamoDB B. CloudFront distribution + convert Lambda to EC2 Reserved + DynamoDB Auto Scaling C. Migrate to RDS MySQL + CloudFront + reduce Lambda timeout/memory + DynamoDB Auto Scaling + DAX D. Migrate to RDS MySQL + API Gateway caching + reduce Lambda timeout/memory + DynamoDB Auto Scaling ✅ D. Migrate to RDS MySQL + API Gateway caching + reduce Lambda timeout/memory + DynamoDB Auto Scaling 🎯 Moving MySQL to AWS eliminates VPN latency (main cost driver), while API Gateway caching reduces Lambda invocations directly. ⚠️ A. Direct Connect is expensive for single app; ElastiCache adds unnecessary cost ⚠️ B. CloudFront caches at edge (wrong layer); EC2 Reserved more expensive at low traffic ⚠️ C. CloudFront wrong caching layer; DAX is microsecond caching (expensive overkill) 📖 Full Explanation The primary issue is Lambda execution time of 4.5 minutes due to VPN latency to on-premises MySQL. Migrating MySQL to Amazon RDS eliminates this latency bottleneck, dramatically reducing Lambda execution time and costs. API Gateway caching reduces the number of Lambda invocations by serving cached responses. Optimizing Lambda memory/timeout settings and DynamoDB Auto Scaling further optimize costs. Direct Connect is expensive for a single application when RDS migration provides better latency. CloudFront is for edge caching, not API response caching. DAX provides microsecond performance but is expensive overkill here.

Company uses AWS Organizations with SCPs attached at organization root restricting all accounts. New acquired account cannot apply AWS Config rules due to SCP restrictions. Need solution without long-term management overhead . Which option allows administrators to update Config rules without introducing long-term management overhead? A. Update root SCPs to remove Config restrictions. Deploy AWS Service Catalog with Config policies organization-wide. B. Add new account to temporary Onboarding OU with SCP allowing Config changes. Make changes before moving to Production OU. C. Remove SCPs from root and apply to Production OU instead. Create temporary Onboarding OU with Config-allowing SCP. Move account through Onboarding then to Production. D. Use allow list instead of deny list on root SCPs. Temporarily add Config service to allow list for new account principals. ✅ C. Move SCPs from root to Production OU, create temporary Onboarding OU 🎯 SCPs at root cannot be overridden by child OUs. Moving SCPs to Production OU allows independent Onboarding OU with Config permissions. ⚠️ A — Removes Config restrictions for ALL accounts organization-wide ⚠️ B — Cannot override explicit deny from root SCP with allow in child OU ⚠️ D — Allow lists create more future management overhead than deny lists 📖 Full Explanation AWS Organizations helps you centrally manage and govern your environment as you grow and scale your AWS resources. Using AWS Organizations, you can programmatically create new AWS accounts and allocate resources, group accounts to organize your workflows, apply policies to accounts or groups for governance, and simplify billing by using a single payment method for all of your accounts. With AWS Organizations, you can consolidate multiple AWS accounts into an organization that you create and centrally manage. You can create member accounts and invite existing accounts to join your organization. You can organize those accounts into groups and attach policy-based controls. Service control policies (SCPs) are a type of organization policy that you can use to manage permissions in your organization. SCPs offer central control over the maximum available permissions for all accounts in your organization. SCPs help you to ensure your accounts stay within your organization's access control guidelines. SCPs are available only in an organization that has all features enabled. An SCP restricts permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts, including the member account's root user. Any account has only those permissions allowed by every parent above it. If a permission is blocked at any level above the account, either implicitly (by not being included in an Allow policy statement) or explicitly (by being included in a Deny policy statement), a user or role in the affected account can't use that permission, even if the account administrator attaches the AdministratorAccess IAM policy with */* permissions to the user. AWS strongly recommends that you don't attach SCPs to the root of your organization without thoroughly testing the impact that the policy has on accounts. Instead, create an OU that you can move your accounts into one at a time, or at least in small numbers, to ensure that you don't inadvertently lock users out of key services.

A company runs a sports web portal with resources in multiple AWS regions (EC2, RDS, IAM). The IT Security Compliance Officer requires a reliable and durable logging solution to track changes to all resources across all regions. The solution must ensure integrity and confidentiality of log data. Which solution would be the best option? A. Create a new trail in AWS CloudTrail with the global services option selected, and create one new Amazon S3 bucket to store the logs. Create IAM roles, S3 bucket policies, and enable Multi Factor Authentication (MFA) Delete on the S3 bucket storing your logs. B. Create three new CloudTrail trails, each with its own S3 bucket to store the logs: one for the AWS Management console, one for AWS SDKs, and one for command line tools. Then create IAM roles and S3 bucket policies for the S3 buckets storing your logs. C. Create a new trail in AWS CloudTrail with the global services option selected, and assign it an existing S3 bucket to store the logs. Create S3 ACLs and enable Multi Factor Authentication (MFA) delete on the S3 bucket storing your logs. D. Create a new trail in CloudTrail and assign it a new S3 bucket to store the logs. Configure AWS SNS to send delivery notifications to your management system. Secure the S3 bucket that stores your logs using IAM roles and S3 bucket policies. ✅ A. CloudTrail with global services + new S3 bucket + IAM roles + MFA Delete 🎯 Global services flag captures IAM events across regions, new S3 bucket ensures confidentiality, MFA Delete provides integrity protection. ⚠️ B — Creates unnecessary multiple trails without global services flag ⚠️ C — Uses existing S3 bucket (compromises confidentiality) and S3 ACLs instead of IAM roles ⚠️ D — Missing global services flag, won't capture IAM events 📖 Full Explanation For most services, events are recorded in the region where the action occurred to its respective AWS CloudTrail. For global services such as AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), AWS STS, Amazon CloudFront, and Route 53, events are delivered to any trail that includes global services (IncludeGlobalServiceEvents flag). AWS CloudTrail service should be your top choice for the scenarios where the application is tracking the changes made by any AWS service, resource, or API. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is integrated with AWS CloudTrail, a service that logs AWS events made by or on behalf of your AWS account. CloudTrail logs authenticate AWS API calls and also AWS sign-in events, and collects this event information in files that are delivered to Amazon S3 buckets. Therefore, the correct answer is: Create a new trail in AWS CloudTrail with the global services option selected, and create one new Amazon S3 bucket to store the logs. Create IAM roles, S3 bucket policies, and enable Multi Factor Authentication (MFA) Delete on the S3 bucket storing your logs. It uses AWS CloudTrail with (includeGlobalServiceEvents flag) Global Option enabled, a single new S3 bucket and IAM Roles so that it has the confidentiality, and MFA on Delete on S3 bucket so that it maintains the data integrity. The option that says: Create a new trail in AWS CloudTrail with the global services option selected, and assign it an existing S3 bucket to store the logs. Create S3 ACLs and enable Multi Factor Authentication (MFA) delete on the S3 bucket storing your logs is incorrect. As an existing S3 bucket is used, it may already be accessed by the user, hence not maintaining the confidentiality, and it is not using IAM roles. The option that says: Create three new CloudTrail trails, each with its own S3 bucket to store the logs: one for the AWS Management console, one for AWS SDKs, and one for command line tools. Then create IAM roles and S3 bucket policies for the S3 buckets storing your logs is incorrect. Although it uses AWS CloudTrail, the Global Option is not enabled, and three S3 buckets are not needed. The option that says: Create a new trail in CloudTrail and assign it a new S3 bucket to store the logs. Configure AWS SNS to send delivery notifications to your management system. Secure the S3 bucket that stores your logs using IAM roles and S3 bucket policies is incorrect. Although it uses AWS CloudTrail, the Global Option is not enabled.

A graphics design startup uses multiple S3 buckets to store high-resolution media files. After partnering with a media company, the partner frequently performs multiple object retrievals from the S3 buckets daily, which increased the startup's data transfer costs . As Solutions Architect, what should you do to help the startup lower their operational costs? A. Advise the media company to create their own S3 bucket, then run aws s3 sync to copy objects so future retrievals use the media company's bucket B. Enable the Requester Pays feature in all startup's S3 buckets to make the media company pay data transfer costs C. Create a new billing account for the media company using AWS Organizations with SCPs for resource access control D. Provide cross-account access for the media company with S3 bucket permissions ✅ B) Enable Requester Pays feature 🎯 Requester Pays shifts data transfer and request costs to the requester while bucket owner pays storage costs. ⚠️ A) S3 sync — Creates duplicate storage costs and initial transfer charges ⚠️ C) AWS Organizations — Uses consolidated billing, doesn't separate costs per account ⚠️ D) Cross-account access — Bucket owner still pays unless Requester Pays enabled 📖 Full Explanation With Requester Pays buckets, the requester pays for requests and data downloads while the bucket owner pays for storage. This requires authentication and x-amz-request-payer header/parameter. Option A creates unnecessary duplication and sync costs. Option C misunderstands AWS Organizations billing (consolidated, not separate). Option D alone doesn't shift transfer costs to the requester.

Financial company deploying Node.js app with RDS MariaDB globally. App runs on on-premises servers AND EC2 instances . Database credentials must be encrypted at rest and in transit . Need secure automated deployment . How should the Architect automate the deployment process in the MOST secure manner? A. SSM Parameter Store + SSM agent + IAM role for all servers + Elastic Beanstalk deployment B. SSM Parameter Store + SSM agent + IAM role for EC2 + IAM Service Role for on-premises + CodeDeploy C. Secrets Manager + SSM agent + IAM role for all servers + Elastic Beanstalk deployment D. SSM Parameter Store + SSM agent + IAM policy attachment + CodeDeploy ✅ B) SSM Parameter Store + IAM role for EC2 + IAM Service Role for on-premises + CodeDeploy 🎯 On-premises servers need IAM Service Roles (not regular roles) to communicate with AWS services. CodeDeploy supports hybrid deployments. ⚠️ A) Elastic Beanstalk cannot deploy to on-premises servers ⚠️ C) Secrets Manager works but Elastic Beanstalk cannot deploy to on-premises ⚠️ D) Must use IAM Roles, not policies, for Parameter Store access 📖 Full Explanation AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store provides secure, hierarchical storage for configuration data management and secrets management. You can store data such as passwords, database strings, and license codes as parameter values. You can store values as plain text or encrypted data. Servers and VMs in a hybrid environment require an IAM role to communicate with the Systems Manager service. The role grants AssumeRole trust to the Systems Manager service. You only need to create the service role for a hybrid environment once for each AWS account. Service role: A service role is an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) that grants permissions to an AWS service so that the service can access AWS resources. If you plan to use Systems Manager to manage on-premises servers and virtual machines (VMs) in what is called a hybrid environment, you must create an IAM role for those resources to communicate with the Systems Manager service.

A serverless forex trading application (AWS SAM) serves millions of global users 24/7. Users complain of slow login times (few minutes) and occasional HTTP 504 errors. Need to optimize performance with minimal cost . Which TWO solutions improve performance with minimal cost? A. Use Lambda@Edge to execute authentication in locations closer to users B. Deploy to multiple regions with Route 53 latency routing C. Increase CloudFront cache hit ratio with Cache-Control max-age D. Set up origin failover with origin groups E. Deploy Lambda functions in multiple regions using transit VPC ✅ A & D: Lambda@Edge + Origin failover 🎯 Lambda@Edge executes authentication closer to users globally, while origin failover prevents 504 errors when primary origin fails. ⚠️ B — Multi-region deployment has significant implementation cost ⚠️ C — Cache optimization doesn't address authentication latency ⚠️ E — Transit VPC adds complexity and cost unnecessarily 📖 Full Explanation Lambda@Edge lets you run Lambda functions to customize the content that CloudFront delivers, executing the functions in AWS locations closer to the viewer. The functions run in response to CloudFront events, without provisioning or managing servers. You can use Lambda functions to change CloudFront requests and responses at the following points: After CloudFront receives a request from a viewer (viewer request), Before CloudFront forwards the request to the origin (origin request), After CloudFront receives the response from the origin (origin response), Before CloudFront forwards the response to the viewer (viewer response). In the given scenario, you can use Lambda@Edge to allow your Lambda functions to customize the content that CloudFront delivers and to execute the authentication process in AWS locations closer to the users. In addition, you can set up an origin failover by creating an origin group with two origins with one as the primary origin and the other as the second origin which CloudFront automatically switches to when the primary origin fails. This will alleviate the occasional HTTP 504 errors that users are experiencing. The option that says: Deploy your application to multiple AWS regions to accommodate your users around the world. Set up a Route 53 record with latency routing policy to route incoming traffic to the region that provides the best latency to the user is incorrect. Although this may resolve the performance issue, this solution entails a significant implementation cost since you have to deploy your application to multiple AWS regions. Remember that the scenario asks for a solution that will improve the performance of the application with minimal cost. The option that says: Increase the cache hit ratio of your CloudFront distribution by configuring your origin to add a Cache-Control max-age directive to your objects, and specify the longest practical value for max-age is incorrect because improving the cache hit ratio for the CloudFront distribution is irrelevant in this scenario. You can improve your cache performance by increasing the proportion of your viewer requests that are served from CloudFront edge caches instead of going to your origin servers for content. However, take note that the problem in the scenario is the sluggish authentication process of your global users and not just the caching of the static objects.

A BPO startup needs a scalable call center system on AWS that can handle thousands of inbound calls with self-service capabilities (password changes, balance checks) without agents. Requirements: automatic speech recognition (ASR) , natural language understanding , and integration with business applications . Which solution should the Solutions Architect implement? A. AWS Ground Station + Amazon Alexa for Business + Lambda B. Amazon Connect + Amazon Comprehend + Lambda C. Amazon Connect + Amazon Lex + Lambda D. AWS Elemental MediaConnect + Amazon Polly + Lambda ✅ C. Amazon Connect + Amazon Lex + Lambda 🎯 Amazon Connect provides cloud contact center functionality, while Amazon Lex offers both ASR and NLU for conversational chatbots that can handle self-service tasks. ⚠️ A. Ground Station is for satellite communications, not contact centers ⚠️ B. Comprehend analyzes text but lacks ASR/NLU for voice interactions ⚠️ D. MediaConnect is for live video transport, Polly only does text-to-speech 📖 Full Explanation Amazon Connect provides a seamless omnichannel experience through a single unified contact center for voice and chat. Amazon Lex is a service for building conversational interfaces into any application using voice and text. Amazon Lex provides the advanced deep learning functionalities of automatic speech recognition (ASR) for converting speech to text and natural language understanding (NLU) to recognize the intent of the text, enabling you to build applications with highly engaging user experiences and lifelike conversational interactions. By using an Amazon Lex chatbot in your Amazon Connect call center, callers can perform tasks such as changing a password, requesting a balance on an account, or scheduling an appointment without needing to speak to an agent. Amazon Lex uses AWS Lambda functions to query your business applications, provide information back to callers, and make updates as requested.

Fashion startup building mobile app expecting millions of users after celebrity promotion. App needs: automatic scaling , user photo storage with 100-character captions, static content distribution. Which solution fulfills these requirements? A. Cognito + DynamoDB + S3 + CloudFront B. SAML Federation + RDS + S3 + AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity + S3 distribution C. Cognito + RDS + S3 + CloudFront D. On-premises AD + LDAP + DynamoDB + S3 + CloudFront ✅ A. Cognito + DynamoDB + S3 + CloudFront 🎯 DynamoDB scales to millions of users better than RDS for simple data. CloudFront provides global CDN for static content distribution. ⚠️ B — SAML doesn't support social logins; should use CloudFront not S3 for distribution ⚠️ C — RDS less scalable than DynamoDB for simple caption data ⚠️ D — On-premises AD unsuitable for public mobile app; use Web Identity Federation instead 📖 Full Explanation Amazon Cognito scales to millions of users and supports sign-in with social identity providers, such as Facebook, Google, and Amazon, and enterprise identity providers via SAML 2.0. Amazon S3 provides a scalable object storage solution. Amazon CloudFront is a Content Delivery Network that helps your system to handle the millions of user views and finally, DynamoDB is a scalable database that can handle millions of records. In this scenario, the top priority is scalability to meet the upcoming surge of users of your mobile app. Since all of these services can provide the scalability that your mobile app needs, the best option that you can choose is the following: 1. Use Cognito to handle user authentication and management. 2. Launch a DynamoDB table to store user data. 3. Create an S3 bucket to store all of the user photos and other static files. 4. Distribute the static contents using CloudFront to improve scalability. The following option is incorrect because a SAML 2.0-based federation doesn't use social media logins and it is better to use CloudFront to distribute static contents compared to an S3 bucket: 1. Set up a SAML 2.0-based Federation that lets the users sign into the app using a third party identity provider such as Amazon, Google or Facebook. 2. Set up an RDS database and an S3 bucket to store the photos. 3.
