Use the AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity API call to assume the IAM role containing the proper permissions to communicate with the RDS database. 4. Distribute the static contents using S3 to improve scalability. The following option is incorrect because using an on-premise Active Directory server is not a suitable solution for this scenario: 1. Configure an on-premises Active Directory (AD) server utilizing SAML 2.0 to manage the application users inside of the on-premises AD server. 2. Develop a custom code that authenticates against the LDAP server. 3. Use DynamoDB as the main database of the app and S3 as the scalable object storage. 4. Grant an IAM role assigned to the STS token to allow the end-user to access the required data in the DynamoDB table. 5. Distribute the static contents using CloudFront to improve scalability. Remember that this is a public mobile app and hence, it is better to set up a Web Identity Federation instead The following option is incorrect because RDS is not as scalable as DynamoDB: 1. Use Cognito to handle user authentication and management. 2. Use an RDS database to store user data. 3. Create an S3 bucket to store all of the user photos and other static files. 4. Distribute the static contents using CloudFront to improve scalability. Based on the type of data you will be storing, a relational database like RDS is not suitable to store simple data sets such as a 100-character caption which does not need multiple tables or relational data models.

Company building CRM portal on AWS using containerized microservices on ECS . Must comply with least privilege security and support security groups and network monitoring at container level . Which provides the MOST secure configuration? A. Use bridge network mode, attach security groups to EC2 instances, use IAM roles for EC2 B. Use awsvpc network mode, attach security groups to ECS tasks, use IAM roles for tasks C. Use App Runner with VPC/security groups, add IAM credentials to environment variables D. Use awsvpc network mode, attach security groups to ECS tasks, pass IAM credentials to container ✅ B. awsvpc network mode + security groups on tasks + IAM roles for tasks 🎯 Only awsvpc mode allows security groups at task level (each task gets its own ENI). IAM roles for tasks follow least privilege vs hardcoded credentials. ⚠️ A. Bridge mode — cannot attach security groups to individual tasks, only EC2 instances ⚠️ C. App Runner — hardcoding IAM credentials in environment variables is a security risk ⚠️ D. Passing credentials — violates least privilege, credentials could be exposed in container 📖 Full Explanation Task definitions are split into separate parts: the task family, the IAM task role, the network mode, container definitions, volumes, task placement constraints, and launch types. The family and container definitions are required in a task definition, while task role, network mode, volumes, task placement constraints, and launch type are optional. You can configure various Docker networking modes that will be used by containers in your ECS task. The valid values are none, bridge, awsvpc, and host. The default Docker network mode is bridge. With IAM roles for Amazon ECS tasks, you can specify an IAM role that can be used by the containers in a task. Applications must sign their AWS API requests with AWS credentials, and this feature provides a strategy for managing credentials for your applications to use, similar to the way that Amazon EC2 instance profiles provide credentials to EC2 instances. Instead of creating and distributing your AWS credentials to the containers or using the EC2 instance's role, you can associate an IAM role with an ECS task definition or RunTask API operation. The applications in the task's containers can then use the AWS SDK or CLI to make API requests to authorized AWS services. If the network mode is set to none, the task's containers do not have external connectivity, and port mappings can't be specified in the container definition. If the network mode is bridge, the task utilizes Docker's built-in virtual network which runs inside each container instance. If the network mode is host, the task bypasses Docker's built-in virtual network and maps container ports directly to the EC2 instance's network interface directly. In this mode, you can't run multiple instantiations of the same task on a single container instance when port mappings are used. If the network mode is awsvpc, the task is allocated an elastic network interface, and you must specify a NetworkConfiguration when you create a service or run a task with the task definition. When you use this network mode in your task definitions, every task that is launched from that task definition gets its own elastic network interface (ENI) and a primary private IP address. The task networking feature simplifies container networking and gives you more control over how containerized applications communicate with each other and other services within your VPCs. Task networking also provides greater security for your containers by allowing you to use security groups and network monitoring tools at a more granular level within your tasks. Because each task gets its own ENI, you can also take advantage of other Amazon EC2 networking features like VPC Flow Logs so that you can monitor traffic to and from your tasks. Additionally, containers that belong to the same task can communicate over the localhost interface. A task can only have one ENI associated with it at a given time.

A data analytics startup will develop a FIFA World Cup statistics system for global access. The system must track game statistics, allow voting for best players/coaches, and handle 10-30 million queries on game days . Requirements: durable storage , high availability , high scalability , and cost-effective . Which is the most cost-effective solution meeting these requirements? A. Multi-AZ RDS + ElastiCache reports + default expire parameters B. Multi-AZ RDS + DynamoDB storage + daily table deletion C. Multi-AZ RDS with Read Replicas + query replicas + daily cleanup D. Multi-AZ RDS with Read Replicas + S3 batch reports + CloudFront CDN with daily TTL ✅ D. Multi-AZ RDS with Read Replicas + S3 batch reports + CloudFront CDN with daily TTL 🎯 Combines scalable database (RDS Multi-AZ + Read Replicas), durable storage (S3), and global distribution (CloudFront) for cost-effective handling of millions of global queries. ⚠️ A. ElastiCache — lacks durable storage and CDN for global distribution ⚠️ B. RDS + DynamoDB — maintaining both databases is not cost-effective ⚠️ C. Read Replicas only — missing durable storage and CDN components 📖 Full Explanation In this scenario, you are required to have the following: A durable storage for the generated reports. A database that is highly available and can scale to handle millions of queries. A Content Delivery Network that can distribute the report files to users all over the world. Amazon S3 is object storage built to store and retrieve any amount of data from anywhere. It's a simple storage service that offers industry leading durability, availability, performance, security, and virtually unlimited scalability at very low costs. Amazon RDS provides high availability and failover support for DB instances using Multi-AZ deployments. In a Multi-AZ deployment, Amazon RDS automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone. The primary DB instance is synchronously replicated across Availability Zones to a standby replica to provide data redundancy, eliminate I/O freezes, and minimize latency spikes during system backups. Amazon RDS uses the MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle, and PostgreSQL DB engines' built-in replication functionality to create a special type of DB instance called a read replica from a source DB instance. The source DB instance becomes the primary DB instance. Updates made to the primary DB instance are asynchronously copied to the read replica. Amazon CloudFront is a web service that speeds up distribution of your static and dynamic web content, such as .html, .css, .js, and image files, to your users. CloudFront delivers your content through a worldwide network of data centers called edge locations. When a user requests content that you're serving with CloudFront, the request is routed to the edge location that provides the lowest latency (time delay), so that content is delivered with the best possible performance. Hence, the following option is the best solution that satisfies all of these requirements: 1. Generate the FIFA reports from MySQL database in Multi-AZ RDS deployments configuration with Read Replicas. 2. Set up a batch job that puts reports in an S3 bucket. 3. Launch a CloudFront distribution to cache the content with a TTL set to expire objects daily. In the above, S3 provides durable storage; Multi-AZ RDS with Read Replicas provide a scalable and highly available database and CloudFront provides the CDN.

A logistics company needs a multi-tier web application (EC2, S3, NoSQL database) in us-east-1 with disaster recovery in us-west-1 . Requirements: same data copy in both regions, quick failover when primary unavailable, automatic failback when primary returns. Which solution meets these requirements? A. AWS Service Catalog for EC2, S3 CRR, Route 53 health checks with manual DNS updates, RDS MySQL cross-region read replica B. CloudFormation StackSets for EC2, S3 CRR, Route 53 failover routing, DynamoDB global tables C. CloudFormation StackSets for EC2, S3 CRR, Route 53 failover routing, Aurora global database D. CloudFormation StackSets for EC2, S3 CRR, CloudFront distribution, DynamoDB tables with S3 backups ✅ B. CloudFormation StackSets + DynamoDB global tables 🎯 DynamoDB global tables provide automatic multi-region replication for NoSQL requirements with seamless failover. CloudFormation StackSets enable consistent multi-region deployments. ⚠️ A — Manual DNS updates don't provide automatic failback, RDS MySQL isn't NoSQL ⚠️ C — Aurora is relational database, not NoSQL as required ⚠️ D — S3 backups create data lag and don't provide real-time sync like global tables 📖 Full Explanation AWS CloudFormation StackSets enable deploying identical infrastructure across multiple regions consistently. S3 Cross-Region Replication handles static content synchronization. Route 53 failover routing provides automatic DNS failover and failback capabilities. DynamoDB global tables offer fully managed, multi-region, multi-active database replication that's perfect for NoSQL requirements with automatic conflict resolution and fast local read/write performance. Option A requires manual intervention and uses wrong database type. Option C uses Aurora (relational) instead of NoSQL. Option D relies on unreliable S3 backup/restore process instead of real-time replication.

A company's CloudFormation stack for a voting application stores high-quality images in S3 and contestant data in RDS . After competition ends, the stack will be terminated but data must be preserved for future use. Which DeletionPolicy configuration BEST preserves both resources? A. Set DeletionPolicy to retain on both RDS and S3 B. Set DeletionPolicy on S3 bucket to snapshot C. Set DeletionPolicy on RDS to snapshot and S3 bucket to retain D. Set RDS to snapshot and enable S3 replication to destination bucket ✅ C. RDS snapshot + S3 retain 🎯 RDS supports snapshot DeletionPolicy for backup, while S3 uses retain to preserve bucket and contents. ⚠️ A. RDS retain keeps instance running (costly) vs snapshot backup ⚠️ B. S3 doesn't support snapshot DeletionPolicy ⚠️ D. Unnecessary complexity - retain is simpler than replication 📖 Full Explanation CloudFormation DeletionPolicy has three options: Delete (default), Retain, and Snapshot. For RDS, snapshot creates a backup before deletion, which is ideal for preserving database data. For S3, retain preserves the bucket and all contents without deletion. The snapshot option doesn't exist for S3 buckets. Retain for RDS would keep the instance running (incurring costs), while replication adds unnecessary complexity when simple retention suffices.

A company runs hundreds of Windows EC2 instances. The Solutions Architect must develop a workflow to automatically identify and apply required patches. Critical requirement: EC2 instances must NOT reboot simultaneously to avoid revenue loss from system unavailability. Which solution meets these requirements? A. Create two Patch Groups with unique tags that you will assign to all of your EC2 Windows Instances. Associate the predefined AWS-DefaultPatchBaseline baseline on both patch groups. Set up two non-overlapping maintenance windows and associate each with a different patch group. Using Patch Group tags, register targets with specific maintenance windows and lastly, assign the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document as a task within each maintenance window which has a different processing start time. B. Create a Patch Group with unique tags that you will assign to all of your EC2 Windows Instances. Associate the predefined AWS-DefaultPatchBaseline baseline on your patch group. Set up a maintenance window and associate it with your patch group. Assign the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document as a task within your maintenance window. C. Create two Patch Groups with unique tags that you will assign to all of your EC2 Windows Instances. Associate the predefined AWS-DefaultPatchBaseline baseline on both patch groups. Create two CloudWatch Events rules which are configured to use a cron expression to automate the execution of patching for the two Patch Groups using the AWS Systems Manager Run command. Set up an AWS Systems Manager State Manager document to define custom commands which will be executed during patch execution. D. Create a Patch Group with unique tags that you will assign to all of your EC2 Windows Instances. Associate the predefined AWS-DefaultPatchBaseline baseline on both patch groups. Create a CloudWatch Events rule configured to use a cron expression to automate the execution of patching in a given schedule using the AWS Systems Manager Run command. Set up an AWS Systems Manager State Manager document to define custom commands which will be executed during patch execution. ✅ A. Two Patch Groups with non-overlapping maintenance windows 🎯 Two patch groups with separate maintenance windows prevent simultaneous reboots, maintaining system availability during patching operations. ⚠️ B — Single patch group causes all instances to reboot simultaneously ⚠️ C — CloudWatch Events + Run Command inappropriate for scheduled patching operations ⚠️ D — Single patch group + wrong services for patch scheduling 📖 Full Explanation AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager automates the process of patching managed instances with both security-related and other types of updates. You can use Patch Manager to apply patches for both operating systems and applications. You can patch fleets of Amazon EC2 instances or your on-premises servers and virtual machines (VMs) by operating system type. This includes supported versions of Windows Server, Ubuntu Server, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES), CentOS, Amazon Linux, and Amazon Linux 2. You can scan instances to see only a report of missing patches, or you can scan and automatically install all missing patches. Patch Manager uses patch baselines, which include rules for auto-approving patches within days of their release, as well as a list of approved and rejected patches. You can install patches on a regular basis by scheduling patching to run as a Systems Manager maintenance window task. You can also install patches individually or to large groups of instances by using Amazon EC2 tags. You can add tags to your patch baselines themselves when you create or update them. You can use a patch group to associate instances with a specific patch baseline. Patch groups help ensure that you are deploying the appropriate patches, based on the associated patch baseline rules, to the correct set of instances. Patch groups can also help you avoid deploying patches before they have been adequately tested. For example, you can create patch groups for different environments (such as Development, Test, and Production) and register each patch group to an appropriate patch baseline. When you run AWS-RunPatchBaseline, you can target managed instances using their instance ID or tags. SSM Agent and Patch Manager will then evaluate which patch baseline to use based on the patch group value that you added to the instance. You create a patch group by using Amazon EC2 tags. Unlike other tagging scenarios across Systems Manager, a patch group must be defined with the tag key: Patch Group. Note that the key is case-sensitive. You can specify any value, for example, "web servers," but the key must be Patch Group. The AWS-DefaultPatchBaseline baseline is primarily used to approve all Windows Server operating system patches that are classified as "CriticalUpdates" or "SecurityUpdates" and that have an MSRC severity of "Critical" or "Important". Patches are auto-approved seven days after release.

Department of Education builds a learning portal on AWS with hybrid on-premises infrastructure. Need to aggregate logs from on-premises servers, automate log analysis for errors, and immediately notify IT Operations when error thresholds are breached . Which solution should the Architect implement? A. Install Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, send logs to Lambda for processing, write metrics to Prometheus, create CloudWatch Alarm for notifications B. Install Kinesis agent, send logs to CloudWatch Logs, create metric filter, use QuickSight to monitor and notify IT Operations C. Install CloudWatch agent, send logs to EventBridge, create metric filter, use Athena to monitor and notify IT Operations D. Install CloudWatch agent, send logs to CloudWatch Logs, create metric filter, create CloudWatch Alarm to monitor and notify IT Operations ✅ D. CloudWatch agent → CloudWatch Logs → metric filter → CloudWatch Alarm 🎯 CloudWatch agent collects on-premises logs, metric filters convert log patterns to metrics, CloudWatch Alarms provide immediate threshold-based notifications. ⚠️ A. Prometheus — designed for container metrics, not log aggregation from on-premises ⚠️ B. Kinesis agent — wrong agent type; QuickSight is for BI dashboards, not real-time alerting ⚠️ C. EventBridge — not the destination for logs; Athena is for querying, not alerting 📖 Full Explanation Amazon CloudWatch monitors AWS resources and applications in real time. The CloudWatch agent collects log data from on-premises servers and sends it to CloudWatch Logs. Metric filters define patterns to look for in log data and convert them into numerical CloudWatch metrics. CloudWatch Alarms can monitor these metrics and send notifications when thresholds are breached, providing immediate notification to IT Operations teams. This creates a complete log aggregation, analysis, and alerting solution.

A company has production, development, and test environments with hundreds of EC2 instances. Ubuntu released critical security patches that must be applied to all environments except production (production will be patched after verification). Each environment has different baseline patch requirements . Using AWS Systems Manager, how should you perform this task with the least amount of effort ? A. Tag each instance based on its OS. Create a patch baseline in AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager for each environment. Categorize EC2 instances based on their tags using Patch Groups and then apply the patches specified in the corresponding patch baseline to each Patch Group. Afterward, verify that the patches have been installed correctly using Patch Compliance. Record the changes to patch and association compliance statuses using AWS Config. B. Tag each instance based on its environment and OS. Create various shell scripts for each environment that specifies which patch will serve as its baseline. Using AWS Systems Manager Run Command, place the EC2 instances into Target Groups and execute the script corresponding to each Target Group. C. Tag each instance based on its environment and OS. Create a patch baseline in AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager for each environment. Categorize EC2 instances based on their tags using Patch Groups and apply the patches specified in the corresponding patch baseline to each Patch Group. D. Schedule a maintenance period in AWS Systems Manager Maintenance Windows for each environment, where the period is after business hours so as not to affect daily operations. During the maintenance period, Systems Manager will execute a cron job that will install the required patches for each EC2 instance in each environment. After that, verify in Systems Manager Managed Instances that your environments are fully patched and compliant. ✅ C. Tag instances by environment+OS, create patch baselines per environment, use Patch Groups 🎯 Patch Manager with environment-based tagging allows different patch baselines per environment while excluding production. This is the most direct approach with minimal configuration. ⚠️ A — Tags only by OS would patch ALL environments including production ⚠️ B — Custom scripts with Run Command requires more effort than native Patch Manager ⚠️ D — Maintenance Windows adds unnecessary complexity for this straightforward patching task 📖 Full Explanation AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager automates the process of patching managed instances with security-related updates. For Linux-based instances, you can also install patches for non-security updates. You can patch fleets of Amazon EC2 instances or your on-premises servers and virtual machines (VMs) by operating system type. Patch Manager uses patch baselines, which include rules for auto-approving patches within days of their release, as well as a list of approved and rejected patches. You can install patches on a regular basis by scheduling patching to run as a Systems Manager Maintenance Window task. You can also install patches individually or to large groups of instances by using Amazon EC2 tags. For each auto-approval rule that you create, you can specify an auto-approval delay. This delay is the number of days of wait after the patch was released, before the patch is automatically approved for patching. A patch group is an optional means of organizing instances for patching. For example, you can create patch groups for different operating systems (Linux or Windows), different environments (Development, Test, and Production), or different server functions (web servers, file servers, databases). Patch groups can help you avoid deploying patches to the wrong set of instances. They can also help you avoid deploying patches before they have been adequately tested. You create a patch group by using Amazon EC2 tags. Unlike other tagging scenarios across Systems Manager, a patch group must be defined with the tag key: Patch Group. After you create a patch group and tag instances, you can register the patch group with a patch baseline. By registering the patch group with a patch baseline, you ensure that the correct patches are installed during the patching execution. Hence, the correct answer is: Tag each instance based on its environment and OS. Create a patch baseline in AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager for each environment. Categorize EC2 instances based on their tags using Patch Groups and apply the patches specified in the corresponding patch baseline to each Patch Group. The option that says: Tag each instance based on its environment and OS. Create various shell scripts for each environment that specifies which patch will serve as its baseline. Using AWS Systems Manager Run Command, place the EC2 instances into Target Groups and execute the script corresponding to each Target Group is incorrect as this option takes more effort to perform because you are using Systems Manager Run Command instead of Patch Manager. The Run Command service enables you to automate common administrative tasks and perform ad hoc configuration changes at scale, however, it takes a lot of effort to implement this solution. You can use Patch Manager instead to perform the task required by the scenario since you need to perform this task with the least amount of effort. The option that says: Tag each instance based on its OS. Create a patch baseline in AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager for each environment. Categorize EC2 instances based on their tags using Patch Groups and then apply the patches specified in the corresponding patch baseline to each Patch Group. Afterward, verify that the patches have been installed correctly using Patch Compliance. Record the changes to patch and association compliance statuses using AWS Config is incorrect. You should be tagging instances based on the environment and its OS type in which they belong and not just its OS type. This is because the type of patches that will be applied varies between the different environments. With this option, the Ubuntu EC2 instances in all of your environments, including in production, will automatically be patched. The option that says: Schedule a maintenance period in AWS Systems Manager Maintenance Windows for each environment, where the period is after business hours so as not to affect daily operations. During the maintenance period, Systems Manager will execute a cron job that will install the required patches for each EC2 instance in each environment. After that, verify in Systems Manager Managed Instances that your environments are fully patched and compliant is incorrect because this is not the simplest way to address the issue using AWS Systems Manager. The AWS Systems Manager Maintenance Windows feature lets you define a schedule for when to perform potentially disruptive actions on your instances such as patching an operating system, updating drivers, or installing software or patches. Each Maintenance Window has a schedule, a maximum duration, a set of registered targets (the instances that are acted upon), and a set of registered tasks. Although this solution may work, it entails a lot of configuration and effort to implement.

A startup develops IoT pet collars that collect biometric data every second and send it via POST API to a web portal. The portal must provide real-time analytics , trends, and health reports to global pet owners with high durability, availability, and scalability . Which architecture best meets these requirements? A. Use Kinesis Data Streams → Kinesis analytics → S3 → Redshift with backups B. SQS queue → Kinesis analytics → RDS MySQL C. S3 bucket → Data Pipeline daily analysis → Redshift OLAP D. EMR instance → Kinesis analytics → DynamoDB ✅ A. Kinesis Data Streams → analytics → S3 → Redshift 🎯 Kinesis Data Streams handles high-frequency streaming data and enables real-time analytics, perfect for second-by-second biometric collection. ⚠️ B. SQS — Not designed for high-frequency streaming data analytics ⚠️ C. Data Pipeline — Daily batch processing, not real-time ⚠️ D. EMR — Not appropriate for data collection, only processing 📖 Full Explanation Amazon Kinesis Data Streams enable you to build custom applications that process or analyze streaming data for specialized needs. Kinesis Data Streams can continuously capture and store terabytes of data per hour from hundreds of thousands of sources. With the Kinesis Client Library (KCL), you can build applications for real-time dashboards, generate alerts, and emit data to other AWS services like S3, Redshift, EMR, and Lambda. The correct architecture uses Kinesis for streaming collection, real-time analytics, S3 for storage, and Redshift for complex analytics with automated backups. Option B is wrong because SQS queues aren't appropriate for high-frequency streaming data. Option C is wrong because Data Pipeline runs daily batch jobs, not real-time processing. Option D is wrong because EMR instances aren't designed for data collection, only processing.

An IT consulting company uses AWS Organizations with multiple accounts grouped into OUs. Security team discovered an unauthorized third-party AWS account was added to the organization with high-level access privileges. No detrimental actions occurred yet. Which actions should the solutions architect take to set up monitoring for changes to AWS accounts ? (Select TWO.) A. Create a trail in Amazon CloudTrail to capture all API calls to your AWS Organizations, including calls from the AWS Organizations console and from code calls to the AWS Organizations APIs. Use Amazon EventBridge and SNS to raise events when administrator-specified actions occur in an organization and send a notification to you. B. Monitor all changes to your organization using Systems Manager and use Amazon EventBridge to notify you of any new activity to your account. C. Use AWS Config to monitor the compliance of your AWS Organizations. Set up an SNS Topic or Amazon EventBridge that will send alerts to you for any changes. D. Configure AWS Control Tower to manage and monitor all child accounts under the organization. Use Amazon Inspector to analyze any possible breach and notify the administrators using AWS SNS. E. Set up a CloudWatch Dashboard to monitor any changes to your organizations and create an SNS topic that would send you a notification. ✅ A & C: CloudTrail + EventBridge/SNS for API calls, AWS Config for compliance monitoring 🎯 CloudTrail captures Organizations API calls, Config aggregates compliance data across accounts - both can trigger EventBridge/SNS for real-time alerts. ⚠️ B: Systems Manager manages EC2/servers, not Organizations structure ⚠️ D: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, not account changes ⚠️ E: CloudWatch Dashboard visualizes metrics, doesn't monitor Organizations configuration 📖 Full Explanation AWS Organizations can work with CloudWatch Events to raise events when administrator-specified actions occur in an organization. For example, because of the sensitivity of such actions, most administrators would want to be warned every time someone creates a new account in the organization or when an administrator of a member account attempts to leave the organization. You can configure CloudWatch Events rules that look for these actions and then send the generated events to administrator-defined targets. Targets can be an Amazon SNS topic that emails or text messages its subscribers. Combining this with Amazon CloudTrail, you can set an event to trigger whenever a matching API call is received. Multi-account, multi-region data aggregation in AWS Config enables you to aggregate AWS Config data from multiple accounts and regions into a single account. Multi-account, multi-region data aggregation is useful for central IT administrators to monitor compliance for multiple AWS accounts in the enterprise. An aggregator is a new resource type in AWS Config that collects AWS Config data from multiple source accounts and regions.

A stocks brokerage firm hosts its legacy application on Amazon EC2 in a private subnet. Employees access it from corporate laptops through a proprietary desktop program via AWS Direct Connect. Security requirement: encrypt network traffic from employee laptops to VPC resources while maintaining Direct Connect performance . Which solution complies with this requirement? A. Create private virtual interface + site-to-site VPN over Internet B. Create public virtual interface + site-to-site VPN over Internet C. Create private virtual interface + site-to-site VPN over DX connection D. Create public virtual interface + site-to-site VPN over DX connection ✅ D. Create public virtual interface + site-to-site VPN over DX connection 🎯 VPN over Direct Connect requires public virtual interface to access AWS VPN endpoints. This maintains DX performance while adding encryption. ⚠️ A — Private VIF can't establish VPN connections to AWS VPN endpoints ⚠️ B — VPN over Internet bypasses Direct Connect, losing performance benefit ⚠️ C — Private VIF can't reach AWS VPN endpoints for encrypted tunnel 📖 Full Explanation To establish VPN over Direct Connect, you need a public virtual interface because AWS VPN endpoints are accessible via public IP addresses. Private virtual interfaces connect directly to VPC resources using private IPs but cannot establish VPN tunnels. Options A and B use Internet routing instead of Direct Connect, losing the performance benefit. Only option D correctly uses public VIF to establish encrypted VPN tunnel while maintaining Direct Connect's reliable performance characteristics.

A multinational financial firm needs multi-regional deployment of its cryptocurrency trading application in US and Europe. The containerized Kubernetes app uses DynamoDB Global Tables and has multiple public-facing ALBs. The Network team wants to make the application available through an apex domain for easier access. Which is the MOST operationally efficient solution to meet these requirements? A. Launch AWS Transit Gateway targeting ALBs. Create CNAME record in Route 53 pointing to Transit Gateway DNS name. B. Set up AWS Transit Gateway with multicast domain targeting ALBs. Create public record in Route 53 using Transit Gateway static IP. C. Set up AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups targeting ALBs in required regions. Create public alias record in Route 53 pointing to accelerator DNS name. D. Launch AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups targeting ALBs. Create Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoint pointing to accelerator CNAME. ✅ C. Global Accelerator + Route 53 alias record 🎯 Global Accelerator optimally routes traffic to healthy ALBs across regions. Route 53 alias records support apex domains (unlike CNAME). ⚠️ A. CNAME records cannot be used with apex domains in Route 53 ⚠️ B. Transit Gateway doesn't distribute traffic to ALBs; multicast is for VPC subnets ⚠️ D. Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoint is for on-premises DNS queries to VPC 📖 Full Explanation AWS Global Accelerator is a service in which you create accelerators to improve the performance of your applications for local and global users. With a standard accelerator, Global Accelerator directs traffic over the AWS global network to endpoints in the nearest Region to the client. For standard accelerators, Global Accelerator uses the AWS global network to route traffic to the optimal regional endpoint based on health, client location, and policies that you configure. Endpoints can be Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers, Amazon EC2 instances, or Elastic IP addresses in one or multiple Regions. To use your custom domain name with Global Accelerator when you use Route 53, you create an alias record that points your custom domain name to the DNS name assigned to your accelerator. An alias record can be created both for the root domain (apex) and subdomains, unlike CNAME records which cannot be used for apex domains.

A media company needs to provide another AWS account access to multiple resources (S3, KMS, OpenSearch) for copying data. Requirements: users retain their original permissions (no role switching), continuous policy monitoring , and access specified by AWS account ID list . Which policy type is MOST suitable? A. Cross-account access with user-based policy + AWS Config rules B. Service-linked role with identity-based policy + Systems Manager rules C. Cross-account access with resource-based policy + AWS Config rules D. Service-linked role with service control policy + Systems Manager rules ✅ C. Cross-account access with resource-based policy + AWS Config rules 🎯 Resource-based policies allow cross-account access while preserving original user permissions (no role switching required). AWS Config provides continuous policy monitoring. ⚠️ A — User-based policies don't provide cross-account resource access ⚠️ B — Service-linked roles are AWS service-specific, not for cross-account access ⚠️ D — Service control policies are for AWS Organizations, not cross-account resource sharing 📖 Full Explanation For some AWS services, you can grant cross-account access to your resources. To do this, you attach a policy directly to the resource that you want to share, instead of using a role as a proxy. The resource that you want to share must support resource-based policies. Unlike a user-based policy, a resource-based policy specifies who (in the form of a list of AWS account ID numbers) can access that resource. Cross-account access with a resource-based policy has some advantages over a role. With a resource that is accessed through a resource-based policy, the user still works in the trusted account and does not have to give up his or her user permissions in place of the role permissions. In other words, the user continues to have access to resources in the trusted account at the same time as he or she has access to the resource in the trusting account. This is useful for tasks such as copying information to or from the shared resource in the other account. AWS Config is a service that enables you to assess, audit, and evaluate the configurations of your AWS resources. Config continuously monitors and records your AWS resource configurations and allows you to automate the evaluation of recorded configurations against desired configurations.

Company launches bug bounty program to find security vulnerabilities. Solutions architect needs to check system vulnerabilities for DDoS attacks. Budget constraints prevent enabling AWS Shield Advanced. Which are the best techniques to help mitigate DDoS attacks for AWS cloud infrastructure? (Select TWO.) A. Use CloudFront distribution for static and dynamic content. Add CloudWatch alerts for high CPUUtilization and NetworkIn metrics to trigger Auto Scaling. B. Add multiple ENIs to each EC2 instance and use Enhanced Networking to increase network bandwidth. C. Use Reserved EC2 instances for maximum performance. Use AWS WAF to protect from web exploits. D. Use ALB to distribute traffic across backend instances. Integrate AWS WAF with ALB to protect from web exploits. E. Use S3 as POSIX storage instead of EBS. Install SSM agent and use Patch Manager. ✅ A & D - CloudFront distribution + ALB with traffic distribution 🎯 CloudFront blocks malformed connections (SYN floods, UDP reflection) at edge. ALB distributes load across instances to prevent overload. ⚠️ B - Multiple ENIs don't help when CPU saturated by DDoS requests ⚠️ C - Reserved instances provide no performance advantage over on-demand ⚠️ E - S3 isn't POSIX-compliant and doesn't address DDoS mitigation 📖 Full Explanation Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that can deliver entire websites including static, dynamic, streaming, and interactive content. It only accepts well-formed connections, preventing common DDoS attacks like SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks from reaching your origin. Larger DDoS attacks can exceed single EC2 instance capacity, so Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic across many backend instances and can auto-scale to manage larger volumes of traffic. CloudWatch alarms trigger Auto Scaling to maintain application availability during unexpected traffic surges. Option B is wrong because multiple ENIs don't help when CPU is saturated. Option C is wrong because Reserved instances don't provide additional performance. Option E is wrong because S3 isn't POSIX-compliant and doesn't address DDoS mitigation.

A media company has hybrid architecture with Direct Connect. 50TB+ digital videos on on-premises tape library used by Media Asset Management (MAM) system. Want automated catalog with facial recognition, minimal disruption, least management overhead . Eventually migrate to AWS. Which solution uses LEAST ongoing management overhead with MINIMAL disruption? A. Use Amazon Kinesis Video Streams to set up video ingestion stream with Amazon Rekognition, build face collection. Stream media files from MAM into Kinesis, configure Rekognition to process streamed files. Launch stream consumer for metadata, push to MAM, store files in S3. B. Set up tape gateway on-premises connected to AWS Storage Gateway. Configure MAM to fetch files from archive, push to tape gateway for Glacier storage. Use Rekognition with Lambda function to process video from tape gateway in real-time. C. Integrate local data center file system to AWS Storage Gateway via file gateway on-premises. MAM extracts files and sends to file gateway. Build Rekognition collection, use Lambda to process files from S3 bucket backing file gateway. D. Request AWS Snowball to migrate files to S3. Provision large EC2 instance, install open-source facial recognition tools like OpenFace/OpenCV. Process files for metadata, push to MAM, copy files to another S3 bucket. ✅ C File Gateway with Rekognition 🎯 File Gateway provides seamless integration with existing MAM system while enabling real-time processing with Rekognition. Tape Gateway can't process files in real-time from Glacier. ⚠️ A Kinesis Video Streams — Requires major MAM changes, designed for streaming not archived files ⚠️ B Tape Gateway — Can't process files real-time from Glacier archive ⚠️ D Snowball + EC2 — High management overhead with open-source tools vs managed Rekognition 📖 Full Explanation Amazon Rekognition can store information about detected faces in server-side containers known as collections. You can use the facial information that's stored in a collection to search for known faces in images, stored videos, and streaming videos. Amazon Rekognition supports the IndexFaces operation. You can use this operation to detect faces in an image and persist information about facial features that are detected in a collection. This is an example of a storage-based API operation because the service persists information on the server. To store facial information, you must first create (CreateCollection) a face collection in one of the AWS Regions in your account. You specify this face collection when you call the IndexFaces operation. After you create a face collection and store facial feature information for all faces, you can search the collection for face matches. To search for faces in an image, call SearchFacesByImage. To search for faces in a stored video, call StartFaceSearch. To search for faces in a streaming video, call CreateStreamProcessor. AWS Storage Gateway offers file-based, volume-based, and tape-based storage solutions. With a tape gateway, you can cost-effectively and durably archive backup data in GLACIER or DEEP_ARCHIVE. A tape gateway provides a virtual tape infrastructure that scales seamlessly with your business needs and eliminates the operational burden of provisioning, scaling, and maintaining a physical tape infrastructure. You can run AWS Storage Gateway either on-premises as a VM appliance, as a hardware appliance, or in AWS as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance. You deploy your gateway on an EC2 instance to provision iSCSI storage volumes in AWS. You can use gateways hosted on EC2 instances for disaster recovery, data mirroring, and providing storage for applications hosted on Amazon EC2. Hence, the correct answer is: Integrate the file system of your local data center to AWS Storage Gateway by setting up a file gateway appliance on-premises. Utilize the MAM solution to extract the media files from the current data store and send them into the file gateway. Build a collection using Amazon Rekognition by populating a catalog of faces from the processed media files. Use an AWS Lambda function to invoke Amazon Rekognition Javascript SDK to have it fetch the media file from the S3 bucket which is backing the file gateway, retrieve the needed metadata, and finally, persist the information into the MAM solution. The option that says: Request for an AWS Snowball Storage Optimized device to migrate all of the media files from the on-premises library into Amazon S3. Provision a large EC2 instance and allow it to access the S3 bucket. Install an open-source facial recognition tool on the instance like OpenFace or OpenCV. Process the media files to retrieve the metadata and push this information into the MAM solution. Lastly, copy the media files to another S3 bucket is incorrect. This entails a lot of ongoing management overhead instead of just using Amazon Rekognition. Moreover, it is more suitable to use the AWS Storage Gateway service rather than an EBS Volume. The option that says: Set up a tape gateway appliance on-premises and connect it to your AWS Storage Gateway. Configure the MAM solution to fetch the media files from the current archive and push them into the tape gateway to be stored in Amazon Glacier. Using Amazon Rekognition, build a collection from the catalog of faces. Utilize a Lambda function which invokes the Rekognition Javascript SDK to have Amazon Rekognition process the video directly from the tape gateway in real-time, retrieve the required metadata, and push the metadata into the MAM solution is incorrect. Although this solution uses the right combination of AWS Storage Gateway and Amazon Rekognition, take note that you can't directly fetch the media files from your tape gateway in real time since this is backed up using Glacier. Although the on-premises data center is using a tape gateway, you can still set up a solution to use a file gateway in order to properly process the videos using Amazon Rekognition. Keep in mind that the tape gateway in the AWS Storage Gateway service is primarily used as an archive solution. The option that says: Use Amazon Kinesis Video Streams to set up a video ingestion stream and with Amazon Rekognition, build a collection of faces. Stream the media files from the MAM solution into Kinesis Video Streams and configure the Amazon Rekognition to process the streamed files. Launch a stream consumer to retrieve the required metadata, and push the metadata into the MAM solution. Finally, configure the stream to store the files in an S3 bucket is incorrect. This approach requires significant changes to the existing MAM solution to stream media files directly into Kinesis Video Streams, potentially causing more disruption to the current workflow. Additionally, Kinesis Video Streams is designed for real-time video streaming and processing, which may not be the most efficient approach for processing pre-existing media files stored in a tape library. Lastly, setting up and managing Kinesis Video Streams, configuring Amazon Rekognition integration, implementing a stream consumer, and storing files in S3 introduces additional complexity and management overhead compared to the File Gateway approach.

A tech startup is launching a global mobile marketplace using AWS Amplify . Backend APIs will be deployed to multiple AWS regions to process sales and financial transactions in the region closest to users. Transactions made in one region must be automatically replicated to other regions. Expected to have millions of users across North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. Which is the most scalable, cost-effective, and highly available architecture? A. Create a Global DynamoDB table with replica tables across several AWS regions. Store transactions to a DynamoDB replica table in each local region. B. Use AWS Control Tower and Amazon Connect to launch and centrally manage multiple DynamoDB tables in various AWS Regions. C. Store transactions to a DynamoDB table in each local region. Set up AWS Lambda function to read recent writes and replay data to DynamoDB tables in all other regions. D. Create Amazon S3 buckets in all required regions. Store transactions in local S3 bucket and replicate using S3 Cross-Region Replication. ✅ A. Create a Global DynamoDB table with replica tables across several AWS regions 🎯 Why correct: DynamoDB Global Tables provides fully managed, multi-region, multi-master database with automatic replication. It eliminates the complexity of manual replication and conflict resolution while providing fast local read/write performance for global applications. ⚠️ B. AWS Control Tower and Amazon Connect AWS Control Tower is for multi-account governance and Amazon Connect is a contact center service. Neither service can set up Global DynamoDB tables or handle database replication across regions. ⚠️ C. Lambda function for replication Using Lambda to manually replicate millions of transactions across multiple regions is not scalable. This approach would require significant compute capacity, custom conflict resolution logic, and complex error handling that Global Tables handles automatically. ⚠️ D. S3 Cross-Region Replication Amazon S3 is designed for object storage, not transactional workloads. While S3 Cross-Region Replication works for objects, it's not suitable for real-time transactional data that requires ACID properties and low-latency access.

When should you choose DynamoDB Global Tables over manual Lambda-based replication for multi-region data synchronization? A. When you need custom conflict resolution logic and complex data transformations during replication B. When you have millions of transactions requiring automatic replication with minimal operational overhead C. When you need to replicate data to non-AWS databases or custom endpoints D. When you want full control over replication timing and batching strategies ✅ B. When you have millions of transactions requiring automatic replication with minimal operational overhead DynamoDB Global Tables • Fully managed multi-master replication • Automatic conflict resolution • Built-in scalability for millions of operations • No custom code required • Eventually consistent across regions Lambda-based Replication • Custom replication logic • Manual conflict resolution • Requires scaling management • Custom error handling needed • Flexible destination targets 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Global Tables when you need managed, scalable, automatic replication between DynamoDB tables. Choose Lambda when you need custom logic, data transformation, or replication to non-DynamoDB targets.

Which statement about DynamoDB Global Tables conflict resolution is correct? A. Global Tables uses a first-write-wins strategy where the earliest timestamp takes precedence B. Global Tables uses a last-write-wins strategy based on the most recent timestamp C. Global Tables requires manual intervention to resolve all write conflicts between regions D. Global Tables prevents write conflicts by implementing region-based write locks ✅ B. Global Tables uses a last-write-wins strategy based on the most recent timestamp 🎯 Why correct: DynamoDB Global Tables automatically resolves conflicts using last-write-wins based on timestamps. This eliminates the need for manual conflict resolution while ensuring eventual consistency across all replica tables. Options A, C, and D describe incorrect conflict resolution mechanisms - Global Tables doesn't use first-write-wins, doesn't require manual intervention, and doesn't implement write locks.

A company needs to store and replicate financial transaction data across multiple AWS regions with ACID properties , sub-millisecond latency , and automatic failover capabilities. Which service best addresses this requirement? A. Amazon RDS with Cross-Region Read Replicas B. DynamoDB Global Tables C. Amazon S3 with Cross-Region Replication D. Amazon ElastiCache Global Datastore ✅ B. DynamoDB Global Tables 🎯 Key insight: DynamoDB Global Tables provides single-digit millisecond latency, automatic multi-region replication, and built-in ACID properties for transactions. It's specifically designed for financial and transactional workloads requiring global distribution. ⚠️ A. RDS Cross-Region Replicas only provide read replicas, not multi-master writes, and have higher latency than DynamoDB. ⚠️ C. S3 is object storage, not suitable for transactional data requiring ACID properties. ⚠️ D. ElastiCache is for caching, not persistent transactional storage with ACID guarantees.

A solutions architect proposes using AWS Lambda functions triggered by DynamoDB Streams to manually replicate transaction data across 5 AWS regions for a high-volume financial application. Why is this problematic? A. DynamoDB Streams cannot trigger Lambda functions across multiple regions B. Lambda functions have execution time limits that may cause replication delays C. The approach lacks automatic scaling and conflict resolution for millions of transactions D. Lambda functions cannot write to DynamoDB tables in different regions ✅ C. The approach lacks automatic scaling and conflict resolution for millions of transactions Manual Lambda-based replication requires custom scaling logic, error handling, retry mechanisms, and conflict resolution. With millions of transactions, this becomes operationally complex and error-prone compared to managed solutions. 🎯 Better approach: Use DynamoDB Global Tables which provides automatic scaling, built-in conflict resolution, and managed replication without custom code. It's specifically designed for high-volume, multi-region transactional workloads.

A company is building a new CRM portal using containerized microservices on Amazon ECS . Requirements: least privilege security , support for security groups at container level , and network monitoring tools at container level to meet strict IT security policies. Which configuration provides the MOST secure setup? A. Bridge network mode, security groups on EC2 instances, IAM roles for EC2 instances B. AWS App Runner with VPC/security groups, IAM credentials in environment variables C. awsvpc network mode, security groups on ECS tasks, IAM roles for tasks D. awsvpc network mode, security groups on ECS tasks, pass IAM credentials at launch ✅ C. awsvpc network mode, security groups on ECS tasks, IAM roles for tasks 🎯 Why correct: awsvpc allocates each task its own ENI and private IP, enabling security groups and network monitoring at the granular task level. IAM roles for tasks provide secure credential management without embedding secrets in containers. ⚠️ A. Bridge network mode Bridge mode uses Docker's built-in virtual network inside container instances. You cannot attach security groups to individual tasks - only to the underlying EC2 instances, which doesn't provide the required container-level granularity for security controls. ⚠️ B. AWS App Runner with credentials in environment While App Runner can deploy containers, storing IAM credentials as environment variables violates security best practices. Credentials can be exposed through container inspection, process lists, or application logs, creating significant security risks. ⚠️ D. Pass IAM credentials at launch Though awsvpc is correct, manually passing IAM credentials into containers is a security anti-pattern. Credentials could be exposed through container runtime, process memory, or application code, violating least privilege principles.

When should you choose awsvpc network mode over bridge network mode for ECS tasks? A. When you need the simplest networking setup with minimal configuration B. When you need task-level security groups and network monitoring capabilities C. When you want to reduce ENI consumption and network overhead D. When you need to run multiple tasks on the same port on one instance ✅ B. When you need task-level security groups and network monitoring capabilities awsvpc Network Mode • Each task gets its own ENI and private IP • Security groups attachable to individual tasks • VPC Flow Logs support at task level • Enhanced network isolation • Required for Fargate launch type bridge Network Mode • Uses Docker's built-in virtual network • Security groups only at EC2 instance level • Simpler setup with less configuration • Lower ENI consumption • Default mode for EC2 launch type 🎯 Decision rule: Choose awsvpc when you need granular security controls, network monitoring, or Fargate. Choose bridge for simpler setups where instance-level security is sufficient.

Which statement about IAM roles for ECS tasks is correct? A. Task roles can only be used with awsvpc network mode B. Task roles provide temporary credentials to containers without embedding secrets C. Task roles require manual credential rotation every 24 hours D. Task roles can only access services within the same VPC ✅ B. Task roles provide temporary credentials to containers without embedding secrets 🎯 Why correct: IAM roles for tasks work similar to EC2 instance profiles - they provide automatic, temporary credential management without requiring developers to embed AWS credentials in container images or environment variables. This follows security best practices and enables least privilege access. Task roles work with any network mode, credentials are automatically rotated by AWS, and can access any AWS service the role permits regardless of VPC boundaries.

A company needs to monitor network traffic flows between individual microservices in their ECS cluster for security compliance and troubleshooting. Which ECS configuration enables this monitoring capability? A. Bridge network mode with CloudTrail logging B. Host network mode with VPC Flow Logs C. awsvpc network mode with VPC Flow Logs D. None network mode with CloudWatch Logs ✅ C. awsvpc network mode with VPC Flow Logs 🎯 Why this trigger maps here: awsvpc mode gives each task its own ENI, making it appear as a separate network entity. This enables VPC Flow Logs to capture traffic at the individual task level, providing the granular monitoring needed for microservices communication analysis. ⚠️ A. Bridge + CloudTrail: CloudTrail logs API calls, not network traffic. Bridge mode shares the host's network interface, preventing task-level flow monitoring. ⚠️ B. Host + VPC Flow Logs: Host mode bypasses Docker networking but still shares the EC2 instance's ENI, so you can't distinguish between different containers' traffic. ⚠️ D. None + CloudWatch: None mode provides no external connectivity, and CloudWatch Logs captures application logs, not network flows.

A solutions architect proposes using bridge network mode with security groups attached to EC2 instances for a microservices architecture requiring container-level security controls. Why is this problematic? A. Bridge mode doesn't support security groups at all B. Security group rules apply to the entire EC2 instance, not individual containers C. Bridge mode requires manual IP address management D. Security groups in bridge mode only work with ALB targets ✅ B. Security group rules apply to the entire EC2 instance, not individual containers In bridge network mode , all containers on an EC2 instance share the host's network interface through Docker's virtual network. Security groups attached to the EC2 instance apply to ALL traffic to/from that instance, making it impossible to implement different security policies for individual containers or microservices running on the same host. 🎯 Better approach: Use awsvpc network mode where each task gets its own ENI, enabling security groups to be attached directly to individual tasks for granular, container-level security controls.

A media company processes videos using Auto Scaling EC2 instances that scale based on SQS queue messages . Videos take 20-40 minutes to process. Current configuration: visibility timeout = 1 hour , maxReceiveCount = 1 , messages failing once go to dead-letter queue . Problem: Videos are appearing in DLQ despite no operational errors and processing within expected time . CloudTrail shows repeated ReceiveMessage API calls for specific videos. Which solution should the solutions architect implement? A. Set a minimum number of EC2 instances on the Auto Scaling group to prevent scale-up delays B. Reconfigure the SQS redrive policy and set maxReceiveCount to 10 C. Update the visibility timeout for the SQS queue to 2 hours D. Configure a higher delivery delay setting on the SQS queue ✅ B. Reconfigure the SQS redrive policy and set maxReceiveCount to 10 🎯 Why correct: The maxReceiveCount of 1 means any single failure (network error, temporary unavailability) immediately sends messages to DLQ. Setting it to 10 allows multiple retry attempts before declaring a message truly failed, accounting for transient issues while still catching genuinely problematic messages. ⚠️ A. Set minimum EC2 instances This doesn't address the core issue of messages prematurely going to DLQ. The Auto Scaling is working correctly based on queue depth. Setting minimum instances wastes cost when no messages are queued and doesn't solve the maxReceiveCount problem. ⚠️ C. Increase visibility timeout to 2 hours The current 1-hour timeout already exceeds the 20-40 minute processing window by a significant margin. The issue isn't processing time but rather the single-failure tolerance. Increasing timeout won't prevent messages from hitting DLQ after one receive attempt. ⚠️ D. Configure higher delivery delay Delivery delay only affects new messages entering the queue, not messages already being processed. This doesn't solve the fundamental issue of maxReceiveCount being too restrictive for handling transient failures during message processing.

Which statement about SQS maxReceiveCount configuration is correct? A. maxReceiveCount should always be set to 1 for fastest error detection B. maxReceiveCount determines how many consumers can process the same message simultaneously C. maxReceiveCount controls how many times a message can be received before moving to DLQ D. maxReceiveCount only applies to FIFO queues, not standard queues ✅ C. maxReceiveCount controls how many times a message can be received before moving to DLQ 🎯 maxReceiveCount is the threshold for message retry attempts. When a message's ReceiveCount exceeds this value, SQS automatically moves it to the configured dead-letter queue. Setting it too low (like 1) causes transient failures to immediately trigger DLQ movement, while setting it appropriately (5-10) allows for retry attempts while still catching genuinely problematic messages. This applies to both standard and FIFO queues, and doesn't control concurrent consumers.

When should you choose a higher maxReceiveCount versus a lower maxReceiveCount for SQS dead-letter queue configuration? A. Higher maxReceiveCount for applications with frequent transient errors B. Lower maxReceiveCount for applications requiring immediate error detection C. Higher maxReceiveCount for FIFO queues only D. Lower maxReceiveCount for better cost optimization ✅ A. Higher maxReceiveCount for applications with frequent transient errors Higher maxReceiveCount (5-10) • Applications with network instability • Transient dependency failures • Temporary resource unavailability • Processing that may timeout occasionally Lower maxReceiveCount (1-3) • Critical applications needing fast failure detection • Well-tested, stable processing logic • Minimal external dependencies • When poison messages must be quickly isolated 🎯 Decision rule: Choose higher when you expect transient failures that should be retried. Choose lower when failures indicate genuine problems requiring immediate attention. Balance between resilience and fast failure detection based on your application's reliability patterns.

A company's message processing system experiences intermittent network connectivity issues and temporary downstream service unavailability . Messages are being moved to the dead-letter queue too frequently, but when manually reprocessed, they succeed. Which SQS configuration change best addresses this pattern? A. Increase visibility timeout from 30 seconds to 5 minutes B. Increase maxReceiveCount from 3 to 10 C. Enable message deduplication on the queue D. Configure exponential backoff on consumer retry logic ✅ B. Increase maxReceiveCount from 3 to 10 🎯 Trigger recognition: "Messages succeed when manually reprocessed" + "intermittent network issues" + "temporary service unavailability" = classic pattern of transient failures . The solution is allowing more retry attempts before giving up, which is exactly what increasing maxReceiveCount accomplishes. This gives the system resilience against temporary issues while still catching genuinely problematic messages.

Requirements: Video processing takes 20-40 minutes , network can have 2-3 minute outages , downstream services occasionally timeout for 30 seconds , must detect genuine failures within 2 hours , cost-effective retry strategy . Which SQS configuration meets ALL requirements? A. Visibility timeout: 45 minutes, maxReceiveCount: 1 B. Visibility timeout: 60 minutes, maxReceiveCount: 8 C. Visibility timeout: 30 minutes, maxReceiveCount: 15 D. Visibility timeout: 90 minutes, maxReceiveCount: 3 ✅ B. Visibility timeout: 60 minutes, maxReceiveCount: 8 🎯 Requirements mapping: 60-minute visibility timeout accommodates 40-minute processing + buffer for delays. maxReceiveCount: 8 provides resilience against 2-3 minute network outages and 30-second service timeouts while keeping total retry window under 2 hours (8 × 15 min average = 2 hours). This balances transient failure tolerance with reasonable failure detection time and cost efficiency.

A company needs deployment solution for AWS application with: 500GB static dataset accessible at boot, auto-scaling capability, multiple daily code deployments , and 48-hour OS patch requirement. Which solution meets all requirements cost-effectively? A. Systems Manager AMI patching + batch job deployments + EFS mounting B. Systems Manager AMI patching + CodeDeploy + EFS mounting C. Amazon Linux AMI replacement + S3 download via user data + CodeDeploy D. Amazon Linux AMI + S3 download + Systems Manager patching + CodeDeploy ✅ B. Systems Manager AMI patching + CodeDeploy + EFS mounting 🎯 Why correct: Systems Manager Patch Manager ensures 48-hour patch compliance, CodeDeploy enables multiple daily deployments, and EFS provides cost-effective shared access to 500GB dataset across all instances without duplicating storage. ⚠️ A. Batch job approach Batch jobs run nightly but developers need multiple deployments per day . This doesn't meet the rapid deployment requirement and forces developers to wait until night for their code updates. ⚠️ C. Amazon Linux AMI replacement Amazon Linux AMI updates take weeks or months to release, far exceeding the 48-hour patch requirement. Also, downloading 500GB from S3 to each instance's EBS volume is more expensive than shared EFS. ⚠️ D. S3 download approach While patching meets requirements, downloading 500GB to each instance's EBS volume creates unnecessary storage costs compared to a single shared EFS volume mounted across all instances.

When should you choose EFS over S3 for storing large datasets accessed by multiple EC2 instances? A. When you need the lowest possible storage cost B. When instances need simultaneous file-level access without downloading C. When you need global accessibility from any region D. When you need object versioning and lifecycle policies ✅ B. When instances need simultaneous file-level access without downloading Amazon EFS • NFS-based file system • Simultaneous multi-instance access • No download required • File-level operations • Higher cost per GB Amazon S3 • Object storage service • Must download to instance storage • Lower cost per GB • Global accessibility • Versioning and lifecycle features 🎯 Decision rule: Choose EFS when multiple instances need shared, simultaneous access to files. Choose S3 when you need cost-effective storage and can download data to local storage.

A company needs to deploy application updates multiple times per day across an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances with zero downtime and rollback capability . Which AWS service best addresses this requirement? A. AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager B. AWS CodeDeploy C. AWS CloudFormation D. AWS Lambda with EC2 API ✅ B. AWS CodeDeploy 🎯 AWS CodeDeploy is specifically designed for application deployments with built-in deployment strategies (blue/green, rolling), automatic rollback capabilities, and integration with Auto Scaling groups for zero-downtime deployments. ⚠️ A. Patch Manager is for OS/security patches, not application code ⚠️ C. CloudFormation deploys infrastructure, not application code updates ⚠️ D. Lambda would require custom scripting without built-in rollback features

Which statement about AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager is correct? A. It only works with Windows instances for security patches B. It can auto-approve patches within specified days of release using patch baselines C. It requires manual approval for each individual patch before installation D. It only installs patches during scheduled maintenance windows ✅ B. It can auto-approve patches within specified days of release using patch baselines 🎯 Patch baselines include rules for auto-approving patches within days of their release, plus approved/rejected patch lists. This enables automated compliance with patch timing requirements like the 48-hour requirement in the scenario. Works with both Windows and Linux, can run outside maintenance windows, and doesn't require manual approval for each patch.

Requirements: 500GB shared dataset , multiple EC2 instances in Auto Scaling group, cost optimization , immediate access at boot , file-level operations . Which storage solution meets ALL requirements? A. Amazon S3 with download via user data script B. Amazon EFS mounted at instance launch C. Amazon EBS volumes attached to each instance D. Instance store volumes with data replication ✅ B. Amazon EFS mounted at instance launch 🎯 Why EFS wins: Shared access (one dataset, multiple instances), immediate availability (no download time), cost-effective (pay for one copy vs multiple), file-level operations (NFS protocol), and Auto Scaling compatible (automatic mounting). ⚠️ A. S3 requires downloading 500GB to each instance's local storage, increasing costs and boot time ⚠️ C. EBS requires separate 500GB volumes per instance, multiplying storage costs unnecessarily ⚠️ D. Instance store is ephemeral and requires complex replication logic for data persistence

A company wants to host an internal web application in AWS using Docker containers for the front-end and MySQL for the backend. They need AWS-managed container services to reduce overhead. Company documents are frequently accessed for 3 months , then rarely accessed, but must be retained for 5 years . The company wants the lowest possible cost . Which implementation is the most cost-effective solution? A. ECS with EC2 On-Demand instances, RDS On-Demand, EFS volume, cron job to copy to S3 Glacier after 3 months B. ECS with Spot Instances, Aurora Serverless v2, encrypted EBS volume shared with containers, cron job to delete after 5 years C. ECS with Spot Instances and draining enabled, RDS Reserved instances, encrypted S3 bucket with lifecycle policy D. EKS with auto-scaling and Spot instances, RDS On-Demand, encrypted S3 bucket with lifecycle policy ✅ C. ECS with Spot Instances and draining enabled, RDS Reserved instances, encrypted S3 bucket with lifecycle policy 🎯 Why correct: This solution combines the most cost-effective options: Spot Instances for compute (up to 90% savings), Reserved Instances for predictable database workloads, and S3 with automatic lifecycle management that transitions to Glacier after 3 months and deletes after 5 years. ⚠️ A. On-Demand with EFS On-Demand instances are significantly more expensive than Spot Instances for this workload. EFS is also more expensive than S3 for document storage, and using cron jobs adds operational complexity compared to native S3 lifecycle policies. ⚠️ B. Aurora Serverless with EBS Aurora Serverless v2 is more expensive than RDS Reserved for predictable workloads. Storing documents on EBS volumes requires more expensive disk space on instances instead of using cost-effective S3 storage. ⚠️ D. EKS with RDS On-Demand EKS has additional management overhead compared to ECS. Using On-Demand instances for continuously running RDS databases is expensive when Reserved Instances would provide significant cost savings for predictable workloads.

When choosing between EC2 Spot Instances and On-Demand Instances for containerized applications, which factor is most important? A. Spot Instances are always better due to lower cost B. On-Demand Instances provide guaranteed availability C. Workload fault tolerance and cost sensitivity determine the choice D. Spot Instances only work with specific instance types ✅ C. Workload fault tolerance and cost sensitivity determine the choice Spot Instances • Up to 90% cost savings • Subject to interruption with 2-minute notice • Best for fault-tolerant workloads • Ideal for batch processing, containerized apps On-Demand Instances • Predictable, guaranteed availability • Higher cost but no interruptions • Best for critical, stateful applications • Ideal for databases, production web servers 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Spot when your application can handle interruptions and you need cost optimization. Choose On-Demand when you need guaranteed availability and can't tolerate interruptions.

Which statement about ECS Spot Instance draining is correct? A. It's enabled by default on all ECS container instances B. It must be manually enabled by adding ECS_ENABLE_SPOT_INSTANCE_DRAINING=true to /etc/ecs/ecs.config C. It only works with Fargate launch type D. It prevents Spot Instance interruptions from occurring ✅ B. It must be manually enabled by adding ECS_ENABLE_SPOT_INSTANCE_DRAINING=true to /etc/ecs/ecs.config 🎯 Key insight: Spot Instance draining is disabled by default and requires manual configuration. When enabled, it gracefully handles Spot interruptions by placing the instance in DRAINING status, stopping PENDING tasks immediately, and starting replacement tasks on available instances. This prevents abrupt task termination during Spot interruptions.

A company needs database hosting for a predictable workload that runs 24/7 with consistent usage patterns . They want to minimize costs while ensuring reliable performance . Which RDS pricing model meets ALL requirements? A. RDS On-Demand Instances B. RDS Reserved Instances C. Aurora Serverless v2 D. RDS Spot Instances ✅ B. RDS Reserved Instances 🎯 Why: Predictable 24/7 workload maps to Reserved Instance cost model (up to 75% savings). Consistent usage means you can commit to 1-3 year terms. Reliable performance is guaranteed since Reserved Instances provide dedicated capacity. ⚠️ A. On-Demand: Most expensive option for continuous workloads ⚠️ C. Serverless: Better for variable/unpredictable workloads, more expensive for consistent 24/7 usage ⚠️ D. Spot: RDS doesn't offer Spot pricing model

A company needs to store documents that are frequently accessed for 3 months , then rarely accessed , but must be retained for 5 years with automatic lifecycle management . Which storage solution best addresses this requirement? A. EFS with manual archival process B. EBS volumes with scheduled snapshots C. S3 with lifecycle policies to transition to Glacier D. Instance store with backup scripts ✅ C. S3 with lifecycle policies to transition to Glacier 🎯 Perfect trigger match: The phrase "automatic lifecycle management" with changing access patterns directly maps to S3 Lifecycle policies . These can automatically transition objects to Glacier after 3 months for cost savings and delete after 5 years for compliance. ⚠️ A. EFS: More expensive than S3, requires manual processes ⚠️ B. EBS: Block storage, not suitable for document archival ⚠️ D. Instance store: Ephemeral storage, data loss risk

A company runs weather pattern simulations generating terabytes of data. Current setup: MySQL 8.0 on EC2 (16 TiB, growing), Ruby on Rails on separate EC2 . Requirements: highly scalable, highly available, 24x7 operation, cost-effective . Which solution BEST meets all requirements? A. Auto Scaling EC2 + ALB, Reserved + On-Demand instances, migrate to Amazon Aurora , create read replica in another AZ B. Convert to Lambda@Edge functions, migrate to RDS MySQL Multi-AZ with storage autoscaling C. Auto Scaling EC2 + ALB, Reserved + On-Demand instances, migrate to RDS MySQL Multi-AZ , manually adjust storage D. Reserved EC2 for app and database, Auto Scaling Multi-AZ, source-replica setup on EC2, use LVM for storage expansion ✅ A. Auto Scaling EC2 + ALB, Reserved + On-Demand instances, migrate to Amazon Aurora, create read replica in another AZ 🎯 Why correct: Aurora automatically scales storage up to 128 TiB (vs RDS 64 TiB limit), provides better cost optimization through automatic scaling, and the mixed Reserved/On-Demand approach optimizes costs while ensuring availability. ⚠️ B. Lambda@Edge + RDS MySQL Multi-AZ Lambda@Edge is designed for CloudFront content customization at edge locations, not for running compute-intensive weather simulation applications. This is architectural mismatch - Lambda@Edge has execution time limits unsuitable for heavy data processing workloads. ⚠️ C. RDS MySQL Multi-AZ with manual storage adjustment Manual storage adjustment creates operational overhead and potential downtime during scaling operations. RDS supports storage autoscaling, making manual adjustment unnecessary. Also, RDS MySQL has a 64 TiB limit vs Aurora's 128 TiB automatic scaling. ⚠️ D. Reserved EC2 with self-managed MySQL Self-managing MySQL on EC2 creates significant operational overhead for patching, backups, failover, and scaling. LVM and EBS volume management adds complexity. This approach lacks the automatic scaling and managed service benefits of Aurora.

When should you choose Amazon Aurora over RDS MySQL for large-scale data workloads? A. When you need exactly 64 TiB of storage with manual scaling control B. When you need automatic storage scaling beyond 64 TiB with pay-per-use pricing C. When you need basic MySQL compatibility with minimal management overhead D. When you need to run on a single Availability Zone for cost optimization ✅ B. When you need automatic storage scaling beyond 64 TiB with pay-per-use pricing Amazon Aurora • Automatic scaling up to 128 TiB • Pay only for storage used • Built-in Multi-AZ replication • 6 copies across 3 AZs • Better performance (5x MySQL) RDS MySQL • Manual or autoscaling up to 64 TiB • Pre-provisioned storage billing • Optional Multi-AZ deployment • Standard MySQL performance • Lower cost for small workloads 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Aurora when you need automatic scaling beyond 64 TiB, better performance, or built-in HA. Choose RDS MySQL for smaller, cost-sensitive workloads with predictable growth.

Which statement about Amazon Aurora storage scaling is correct? A. Aurora requires manual intervention to add storage volumes when capacity is exceeded B. Aurora automatically scales storage up to 128 TiB and charges only for space actually used C. Aurora storage must be pre-provisioned in fixed increments like standard EBS volumes D. Aurora storage scaling requires downtime during expansion operations ✅ B. Aurora automatically scales storage up to 128 TiB and charges only for space actually used 🎯 Key insight: Aurora's storage layer is fundamentally different from traditional databases. It automatically grows in 10GB increments as needed, eliminating capacity planning and reducing costs by charging only for consumed space. This contrasts with RDS which requires pre-provisioned storage volumes.

A company has a database that currently stores 16 TiB and is expected to grow continuously from complex simulations. They need automatic scaling without manual intervention and cost optimization through pay-per-use . Which database service best addresses these requirements? A. Amazon RDS MySQL with storage autoscaling enabled B. Amazon Aurora MySQL with automatic storage scaling C. Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand billing D. Amazon Redshift with elastic resize capability ✅ B.
