Spot Fleet with diversified allocation strategy and Auto Scaling 🎯 Why correct: Spot instances are most cost-effective for temporary peak loads. Diversified allocation strategy spreads instances across multiple AZs and instance types, ensuring capacity availability even if one AZ fails. Auto Scaling provides automatic recovery and scaling capabilities. ⚠️ A. Spot and On-Demand combination Missing Auto Scaling Groups which are essential for automatic recovery when an AZ fails. Manual scaling cannot provide the quick recovery required during peak load scenarios. ⚠️ B. Reserved and On-Demand combination Lacks Auto Scaling Groups for automatic recovery. Also uses more expensive Reserved Instances for peak load instead of cost-effective Spot instances . ⚠️ C. Auto Scaling with Reserved instances While it includes Auto Scaling, using Reserved Instances for peak load is significantly more expensive than Spot instances for handling temporary, variable workloads.

When should you choose Spot Fleet over Auto Scaling Groups for handling variable workloads? A. When you need guaranteed capacity and predictable costs B. When you need maximum cost savings for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads C. When you require persistent storage and long-running processes D. When you need consistent performance for mission-critical applications ✅ B. When you need maximum cost savings for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads Spot Fleet • Up to 90% cost savings vs On-Demand • Best for fault-tolerant workloads • Diversified allocation across instance types/AZs • Can be interrupted with 2-minute notice • Ideal for batch processing, web servers Auto Scaling Groups • Predictable capacity and costs • Guaranteed availability • Works with On-Demand/Reserved instances • No interruption risk • Better for mission-critical applications 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Spot Fleet when cost optimization is priority and workload can handle interruptions. Choose Auto Scaling Groups when you need guaranteed capacity and consistent performance.

Which statement about Spot Fleet diversified allocation strategy is correct? A. It launches instances only in the lowest-priced Availability Zone to minimize costs B. It distributes instances across multiple instance types and AZs to improve availability C. It automatically converts Spot instances to On-Demand when capacity is low D. It reserves capacity in advance to guarantee instance availability ✅ B. It distributes instances across multiple instance types and AZs to improve availability 🎯 Key insight: Diversified allocation strategy spreads Spot Fleet requests across different instance families , sizes , and Availability Zones . This reduces the risk of all instances being terminated simultaneously and improves overall fleet stability. It doesn't guarantee capacity (that's Reserved Instances) or automatically convert to On-Demand (that's a separate configuration). Options A, C, and D describe incorrect behaviors. Diversified strategy prioritizes availability over lowest cost, doesn't auto-convert instance types, and cannot reserve capacity like Reserved Instances.

A company runs batch processing jobs that can tolerate interruptions, need to scale from 10 to 1000 instances quickly during peak hours, and must minimize costs while maintaining some capacity even during Spot price spikes. Which EC2 purchasing option best addresses these requirements? A. Auto Scaling Group with On-Demand instances B. Spot Fleet with diversified allocation strategy C. Reserved Instances with scheduled scaling D. Mixed Instance Types Auto Scaling Group ✅ B. Spot Fleet with diversified allocation strategy 🎯 Perfect match: Spot Fleet provides up to 90% cost savings ideal for fault-tolerant batch jobs . Diversified allocation spreads across multiple instance types and AZs, ensuring some capacity remains available even during Spot price fluctuations or capacity constraints in specific instance families. ⚠️ A. Auto Scaling with On-Demand: Provides guaranteed capacity but at full price, eliminating the cost optimization requirement. ⚠️ C. Reserved Instances: Requires 1-3 year commitment and doesn't provide the massive scaling flexibility needed. ⚠️ D. Mixed Instance Types: Still uses On-Demand pricing tiers, not achieving maximum cost savings.

Requirements: 90% cost reduction for peak load handling, automatic recovery from AZ failures, support for stateless web applications , and ability to scale quickly during traffic spikes while maintaining some capacity during Spot interruptions. Which combination of services meets ALL requirements? A. Auto Scaling Groups + Reserved Instances + Application Load Balancer B. Spot Fleet + Auto Scaling + Application Load Balancer + Diversified allocation C. Elastic Beanstalk + On-Demand instances + Network Load Balancer D. ECS Fargate + Spot capacity providers + Application Load Balancer ✅ B. Spot Fleet + Auto Scaling + Application Load Balancer + Diversified allocation 🎯 Requirements mapping: • 90% cost reduction: Spot instances provide up to 90% savings • Automatic recovery: Auto Scaling detects and replaces failed instances • Stateless web apps: ALB distributes traffic effectively • Quick scaling: Auto Scaling + Spot Fleet rapid provisioning • Capacity during interruptions: Diversified allocation across instance types/AZs ⚠️ A: Reserved Instances don't provide 90% cost reduction and aren't suitable for variable peak loads ⚠️ C: On-Demand instances don't meet the cost reduction requirement ⚠️ D: While cost-effective, ECS Fargate has different scaling characteristics and may not achieve 90% savings

An enterprise CMS application runs on Auto Scaling EC2 instances behind an ALB . Instances are in private subnets , ALB in public subnets. Systems Manager Session Manager provides access. After deploying a new application version, instances are marked unhealthy by ALB and terminated by Auto Scaling . CloudWatch Logs show no definitive errors, but instances terminate before troubleshooting is possible. Which is the quickest way to troubleshoot the problem? A. Update application log settings for verbose logging and ensure CloudWatch agent is running B. Select one EC2 instance and enable termination protection, then access via Session Manager C. Create temporary EC2 instance with new app version, login via SSH, add to ALB D. Suspend the "Terminate" process for the ASG, then login via Session Manager ✅ D. Suspend the "Terminate" process for the ASG, then login via Session Manager 🎯 Why correct: Auto Scaling processes can be individually suspended without affecting the entire ASG. Suspending only the "Terminate" process prevents instance replacement while maintaining other ASG functionality, giving time to troubleshoot via Session Manager. ⚠️ A. Verbose logging approach This won't solve the core issue of instances being terminated before logs can be collected. Even with verbose logging, instances may terminate before generating useful logs, and this doesn't address the immediate need to access unhealthy instances. ⚠️ B. EC2 termination protection Termination protection only prevents manual termination or API calls. Auto Scaling groups have the authority to terminate instances they created, even with termination protection enabled. The ASG will override instance-level protection. ⚠️ C. Temporary instance approach Creating a separate instance is unnecessarily complex and time-consuming. It requires multiple steps (launch, configure, deploy, attach to ALB) and doesn't directly troubleshoot the actual unhealthy instances in the ASG environment.

Which statement about Auto Scaling Group process suspension is correct? A. Suspending processes affects all Auto Scaling groups in the account B. Individual processes can be suspended while others continue running C. Process suspension automatically enables detailed monitoring D. Suspended processes cannot be resumed without recreating the ASG ✅ B. Individual processes can be suspended while others continue running 🎯 Key insight: Auto Scaling processes (Launch, Terminate, HealthCheck, ReplaceUnhealthy, AZRebalance, AlarmNotification, ScheduledActions, AddToLoadBalancer) can be suspended individually. This granular control allows troubleshooting specific issues without disrupting all ASG functionality. Suspended processes can be easily resumed.

When troubleshooting EC2 instances, when should you use EC2 termination protection vs Auto Scaling process suspension? A. Always use termination protection as it provides stronger protection B. Use process suspension for ASG instances, termination protection for standalone instances C. Both provide identical protection for ASG instances D. Use termination protection only for instances with EBS root volumes ✅ B. Use process suspension for ASG instances, termination protection for standalone instances EC2 Termination Protection • Prevents manual/API termination • Works for standalone instances • Overridden by Auto Scaling groups • Instance-level setting ASG Process Suspension • Controls Auto Scaling behavior • Prevents ASG from terminating instances • Granular process control • Group-level setting 🎯 Decision rule: Use termination protection for standalone instances you want to protect from accidental termination. Use ASG process suspension when troubleshooting ASG-managed instances, as ASGs override instance-level protection.

A company needs to access EC2 instances in private subnets without managing SSH keys, bastion hosts, or opening inbound ports for security compliance. Which service best addresses this requirement? A. AWS Systems Manager Session Manager B. AWS Direct Connect with VPN C. EC2 Instance Connect D. AWS Client VPN ✅ A. AWS Systems Manager Session Manager 🎯 Perfect fit: Session Manager provides secure, auditable access to EC2 instances without SSH keys, bastion hosts, or inbound security group rules. It works through the Systems Manager Agent and AWS APIs, ideal for private subnet access with zero infrastructure overhead. ⚠️ B. Direct Connect + VPN: Provides network connectivity but still requires managing access credentials and doesn't eliminate SSH key management. ⚠️ C. EC2 Instance Connect: Still uses SSH and requires temporary key injection, doesn't fully eliminate SSH key management. ⚠️ D. Client VPN: Provides network access but doesn't solve SSH key management or eliminate need for bastion-like infrastructure.

Requirements: Real-time troubleshooting of ASG instances, no infrastructure changes , immediate implementation , and preserve ASG functionality during investigation. Which approach meets ALL requirements? A. Create new instances outside ASG for testing B. Suspend ASG "Terminate" process and use Session Manager C. Enable detailed CloudWatch monitoring and wait for logs D. Temporarily disable ALB health checks ✅ B. Suspend ASG "Terminate" process and use Session Manager 🎯 Requirements mapping: Real-time troubleshooting ✓ (Session Manager), No infrastructure changes ✓ (uses existing setup), Immediate implementation ✓ (simple console action), Preserve ASG functionality ✓ (other processes continue) ⚠️ A. New instances: Requires infrastructure changes and doesn't troubleshoot actual problem instances. ⚠️ C. CloudWatch monitoring: Not real-time troubleshooting, passive monitoring only. ⚠️ D. Disable health checks: Doesn't preserve ASG functionality, affects load balancer behavior.

A company uses AWS Fargate for production and wants to deploy development workloads on-premises to leverage existing investments. Requirements: same cluster management for both environments, easy migration from dev to production, and consistent tooling/API experience across container workloads. Which solution is MOST operationally efficient? A. Use Amazon EKS Anywhere for on-premises Kubernetes management, then migrate to EKS on Fargate B. Install AWS Outposts and run Amazon ECS on Outposts, then migrate to AWS Fargate C. Install AWS Outposts and run Amazon EKS Anywhere on Outposts, then migrate to AWS Fargate D. Use Amazon ECS Anywhere to manage containers on-premises and AWS with standardized orchestration ✅ D. Amazon ECS Anywhere 🎯 Why correct: ECS Anywhere allows on-premises compute, EC2 instances, and Fargate to coexist in the same ECS cluster , providing unified management and seamless migration paths with consistent tooling. ⚠️ A. EKS Anywhere EKS Anywhere is designed for on-premises only and does not integrate with AWS Cloud services like Fargate. You cannot have EKS Anywhere and cloud EKS in the same cluster for unified management. ⚠️ B. ECS on Outposts AWS Fargate is not supported on Outposts. ECS on Outposts requires EC2 instances as compute capacity providers, preventing seamless migration to Fargate-based production. ⚠️ C. EKS Anywhere on Outposts EKS Anywhere is not designed to run on Outposts. It's intended for customer-managed infrastructure and doesn't integrate with AWS-managed services or support Fargate migration.

When should you choose ECS Anywhere over EKS Anywhere for hybrid container deployments? A. When you need Kubernetes-native tooling and existing Kubernetes expertise B. When you want unified cluster management between on-premises and AWS Cloud services C. When you require complex multi-cluster networking across environments D. When you need to run serverless containers only on-premises ✅ B. Unified cluster management between on-premises and AWS Cloud services ECS Anywhere • Single cluster spans on-premises + AWS • Integrates with Fargate and EC2 • AWS-managed control plane • Seamless cloud migration • No Kubernetes knowledge required EKS Anywhere • On-premises Kubernetes only • No integration with AWS EKS • Customer-managed control plane • Requires separate cloud clusters • Kubernetes expertise needed 🎯 Decision rule: Choose ECS Anywhere when you need hybrid cloud integration and easy migration. Choose EKS Anywhere when you want pure on-premises Kubernetes with full control.

A company wants to gradually migrate containerized workloads from on-premises to AWS while maintaining consistent operational tools and keeping some workloads on-premises permanently. Which AWS service best addresses this migration pattern? A. AWS App2Container with EKS B. Amazon ECS Anywhere C. AWS Outposts with ECS D. Amazon EKS Anywhere ✅ B. Amazon ECS Anywhere 🎯 Trigger phrase 'gradually migrate' maps to ECS Anywhere's ability to have on-premises and cloud resources in the same cluster, enabling workload mobility with consistent tooling across environments. ⚠️ A. App2Container: Migration tool, not ongoing hybrid management ⚠️ C. Outposts: AWS infrastructure on-premises, not true hybrid clusters ⚠️ D. EKS Anywhere: On-premises only, no cloud integration

Which statement about AWS Fargate compatibility is correct? A. Fargate can run on AWS Outposts for edge computing scenarios B. Fargate tasks can be managed alongside on-premises containers in ECS Anywhere C. Fargate requires EC2 instances as underlying compute infrastructure D. Fargate integrates directly with EKS Anywhere for hybrid deployments ✅ B. Fargate tasks can be managed alongside on-premises containers in ECS Anywhere 🎯 Key insight: ECS Anywhere creates a unified cluster where Fargate, EC2, and on-premises compute can coexist under single management plane. Fargate is not supported on Outposts and doesn't integrate with EKS Anywhere. Fargate is serverless - no EC2 instances required.

Requirements: Container workloads must run on existing on-premises servers, integrate with AWS compliance reporting via Artifact, support seamless migration to cloud, and provide consistent API experience across environments. Which solution meets ALL requirements? A. Docker Swarm with custom AWS integration B. Amazon ECS Anywhere C. Kubernetes with AWS Controllers D. Amazon EKS Anywhere ✅ B. Amazon ECS Anywhere 🎯 Requirements mapping: On-premises servers ✓ (external instances), AWS compliance ✓ (native AWS service), seamless migration ✓ (unified clusters), consistent APIs ✓ (same ECS APIs everywhere) ⚠️ A. Docker Swarm: No native AWS integration or compliance features ⚠️ C. Kubernetes: Requires custom integration work, no seamless migration ⚠️ D. EKS Anywhere: On-premises only, no cloud migration path

A tech company created an S3 bucket named "www.tutorialsdojo.com" in us-west-2, enabled static website hosting , uploaded content including index.html, registered the custom domain with Route 53 , and created an Alias record pointing to the S3 website endpoint. Users cannot see any content on both tutorialsdojo.com and www.tutorialsdojo.com. Which is the MOST likely cause of this issue? A. The URL needs to include a filename (www.tutorialsdojo.com/index.html) B. The error.html file value is missing, which is required C. Route 53 is still propagating changes (wait 12 hours) D. The S3 bucket lacks public read access ✅ D. The S3 bucket lacks public read access 🎯 Why correct: S3 static websites require public read access to serve content to visitors. Without this permission, users receive access denied errors even when all other configuration is correct. ⚠️ A. URL filename requirement S3 static websites automatically serve the index document (index.html) when accessing the root URL. Manually appending filenames is not required for basic functionality. ⚠️ B. Missing error.html The error document is optional for S3 static websites. While recommended for better user experience, its absence won't prevent the site from loading successfully. ⚠️ C. Route 53 propagation delay Route 53 propagates DNS changes to its global network within 60 seconds under normal conditions, not 12 hours. This timeframe is excessive for Route 53.

Which statement about S3 static website hosting requirements is correct? A. The bucket name must match the domain name exactly B. HTTPS is automatically enabled for all S3 static websites C. The error.html file is mandatory for website functionality D. Private buckets can serve static websites with signed URLs ✅ A. The bucket name must match the domain name exactly 🎯 Critical requirement: For Route 53 Alias records to work with S3 static websites, the bucket name must exactly match the domain (e.g., www.example.com bucket for www.example.com domain). HTTPS requires CloudFront , error.html is optional, and static websites require public read access , not signed URLs.

A company needs to host a static website with: custom domain , HTTPS encryption , global performance , and cost optimization . Which architecture meets ALL requirements? A. S3 static website + Route 53 only B. S3 static website + CloudFront + Route 53 C. EC2 web server + Application Load Balancer D. S3 static website + API Gateway ✅ B. S3 static website + CloudFront + Route 53 🎯 Why this meets all requirements: S3 provides cost-effective static hosting, CloudFront adds HTTPS support and global edge caching for performance, Route 53 enables custom domain routing. S3 alone lacks HTTPS, EC2 is more expensive, API Gateway doesn't serve static content efficiently.

A solutions architect proposes using S3 bucket policies to restrict static website access to specific IP addresses. Why is this problematic? A. S3 bucket policies don't support IP-based conditions B. Static website endpoints bypass bucket policies entirely C. IP restrictions require VPC endpoints instead D. Route 53 aliases don't work with restricted buckets ✅ B. Static website endpoints bypass bucket policies entirely S3 static website endpoints use a different access path that ignores bucket policies, including IP restrictions. The website endpoint serves content based on public read permissions only. 🎯 Better approach: Use CloudFront with Web Application Firewall (WAF) or geographic restrictions to control access to static websites while maintaining performance.

A company reports their S3 static website works intermittently - sometimes loads content, sometimes shows "Access Denied" errors, despite correct DNS configuration. Which issue most likely causes this behavior? A. Inconsistent Route 53 DNS propagation B. Mixed bucket permissions (some objects public, others private) C. S3 eventual consistency causing access delays D. CloudFront caching stale permission data ✅ B. Mixed bucket permissions (some objects public, others private) 🎯 Intermittent failures in S3 static websites typically indicate that some objects have public read access while others remain private. Users can access public objects but receive "Access Denied" for private ones, creating inconsistent behavior across different pages or resources.

A company is decommissioning its legacy web application (Auto Scaling EC2 + ALB) and building a new serverless architecture using AWS Lambda , API Gateway , and DynamoDB . The solution requires a CI/CD pipeline to automate builds and support gradual deployments . Which is the most suitable way to build, test, and deploy the new architecture? A. Use AWS Serverless Application Repository to organize components and deploy as versioned entities B. Use AWS SAM and set up CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline for CI/CD C. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to deploy the application D. Use CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CodePipeline with Systems Manager Automation ✅ B. Use AWS SAM and set up CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline for CI/CD 🎯 Why correct: AWS SAM is specifically designed for building, testing, and deploying serverless applications with Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB. Combined with the AWS Code services, it provides native support for gradual deployments and automated CI/CD workflows for serverless architectures. ⚠️ A. Serverless Application Repository This is just a managed repository for discovering and sharing serverless applications. It doesn't provide the build, test, and CI/CD pipeline capabilities needed for development workflows - it's only for deployment of pre-built applications. ⚠️ C. AWS Elastic Beanstalk Elastic Beanstalk is designed for deploying traditional applications on EC2 instances, not serverless architectures. It cannot manage Lambda functions, API Gateway, or DynamoDB in a serverless context. ⚠️ D. Systems Manager Automation Systems Manager Automation is primarily for managing and configuring EC2 instances through runbooks, not for building and deploying serverless applications. It lacks the serverless-specific deployment capabilities that SAM provides.

When should you choose AWS SAM over AWS CDK for serverless application development? A. When you need multi-language support and complex infrastructure B. When you want serverless-focused templates with built-in best practices C. When you need to deploy non-serverless AWS resources D. When you prefer object-oriented programming paradigms ✅ B. When you want serverless-focused templates with built-in best practices AWS SAM • Serverless-focused framework • Simplified YAML templates • Built-in serverless best practices • Local testing capabilities • Gradual deployment support AWS CDK • General-purpose IaC framework • Multiple programming languages • Object-oriented constructs • Broader AWS service support • More flexibility but complexity 🎯 Decision rule: Choose SAM when building pure serverless applications with Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB. Choose CDK when you need complex infrastructure, multiple languages, or non-serverless resources.

Which statement about AWS SAM local testing capabilities is correct? A. SAM CLI can only test Lambda functions, not API Gateway endpoints B. Local testing requires deploying resources to AWS first C. SAM CLI can locally simulate Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB D. Local testing is only available for Node.js runtime ✅ C. SAM CLI can locally simulate Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB 🎯 SAM CLI local capabilities: The sam local command can simulate an entire serverless application locally using Docker containers, including Lambda functions, API Gateway endpoints, and DynamoDB tables. This enables rapid development and testing without AWS deployment costs. It supports all Lambda runtimes, not just Node.js, and doesn't require prior AWS deployment.

A development team needs to implement blue/green deployments for their Lambda-based API with automatic rollback if error rates exceed 5% and gradual traffic shifting over 10 minutes. Which deployment approach best addresses these requirements? A. AWS CodeDeploy with Lambda deployment configuration B. AWS SAM with gradual deployment preferences C. AWS Lambda aliases with weighted routing D. AWS API Gateway stage variables ✅ B. AWS SAM with gradual deployment preferences 🎯 SAM gradual deployments integrate with CodeDeploy to provide built-in blue/green deployment patterns with automatic rollback triggers based on CloudWatch alarms (like error rate thresholds) and configurable traffic shifting policies (linear or canary). This provides the complete automated deployment solution the scenario requires. ⚠️ A. CodeDeploy alone provides the deployment mechanism but requires additional SAM/CloudFormation integration for serverless-specific configurations. ⚠️ C. Lambda aliases enable traffic splitting but don't provide automated rollback based on metrics. ⚠️ D. API Gateway stages are for environment separation, not gradual deployments.

Requirements: Serverless application with Lambda functions, infrastructure as code , local development/testing , CI/CD integration , and gradual deployments with rollback . Which combination meets ALL requirements? A. Terraform + Jenkins + Lambda aliases B. AWS SAM + CodePipeline + CodeDeploy C. CloudFormation + CodeBuild + API Gateway stages D. Serverless Framework + GitLab CI + Route 53 weighted routing ✅ B. AWS SAM + CodePipeline + CodeDeploy 🎯 Complete serverless solution: SAM provides IaC with serverless focus + local testing via SAM CLI. CodePipeline handles CI/CD automation. CodeDeploy (integrated with SAM) enables gradual deployments with automatic rollback based on CloudWatch metrics. This combination addresses every requirement natively. ⚠️ A. Terraform + Jenkins: No native serverless local testing capabilities and Lambda aliases alone don't provide automated rollback based on metrics. ⚠️ C. CloudFormation + CodeBuild: Missing local testing capabilities and API Gateway stages don't provide gradual deployment functionality. ⚠️ D. Serverless Framework: While capable, Route 53 weighted routing is complex for application-level deployments and lacks integrated rollback mechanisms.

A global financial company is launching a cryptocurrency trading platform in AWS. To comply with anti-money laundering (AML/CFT) measures , all report files must be blocked from accessing certain blacklisted countries on the FATF list. The solution must still deliver content globally with low latency . What is the best way to satisfy this security requirement while maintaining global low-latency access? A. Create a CloudFront distribution with Geo-Restriction enabled to block all blacklisted countries B. Deploy using Elastic Beanstalk and deny traffic from blacklisted IPs in VPC Network ACL C. Use Route 53 with Geolocation routing policy to block blacklisted countries D. Use Route 53 with Geoproximity routing policy to block blacklisted countries ✅ A. Create a CloudFront distribution with Geo-Restriction enabled 🎯 Why correct: CloudFront geo-restriction provides both country-level blocking AND global low-latency content delivery through edge locations. It's designed specifically for this use case of geographic content filtering while maintaining performance. ⚠️ B. Elastic Beanstalk with Network ACL IP blocking Network ACLs have limited entries and blocking entire countries by IP ranges is operationally complex and error-prone. This approach doesn't provide the global low-latency delivery that CloudFront offers through edge caching. ⚠️ C. Route 53 Geolocation routing Route 53 only provides DNS resolution and routing decisions - it doesn't block access or provide content caching. Users from blocked countries could still access content directly via IP addresses, and there's no low-latency content delivery. ⚠️ D. Route 53 Geoproximity routing Geoproximity routing is for directing traffic based on resource location and traffic shifting, not for blocking access. Like Geolocation, it only handles DNS routing and provides no content blocking or edge caching capabilities.

When should you choose CloudFront geo-restriction over Route 53 geolocation routing for content access control? A. When you need to block content access from specific countries while maintaining global performance B. When you need to route users to different application versions based on location C. When you need to perform DNS-level geographic routing for backend services D. When you need to distribute traffic across multiple regions based on user proximity ✅ A. When you need to block content access from specific countries while maintaining global performance CloudFront Geo-Restriction • Blocks content at edge locations • Provides low-latency global delivery • Country-level access control • Content caching and acceleration Route 53 Geolocation • DNS-level routing decisions • Routes to different endpoints • No content blocking capability • No content caching or acceleration 🎯 Decision rule: Choose CloudFront when you need to block access while delivering content globally. Choose Route 53 when you need to route users to different application endpoints based on location.

A financial services company must comply with regulatory requirements that prohibit serving certain documents to users in specific countries, while ensuring fast global access for authorized regions. Which AWS service combination best addresses this compliance requirement? A. CloudFront with geo-restriction and S3 origin B. Route 53 with geolocation routing and ALB targets C. API Gateway with resource policies and Lambda authorizers D. WAF with geo-match conditions and CloudFormation templates ✅ A. CloudFront with geo-restriction and S3 origin 🎯 Key insight: Regulatory content blocking + global performance requirements = CloudFront geo-restriction. It provides country-level blocking at edge locations while caching content globally for fast access in allowed regions. ⚠️ B. Route 53 geolocation: Only routes DNS queries, doesn't block content access ⚠️ C. API Gateway: More complex, lacks built-in geographic content caching ⚠️ D. WAF geo-match: Adds complexity, doesn't provide content acceleration

Which statement about CloudFront geo-restriction capabilities is correct? A. It can block access at city and state level within countries B. It operates at the country level and can use whitelist or blacklist approaches C. It requires custom Lambda@Edge functions to implement geographic blocking D. It only works with static content stored in S3, not dynamic content ✅ B. It operates at the country level and can use whitelist or blacklist approaches 🎯 Key concept: CloudFront geo-restriction is a built-in feature that works at the country level and supports both whitelist (allow only specified countries) and blacklist (block specified countries) configurations. For finer granularity, you need third-party geolocation services. ⚠️ A. City/state level: Built-in geo-restriction only works at country level ⚠️ C. Lambda@Edge required: Geo-restriction is a native CloudFront feature ⚠️ D. Only static content: Works with any origin type, including dynamic content

A solutions architect proposes using VPC Network ACLs to block entire countries' IP ranges for compliance requirements. Why is this approach problematic? A. Network ACLs don't support geographic IP range blocking B. Network ACLs have rule limits and countries have dynamic IP ranges making this operationally complex C. Network ACLs only work at the subnet level, not at the country level D. Network ACLs are stateful and would block return traffic ✅ B. Network ACLs have rule limits and countries have dynamic IP ranges making this operationally complex Network ACLs have a limited number of rules (typically 20 per ACL), and countries have thousands of IP ranges that change frequently. This creates an operational nightmare of constantly updating and managing multiple ACLs across subnets. 🎯 Better approach: Use CloudFront geo-restriction which handles country-level blocking automatically at edge locations without rule limits or IP range management overhead.

A company uses LDAP for employee authentication and plans to release a mobile app with federated AWS access. The app must use a custom-built authentication solution and IAM roles for permissions. Due to strict security requirements, the solution must be custom-built. Which TWO options enable authentication and authorization for the mobile application? A. Build a custom SAML-compatible solution to handle authentication and authorization. Configure the solution to use LDAP for user authentication and use SAML assertion to perform authorization to the IAM identity provider. B. Build a custom LDAP connector using Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda function for user authentication. Use Amazon DynamoDB to store user authorization tokens. C. Build a custom OpenID Connect-compatible solution for the user authentication functionality. Use Amazon Cognito Identity Pools for authorizing access to AWS resources. D. Build a custom SAML-compatible solution for user authentication. Leverage AWS IAM Identity Center for authorizing access to AWS resources. E. Build a custom OpenID Connect-compatible solution in combination with AWS IAM Identity Center to create authentication and authorization functionality for the application. ✅ A & C. SAML with LDAP authentication + OpenID Connect with Cognito Identity Pools 🎯 Why correct: Both solutions provide custom authentication while properly integrating with AWS federation. SAML assertions enable IAM role assumption, while OpenID Connect with Cognito Identity Pools provides temporary AWS credentials for mobile federated access. ⚠️ B. Custom LDAP connector with DynamoDB token storage Storing authorization tokens permanently in DynamoDB violates security best practices. Tokens should be temporary and generated upon authentication, not persistently stored. This approach also doesn't leverage AWS federation mechanisms properly. ⚠️ D. SAML with IAM Identity Center IAM Identity Center supports single sign-on to business applications through web browsers only, not mobile applications. The requirement specifically mentions mobile app access, making this solution incompatible. ⚠️ E. OpenID Connect with IAM Identity Center IAM Identity Center only supports SAML 2.0-based applications, not OpenID Connect. This combination is technically incompatible and won't work for the mobile authentication scenario.

When should you choose SAML federation over OpenID Connect for AWS mobile authentication? A. When you need to integrate with existing enterprise LDAP systems and require assertion-based authorization B. When you need simple social login integration with minimal enterprise requirements C. When you want to avoid custom development and use managed authentication services D. When you need to support only web-based applications without mobile access ✅ A. When you need to integrate with existing enterprise LDAP systems and require assertion-based authorization SAML Federation • Enterprise identity integration • Assertion-based authorization • Complex attribute mapping • LDAP/AD compatibility • Role-based access control OpenID Connect • Simple token-based auth • Social identity providers • JSON Web Tokens (JWT) • Lightweight mobile integration • Modern web standards 🎯 Decision rule: Choose SAML when integrating with enterprise directories and complex authorization needs. Choose OpenID Connect for modern mobile apps with simpler authentication requirements.

Which statement about Amazon Cognito Identity Pools is correct? A. Identity Pools store user credentials and handle password authentication directly B. Identity Pools provide temporary AWS credentials for authenticated and unauthenticated users C. Identity Pools can only work with Amazon Cognito User Pools, not external identity providers D. Identity Pools require permanent IAM users to be created for each federated user ✅ B. Identity Pools provide temporary AWS credentials for authenticated and unauthenticated users 🎯 Key insight: Cognito Identity Pools act as a credential broker, exchanging identity tokens from various providers (including OpenID Connect, SAML, User Pools, or social providers) for temporary AWS credentials. This enables secure, temporary access to AWS resources without permanent IAM users. Option A describes User Pools, not Identity Pools. Option C is wrong because Identity Pools work with many external providers. Option D contradicts the fundamental purpose of federation.

A mobile application needs to authenticate users against an existing corporate LDAP directory and provide them with temporary AWS access using custom authentication logic . The solution must support mobile devices and follow enterprise security standards. Which authentication approach best addresses these requirements? A. AWS IAM Identity Center with SAML integration B. Custom SAML IdP with LDAP backend and IAM role assumption C. Amazon Cognito User Pools with LDAP integration D. Direct LDAP authentication with stored DynamoDB tokens ✅ B. Custom SAML IdP with LDAP backend and IAM role assumption 🎯 Perfect match: Custom SAML solution allows integration with existing LDAP while providing enterprise-grade federation. SAML assertions enable temporary AWS credential generation through IAM role assumption, meeting both custom authentication and mobile access requirements. ⚠️ A: IAM Identity Center only supports web browsers, not mobile apps ⚠️ C: Cognito User Pools can't directly integrate with LDAP directories ⚠️ D: Storing tokens permanently violates security best practices

A solutions architect proposes using AWS IAM Identity Center for mobile application authentication with federated AWS access. Why is this approach problematic? A. IAM Identity Center doesn't support SAML 2.0 authentication protocols B. IAM Identity Center only supports web browser-based SSO, not mobile applications C. IAM Identity Center requires separate IAM users for each federated identity D. IAM Identity Center cannot integrate with external identity providers ✅ B. IAM Identity Center only supports web browser-based SSO, not mobile applications IAM Identity Center is designed for enterprise SSO to business applications through web browsers. It lacks the mobile SDK and token-based authentication mechanisms needed for mobile app integration. Mobile apps require different authentication flows and credential management. 🎯 Better approach: Use Amazon Cognito Identity Pools with OpenID Connect or custom SAML IdP for mobile authentication. These services provide mobile SDKs and support token-based authentication suitable for mobile applications.

An accounting firm runs 200+ EC2 instances (Windows and Linux) in production. They need monthly performance checks collecting system details like memory usage, disk space , and other metrics. System logs must be analyzed with AWS Analytics tools and results stored in S3 . Which is the most efficient way to collect and analyze logs with minimal effort? A. Set up unified CloudWatch Logs agent on each instance, analyze with CloudWatch Logs Insights B. Enable Traffic Mirroring, install AWS CDK, create custom daemon script for CloudWatch Logs C. Install AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) on each instance for CloudWatch Logs D. Install AWS Inspector Agent on each instance, use CloudWatch dashboard for analysis ✅ A. Set up unified CloudWatch Logs agent on each instance, analyze with CloudWatch Logs Insights 🎯 Why correct: The unified CloudWatch agent collects both logs and metrics with one installation, supports Windows/Linux, provides better performance, and CloudWatch Logs Insights enables interactive log analysis with purpose-built query language. ⚠️ B. Traffic Mirroring + AWS CDK + custom daemon Requires significant development effort to create custom monitoring solution. Traffic Mirroring only copies network traffic from ENIs, not system metrics. This violates the "minimal effort" requirement and is unnecessarily complex. ⚠️ C. AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) While valid, SSM Agent requires manual connection to instances for log troubleshooting, making it time-consuming. CloudWatch Agent is more efficient for monitoring and automatically sends data to CloudWatch Logs. ⚠️ D. AWS Inspector Agent + CloudWatch dashboard Inspector is a security assessment service for vulnerability scanning, not system performance monitoring. CloudWatch dashboards are for resource monitoring across regions, not interactive log analysis like the scenario requires.

When should you choose CloudWatch Agent over SSM Agent for EC2 monitoring? A. When you need remote command execution capabilities B. When you need automated log collection and real-time monitoring C. When you need patch management functionality D. When you need session management for shell access ✅ B. When you need automated log collection and real-time monitoring CloudWatch Agent • Automated log and metric collection • Real-time performance monitoring • Custom metrics (memory, disk) • Better performance for monitoring • Unified logs + metrics collection SSM Agent • Remote command execution • Patch management • Session Manager (shell access) • Configuration management • Manual log file access 🎯 Decision rule: Choose CloudWatch Agent for automated monitoring and log analysis. Choose SSM Agent for systems management tasks like patching and remote access.

Which statement about CloudWatch Logs Insights is correct? A. It requires setting up Elasticsearch clusters for log indexing B. It provides a purpose-built query language for interactive log analysis C. It only works with application logs, not system metrics D. It stores queries permanently and requires manual refresh for new data ✅ B. It provides a purpose-built query language for interactive log analysis 🎯 Why correct: CloudWatch Logs Insights has a built-in query language with simple commands, autocompletion, field discovery, and sample queries for AWS services. It enables real-time interactive analysis without external tools. The other options are incorrect: no Elasticsearch needed, works with all log types, and queries run against live data automatically.

A company needs to collect memory usage and disk space metrics from 200+ EC2 instances running both Windows and Linux . The solution must work with minimal configuration effort . Which service best addresses this requirement? A. AWS Systems Manager Session Manager B. Unified CloudWatch Agent C. AWS Config Rules D. Amazon Inspector ✅ B. Unified CloudWatch Agent 🎯 Key trigger: "Memory usage and disk space metrics" + "Windows and Linux" + "minimal effort" = CloudWatch Agent. It's the only service that collects custom system metrics from both OS types with single agent installation. ⚠️ A. Session Manager provides shell access, not metric collection ⚠️ C. Config Rules track configuration compliance, not performance metrics ⚠️ D. Inspector performs security assessments, not system monitoring

A solutions architect proposes using Traffic Mirroring with custom scripts to collect EC2 system metrics. Why is this problematic? A. Traffic Mirroring only copies network traffic, not system performance data B. Traffic Mirroring is too expensive for 200+ instances C. Traffic Mirroring doesn't support Windows instances D. Traffic Mirroring requires VPC peering connections ✅ A. Traffic Mirroring only copies network traffic, not system performance data Traffic Mirroring is a VPC feature that copies network packets from ENIs to analysis appliances. It cannot access system metrics like memory usage or disk space that exist within the operating system. 🎯 Better approach: Use CloudWatch Agent which runs inside the EC2 instance and can access system-level metrics directly through the operating system APIs.

A company launched a central employee registry application with microservices architecture in Docker. Management teams in different VPCs need to connect to this central repository. Requirements: Traffic must not traverse public Internet and IT Security must be notified of denied requests with source IPs . How should the Solutions Architect implement this architecture? A. Set up Transit VPC with third-party VPN appliances and AWS Config rules B. Set up IPSec Tunnels between VPCs with VPC Flow Logs C. Link VPCs using VPC Peering with VPC Flow Logs D. Use AWS Direct Connect between VPCs with VPC Flow Logs ✅ C. Link VPCs using VPC Peering with VPC Flow Logs 🎯 Why correct: VPC Peering enables private routing between VPCs within AWS network, avoiding public Internet. VPC Flow Logs capture rejected traffic with source IPs, meeting both security requirements perfectly. ⚠️ A. Transit VPC with VPN appliances VPN appliances use public Internet for data transfer, violating the requirement. AWS Config rules cannot capture source IPs of incoming requests - this is not their function. ⚠️ B. IPSec Tunnels IPSec tunnels use the Internet to transfer data between VPCs, directly violating the requirement that traffic must not traverse public Internet. ⚠️ D. AWS Direct Connect Direct Connect cannot be set up between different VPCs - it's designed for dedicated connections between on-premises data centers and AWS VPCs, not VPC-to-VPC connectivity.

When connecting multiple VPCs within AWS, when should you choose VPC Peering over AWS Transit Gateway? A. When you need hub-and-spoke connectivity with centralized routing B. When you have simple point-to-point connectivity between a few VPCs C. When you need to connect thousands of VPCs with complex routing D. When you require on-premises connectivity through VPN or Direct Connect ✅ B. When you have simple point-to-point connectivity between a few VPCs VPC Peering • Direct point-to-point connection • No additional hops or latency • Cost-effective for simple scenarios • No transitive routing • Mesh topology for multiple VPCs AWS Transit Gateway • Hub-and-spoke architecture • Centralized routing and management • Supports thousands of connections • Transitive routing capabilities • On-premises integration 🎯 Decision rule: Choose VPC Peering for simple, direct connections between few VPCs. Choose Transit Gateway for complex, scalable network topologies with centralized management needs.

Which statement about VPC Flow Logs is correct? A. Flow Logs capture application-level data and can decrypt encrypted traffic B. Flow Logs impact network performance and add latency to traffic C. Flow Logs collect data outside the network traffic path without affecting performance D. Flow Logs can only be published to Amazon S3, not CloudWatch Logs ✅ C. Flow Logs collect data outside the network traffic path without affecting performance 🎯 Key insight: VPC Flow Logs operate as a passive monitoring service that captures IP traffic metadata without interfering with actual network traffic flow. They can publish to both CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3 , capture network-level (not application-level) data, and cannot decrypt encrypted traffic.

A solutions architect proposes using AWS Config rules to monitor and capture source IP addresses of denied network requests for security auditing. Why is this approach problematic? A. AWS Config rules are too expensive for network monitoring B. AWS Config rules monitor resource configuration compliance, not network traffic C. AWS Config rules only work with EC2 instances, not VPCs D. AWS Config rules require root access to function properly ✅ B. AWS Config rules monitor resource configuration compliance, not network traffic AWS Config is designed to track resource configuration changes and evaluate compliance against rules - it cannot capture real-time network traffic data like source IPs of denied requests. This is fundamentally outside its service scope. 🎯 Better approach: Use VPC Flow Logs to capture network traffic metadata including source IPs, security group actions, and connection details. Flow Logs are specifically designed for network monitoring and security analysis.

A company needs to monitor all network traffic flowing through their VPC, including source and destination IPs , for security compliance and troubleshooting without impacting network performance . Which AWS service best addresses this requirement? A. AWS CloudTrail B. Amazon GuardDuty C. VPC Flow Logs D. AWS Config ✅ C. VPC Flow Logs 🎯 Perfect match: VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata (source/destination IPs, ports, protocols) for all network interfaces in a VPC. Data collection occurs outside the traffic path, ensuring zero performance impact while providing comprehensive network visibility for security and troubleshooting. CloudTrail: Logs API calls, not network traffic GuardDuty: Threat detection service, doesn't provide raw traffic logs Config: Tracks resource configuration, not network flows

A company's flagship product page on a three-tier .NET web application with MySQL database experienced downtime during traffic surge. Management wants to migrate to AWS with infrastructure capable of handling 300,000 peak users while being highly available, scalable, and cost-effective . Which design option satisfies these requirements? A. Elastic Beanstalk with EC2 Auto Scaling behind Network Load Balancer and RDS MySQL Multi-AZ B. CloudFormation stack with EC2 Auto Scaling behind Application Load Balancer and Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ with "retain" deletion policy C. CloudFormation stack with ECS cluster using Spot Instances behind ALB and RDS MySQL Multi-AZ with "snapshot" deletion policy D. Elastic Beanstalk across two regions with ALB in each region and Aurora MySQL with cross-region read replica ✅ B. CloudFormation stack with EC2 Auto Scaling behind Application Load Balancer and Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ with "retain" deletion policy 🎯 Why correct: ALB provides Layer 7 load balancing ideal for web applications, Auto Scaling handles traffic surges across multiple AZs for high availability, Aurora MySQL offers better performance than RDS MySQL, and "retain" deletion policy prevents accidental data loss during stack operations. ⚠️ A. Elastic Beanstalk with Network Load Balancer Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 (TCP) and cannot handle HTTP/HTTPS routing decisions based on application attributes like headers or cookies that web applications require. ALB is the correct choice for web applications. ⚠️ C. ECS with Spot Instances Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS based on supply and demand, causing reliability issues for a flagship product page. The "snapshot" deletion policy requires significant restoration time if the stack is deleted accidentally. ⚠️ D. Multi-region deployment Deploying across two regions is unnecessarily expensive and complex for this requirement. Multi-AZ deployment within a single region provides sufficient high availability. The read replica setup forces all writes to the primary region, adding latency.

When should you choose Application Load Balancer over Network Load Balancer for web applications? A. When you need Layer 4 load balancing for maximum performance B. When you need HTTP/HTTPS routing and content-based routing decisions C. When you need to handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency D. When you need static IP addresses for whitelisting in firewalls ✅ B. When you need HTTP/HTTPS routing and content-based routing decisions Application Load Balancer (ALB) • Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) load balancing • Content-based routing (path, host, headers) • WebSocket and HTTP/2 support • Integration with WAF • SSL termination with SNI Network Load Balancer (NLB) • Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) load balancing • Ultra-high performance (millions RPS) • Static IP addresses • Preserves source IP • Lower latency than ALB 🎯 Decision rule: Choose ALB for web applications needing HTTP routing, SSL termination, or content-based decisions. Choose NLB for non-HTTP protocols, extreme performance requirements, or when static IPs are needed.

Which statement about CloudFormation deletion policies is correct? A. "Snapshot" policy immediately creates a backup and deletes the resource B. "Retain" policy keeps the resource and removes it from CloudFormation management C. "Delete" policy is the safest option for production databases D. Deletion policies only apply to S3 buckets and cannot be used with RDS ✅ B. "Retain" policy keeps the resource and removes it from CloudFormation management 🎯 Why correct: The "Retain" policy preserves the resource when the stack is deleted but removes CloudFormation's ability to manage it. "Snapshot" creates a backup but still deletes the resource, requiring restoration time. "Delete" removes the resource entirely, which is risky for production data. Deletion policies work with many resource types including RDS, EBS, and S3.

A company needs to handle sudden traffic spikes for their web application while maintaining high availability and cost efficiency . The application must scale automatically based on demand. Which AWS service combination best addresses this requirement? A. Reserved Instances with manual scaling B. Auto Scaling Groups with Application Load Balancer C. Spot Fleet with Network Load Balancer D. Elastic Beanstalk with single Availability Zone deployment ✅ B. Auto Scaling Groups with Application Load Balancer 🎯 Perfect match: Auto Scaling Groups automatically add/remove instances based on demand (handles spikes), ALB distributes traffic across healthy instances (high availability), and you only pay for instances when needed (cost efficient). Reserved Instances require capacity planning and don't auto-scale. Spot Fleet risks instance reclamation during traffic spikes. Single AZ deployment lacks high availability.

Requirements: MySQL-compatible database , Multi-AZ deployment , better performance than standard RDS , automatic failover , and cost optimization for read-heavy workloads . Which database service meets ALL requirements? A. Amazon RDS MySQL Multi-AZ B. Amazon Aurora MySQL C. Amazon DynamoDB D. Amazon DocumentDB ✅ B. Amazon Aurora MySQL 🎯 Why Aurora wins: MySQL-compatible ✓, Multi-AZ by design ✓, 5x better performance than RDS MySQL ✓, automatic failover in seconds ✓, and Aurora Replicas provide cost-effective read scaling ✓. RDS MySQL lacks the performance advantage and read replica cost efficiency. RDS MySQL meets basic requirements but lacks Aurora's performance benefits. DynamoDB is NoSQL, not MySQL-compatible. DocumentDB is MongoDB-compatible, not MySQL.

A company migrates Docker containers to AWS Fargate on a private subnet with no direct internet connection . When launching Fargate tasks, they receive: CannotPullContainerError: API error (500): Get https://111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/v2/: net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection Which solution fixes this ECR image pull issue? A. Switch from "awsvpc" to "bridge" network mode to allow internet connections B. Set auto-assign public IP to DISABLED and launch NAT gateway on private subnet C. Set auto-assign public IP to ENABLED and create gateway VPC endpoint for ECR D. Set auto-assign public IP to DISABLED and launch NAT gateway on public subnet ✅ D. Set auto-assign public IP to DISABLED and launch NAT gateway on public subnet 🎯 Why correct: Private subnet Fargate tasks need internet access to pull ECR images. NAT gateway must be in public subnet with IGW route to provide outbound internet access for private resources. ⚠️ A. Switch to bridge network mode Fargate only supports awsvpc network mode - each task gets its own ENI. Bridge mode is not available in Fargate, making this technically impossible. ⚠️ B. NAT gateway on private subnet NAT gateway requires a public IP and direct IGW route. Placing it on private subnet creates the same connectivity limitation as the Fargate tasks themselves. ⚠️ C. Enable public IP with gateway VPC endpoint Private subnet tasks shouldn't have public IPs. Also, ECR requires interface VPC endpoints, not gateway endpoints. Gateway endpoints only support S3 and DynamoDB.

Which statement about AWS Fargate networking is correct? A. Fargate supports both awsvpc and bridge network modes for flexibility B. Each Fargate task receives its own elastic network interface (ENI) C. Fargate tasks can share ENIs to reduce IP address consumption D. Bridge network mode provides better security isolation than awsvpc ✅ B. Each Fargate task receives its own elastic network interface (ENI) 🎯 Key concept: Fargate only supports awsvpc network mode, where each task gets a dedicated ENI for VPC communication and security isolation. This provides task-level network isolation but requires more IP addresses. Bridge mode is not supported in Fargate - it's an EC2 container feature only.

When should you use NAT Gateway versus VPC Endpoints for private subnet internet access? A. Always use VPC Endpoints as they're more secure than NAT Gateway B. Use NAT Gateway for general internet access, VPC Endpoints for specific AWS services C. VPC Endpoints are cheaper so should be used whenever possible D. NAT Gateway only works with public subnets, VPC Endpoints work with private subnets ✅ B. Use NAT Gateway for general internet access, VPC Endpoints for specific AWS services NAT Gateway • General internet/external API access • ECR image pulls from internet • Third-party service calls • Software updates/packages • Charges for data processing VPC Endpoints • Direct private access to AWS services • S3, DynamoDB (Gateway endpoints) • ECR, ECS, other services (Interface endpoints) • No internet gateway required • No data processing charges 🎯 Decision rule: Use NAT Gateway when tasks need general internet access. Use VPC Endpoints when accessing AWS services privately without internet routing.

A company runs Fargate tasks in private subnets that need to pull images from ECR and access S3 buckets , but they want to minimize data transfer costs and avoid internet routing for AWS service calls. Which combination provides the most cost-effective solution? A. NAT Gateway only for all external access B. Interface VPC Endpoints for ECR and Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 C. Public subnets with Internet Gateway for direct access D. Interface VPC Endpoints for both ECR and S3 ✅ B. Interface VPC Endpoints for ECR and Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 🎯 Cost optimization: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) have no hourly charges, only Interface endpoints have hourly fees. This hybrid approach minimizes VPC endpoint costs while avoiding NAT Gateway data processing charges for AWS service access. A is expensive due to NAT Gateway data processing fees. C violates private subnet requirement. D unnecessarily uses costly Interface endpoint for S3 when free Gateway endpoint is available.

A solutions architect proposes placing NAT Gateway in the same private subnet as Fargate tasks to reduce network hops. Why is this problematic? A. NAT Gateway cannot be deployed in private subnets due to service limitations B. NAT Gateway needs public IP and Internet Gateway route, unavailable in private subnets C. Private subnet NAT Gateway creates circular routing dependencies D. Fargate tasks cannot communicate with NAT Gateway in same subnet ✅ B. NAT Gateway needs public IP and Internet Gateway route, unavailable in private subnets NAT Gateway requires a public IP address and direct route to Internet Gateway to function. Private subnets by definition lack these internet connectivity components, making the NAT Gateway unable to provide outbound internet access. 🎯 Better approach: Deploy NAT Gateway in public subnet with IGW route, then configure private subnet route table to send 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to the NAT Gateway for internet access.

A company hosts its online immigration system on one large EC2 instance with attached EBS volumes . The system accepts documents and photos, performs automated verification, but becomes unavailable during surges . Processing takes too long and EBS storage is insufficient for growing data uploads. Which option provides high availability and scalable storage? A. Upgrade to EBS with Provisioned IOPS and use SQS queue with Auto Scaling EC2 instances B. Use SNS to distribute tasks to EC2 instances with Auto Scaling based on SQS queue length C. Use EBS with Provisioned IOPS, SNS for task distribution, Auto Scaling based on SNS notifications D. Use S3 with cross-region replication, SQS queue, Auto Scaling EC2 instances, CloudFormation for multi-region deployment ✅ D. S3 with cross-region replication, SQS queue, Auto Scaling EC2 instances, CloudFormation for multi-region deployment 🎯 Why correct: S3 provides unlimited scalable storage for documents/photos, SQS enables reliable task distribution to multiple EC2 instances, Auto Scaling handles surge capacity, and cross-region replication ensures high availability. ⚠️ A. EBS with Provisioned IOPS and SQS EBS volumes have size limits and don't scale automatically like S3. Each EC2 instance would need its own EBS volume, making data synchronization complex and expensive compared to centralized S3 storage. ⚠️ B. SNS for task distribution SNS is for notifications, not task queuing. It doesn't provide message persistence or retry logic needed for processing tasks. SQS is designed for reliable task distribution with dead letter queues and visibility timeouts. ⚠️ C. EBS storage with SNS Combines two problems: EBS lacks scalability for growing file storage, and SNS isn't appropriate for task queuing. This doesn't solve the core storage scalability issue or provide proper task distribution.

When should you choose SQS over SNS for distributing processing tasks? A. When you need real-time notifications to multiple subscribers B. When you need reliable task queuing with message persistence and retry logic C. When you need to broadcast messages to email and SMS endpoints D. When you need fan-out messaging to multiple services simultaneously ✅ B. When you need reliable task queuing with message persistence and retry logic SQS (Simple Queue Service) • Message persistence and durability • Visibility timeout for processing • Dead letter queues for failed messages • Polling-based message consumption • Task distribution and load balancing SNS (Simple Notification Service) • Real-time push notifications • Fan-out to multiple subscribers • Email, SMS, HTTP endpoints • Fire-and-forget delivery • Event-driven architecture 🎯 Decision rule: Choose SQS when you need reliable task processing with retries and persistence. Choose SNS when you need to notify multiple subscribers immediately about events.

Which statement about S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) is correct? A. CRR automatically replicates all existing objects when first enabled B. CRR only replicates objects uploaded after replication is enabled C. CRR requires both source and destination buckets to be in the same AWS account D. CRR works without versioning enabled on the source bucket ✅ B. CRR only replicates objects uploaded after replication is enabled 🎯 Key insight: CRR is prospective only - existing objects must be copied separately using S3 Batch Operations or AWS CLI. Versioning must be enabled on both buckets, and cross-account replication is supported with proper IAM roles.

A company needs storage that: scales automatically , supports millions of files , provides high durability (99.999999999%) , and allows concurrent access from multiple EC2 instances . Which service meets ALL requirements? A. EBS with Provisioned IOPS B. EFS (Elastic File System) C. S3 (Simple Storage Service) D. Instance Store volumes ✅ C. S3 (Simple Storage Service) 🎯 Why S3 wins: Automatic scaling (no limits), 99.999999999% durability, designed for millions/billions of objects, RESTful API allows concurrent access from any number of EC2 instances without mounting complexity. EBS: Limited to single AZ, size limits, requires manual scaling EFS: Good for file system access but more expensive than S3 for pure object storage Instance Store: Ephemeral storage, lost when instance stops

A company's application experiences unpredictable traffic spikes that overwhelm their single EC2 instance, causing service unavailability . They need to distribute workload automatically when demand increases. Which combination best addresses this scaling challenge? A. Application Load Balancer + Static EC2 instances B. Auto Scaling Group + SQS + CloudWatch metrics C. Lambda functions + API Gateway D. Elastic Beanstalk + Manual scaling ✅ B. Auto Scaling Group + SQS + CloudWatch metrics 🎯 Perfect trigger match: Auto Scaling responds to demand spikes, SQS decouples and queues work during surges, CloudWatch metrics (like SQS queue depth) trigger scaling actions automatically. A: Static instances can't scale with demand C: Good for event-driven but may not suit all application types D: Manual scaling defeats the purpose of automation

A company hosts production applications in Docker containers on self-managed VMs with commercial Oracle Java SE (expensive licensing). MySQL databases use source-replica setup for HA. Company wants to migrate to AWS Cloud to gain flexibility and agility , switch to OpenJDK to save licensing costs, with minimal application changes . Which migration strategy meets these requirements? A. Re-factor/re-architect: Convert Docker containers to AWS Lambda Functions, MySQL to DynamoDB using AWS SCT B. Re-platform: Deploy Docker containers on AWS App Runner, MySQL to DynamoDB using AWS SCT C. Re-host: Mirror current setup on EC2 instances, manual MySQL dump to S3 and restore D. Re-platform: Run Docker containers on Amazon ECS, migrate MySQL to RDS using DMS ✅ D. Re-platform with Amazon ECS and RDS migration 🎯 Why correct: Re-platforming provides cloud benefits (elasticity, managed services) while minimizing application changes. ECS handles Docker containers natively, RDS provides managed MySQL with built-in HA, and DMS enables seamless database migration. ⚠️ A. Re-factor/re-architect with Lambda + DynamoDB Requires major application changes to convert Docker containers to serverless functions. Converting relational MySQL to NoSQL DynamoDB needs significant application refactoring, violating the "minimal changes" requirement. ⚠️ B. Re-platform with App Runner + DynamoDB While App Runner supports containers, converting MySQL to DynamoDB requires major application changes and schema redesign. The scenario doesn't justify moving from relational to NoSQL database. ⚠️ C. Re-host with EC2 mirroring Lift-and-shift approach doesn't leverage cloud benefits like elasticity and managed services. Manual database migration is error-prone compared to DMS, and self-managing MySQL on EC2 loses HA benefits of RDS.

When should you choose Amazon ECS over AWS Lambda for containerized applications? A. When you need event-driven, stateless functions with automatic scaling B. When you have long-running processes, persistent connections, or need full container control C. When you want to avoid managing any infrastructure whatsoever D. When you need sub-second response times for simple compute tasks ✅ B. When you have long-running processes, persistent connections, or need full container control Amazon ECS • Long-running applications • Persistent connections/state • Full container orchestration • Custom networking/security • Existing Docker workflows AWS Lambda • Event-driven functions • Stateless processing • 15-minute execution limit • Automatic scaling • Pay-per-invocation 🎯 Decision rule: Choose ECS when you need container orchestration for traditional applications. Choose Lambda when you can refactor to stateless, event-driven functions under 15 minutes.

Which statement about AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is correct? A. DMS can only migrate between identical database engines (MySQL to MySQL) B. DMS requires downtime during the entire migration process C. DMS supports homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations with continuous data replication D. DMS automatically converts application code to work with the target database ✅ C. DMS supports homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations with continuous data replication 🎯 Why correct: DMS supports both same-engine (homogeneous) and different-engine (heterogeneous) migrations. It uses Change Data Capture (CDC) to continuously replicate changes, minimizing downtime. For schema conversion in heterogeneous migrations, you use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) separately. ⚠️ A: DMS supports heterogeneous migrations between different engines. ⚠️ B: DMS minimizes downtime with CDC replication. ⚠️ D: DMS migrates data; application code changes require separate tools like SCT for schema conversion.

A company needs to migrate MySQL databases from on-premises to AWS with minimal downtime and wants to maintain the same database engine for compatibility . Which combination of services best addresses this requirement? A. AWS SCT + Amazon DynamoDB B. AWS DMS + Amazon RDS MySQL C. AWS DataSync + Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL D. AWS Backup + Amazon DocumentDB ✅ B. AWS DMS + Amazon RDS MySQL 🎯 Perfect match: DMS provides continuous data replication for minimal downtime migration. RDS MySQL maintains the same engine for full compatibility. This is a homogeneous migration requiring no schema changes. ⚠️ A: SCT + DynamoDB changes from relational to NoSQL, breaking compatibility. ⚠️ C: DataSync is for file migration, and PostgreSQL changes the database engine. ⚠️ D: Backup doesn't provide continuous replication, and DocumentDB is for MongoDB workloads.

Requirements: Containerized applications with Docker, managed container orchestration , integration with AWS services , cost optimization , and minimal operational overhead . Which service meets ALL requirements? A. Self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 B. Amazon ECS with Fargate C. AWS Lambda with container images D. Docker containers on EC2 instances ✅ B. Amazon ECS with Fargate 🎯 Why: Managed orchestration ✓ (ECS handles scheduling), AWS integration ✓ (native IAM, VPC, ALB), Cost optimization ✓ (Fargate pay-per-use), Minimal overhead ✓ (serverless containers, no EC2 management). ⚠️ A: Self-managed Kubernetes requires significant operational overhead for cluster management. ⚠️ C: Lambda has 15-minute execution limits, not suitable for long-running containerized applications. ⚠️ D: Docker on EC2 requires manual container orchestration and instance management.

A company wants to migrate three-tier web applications from on-premises VMs to AWS with the following requirements: • Import VM images to AWS • Synchronize changes until production cutover • Minimal downtime during cutover • Migrate both root volumes and terabytes of data volumes • Minimal operational overhead Which solution meets all requirements? A. Use AWS Application Discovery Service and Migration Hub to group VMs. Write AWS CLI scripts for VM Import/Export to import VMs as AMIs at regular intervals. B. Use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) for root volumes only. Import data volumes separately using CLI import-snapshot commands. C. Use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) to migrate entire VMs. Install replication agents on each tier for continuous sync. D. Write AWS CLI scripts using VM Import/Export for complete VM migration. Schedule regular runs for synchronization. ✅ C. AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) with replication agents 🎯 Why correct: MGN provides continuous replication with minimal operational overhead, supports both root and data volumes automatically, and enables quick cutover with minimal downtime through its automated lift-and-shift process. ⚠️ A. Discovery Service + VM Import/Export VM Import/Export cannot sync incremental changes - it requires full VM re-import after each change, creating massive operational overhead and extended downtime windows for terabyte-scale data. ⚠️ B. MGN for root volumes + manual data import Separating root and data volume migration adds unnecessary operational complexity when MGN can handle both automatically, violating the minimal overhead requirement. ⚠️ D. Scheduled VM Import/Export scripts VM Import/Export fundamentally cannot perform incremental synchronization - each "sync" requires importing the entire multi-terabyte VM again, making this approach operationally impossible.

When should you choose AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) over VM Import/Export for server migration? A. When you need one-time migration of static VM images with no ongoing changes B. When you need continuous synchronization with minimal downtime cutover C. When you only need to migrate virtual machine templates for future use D. When you want to convert VMs to container images ✅ B. When you need continuous synchronization with minimal downtime cutover AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) • Continuous replication with incremental sync • Automated cutover process • Minimal downtime (minutes) • Handles live, changing servers • Built-in testing capabilities • Supports both root and data volumes automatically VM Import/Export • One-time import of static VM images • No incremental sync capabilities • Requires full re-import for changes • Best for inactive/template VMs • Manual process with higher complexity • Good for disaster recovery scenarios 🎯 Decision rule: Choose MGN when migrating active production servers that need ongoing sync and quick cutover. Choose VM Import/Export for static VM templates or one-time migrations of inactive systems.

A company needs to migrate 50 production servers from VMware to AWS. The servers must remain operational during migration, with changes continuously synchronized until a planned cutover weekend. The solution must minimize manual intervention and support both Linux and Windows servers. Which AWS service best addresses this requirement? A. AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) B. AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) C. AWS DataSync D. AWS VM Import/Export ✅ B. AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) 🎯 Key trigger phrases: "production servers remain operational", "continuously synchronized", "planned cutover", and "minimize manual intervention" all point to MGN's continuous replication and automated cutover capabilities. ⚠️ A. DMS: Designed for database migration, not full server migration ⚠️ C. DataSync: File transfer service, not server migration ⚠️ D. VM Import/Export: Cannot maintain continuous sync of operational servers

Which statement about AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) replication agents is correct? A. Replication agents only work with VMware vSphere environments B. Agents must be installed on a separate dedicated server in each network C. Agents are installed directly on source servers and support both Linux and Windows D. Agents require root/administrator access and will restart the source server during installation ✅ C. Agents are installed directly on source servers and support both Linux and Windows 🎯 MGN replication agents are lightweight software installed on each source server (physical, virtual, or cloud) that you want to migrate. They work across multiple hypervisors and cloud platforms, not just VMware. Installation is non-disruptive and doesn't require server restarts, making them ideal for production environments. ⚠️ A: MGN works with any x86-based server, not just VMware environments ⚠️ B: Agents install on the actual servers being migrated, not separate infrastructure ⚠️ D: While admin access is needed, installation doesn't require server restarts

Requirements for a migration project: • Multi-terabyte data volumes attached to VMs • Zero data loss during migration • Continuous operations during migration process • Automated failback capability if issues occur • Cross-platform support (physical, VMware, Hyper-V) Which service meets ALL requirements? A. AWS Storage Gateway B. AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) C. AWS DataSync with scheduled transfers D. AWS VM Import/Export with EBS snapshots ✅ B. AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) 🎯 Requirements mapping: • Multi-terabyte volumes: MGN handles any size automatically • Zero data loss: Continuous block-level replication • Continuous operations: Non-disruptive agent installation • Automated failback: Built-in cutover and failback capabilities • Cross-platform: Supports physical, VMware, Hyper-V, and cloud servers ⚠️ A. Storage Gateway: Hybrid storage solution, not a migration service ⚠️ C. DataSync: File transfer only, no server migration or failback ⚠️ D. VM Import/Export: No continuous operations support, manual process

A multinational investment bank uses a single 1 Gbps Direct Connect to connect 10 VPCs to on-premises. Recent IT audit identified this as a single point of failure requiring immediate resolution. Which is the MOST cost-effective solution to improve connection redundancy? A. Establish MPLS connection to all 10 VPCs with BGP active/passive routing B. Establish another 1 Gbps Direct Connect with private VIFs to all 10 VPCs C. Establish another 1 Gbps Direct Connect with public VIF and VPN tunnels D. Establish VPN tunnels to each VPC terminating at VGWs with BGP ✅ D. Establish VPN tunnels to each VPC terminating at VGWs with BGP 🎯 Why correct: VPN provides cost-effective redundancy for Direct Connect. Creating a second Direct Connect is expensive for failover, while VPN offers encrypted backup connectivity at much lower cost with acceptable bandwidth reduction during failover scenarios. ⚠️ A. MPLS connection You cannot directly connect MPLS to AWS VPCs. MPLS requires colocation setup with Direct Connect facility for local cross-connect, making this solution more complex and expensive than VPN backup. ⚠️ B. Another Direct Connect with private VIFs While technically sound for redundancy, establishing another 1 Gbps Direct Connect connection is expensive compared to VPN backup. The question specifically asks for most cost-effective solution. ⚠️ C. Direct Connect with public VIF and VPN This adds unnecessary complexity and cost by requiring another Direct Connect connection. Public VIF for VPN tunnels doesn't provide cost advantage over direct VPN connections from on-premises.

When designing redundancy for hybrid connectivity, when should you choose a second Direct Connect over VPN backup? A. When cost optimization is the primary concern B. When consistent high bandwidth is critical even during failover C. When encryption is required for compliance D. When connecting fewer than 5 VPCs ✅ B. When consistent high bandwidth is critical even during failover Second Direct Connect • Maintains full bandwidth during failover • Higher cost but consistent performance • Best for bandwidth-critical applications • Requires dedicated circuit provisioning VPN Backup • Cost-effective redundancy option • Reduced bandwidth during failover • Quick to provision and configure • Built-in encryption capabilities 🎯 Decision rule: Choose second Direct Connect when applications cannot tolerate bandwidth reduction during failover. Choose VPN backup when cost optimization is priority and bandwidth reduction is acceptable.

Which statement about AWS Direct Connect Virtual Interfaces (VIFs) is correct? A. Public VIFs can directly connect to VPC private subnets B. Private VIFs require BGP peering for each VPC connection C. Transit VIFs can connect to multiple VPCs through Transit Gateway D. VIFs automatically provide encryption for all traffic ✅ C. Transit VIFs can connect to multiple VPCs through Transit Gateway 🎯 Why correct: Transit VIFs connect Direct Connect to AWS Transit Gateway, enabling connectivity to multiple VPCs through a single VIF. This simplifies network architecture compared to multiple private VIFs. Public VIFs connect to AWS public services, private VIFs connect to single VPC, and Direct Connect doesn't provide encryption by default.
