A company needs to establish backup connectivity for their existing Direct Connect with minimal cost and encryption requirements for compliance. Which solution best addresses these requirements? A. Second Direct Connect with MACsec encryption B. Site-to-Site VPN with customer gateway C. AWS PrivateLink endpoints D. Internet Gateway with NAT Gateway ✅ B. Site-to-Site VPN with customer gateway 🎯 Perfect match: Site-to-Site VPN provides cost-effective backup connectivity with built-in IPsec encryption for compliance. Quick to provision and ideal failover for Direct Connect. ⚠️ A. Second Direct Connect: Expensive and doesn't meet minimal cost requirement ⚠️ C. PrivateLink: For service connectivity, not backup site connectivity ⚠️ D. Internet Gateway: Doesn't provide encrypted backup connectivity

Requirements: Connect 15 VPCs to on-premises, cost optimization priority , centralized routing management , bandwidth up to 100 Gbps , and simplified network architecture . Which service combination meets ALL requirements? A. Direct Connect with 15 private VIFs B. Direct Connect with Transit VIF and Transit Gateway C. Site-to-Site VPN to each VPC D. AWS PrivateLink with VPC endpoints ✅ B. Direct Connect with Transit VIF and Transit Gateway 🎯 Perfect alignment: Transit Gateway provides centralized routing for all 15 VPCs through single Transit VIF, reducing complexity and cost. Direct Connect supports up to 100 Gbps bandwidth requirement that VPN cannot match. ⚠️ A. 15 private VIFs: More complex management, higher costs ⚠️ C. VPN to each VPC: Cannot achieve 100 Gbps bandwidth ⚠️ D. PrivateLink: For service access, not site-to-site connectivity

A retail company's web application on Auto Scaling EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer experienced downtime. The target group health check queries a database page, but when RDS MySQL CPU usage spiked , health checks timed out, causing Auto Scaling to continuously replace healthy instances. Web server metrics were normal. Which TWO solutions prevent this issue and improve scalability? A. Create CloudWatch alarm to monitor RDS and set alarm action to recover the instance by rebooting B. Change health check to simple HTML page, use Route 53 health check for database monitoring with CloudWatch alarms C. Create RDS read replicas and configure application to use single reader endpoint for reads D. Change to TCP health check on EC2 instances, use Route 53 for database monitoring E. Add ElastiCache cluster to cache frequent database queries ✅ B and E. Simple HTML health checks + Route 53 monitoring, and ElastiCache caching 🎯 Why correct: Health checks that query the database create cascading failures during DB stress. Decoupling health checks from DB dependency while adding caching reduces database load and prevents false positive failures. ⚠️ A. CloudWatch RDS recovery Rebooting the database causes downtime and doesn't address the root cause. With Multi-AZ, the standby would also become overwhelmed. Recovery actions should scale, not restart resources. ⚠️ C. Read replicas only While read replicas help performance, this doesn't solve the health check problem. The same repetitive health check queries will still hit the database tier, causing the original timeout issue. ⚠️ D. TCP health checks Application Load Balancers only support HTTP/HTTPS health checks, not TCP. This is technically impossible to implement and wouldn't solve the database dependency issue anyway.

When should you use Application Load Balancer health checks versus Route 53 health checks for monitoring? A. ALB for external monitoring, Route 53 for internal target health B. ALB for target availability, Route 53 for application functionality C. ALB for database queries, Route 53 for simple page checks D. Both should always use identical health check configurations ✅ B. ALB for target availability, Route 53 for application functionality ALB Health Checks • Target instance availability • High frequency (every 30 seconds) • Simple HTTP/HTTPS only • Multiple simultaneous checks • Triggers Auto Scaling actions Route 53 Health Checks • End-to-end functionality • Lower frequency options • Complex application testing • External perspective • DNS failover integration 🎯 Decision rule: Use ALB for basic target health to prevent traffic routing to failed instances. Use Route 53 for comprehensive application monitoring including database connectivity without overwhelming backend systems.

Which statement about ElastiCache implementation for retail applications is correct? A. ElastiCache should cache all database queries including writes and updates B. ElastiCache is most effective for read-heavy workloads with frequent product searches C. ElastiCache eliminates the need for RDS read replicas in all scenarios D. ElastiCache automatically synchronizes with RDS without application changes ✅ B. ElastiCache is most effective for read-heavy workloads with frequent product searches 🎯 Why correct: Retail applications have high read-to-write ratios with customers browsing products. Caching frequent searches, product details, and catalog queries significantly reduces database load. ElastiCache requires application-level integration for cache-aside or write-through patterns. ⚠️ Wrong options: A) Never cache writes - causes data consistency issues. C) Read replicas handle different use cases than caching. D) Requires application code changes for cache integration.

A company reports that their Auto Scaling group keeps replacing healthy EC2 instances during database performance issues, even though the web servers themselves are functioning normally. Which root cause best explains this cascading failure pattern? A. Auto Scaling group minimum size is set too low B. Health check endpoint has database dependency creating false failures C. Application Load Balancer is misconfigured for multi-AZ deployment D. CloudWatch metrics are not properly configured for the instances ✅ B. Health check endpoint has database dependency creating false failures 🎯 Trigger recognition: When healthy compute resources are replaced during database issues, it indicates health checks are testing database connectivity rather than instance health. This creates a cascading failure where database problems cause infrastructure churn. A) Minimum size affects scale-down, not replacement behavior. C) Multi-AZ ALB configuration doesn't cause this pattern. D) CloudWatch metrics don't directly trigger Auto Scaling replacements.

Requirements: Monitor application health without impacting database performance , maintain Auto Scaling functionality , get notifications when application logic fails , support HTTP-based monitoring . Which monitoring architecture meets ALL requirements? A. TCP health checks with CloudWatch database alarms B. Simple ALB health checks plus Route 53 application monitoring C. Database-dependent ALB checks with ElastiCache D. CloudWatch custom metrics with Lambda health checkers ✅ B. Simple ALB health checks plus Route 53 application monitoring 🎯 Why this meets all requirements: Simple ALB checks (no DB impact) maintain Auto Scaling triggers, Route 53 monitors application logic with notifications, both support HTTP, and architecture decouples infrastructure health from application functionality. A) ALB doesn't support TCP checks. C) Still impacts database performance. D) Custom metrics add complexity without addressing the core health check separation need.

A fintech startup has a cloud-based payment processing system on AWS using EC2, DynamoDB, S3, and CloudFront . They process credit card payments and cryptocurrencies but failed PCI DSS compliance because credit card numbers are not properly encrypted. You need to fix encryption and improve CloudFront cache hit ratio . What is the best option to protect sensitive credit card information and improve cache performance? A. Add custom SSL in CloudFront. Configure origin to add User-Agent and Host headers to objects. B. Create Origin Access Control (OAC) and add to CloudFront. Configure origin to add User-Agent and Host headers. C. Configure CloudFront to use Signed URLs. Add Cache-Control max-age directive with longest practical value. D. Configure CloudFront with HTTPS and field-level encryption. Add Cache-Control max-age directive with longest practical value. ✅ D. Configure CloudFront with HTTPS and field-level encryption plus Cache-Control max-age 🎯 Why correct: Field-level encryption encrypts sensitive data at the edge and keeps it encrypted throughout the application stack, meeting PCI DSS requirements. Cache-Control max-age increases cache hit ratio by keeping objects cached longer at edge locations. ⚠️ A. Custom SSL + User-Agent/Host headers While SSL provides transport security, it doesn't encrypt specific fields like credit card numbers for PCI DSS compliance. User-Agent and Host headers actually decrease cache hit ratio by creating more cache variations. ⚠️ B. OAC + User-Agent/Host headers OAC restricts access to S3 objects but provides no encryption for sensitive data fields. User-Agent and Host headers create cache fragmentation, reducing hit ratios instead of improving them. ⚠️ C. Signed URLs + Cache-Control max-age Signed URLs control access to private content but don't encrypt credit card data at the field level. This fails to address the core PCI DSS compliance requirement for data encryption.

Which statement about CloudFront field-level encryption is correct? A. It can encrypt up to 50 data fields in a single POST request B. It encrypts data at the origin server before sending to CloudFront C. It encrypts data at CloudFront edge locations and keeps it encrypted throughout the application stack D. It only works with GET requests, not POST requests ✅ C. It encrypts data at CloudFront edge locations and keeps it encrypted throughout the application stack 🎯 Key benefit: Field-level encryption protects sensitive data from the moment it hits the edge until only authorized applications decrypt it. This ensures end-to-end protection for PCI DSS compliance. The limit is 10 fields (not 50), it works with POST requests (not GET), and encryption happens at the edge (not origin).

When should you choose field-level encryption over standard HTTPS for protecting sensitive data? A. When you need to protect data only during transport B. When you need to encrypt specific form fields and keep them encrypted throughout your application C. When you want to reduce CloudFront costs D. When you need to cache sensitive data at edge locations ✅ B. When you need to encrypt specific form fields and keep them encrypted throughout your application HTTPS Only • Encrypts data in transit • Decrypted at origin server • All backend systems see plaintext • Good for general transport security Field-Level Encryption • Encrypts specific fields at edge • Stays encrypted through application • Only authorized apps can decrypt • Required for PCI DSS compliance 🎯 Decision rule: Choose HTTPS for general transport security. Choose field-level encryption when you need specific sensitive fields (like credit cards) to remain encrypted even after reaching your servers.

A company wants to improve CloudFront cache hit ratio. They currently have many cache misses due to varying request headers. Requirements: maximize cache efficiency , reduce origin load , maintain functionality . Which Cache-Control strategy meets ALL requirements? A. Add User-Agent and Host headers to cache key B. Set Cache-Control: no-cache on all objects C. Configure Cache-Control max-age with the longest practical value D. Use Cache-Control: must-revalidate for all content ✅ C. Configure Cache-Control max-age with the longest practical value 🎯 Why this works: Longer max-age values keep objects cached at edge locations longer, reducing requests to origin and improving cache hit ratio. User-Agent/Host headers create cache fragmentation. No-cache and must-revalidate force frequent origin requests, defeating the cache purpose.

A solutions architect suggests using Origin Access Control (OAC) to encrypt credit card data for PCI DSS compliance. Why is this approach problematic? A. OAC only works with S3, not with EC2 origins B. OAC controls access but doesn't provide data encryption C. OAC increases CloudFront costs significantly D. OAC requires custom SSL certificates ✅ B. OAC controls access but doesn't provide data encryption Common misconception: OAC is an access control mechanism that restricts who can access your S3 content through CloudFront. It doesn't encrypt data fields or provide the end-to-end encryption required for PCI DSS compliance with credit card information. 🎯 Better approach: Use field-level encryption which actually encrypts sensitive data fields at the edge and keeps them encrypted throughout your application stack, meeting PCI DSS requirements.

A university's serverless online portal using Lambda and API Gateway was compromised by an SQL injection attack through the login page, causing complete data loss. The university needs a cost-effective solution to prevent future SQL injection attacks and track historical changes to firewall rules and metrics. Which solution best prevents SQL injection attacks while tracking firewall changes cost-effectively? A. Use AWS WAF with web ACL in front of Lambda functions. Use AWS Firewall Manager to track changes. B. Block attacker IP in VPC NACL, set up CloudFront with WAF web ACL. Use AWS Config to track changes. C. Create ALB with WAF, place API Gateway behind ALB with web ACL. Use AWS Firewall Manager to track changes. D. Use AWS WAF with web ACL in front of API Gateway. Use AWS Config to track changes. ✅ D. Use AWS WAF with web ACL in front of API Gateway. Use AWS Config to track changes. 🎯 Why correct: AWS WAF directly integrates with API Gateway to filter malicious requests before they reach Lambda functions. AWS Config is specifically designed to track configuration changes to AWS resources including WAF web ACLs, making it the most cost-effective monitoring solution. ⚠️ A. WAF in front of Lambda with Firewall Manager AWS WAF cannot be placed directly in front of Lambda functions - it must be associated with API Gateway, CloudFront, or ALB. AWS Firewall Manager is designed for multi-account firewall management across AWS Organizations, not for tracking individual WAF configuration changes. ⚠️ B. CloudFront with WAF and IP blocking While technically valid, adding CloudFront introduces unnecessary costs and complexity when the portal doesn't require global distribution. Blocking single IP addresses in NACLs is ineffective as attackers can easily change IP addresses. ⚠️ C. ALB with WAF and Firewall Manager Adding an Application Load Balancer creates additional costs and architectural complexity when API Gateway can directly integrate with WAF. AWS Firewall Manager is designed for multi-account scenarios, not individual WAF configuration tracking.

When should you choose AWS Config over AWS Firewall Manager for WAF monitoring? A. When you need to manage firewalls across multiple AWS accounts B. When you need to track configuration changes to individual WAF resources C. When you need to apply firewall policies organization-wide D. When you need centralized firewall rule management ✅ B. When you need to track configuration changes to individual WAF resources AWS Config • Tracks configuration changes to AWS resources • Records WAF web ACL rule modifications • Provides configuration history and compliance • Single account focused AWS Firewall Manager • Manages firewall policies across accounts • Centralized security policy enforcement • Organization-wide firewall management • Multi-account governance tool 🎯 Decision rule: Choose AWS Config when you need detailed configuration change tracking for individual resources. Choose AWS Firewall Manager when you need centralized firewall policy management across multiple AWS accounts in an organization.

Which statement about AWS WAF integration is correct? A. AWS WAF can be directly attached to Lambda functions for request filtering B. AWS WAF can only be used with CloudFront distributions C. AWS WAF integrates with API Gateway, CloudFront, and Application Load Balancer D. AWS WAF requires a VPC to function properly ✅ C. AWS WAF integrates with API Gateway, CloudFront, and Application Load Balancer 🎯 AWS WAF integration points: AWS WAF can be associated with API Gateway (for REST and HTTP APIs), CloudFront distributions, and Application Load Balancers. It cannot be directly attached to Lambda functions - requests must pass through one of these supported services first. WAF operates at the application layer and doesn't require VPC configuration, making it suitable for both VPC and non-VPC resources.

A company's web application faces SQL injection attacks and needs to block malicious requests before they reach the backend. The solution must be cost-effective and provide custom rule creation capabilities. Which AWS service best addresses this security requirement? A. AWS Shield Advanced B. AWS WAF C. Amazon GuardDuty D. AWS Security Hub ✅ B. AWS WAF 🎯 SQL injection protection trigger: When you need to filter and block specific web exploits like SQL injection at the application layer, AWS WAF provides customizable web security rules that can inspect HTTP requests and block malicious patterns before they reach your application. ⚠️ AWS Shield Advanced focuses on DDoS protection, not application-layer attacks like SQL injection. ⚠️ Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that identifies suspicious activity but doesn't actively block requests. ⚠️ AWS Security Hub is a security posture management service that aggregates findings but doesn't provide request filtering.

Requirements: Block SQL injection attacks on API Gateway, minimal additional infrastructure , cost-effective solution , and track all security rule changes for compliance. Which combination of services meets ALL requirements? A. CloudFront + WAF + CloudTrail B. API Gateway + WAF + Config C. ALB + WAF + CloudWatch D. Lambda + Shield + GuardDuty ✅ B. API Gateway + WAF + Config 🎯 Requirements mapping: API Gateway directly integrates with WAF for SQL injection blocking without additional infrastructure. AWS Config specifically tracks configuration changes to WAF rules for compliance. This combination is the most cost-effective as it leverages existing API Gateway without adding CloudFront or ALB layers. ⚠️ Option A adds unnecessary CloudFront costs and complexity when global distribution isn't required. ⚠️ Option C introduces additional ALB infrastructure costs that aren't needed for the existing API Gateway setup. ⚠️ Option D doesn't address SQL injection attacks as Shield focuses on DDoS and GuardDuty only detects threats without blocking.

A company develops new mobile apps for Android and iOS. They want to store user customization data (4 KB per user) in AWS for a uniform cross-platform experience. They expect 3 million regular users who will authenticate using social login accounts . The solution must be highly available, cost-effective, scalable, and secure . How should the Solutions Architect design this solution? A. Provision a table in DynamoDB containing an item for each user having the necessary attributes to hold the user preferences. The mobile app will query the user preferences directly from the table. Use STS, Web Identity Federation, and DynamoDB's Fine-Grained Access Control for authentication and authorization. B. Create an RDS MySQL instance with multiple read replicas in 2 availability zones to store the user preference data. The mobile application will then query the user preferences from the read replicas. Finally, utilize MySQL's user management and access privilege system to handle the security and access credentials of the users. C. Have the user preference data stored in S3, and set up a DynamoDB table with an item for each user and an item attribute referencing the user's S3 object. The mobile app will retrieve the S3 URL from DynamoDB and then access the S3 object directly utilizing STS, Web identity Federation, and S3 Access Points. D. Launch an RDS MySQL instance in 2 availability zones to contain the user preference data. Deploy a public-facing application on a server in front of the database which will manage authentication and access controls. ✅ A. DynamoDB with Web Identity Federation and Fine-Grained Access Control 🎯 Why correct: DynamoDB provides serverless scalability for 3 million users and cost-effective storage for small 4KB items. Web Identity Federation integrates perfectly with social logins, eliminating custom authentication code while providing secure temporary credentials through STS. ⚠️ B. RDS MySQL with read replicas RDS MySQL requires capacity planning and is more expensive than DynamoDB for this use case. MySQL's built-in user management cannot integrate with social identity providers like Facebook/Google, requiring custom authentication logic that defeats the purpose of using social logins. ⚠️ C. S3 with DynamoDB metadata Unnecessarily complex architecture for 4KB data that fits perfectly in DynamoDB items. S3 Access Points add overhead without benefit, and this design creates additional latency with two API calls instead of one direct DynamoDB query. ⚠️ D. RDS with public application server Introduces a single point of failure with the application server and requires managing EC2 instances. RDS lacks native integration with social identity providers, forcing custom authentication development that increases complexity and security risks.

When should you choose DynamoDB over RDS for mobile application user data? A. When you need complex queries with JOINs across multiple tables B. When you have millions of users with small data records and need automatic scaling C. When you require ACID transactions across multiple database operations D. When you need to perform complex analytical queries with GROUP BY operations ✅ B. When you have millions of users with small data records and need automatic scaling DynamoDB • Serverless automatic scaling • Cost-effective for small records • Single-digit millisecond latency • Built-in security with IAM • No capacity planning required RDS • Complex relational queries • ACID compliance • SQL compatibility • Cross-table JOINs • Analytical workloads 🎯 Decision rule: Choose DynamoDB when you need simple key-value access patterns with massive scale and variable traffic. Choose RDS when you need complex queries, relationships, or SQL compatibility.

Which statement about Web Identity Federation with mobile apps is correct? A. Mobile apps must store permanent AWS credentials locally for user authentication B. Users exchange social login tokens for temporary AWS credentials through STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity C. Web Identity Federation requires a custom authentication server deployed in your VPC D. Social login tokens can be used directly as AWS API credentials without conversion ✅ B. Users exchange social login tokens for temporary AWS credentials through STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity 🎯 Why correct: Web Identity Federation allows mobile apps to obtain temporary AWS credentials by exchanging social login tokens (from Facebook, Google, etc.) through STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity . This eliminates the need to store permanent credentials in mobile apps and leverages existing social identity providers for authentication. Options A and D are security anti-patterns - never store permanent credentials in mobile apps or use social tokens directly. Option C is incorrect as Web Identity Federation is a managed AWS service requiring no custom infrastructure.

A mobile app needs to store small user preference files (under 10KB each) for millions of users with single-digit millisecond response times and automatic scaling without capacity planning. Which storage service best addresses these requirements? A. Amazon S3 with CloudFront for caching B. Amazon EFS with Provisioned Throughput C. Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand billing D. Amazon RDS with read replicas ✅ C. Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand billing 🎯 Trigger mapping: "Single-digit millisecond response times" + "automatic scaling" + "small records" + "millions of users" = DynamoDB. The on-demand billing mode automatically scales without capacity planning, perfect for variable mobile app traffic patterns. S3 has higher latency than DynamoDB. EFS is for file systems, not key-value data. RDS requires capacity planning and has higher latency than DynamoDB for simple lookups.

Requirements: 3 million mobile users , 4KB preference data per user , social login integration , cost optimization , and serverless architecture . Which combination of services meets ALL requirements? A. RDS MySQL + Application Load Balancer + EC2 auto scaling B. DynamoDB + STS + Web Identity Federation C. S3 + Lambda + API Gateway + Cognito User Pools D. ElastiCache + RDS + EC2 + Classic Load Balancer ✅ B. DynamoDB + STS + Web Identity Federation 🎯 Requirements mapping: • 3M users + 4KB data → DynamoDB's automatic scaling • Social login → Web Identity Federation • Cost optimization → Serverless DynamoDB (no servers to manage) • Serverless → No EC2/RDS instances required Option A uses EC2/RDS (not serverless). Option C over-engineers with S3 for small data. Option D uses outdated Classic Load Balancer and isn't serverless.

A government agency has multiple VPCs in various AWS regions across the United States that need to be linked up to an on-premises central office network in Washington, D.C. The central office requires inter-region VPC access over a private network that is dedicated to each region for enhanced security and more predictable data transfer performance. Your team needs to quickly build this network mesh and minimize management overhead. Which option provides the most secure, highly available, and durable solution for this interconnectivity? A. Utilize AWS Direct Connect Gateway for inter-region VPC access. Create a virtual private gateway in each VPC, then create a private virtual interface for each AWS Direct Connect connection to the Direct Connect gateway. B. Enable inter-region VPC peering which allows peering relationships to be established between VPCs across different AWS regions. C. Implement a hub-and-spoke network topology in each region using AWS Transit Gateway. Route traffic between VPCs and the on-premise network over AWS Site-to-Site VPN. D. Create a link aggregation group (LAG) with AWS Direct Connect Gateway and create public virtual interfaces for each connection. ✅ A. AWS Direct Connect Gateway with private virtual interfaces 🎯 Why correct: Direct Connect Gateway provides dedicated network connections with predictable performance across multiple regions while minimizing management overhead. Private virtual interfaces ensure traffic stays within AWS backbone without traversing public internet, meeting the security and performance requirements. ⚠️ B. Inter-region VPC peering While VPC peering keeps traffic on AWS backbone, it requires extensive manual setup and management overhead to create a functional multi-region network mesh. The connections are not dedicated and don't provide the enhanced performance guarantees required by the government agency. ⚠️ C. Transit Gateway with Site-to-Site VPN Site-to-Site VPN uses internet-based connections rather than dedicated private network connections. This doesn't meet the requirement for dedicated network connectivity and enhanced security that the government agency specifically needs. ⚠️ D. LAG with public virtual interfaces Public virtual interfaces are used for accessing AWS public services, not VPC resources. The scenario requires private connectivity to VPC resources. Additionally, LAG is unnecessary complexity for this use case and doesn't address the core connectivity requirements.

When should you choose AWS Direct Connect over AWS Site-to-Site VPN for hybrid connectivity? A. When you need quick setup with minimal upfront costs and can tolerate internet-dependent performance B. When you require dedicated bandwidth, predictable performance, and enhanced security for high-throughput workloads C. When you only need occasional access to AWS resources with basic encryption requirements D. When you want to avoid any hardware requirements at your on-premises location ✅ B. When you require dedicated bandwidth, predictable performance, and enhanced security AWS Direct Connect • Dedicated physical connection • Predictable bandwidth and latency • Higher throughput (up to 100 Gbps) • Enhanced security (private connection) • Lower data transfer costs at scale • Requires hardware investment AWS Site-to-Site VPN • Internet-based encrypted tunnel • Variable performance (internet-dependent) • Lower throughput (up to 1.25 Gbps per tunnel) • Standard IPSec encryption • Higher per-GB transfer costs • Quick setup, minimal hardware 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Direct Connect when you need guaranteed performance, high throughput, and dedicated connectivity. Choose VPN for quick setup, lower upfront costs, and moderate bandwidth requirements.

Which statement about AWS Direct Connect Gateway is correct? A. It can only connect to VPCs within the same AWS region as the Direct Connect location B. It requires a separate BGP session for each VPC connection to manage routing effectively C. It enables a single Direct Connect connection to access multiple VPCs across different regions D. It automatically provides load balancing across multiple Direct Connect connections ✅ C. It enables a single Direct Connect connection to access multiple VPCs across different regions 🎯 Key capability: Direct Connect Gateway acts as a global resource that allows one Direct Connect connection to reach VPCs in multiple regions through a single private virtual interface. This eliminates the need for multiple BGP sessions per VPC and significantly reduces management complexity. Options A and B are incorrect because the gateway specifically enables cross-region connectivity and simplifies BGP management. Option D is wrong because load balancing requires additional configuration like LAG.

A financial services company needs to connect their on-premises data center to multiple VPCs across different regions with dedicated bandwidth and wants to minimize the number of connections and reduce BGP session management overhead . Which AWS service best addresses these requirements? A. AWS Transit Gateway B. AWS Direct Connect Gateway C. AWS VPN CloudHub D. Inter-Region VPC Peering ✅ B. AWS Direct Connect Gateway 🎯 Perfect trigger match: The combination of "multiple VPCs across different regions," "dedicated bandwidth," "minimize connections," and "reduce BGP management" directly maps to Direct Connect Gateway's core value proposition - one connection reaching multiple regions with simplified routing. ⚠️ A. Transit Gateway: Provides connectivity within a region but doesn't offer dedicated bandwidth from on-premises or cross-region capabilities without additional services. ⚠️ C. VPN CloudHub: Uses internet-based connections, not dedicated bandwidth, and doesn't reduce BGP complexity for multiple VPCs. ⚠️ D. VPC Peering: Doesn't provide on-premises connectivity and actually increases management overhead with multiple peering relationships.

A government contractor has requirements for: dedicated private network connectivity , predictable performance for classified data transfer , connection to VPCs in 4 different regions , and minimal operational complexity for network management. Which service combination meets ALL requirements? A. Multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections with Transit Gateway in each region B. AWS Direct Connect with Direct Connect Gateway and private virtual interfaces C. Inter-Region VPC Peering with AWS PrivateLink endpoints D. AWS Client VPN with AWS Global Accelerator ✅ B. AWS Direct Connect with Direct Connect Gateway and private virtual interfaces 🎯 Requirements mapping: Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity and predictable performance. Direct Connect Gateway enables cross-region access to all 4 VPCs through a single connection. Private virtual interfaces ensure classified data stays off public internet. Single BGP session minimizes operational complexity. ⚠️ A. Site-to-Site VPN: Uses internet-based connections, not dedicated private network, and doesn't provide predictable performance required for classified data. ⚠️ C. VPC Peering + PrivateLink: Doesn't provide on-premises connectivity and increases management complexity with multiple peering relationships across regions. ⚠️ D. Client VPN + Global Accelerator: Designed for end-user access, not site-to-site connectivity, and uses internet-based connections rather than dedicated private networks.

A company hosts an online delivery system on EC2 instances behind an ALB across multiple AZs in ap-southeast-1, using MySQL RDS. They need disaster recovery with RTO , RPO = 15 minutes , and automatic PII/IP protection in the most cost-effective manner. Which disaster recovery strategy meets these requirements? A. Schedule DB backup to AWS Storage Gateway hourly, transaction logs to S3 every 5 minutes. Use AWS Shield for PII/IP protection. B. Schedule 15-minute DB backups to Glacier, transaction logs to S3 every 5 minutes. Use Amazon Macie for data protection. C. Schedule DB backup to S3 hourly, transaction logs to separate S3 bucket every 5 minutes. Use Amazon Macie for data protection. D. Set up Multi-AZ asynchronous replication. Use AWS Shield for PII/IP protection from RDS. ✅ C. Schedule DB backup to S3 hourly, transaction logs to separate S3 bucket every 5 minutes. Use Amazon Macie for data protection. 🎯 Why correct: S3 enables fast data retrieval for RTO compliance. Transaction logs every 5 minutes ensure RPO ≤ 15 minutes. Amazon Macie automatically discovers and classifies PII/IP in S3 data stores. ⚠️ A. Storage Gateway + Shield Storage Gateway is for hybrid cloud scenarios not mentioned here. AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks, not PII discovery/classification. This adds unnecessary complexity without meeting the core requirements. ⚠️ B. Glacier Storage Glacier Standard retrieval takes 3-5 hours, violating the RTO requirement. Expedited retrieval (1-5 minutes) adds significant cost, making this less cost-effective than S3. ⚠️ D. Multi-AZ + Shield Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication, not asynchronous. Multi-AZ doesn't provide cross-region DR for regional outages. Shield doesn't discover/classify PII - that's Macie's function.

When should you choose Amazon Macie over AWS Shield for data protection? A. When you need DDoS attack protection for web applications B. When you need to automatically discover and classify PII in S3 buckets C. When you need network-level threat protection D. When you need to protect against volumetric attacks ✅ B. When you need to automatically discover and classify PII in S3 buckets Amazon Macie • Machine learning-based data discovery • Automatically identifies PII and sensitive data • Monitors S3 data access patterns • Provides data classification and protection • Generates alerts for data security risks AWS Shield • DDoS protection service • Network and application layer defense • Protects against volumetric attacks • Always-on detection and mitigation • Integration with CloudFront and Route 53 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Macie when you need data discovery, classification, and monitoring of sensitive information in storage. Choose Shield when you need protection against network attacks and DDoS threats.

Which statement about RDS Multi-AZ deployments is correct? A. Multi-AZ uses asynchronous replication for better performance B. Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication and provides automatic failover within the same region C. Multi-AZ standby instances can be used for read scaling D. Multi-AZ automatically replicates data across multiple AWS regions ✅ B. Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication and provides automatic failover within the same region 🎯 Key facts: Multi-AZ provides high availability through synchronous replication to a standby instance in a different AZ within the same region. The standby is not accessible for reads (unlike Read Replicas which use asynchronous replication). Multi-AZ does not provide cross-region disaster recovery - that requires Read Replicas or manual backup strategies.

A company needs a backup solution with: RPO of 15 minutes , RTO under 3 hours , cost-effective storage , and fast retrieval for disaster recovery . Which storage solution meets ALL requirements? A. Amazon Glacier with expedited retrieval B. Amazon S3 Standard C. Amazon EBS snapshots D. AWS Storage Gateway ✅ B. Amazon S3 Standard 🎯 Why S3 Standard wins: Immediate access (meets RTO), supports frequent backups (meets RPO), cost-effective for backup storage, and network-accessible from anywhere for quick disaster recovery. Glacier has retrieval delays, EBS snapshots are region-specific, and Storage Gateway adds hybrid complexity.

A financial services company stores customer transaction data in S3 and needs to automatically identify credit card numbers, social security numbers, and other PII across terabytes of documents. Which service best addresses this requirement? A. AWS Config B. Amazon Macie C. AWS CloudTrail D. Amazon Inspector ✅ B. Amazon Macie 🎯 Perfect match: Macie uses machine learning to automatically scan S3 buckets and identify sensitive data patterns like credit card numbers, SSNs, and PII. It provides continuous monitoring, classification, and alerting for data security compliance. Config tracks resource configuration changes, CloudTrail logs API calls, and Inspector assesses application security - none perform content-based PII discovery.

A multinational corporation uses AWS Organizations to consolidate billing for multiple business units (Beauty, Baby, Health, Home Care). The Baby products unit purchased 10 Reserved Instances for a new application launching in 3 months. They want to prevent other business units from sharing their RI discounts . Which solution prevents RI discount sharing for the Baby products unit? A. Since the Baby product business unit is part of an AWS Organization, the Reserved Instances will always be shared across other member accounts. There is no way to disable this setting. B. Remove the AWS account of the Baby products business unit out of the AWS Organization. C. Set the Reserved Instance (RI) sharing to private on the AWS account of the Baby products business unit. D. Turn off the Reserved Instance (RI) sharing on the master account for all of the member accounts in the Baby products business unit. ✅ D. Turn off Reserved Instance (RI) sharing on the master account for the Baby products business unit 🎯 Why correct: Only the master/payer account can control RI sharing settings for member accounts through the Billing and Cost Management console Preferences page. This allows granular control per business unit while maintaining organizational structure. ⚠️ A. Always shared with no way to disable This is factually incorrect. AWS Organizations provides the capability to disable RI sharing through the master account's billing preferences, giving organizations control over discount distribution. ⚠️ B. Remove account from organization This eliminates consolidated billing benefits and organizational governance. It's an extreme solution when a simple preference change in the master account achieves the same goal without losing organizational benefits. ⚠️ C. Set RI sharing to private on member account Member accounts cannot control their own RI sharing settings - this capability only exists in the master/payer account. Additionally, there is no "private" option in the RI sharing settings interface.

Which statement about Reserved Instance discount sharing in AWS Organizations is correct? A. Member accounts can individually control their own RI sharing preferences B. Only the master/payer account can control RI sharing settings for member accounts C. RI sharing cannot be disabled once an organization is created D. Each organizational unit (OU) can set its own RI sharing policies ✅ B. Only the master/payer account can control RI sharing settings for member accounts 🎯 Key insight: RI sharing control is centralized at the master account level through the Billing and Cost Management console. This prevents member accounts from unilaterally opting out while giving the organization centralized control over discount distribution policies.

When should you turn off RI sharing versus keeping it enabled in AWS Organizations? A. Turn off when you want to isolate costs by business unit B. Keep enabled when you want maximum cost optimization across all accounts C. Turn off when you have compliance requirements for cost segregation D. All of the above are valid considerations ✅ D. All of the above are valid considerations RI Sharing OFF • Isolates costs by business unit • Prevents cross-subsidization • Meets compliance requirements • Higher overall costs possible RI Sharing ON (Default) • Maximum cost optimization • Utilizes unused RI capacity • Lower overall organizational costs • Shared cost benefits 🎯 Decision rule: Turn off RI sharing when cost isolation and accountability outweigh optimization. Keep enabled when overall cost reduction is the priority.

A company has separate AWS accounts for development, staging, and production environments under AWS Organizations. The production account purchases significant Reserved Instance capacity, but development often has unused EC2 capacity that could benefit from RI discounts. Which configuration maximizes cost optimization across environments? A. Keep RI sharing enabled (default) B. Turn off RI sharing for all accounts C. Enable RI sharing only between dev and staging D. Purchase separate RIs for each environment ✅ A. Keep RI sharing enabled (default) 🎯 Why: With RI sharing enabled, unused RI capacity from production automatically benefits development and staging workloads, maximizing utilization and cost savings across all environments without requiring separate RI purchases. ⚠️ Options B, C, D would result in higher costs by preventing optimal RI utilization across accounts or requiring duplicate RI purchases.

A financial services company needs to: isolate costs between trading and investment divisions , maintain consolidated billing benefits , prevent cross-division RI discount sharing , and comply with regulatory cost segregation requirements . Which approach meets ALL requirements? A. Separate AWS Organizations for each division B. Single organization with RI sharing disabled for specific accounts C. Cost allocation tags with RI sharing enabled D. Separate master accounts with linked billing ✅ B. Single organization with RI sharing disabled for specific accounts 🎯 Why: This meets ALL requirements - consolidated billing (✓), cost isolation through disabled RI sharing (✓), regulatory compliance (✓), while maintaining organizational governance benefits that separate organizations would lose.

A photo hosting company processes petabytes of images monthly using an on-premises HPC cluster with 5,000 cores . Processing takes a week with parallel jobs. The data center is nearing capacity , forcing job spreading throughout the month. Need a scalable solution exceeding current capacity with least management overhead while maintaining durability. Which solution meets the requirements while being cost-effective? A. EMR cluster with Spark, On-demand/Reserved instances, DynamoDB job listing B. Docker on Amazon EKS with auto-scaling, EBS SC1 volumes for temporary storage C. AWS Batch with Managed Compute Environments using Spot Instances and S3 storage D. SQS queue with EC2 Spot Auto Scaling Group, Amazon EFS for data sharing ✅ C. AWS Batch with Managed Compute Environments using Spot Instances and S3 storage 🎯 Why correct: AWS Batch provides fully managed batch computing with dynamic scaling, no infrastructure management overhead, and Spot Instances for cost optimization. S3 provides the required durability and scales to petabytes seamlessly. ⚠️ A. EMR with Spark Managing EMR clusters and Apache Spark adds significant operational overhead, contradicting the "least management overhead" requirement. Reserved instances also mean paying for constantly running infrastructure even during low job periods. ⚠️ B. Docker on EKS Converting applications to containers and managing EKS clusters increases complexity. EBS SC1 volumes cannot be quickly resized and provisioning petabyte-scale volumes upfront is extremely cost-ineffective compared to S3's pay-per-use model. ⚠️ D. SQS with Auto Scaling Group Amazon EFS is significantly more expensive than S3 for storing petabytes of raw data. SQS message processing can also lead to duplicate job execution if Spot instances terminate unexpectedly during processing.

When should you choose AWS Batch over Amazon EMR for large-scale parallel processing? A. When you need Apache Spark or Hadoop ecosystem tools B. When you want minimal management overhead for containerized batch jobs C. When processing streaming data in real-time D. When you need persistent HDFS storage ✅ B. When you want minimal management overhead for containerized batch jobs AWS Batch • Fully managed batch computing • No cluster management required • Automatic scaling and provisioning • Container-based jobs • Pay only for compute resources used Amazon EMR • Managed Hadoop/Spark clusters • Requires cluster configuration • Big data analytics frameworks • Persistent clusters possible • More complex but powerful for analytics 🎯 Decision rule: Choose AWS Batch when you need simple, managed batch processing with containers. Choose EMR when you need Hadoop ecosystem tools or complex big data analytics workflows.

Which statement about AWS Batch Managed Compute Environments is correct? A. You must pre-provision EC2 instances before submitting jobs B. AWS automatically provisions and scales compute resources based on job queue demands C. Only On-Demand instances can be used in managed environments D. Compute environments require manual scaling configuration ✅ B. AWS automatically provisions and scales compute resources based on job queue demands 🎯 Key insight: Managed Compute Environments handle all infrastructure provisioning automatically. AWS Batch scales compute resources up and down based on job queue requirements, supporting both On-Demand and Spot instances. This eliminates the need for manual capacity planning or pre-provisioning, making it ideal for variable workloads like the image processing scenario.

A company needs to process variable workloads with unpredictable timing , wants to minimize management overhead , and requires automatic scaling for containerized batch jobs. Which service best addresses this requirement? A. Amazon ECS with manual scaling B. AWS Batch with Managed Compute Environments C. Amazon EKS with Cluster Autoscaler D. EC2 Auto Scaling Groups with custom scripts ✅ B. AWS Batch with Managed Compute Environments 🎯 Perfect match: AWS Batch is specifically designed for variable batch workloads with automatic provisioning and scaling. It requires zero infrastructure management while handling unpredictable job timing through dynamic compute resource allocation. ECS requires manual scaling configuration and cluster management. EKS adds Kubernetes complexity. EC2 Auto Scaling requires custom job scheduling logic.

Requirements: Process petabytes of data , high durability , cost-effective storage , and ability to scale storage independently from compute resources. Which storage solution meets ALL requirements? A. Amazon EBS GP2 volumes attached to EC2 instances B. Amazon EFS for shared file system access C. Amazon S3 with appropriate storage classes D. Amazon EBS SC1 cold storage volumes ✅ C. Amazon S3 with appropriate storage classes 🎯 Requirements mapping: S3 provides virtually unlimited scalability for petabytes, 11 9's durability, pay-per-use cost model, and complete independence from compute resources. Storage classes like S3 Standard-IA or Glacier can optimize costs based on access patterns. EBS volumes are limited in size and tied to specific instances. EFS is more expensive than S3 for large-scale storage. EBS SC1 still requires pre-provisioning and instance attachment.

A company runs multiple Amazon EC2 clusters . Security team identified unusual API activity and port scanning from a specific IP address. Solutions architect must immediately block the offending IP and fortify infrastructure against frequent network/transport layer DDoS attacks . Which method best satisfies these requirements? A. Change Windows Firewall settings to deny IP access. Use GuardDuty and Systems Manager Patch Manager. B. Block IP using Route 53. Use Amazon Macie for DDoS protection. C. Deny IP access in Network ACL. Use AWS Shield Advanced. D. Add deny rule to all Security Groups. Use AWS WAF and AWS Config. ✅ C. Deny IP access in Network ACL. Use AWS Shield Advanced. 🎯 Why correct: Network ACLs operate at subnet level and can explicitly DENY traffic (stateless firewall). AWS Shield Advanced specifically protects against network/transport layer (L3/L4) DDoS attacks with always-on detection and automatic mitigation. ⚠️ A. Windows Firewall + GuardDuty Why wrong: Windows Firewall only protects individual instances, not network-level blocking. GuardDuty detects threats but doesn't provide DDoS protection. Systems Manager Patch Manager handles patching, not DDoS mitigation. ⚠️ B. Route 53 + Macie Why wrong: Route 53 cannot block specific IP addresses - it's a DNS service. Amazon Macie is for data classification and protection, not DDoS attacks. This combination addresses neither requirement. ⚠️ D. Security Groups + WAF/Config Why wrong: Security Groups cannot explicitly DENY (only allow) and are stateful. AWS WAF protects web applications (L7), not network/transport layers. AWS Config is for compliance monitoring, not DDoS protection.

When should you use Network ACLs over Security Groups for IP blocking? A. When you need stateful filtering with automatic return traffic handling B. When you need to explicitly DENY specific IP addresses at subnet level C. When you need to allow traffic and let AWS handle the rest automatically D. When you need instance-level protection with connection tracking ✅ B. When you need to explicitly DENY specific IP addresses at subnet level Network ACLs • Subnet-level firewall • Stateless (no connection tracking) • Can explicitly ALLOW or DENY • Processed in rule number order • Separate inbound/outbound rules Security Groups • Instance-level firewall • Stateful (connection tracking) • Can only ALLOW (implicit deny) • All rules evaluated together • Return traffic automatically allowed 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Network ACLs when you need explicit DENY rules or subnet-wide protection. Choose Security Groups for typical allow-based access control with stateful behavior.

Which statement about AWS Shield Advanced is correct? A. It only protects web applications against Layer 7 attacks B. It provides always-on detection and automatic mitigation for network and transport layer DDoS attacks C. It requires manual activation during an attack to be effective D. It only works with Amazon CloudFront distributions ✅ B. It provides always-on detection and automatic mitigation for network and transport layer DDoS attacks 🎯 Key insight: AWS Shield Advanced offers proactive, always-on DDoS protection for Layer 3 and 4 attacks (network/transport layers). It includes automatic mitigation, 24/7 DDoS Response Team access, and protection for EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Route 53, and Global Accelerator. Unlike WAF which handles Layer 7, Shield focuses on infrastructure-level attacks.

A company experiences volumetric network floods and protocol attacks targeting their EC2 instances. They need automatic protection without manual intervention during attacks. Which service best addresses this requirement? A. AWS WAF with rate limiting rules B. Amazon GuardDuty with threat detection C. AWS Shield Advanced with always-on mitigation D. AWS Config with compliance monitoring ✅ C. AWS Shield Advanced with always-on mitigation 🎯 Trigger mapping: "Volumetric network floods and protocol attacks" = Layer 3/4 DDoS attacks . "Automatic protection without manual intervention" = always-on detection and mitigation . AWS Shield Advanced is specifically designed for this scenario. ⚠️ A. AWS WAF: Protects against Layer 7 (application) attacks, not network floods ⚠️ B. GuardDuty: Detects threats but doesn't mitigate DDoS attacks ⚠️ D. AWS Config: Monitors compliance, not DDoS protection

A solutions architect proposes using Security Groups to block a malicious IP address by adding a DENY rule. Why is this problematic? A. Security Groups are too slow to process DENY rules B. Security Groups cannot contain explicit DENY rules - they only support ALLOW rules C. Security Groups only work at the application layer, not network layer D. Security Groups require additional licensing for DENY functionality ✅ B. Security Groups cannot contain explicit DENY rules - they only support ALLOW rules Security Groups use an implicit deny model - if traffic isn't explicitly allowed, it's automatically denied. You cannot add explicit DENY rules to Security Groups. This makes them unsuitable for blocking specific IP addresses since you'd need to allow all other IPs, which is impractical and insecure. 🎯 Better approach: Use Network ACLs which support explicit DENY rules and operate at the subnet level, providing network-wide protection against malicious IPs.

A fitness tracking app company serves North American and Asian users with a read-heavy application that pings servers regularly for authorization. Requirements: fault-tolerant across regions , highly-available database writes in single region , multi-region read capability , resilient application tier per region , and relational database semantics . Which TWO options meet these requirements? A. Deploy Auto Scaling groups in each region with RDS MySQL per region for local read/write, enable cross-region replication, store snapshots in S3 B. Create Route 53 geolocation routing to direct users to designated regions, combine with failover routing and health checks C. Deploy Auto Scaling groups in active-active configuration with Aurora Global Database cluster, use in-region endpoints for read/write D. Create Route 53 geoproximity routing to closest endpoints, combine with multivalue answer routing and health checks ✅ B & C. Route 53 geolocation + failover routing, and Aurora Global Database with active-active configuration 🎯 Why correct: Aurora Global Database provides single-region writes with multi-region reads and sub-second replication. Geolocation routing ensures users reach their designated regions while failover provides fault tolerance across regions. ⚠️ A. RDS MySQL with cross-region replication Cannot sync two MySQL master databases that both accept writes in their respective regions. Cross-region replication doesn't support bi-directional writes, violating the single-region write requirement. ⚠️ D. Geoproximity + multivalue routing Multivalue answer routing randomly selects healthy records, potentially sending users to regions far from their location, degrading performance for the read-heavy application that requires low latency.

When should you choose Aurora Global Database over RDS Cross-Region Read Replicas for a multi-region application? A. When you need sub-second replication latency and fast regional failover capabilities B. When you want to minimize costs and can accept higher replication latency C. When you need different database engines across regions D. When you only need read replicas in the same region as the primary ✅ A. Sub-second replication latency and fast regional failover Aurora Global Database • Sub-second cross-region replication • Up to 5 secondary regions • Promote secondary to primary in • Dedicated replication infrastructure • Single logical database spanning regions RDS Cross-Region Read Replicas • Higher replication latency (minutes) • Manual promotion process • Uses standard replication protocols • Lower cost option • Independent database instances 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Aurora Global Database when you need fast failover, low replication latency, and seamless global scaling. Choose RDS Read Replicas when cost optimization is priority and longer failover times are acceptable.

Which statement about Route 53 routing policies is correct for global applications? A. Geoproximity routing always directs users to the geographically closest endpoint B. Multivalue answer routing provides automatic failover to healthy endpoints C. Geolocation routing can be combined with failover routing for fault-tolerant regional distribution D. Latency-based routing guarantees the fastest response time for all users ✅ C. Geolocation routing can be combined with failover routing for fault-tolerant regional distribution 🎯 Why correct: Route 53 allows combining routing policies - geolocation directs users to designated regions based on their location, while failover routing provides automatic switching to healthy regions when primary regions fail. Options A, B, and D make incorrect assumptions about guaranteed behavior or automatic capabilities that these routing policies don't provide.

A company needs a relational database that can handle writes in one region and reads from multiple regions with minimal replication lag for a global application. Which AWS service best addresses this requirement? A. RDS MySQL with Cross-Region Read Replicas B. Aurora Global Database C. DynamoDB Global Tables D. ElastiCache Global Datastore ✅ B. Aurora Global Database 🎯 Perfect match: Aurora Global Database provides single-region writes with up to 5 read-only secondary regions, sub-second replication latency using dedicated infrastructure, and maintains full relational database semantics with ACID compliance. ⚠️ A: RDS Cross-Region Read Replicas have higher latency and manual promotion complexity ⚠️ C: DynamoDB Global Tables is NoSQL, not relational ⚠️ D: ElastiCache is for caching, not primary database storage

Requirements: Active-active configuration across two regions, automatic health-check failover , geographic user routing , and sub-second database replication for a read-heavy fitness app. Which architecture meets ALL requirements? A. Auto Scaling + RDS MySQL Multi-AZ + Route 53 weighted routing B. Auto Scaling + Aurora Global Database + Route 53 geolocation + failover routing C. Lambda + DynamoDB Global Tables + CloudFront geographic restrictions D. ECS Fargate + RDS PostgreSQL + Route 53 latency-based routing ✅ B. Auto Scaling + Aurora Global Database + Route 53 geolocation + failover routing 🎯 Requirement mapping: Auto Scaling provides active-active resilient compute, Aurora Global Database delivers sub-second replication across regions, Route 53 geolocation ensures geographic routing, and failover routing adds automatic health-check based failover capability. ⚠️ A: RDS Multi-AZ only protects within region, doesn't provide cross-region replication ⚠️ C: Lambda may have cold starts affecting read-heavy performance, CloudFront restrictions aren't routing ⚠️ D: Standard RDS PostgreSQL lacks sub-second cross-region replication capability

A company needs to migrate 60 TB of data from on-premises Oracle data warehouse to Amazon Redshift . The database receives daily minor updates and monthly major updates . Migration must complete within 30 days before next major update. Only 50 Mbps Internet allocated to avoid impacting business operations. Keep costs low . Which migration approach satisfies all requirements? A. Provision 1 Gbps AWS Direct Connect, launch Oracle RAC on EC2, replicate data, then use AWS DMS with SCT to migrate to Redshift B. Create Oracle RDS, configure Site-to-Site VPN, replicate to RDS, then use SCT with DMS to migrate to Redshift C. Use Snowball Edge for bulk export, import to RDS Oracle, then use SCT with DMS to migrate to Redshift, copy daily updates over Internet D. Use Snowball Edge with SCT extraction agent for bulk migration, then configure local and DMS tasks for ongoing replication ✅ D. Use Snowball Edge with SCT extraction agent for bulk migration, then configure local and DMS tasks for ongoing replication 🎯 Why correct: Snowball Edge handles 60TB efficiently within bandwidth constraints, SCT extraction agent processes data locally, and DMS handles ongoing updates. This approach minimizes Internet usage and keeps costs low while meeting the 30-day timeline. ⚠️ A. Direct Connect approach While technically feasible, provisioning 1 Gbps Direct Connect for a one-time migration is not cost-effective. The scenario specifically requires keeping costs low, and Direct Connect has setup fees and monthly charges that aren't justified for temporary migration. ⚠️ B. VPN with RDS replication Replicating 60TB over 50 Mbps Internet connection would take much longer than 30 days and could impact business operations. The limited bandwidth constraint makes this approach infeasible for the data volume. ⚠️ C. Snowball to RDS intermediate step This adds unnecessary complexity and cost by requiring an intermediate RDS instance. The data doesn't need to go through RDS - SCT can migrate directly from S3 (populated by Snowball) to Redshift, eliminating the extra step and associated costs.

When migrating large datasets (50+ TB) to AWS, when should you choose AWS Snowball Edge over Direct Connect? A. When you need ongoing high-bandwidth connectivity for multiple applications B. When you have limited Internet bandwidth and need one-time bulk data transfer C. When you require real-time data replication with sub-second latency D. When you need dedicated network connection for regulatory compliance ✅ B. When you have limited Internet bandwidth and need one-time bulk data transfer AWS Snowball Edge • Up to 100TB capacity per device • One-time or infrequent transfers • Bypasses Internet bandwidth limits • Cost-effective for large datasets • 1-2 week shipping timeline AWS Direct Connect • Dedicated 1Gbps-100Gbps connection • Ongoing high-bandwidth needs • Consistent network performance • Monthly recurring costs • Setup time: weeks to months 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Snowball Edge for one-time bulk transfers when Internet bandwidth is limited. Choose Direct Connect for ongoing high-bandwidth requirements or when you need dedicated connectivity for multiple workloads.

Which statement about AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) extraction agents is correct? A. Extraction agents must run on the same server as the source database B. Extraction agents can only work when AWS SCT application is actively running C. Extraction agents act as listeners and can work in background when SCT is closed D. Extraction agents require Direct Connect connectivity to function properly ✅ C. Extraction agents act as listeners and can work in background when SCT is closed 🎯 Key insight: SCT extraction agents are independent processes that run as listeners on separate servers. They receive instructions from AWS SCT and continue data extraction in the background even when the SCT application is closed. This allows for efficient, uninterrupted data migration processes. Agents can be installed on separate servers from the database and work over standard network connections.

A company needs to migrate 80TB of data from an on-premises data warehouse to AWS within 4 weeks. They have limited Internet bandwidth (100 Mbps) and want to minimize impact on daily operations while keeping migration costs low. Which AWS service best addresses this scenario? A. AWS DataSync with VPC endpoints B. AWS Snowball Edge with extraction agents C. AWS Direct Connect with enhanced networking D. AWS Storage Gateway in cached volume mode ✅ B. AWS Snowball Edge with extraction agents 🎯 Trigger mapping: Large dataset (80TB) + limited bandwidth + time constraint + cost optimization = Snowball Edge . The physical device bypasses Internet limitations, handles the data volume, meets timeline, and avoids ongoing connectivity costs. ⚠️ A. DataSync: Would struggle with 80TB over 100 Mbps within 4 weeks and impact operations ⚠️ C. Direct Connect: High setup cost and time for one-time migration ⚠️ D. Storage Gateway: Designed for hybrid scenarios, not bulk migration

Requirements: Migrate Oracle data warehouse to Redshift, handle ongoing daily updates during migration, minimize Internet bandwidth usage, complete within 30 days, cost-effective approach. Which service combination meets ALL requirements? A. AWS DataSync + AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) B. AWS Snowball Edge + AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) + DMS C. AWS Direct Connect + AWS Glue + Amazon EMR D. Amazon RDS + AWS DMS + Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration ✅ B. AWS Snowball Edge + AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) + DMS 🎯 Requirements mapping: • Bulk migration: Snowball Edge handles large dataset offline • Schema conversion: SCT converts Oracle to Redshift format • Ongoing updates: DMS replicates daily changes • Bandwidth minimal: Snowball bypasses Internet for bulk data • Cost-effective: No ongoing connectivity charges

A company runs a hybrid mobile application with a 3TB MySQL database on-premises handling write-intensive requests, connected to AWS via VPN . AWS components include Lambda functions , API Gateway , and DynamoDB . The company notices exponential Lambda costs due to 4.5-minute execution times with most time being wait time from latency to the on-premises MySQL server. User traffic is unpredictable with 20% monthly growth . Which solution should the Solutions Architect implement to reduce overall costs? A. Provision AWS Direct Connect instead of VPN to reduce network latency B. Create CloudFront distribution with API Gateway origin to cache responses C. Convert Lambda to EC2 Reserved Instances with Auto Scaling and Spot instances D. Migrate MySQL to RDS, enable API Gateway caching, optimize Lambda settings, configure DynamoDB Auto Scaling ✅ D. Migrate MySQL to RDS, enable API Gateway caching, optimize Lambda settings, configure DynamoDB Auto Scaling 🎯 Why correct: This addresses the root cause (latency) by moving the database to AWS, reduces Lambda invocations through API caching, and optimizes costs across all components. The 4.5-minute Lambda execution time is primarily wait time, so eliminating network latency between AWS Lambda and the database provides the greatest cost reduction. ⚠️ A. Direct Connect only While Direct Connect reduces latency compared to VPN, it's expensive to provision for a single application and doesn't address the fundamental issue. Keeping the database on-premises still introduces latency, and the cost of Direct Connect may exceed Lambda savings. ⚠️ B. CloudFront caching CloudFront is designed for static content caching at edge locations, not for API response caching. API Gateway has built-in caching specifically designed for API responses, making it more appropriate and cost-effective for this use case. ⚠️ C. EC2 Reserved Instances With unpredictable traffic and 20% monthly growth, Reserved Instances could be more expensive than Lambda during low-traffic periods. Lambda's pay-per-execution model is more cost-effective for variable workloads when optimized properly.

Which statement about AWS Lambda pricing and execution time is correct? A. Lambda charges for the total time allocated, regardless of actual execution time B. Lambda duration is calculated from code execution start until termination, rounded to nearest 1ms C. Lambda pricing is based only on memory allocation, not execution time D. Lambda wait time during external API calls is not included in billable duration ✅ B. Lambda duration is calculated from code execution start until termination, rounded to nearest 1ms 🎯 Key insight: Lambda charges for actual execution duration including wait time for external calls. This is why the 4.5-minute execution time with mostly wait time in the scenario created exponential costs. Reducing latency to external dependencies directly reduces Lambda costs. Options A, C, and D misunderstand Lambda pricing - you pay for both requests AND duration (including wait time), not just allocation or memory alone.

When should you choose API Gateway caching over CloudFront for API response caching? A. When you need global edge location caching B. When caching dynamic API responses with TTL control C. When serving static website content D. When you need the lowest possible latency worldwide ✅ B. When caching dynamic API responses with TTL control API Gateway Caching • Built-in caching for API responses • TTL control (300-3600 seconds) • Reduces backend invocations • Cost-effective for APIs • Stage-level configuration CloudFront • Global edge location caching • Best for static content • Geographic distribution • Lower latency worldwide • More complex for APIs 🎯 Decision rule: Choose API Gateway caching for dynamic API responses that need quick TTL updates. Choose CloudFront for static content that benefits from global edge caching.

A company has Lambda functions with 4.5-minute execution times where most time is spent waiting for responses from an on-premises database connected via VPN. Which approach provides the greatest cost reduction? A. Upgrade VPN to Direct Connect B. Migrate database to AWS RDS C. Increase Lambda memory allocation D. Implement connection pooling ✅ B. Migrate database to AWS RDS 🎯 Root cause solution: Moving the database to AWS eliminates network latency between Lambda and database, directly addressing the wait time that's driving high costs. This provides the most dramatic reduction in execution duration and therefore Lambda costs. Direct Connect improves latency but keeps the fundamental cross-network dependency. Memory allocation and connection pooling don't address the core latency issue.

Requirements: Unpredictable traffic with 20% monthly growth , cost optimization priority , serverless architecture preference , and ability to handle traffic spikes . Which compute solution meets ALL requirements? A. EC2 Reserved Instances with Auto Scaling B. Lambda with optimized configuration C. EC2 Spot Instances only D. Elastic Container Service (ECS) ✅ B. Lambda with optimized configuration 🎯 Requirements mapping: Lambda provides serverless architecture ✓, pay-per-execution for unpredictable traffic ✓, automatic scaling for spikes ✓, and cost optimization when properly configured ✓. Reserved Instances are cost-ineffective for unpredictable workloads with growth patterns.

A company uses AWS Organizations with all accounts in a single Production OU. SCPs are attached at the root , restricting services across all accounts. A newly acquired company's AWS account was invited via InviteAccountToOrganization but administrators cannot apply required AWS Config rules due to SCP restrictions. Which option allows Config rule updates without long-term management overhead? A. Update root SCPs to remove Config restrictions, deploy Service Catalog with Config policies B. Add account to temporary Onboarding OU with SCP allowing Config changes C. Move SCPs from root to Production OU, create temporary Onboarding OU with Config permissions D. Use allow list instead of deny list, temporarily add Config service for new account ✅ C. Move SCPs from root to Production OU, create temporary Onboarding OU with Config permissions 🎯 Why correct: AWS strongly recommends against attaching SCPs to the organization root. Moving SCPs to the Production OU allows creating an independent Onboarding OU with different permissions for temporary Config setup. ⚠️ A. Service Catalog approach Removing Config restrictions at the root level affects ALL accounts permanently, allowing any administrator to modify Config rules. Service Catalog doesn't solve the underlying SCP permission issue. ⚠️ B. Temporary OU with root SCPs intact SCPs use inheritance - an explicit deny at the root cannot be overridden by an allow policy at the OU level. The Config restriction would still apply. ⚠️ D. Allow list modification While technically possible, this creates ongoing management overhead as the allow list must be continuously updated for any new services users require in the future.

Which statement about SCP inheritance in AWS Organizations is correct? A. Child OUs can override explicit deny statements from parent SCPs with explicit allow statements B. SCPs use additive inheritance where child permissions are added to parent permissions C. An explicit deny at any parent level cannot be overridden by child policies D. Root-level SCPs only apply to the management account, not member accounts ✅ C. An explicit deny at any parent level cannot be overridden by child policies 🎯 SCP inheritance follows a restrictive model: If a permission is blocked at any parent level (root or OU), child policies cannot grant that permission back. This is why root-level SCPs are problematic - they cannot be selectively overridden for specific accounts or OUs.

A company needs to temporarily grant AWS Config permissions to a newly acquired account while maintaining strict security controls on existing production accounts. Current SCPs deny Config changes at the root level . Which architectural approach meets ALL requirements? A. Create exception rules in root-level SCPs for the specific account B. Restructure SCPs to OU-level and create temporary onboarding OU C. Use cross-account IAM roles to bypass SCP restrictions D. Temporarily disable SCPs organization-wide during onboarding ✅ B. Restructure SCPs to OU-level and create temporary onboarding OU 🎯 Why this works: Moving SCPs from root to Production OU maintains security for existing accounts while allowing an independent Onboarding OU with different permissions. The new account can be moved between OUs as needed without affecting production security posture.

A solutions architect proposes using AWS Service Catalog to solve SCP Config restrictions by deploying approved Config policies organization-wide. Why is this approach problematic? A. Service Catalog cannot deploy Config resources across multiple accounts B. Service Catalog doesn't address the underlying SCP permission denial C. Config rules cannot be packaged as Service Catalog products D. Service Catalog requires separate deployment in each OU ✅ B. Service Catalog doesn't address the underlying SCP permission denial Service Catalog operates within existing IAM/SCP boundaries - it cannot grant permissions that are explicitly denied by SCPs. Even with approved Config templates, users still cannot deploy them if SCPs block Config service access. 🎯 Better approach: Address the SCP architecture first by restructuring permissions at the OU level, then optionally use Service Catalog for standardized Config deployments.

When should you attach SCPs at the Organization root versus OU level? A. Root level for universal policies, OU level for account-specific restrictions B. Root level for emergency controls only, OU level for operational policies C. Root level for management account controls, OU level for member accounts D. OU level is preferred for flexibility, root level should be avoided ✅ D. OU level is preferred for flexibility, root level should be avoided Root Level SCPs • Apply to ALL accounts • Cannot be overridden • Risk of locking out services • Difficult to manage exceptions OU Level SCPs • Selective application • Independent policy management • Easy account movement • Gradual rollout capability 🎯 Decision rule: Use OU-level SCPs for operational flexibility and easier exception handling. Avoid root-level SCPs unless absolutely necessary for organization-wide security mandates.

A sports web portal company runs resources across multiple AWS regions including EC2 instances and RDS databases. The IT Security Compliance Officer requires a reliable and durable logging solution to track changes to all EC2, IAM, and RDS resources in all regions. The solution must ensure integrity and confidentiality of log data. Which solution best meets these requirements? A. Create a new trail in AWS CloudTrail with the global services option selected, and create one new Amazon S3 bucket to store the logs. Create IAM roles, S3 bucket policies, and enable Multi Factor Authentication (MFA) Delete on the S3 bucket storing your logs. B. Create three new CloudTrail trails, each with its own S3 bucket to store the logs: one for the AWS Management console, one for AWS SDKs, and one for command line tools. Then create IAM roles and S3 bucket policies for the S3 buckets storing your logs. C. Create a new trail in AWS CloudTrail with the global services option selected, and assign it an existing S3 bucket to store the logs. Create S3 ACLs and enable Multi Factor Authentication (MFA) delete on the S3 bucket storing your logs. D. Create a new trail in CloudTrail and assign it a new S3 bucket to store the logs. Configure AWS SNS to send delivery notifications to your management system. Secure the S3 bucket that stores your logs using IAM roles and S3 bucket policies. ✅ A. CloudTrail with global services, new S3 bucket, IAM roles, and MFA Delete 🎯 Why correct: The IncludeGlobalServiceEvents flag captures IAM events across all regions. A new S3 bucket ensures confidentiality, while MFA Delete protects log integrity and IAM roles provide proper access control. ⚠️ B. Three separate trails Creates unnecessary complexity with three S3 buckets when one trail can capture all API calls regardless of source (console, SDK, CLI). Missing the global services option means IAM events won't be captured properly. ⚠️ C. Existing S3 bucket with ACLs Using an existing bucket compromises confidentiality since it may already have other access permissions. S3 ACLs are less secure than IAM roles and bucket policies for this use case. ⚠️ D. No global services option Without the global services flag, IAM events won't be captured. SNS notifications are nice-to-have but don't address the core logging requirements for multi-region resource tracking.

Which statement about AWS CloudTrail's global services option is correct? A. It only captures events from services deployed in the us-east-1 region B. It captures IAM, STS, CloudFront, and Route 53 events regardless of which region's trail is configured C. It requires separate trails in each region to capture global service events D. It automatically encrypts all log files with AWS KMS keys ✅ B. It captures IAM, STS, CloudFront, and Route 53 events regardless of which region's trail is configured 🎯 Global services like IAM don't belong to any specific region, so their events are delivered to any trail with the IncludeGlobalServiceEvents flag enabled. This prevents the need for multiple trails just to capture these events. Option A is wrong because global services aren't limited to us-east-1. Option C is wrong because one trail with global services enabled is sufficient. Option D confuses the global services feature with encryption settings.

A company needs to ensure log file integrity for compliance audits, prevent accidental deletion of critical audit logs, and maintain confidentiality of sensitive API call data stored in S3. Which combination of S3 security features best meets ALL requirements? A. S3 Object Lock with Legal Hold and bucket-level public read blocking B. MFA Delete, IAM roles with least privilege, and S3 bucket policies C. S3 versioning with Cross-Region Replication and KMS encryption D. S3 Access Control Lists (ACLs) and CloudWatch monitoring ✅ B. MFA Delete, IAM roles with least privilege, and S3 bucket policies 🎯 MFA Delete prevents accidental deletion (integrity), IAM roles provide fine-grained access control (confidentiality), and bucket policies add an additional layer of access restrictions.
