Strict security requirements mandate encryption of all network traffic from employee laptops to VPC resources while maintaining consistent network performance of Direct Connect. Which solution complies with this requirement while maintaining Direct Connect performance? A. Create private virtual interface on DX, create site-to-site VPN over Internet, configure laptops to connect to VPN B. Create public virtual interface on DX, create site-to-site VPN over Internet, configure laptops to connect to VPN C. Create private virtual interface on DX, create site-to-site VPN using BGP over DX connection, route employee traffic to VPN D. Create public virtual interface on DX, create site-to-site VPN using BGP over DX connection, route employee traffic to VPN ✅ D. Create public virtual interface on DX, create site-to-site VPN using BGP over DX connection, route employee traffic to VPN 🎯 Why correct: To establish VPN over Direct Connect, you MUST use a public virtual interface (not private) because VPN endpoints are AWS public services. The VPN runs over the DX connection (not Internet) to maintain performance while providing encryption. ⚠️ A. Private VIF + Internet VPN Wrong interface type AND wrong path. Private virtual interfaces cannot establish VPN connections to AWS public endpoints. Additionally, routing VPN over Internet defeats the performance requirement of maintaining Direct Connect benefits. ⚠️ B. Public VIF + Internet VPN Correct interface type but wrong routing path. While public VIF is needed for VPN, routing the VPN over Internet instead of through the DX connection eliminates the consistent performance requirement and doesn't leverage the existing DX investment. ⚠️ C. Private VIF + DX VPN Wrong interface type despite correct routing path. Private virtual interfaces connect to resources via private IP addresses only and cannot establish VPN connections to AWS VPN endpoints, which are public services requiring public virtual interfaces.

When establishing VPN connectivity, when should you choose VPN over Direct Connect vs VPN over Internet? A. Always use VPN over Internet for better encryption B. Use VPN over Direct Connect when you need consistent performance with existing DX investment C. VPN over Internet is required for financial compliance D. Both provide identical performance and security ✅ B. Use VPN over Direct Connect when you need consistent performance with existing DX investment VPN over Direct Connect • Leverages existing DX bandwidth and reliability • Consistent, predictable performance • Lower latency than Internet • Requires public virtual interface • Higher cost but better SLA VPN over Internet • Variable performance based on Internet conditions • Lower upfront costs • Easier to implement quickly • No DX infrastructure required • Suitable for backup connections 🎯 Decision rule: Choose VPN over DX when you have existing Direct Connect and need guaranteed performance. Choose VPN over Internet for cost-sensitive, less critical workloads or quick implementations.

Which statement about Direct Connect virtual interfaces is correct? A. Private virtual interfaces can establish VPN connections to AWS public endpoints B. Public virtual interfaces are required to establish VPN connections over Direct Connect C. Both private and public virtual interfaces provide the same connectivity options D. Virtual interfaces are automatically created when establishing Direct Connect ✅ B. Public virtual interfaces are required to establish VPN connections over Direct Connect 🎯 Key insight: VPN endpoints are AWS public services with public IP addresses. Private virtual interfaces only connect to resources via private IP addresses within VPCs, while public virtual interfaces connect to AWS public endpoints and services. To establish VPN over Direct Connect, you must use a public VIF to reach the VPN service endpoints.

A financial services company requires encrypted network traffic between on-premises and AWS while maintaining consistent network performance and leveraging their existing Direct Connect connection . Which AWS service combination best addresses this requirement? A. AWS PrivateLink with Interface Endpoints B. Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect with Public Virtual Interface C. Transit Gateway with VPC Peering D. AWS Client VPN with certificate-based authentication ✅ B. Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect with Public Virtual Interface 🎯 Trigger mapping: "Encrypted traffic" + "consistent performance" + "existing Direct Connect" = VPN over DX. This provides IPSec encryption while maintaining DX performance characteristics and leveraging existing infrastructure investment. ⚠️ A. PrivateLink: Provides private connectivity but doesn't encrypt traffic in transit and is designed for AWS service access, not general network connectivity. ⚠️ C. Transit Gateway: Facilitates routing but doesn't provide encryption or leverage Direct Connect for performance. ⚠️ D. Client VPN: Designed for individual client connections, not site-to-site connectivity between networks.

Requirements: Encrypt all traffic between corporate network and AWS VPC, maintain existing Direct Connect performance , minimize additional infrastructure costs , and support BGP routing . Which solution meets ALL requirements? A. Replace Direct Connect with multiple Internet-based VPN connections B. Add Site-to-Site VPN over existing Direct Connect using public virtual interface C. Deploy AWS PrivateLink endpoints for all services D. Implement application-layer encryption with existing Direct Connect ✅ B. Add Site-to-Site VPN over existing Direct Connect using public virtual interface 🎯 Requirements mapping: Encryption = IPSec VPN tunnels, Performance = leverage existing DX bandwidth, Cost = reuse DX infrastructure, BGP = VPN supports BGP for dynamic routing. Only option B satisfies all four constraints simultaneously.

A multinational financial firm is deploying a cryptocurrency trading application across multiple regions (US and Europe). The containerized app uses Kubernetes with DynamoDB Global Tables and has public-facing ALBs in each region. The Network team manages DNS internally and wants the application available through an apex domain . S3 Multi-Region Access Points are used for static assets. Which is the MOST operationally efficient solution to meet these requirements? A. Launch an AWS Transit Gateway that targets specific ALBs on the required AWS Regions. Create a CNAME record in Amazon Route 53 that directly points your custom domain name to the DNS name assigned to the AWS Transit Gateway. B. Set up an AWS Transit Gateway with a multicast domain that targets specific ALBs on the required AWS Regions. Create a public record in Amazon Route 53 using the static IP address of the AWS Transit Gateway. C. Set up an AWS Global Accelerator, which has several endpoint groups that target specific endpoints and ALBs on the required AWS Regions. Create a public alias record in Amazon Route 53 that points your custom domain name to the DNS name assigned to your accelerator. D. Launch an AWS Global Accelerator with several endpoint groups that target the ALBs in all the relevant AWS Regions. Create an Amazon Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoint that points your custom domain name to the CNAME assigned to your accelerator. ✅ C. Set up AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups targeting ALBs and create a Route 53 alias record 🎯 Why correct: Global Accelerator provides intelligent traffic routing to multiple ALBs across regions using AWS backbone network, while Route 53 alias records support apex domains (unlike CNAME records). ⚠️ A. Transit Gateway with CNAME Transit Gateway is for VPC connectivity, not load balancing to ALBs. CNAME records cannot be used for apex domains in Route 53 - only alias records support root domain configuration. ⚠️ B. Transit Gateway with multicast domain Multicast domains route traffic between VPC subnets for multicast applications, not to Application Load Balancers. Transit Gateway doesn't provide the global traffic optimization needed for this multi-regional trading application. ⚠️ D. Global Accelerator with Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoint While Global Accelerator is correct, Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoints are for DNS queries from on-premises to VPC, not for public domain resolution. An alias record is needed instead.

When should you choose AWS Global Accelerator over Amazon CloudFront for a multi-regional application? A. When you need to cache static content like images and videos B. When you need intelligent traffic routing to multiple Application Load Balancers across regions C. When you want to reduce costs for content delivery D. When you only need to serve content to users in a single region ✅ B. When you need intelligent traffic routing to multiple Application Load Balancers across regions AWS Global Accelerator • Routes traffic to optimal healthy endpoints • Works with ALBs, NLBs, EC2, EIPs • Provides static anycast IP addresses • Uses AWS backbone network • Best for dynamic content and APIs Amazon CloudFront • Caches content at edge locations • Optimizes delivery of static assets • Reduces origin server load • Lower costs for cacheable content • Best for static websites and media 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Global Accelerator when you need to route traffic to multiple backend services across regions. Choose CloudFront when you need to cache and deliver static content globally.

Which statement about Route 53 alias records is correct? A. Alias records can only point to subdomains, not apex domains B. Alias records can point to apex domains and are automatically resolved to IP addresses C. Alias records are identical to CNAME records in functionality D. Alias records require manual IP address updates when targets change ✅ B. Alias records can point to apex domains and are automatically resolved to IP addresses Why correct: Alias records are a Route 53 extension that can be used for both apex domains (example.com) and subdomains (www.example.com), unlike CNAME records which cannot be used for apex domains. Route 53 automatically resolves alias records to the current IP addresses of the target resource. Why others are wrong: A is incorrect because alias records specifically support apex domains. C is wrong because alias records have unique capabilities that CNAME records lack. D is incorrect because alias records automatically update when target IP addresses change.

A company needs to improve application performance for global users by routing traffic to the nearest healthy endpoint across multiple AWS regions, without caching content. Which service best addresses this requirement? A. Amazon CloudFront B. AWS Global Accelerator C. AWS Transit Gateway D. Elastic Load Balancing ✅ B. AWS Global Accelerator 🎯 Key trigger: "routing traffic to nearest healthy endpoint" + "multiple regions" + "without caching" = Global Accelerator. It uses AWS backbone network for intelligent routing to optimal endpoints based on health and proximity. ⚠️ A. CloudFront is for caching content, not routing to application endpoints ⚠️ C. Transit Gateway connects VPCs, not for global traffic routing ⚠️ D. ELB works within a single region, not across multiple regions

A solutions architect proposes using AWS Transit Gateway to distribute traffic to Application Load Balancers across multiple regions for a global application. Why is this problematic? A. Transit Gateway doesn't support cross-region connectivity B. Transit Gateway is designed for VPC-to-VPC connectivity, not for load balancing to ALBs C. Transit Gateway is more expensive than other solutions D. Transit Gateway requires complex routing table configurations ✅ B. Transit Gateway is designed for VPC-to-VPC connectivity, not for load balancing to ALBs Transit Gateway creates a hub for connecting VPCs and on-premises networks, but it doesn't provide intelligent traffic distribution to application endpoints or load balancers. It operates at the network connectivity layer, not the application load balancing layer. 🎯 Better approach: Use AWS Global Accelerator which is specifically designed to route traffic to ALBs, NLBs, and other endpoints across multiple regions with intelligent health-based routing and performance optimization.

A media company needs to provide another AWS account access to S3 , KMS , and OpenSearch Service resources. Requirements: users must retain their existing permissions while accessing shared resources, solution must support continuous auditing of policy configurations, and access is granted via AWS account ID list . Which policy type and monitoring solution should be implemented? A. Cross-account access with user-based policy + AWS Config rules B. Service-linked role with identity-based policy + AWS Systems Manager rules C. Cross-account access with resource-based policy + AWS Config rules D. Service-linked role with service control policy + AWS Systems Manager rules ✅ C. Cross-account access with resource-based policy + AWS Config rules 🎯 Why correct: Resource-based policies allow users to retain their existing permissions while accessing shared resources across accounts. AWS Config provides continuous monitoring and auditing of policy configurations. ⚠️ A. User-based policy User-based policies map access to specific IAM users, not AWS resources. This doesn't enable cross-account resource sharing and doesn't meet the requirement to grant access via AWS account ID list. ⚠️ B. Service-linked role + Systems Manager Service-linked roles are predefined by AWS services and cannot be customized for cross-account access. Systems Manager doesn't provide policy configuration auditing like AWS Config does. ⚠️ D. Service control policy + Systems Manager Service control policies are used in AWS Organizations for governance, not cross-account resource access. Service-linked roles are service-managed and inappropriate for custom cross-account scenarios.

When should you use resource-based policies versus role-based cross-account access? A. Always use roles for better security B. Use resource-based when users need to retain existing permissions C. Use roles when sharing with multiple accounts D. Resource-based policies are only for S3 buckets ✅ B. Use resource-based when users need to retain existing permissions Resource-Based Policies • Users keep existing permissions • Access both accounts simultaneously • Ideal for data copying/sharing • Supported by S3, KMS, SNS, SQS Role-Based Access • Users assume role permissions only • Must switch between accounts • Better for administrative tasks • Works with all AWS services 🎯 Decision rule: Choose resource-based when users need to work with resources in both accounts simultaneously. Choose roles when users can temporarily switch contexts.

Which statement about AWS Config rules is correct? A. Config rules can prevent non-compliant resource creation B. Config rules continuously monitor and evaluate resource configurations C. Config rules automatically remediate all compliance violations D. Config rules only work with EC2 instances ✅ B. Config rules continuously monitor and evaluate resource configurations 🎯 Key insight: AWS Config is detective, not preventive. It monitors existing resources against compliance rules but doesn't block creation. Remediation requires additional setup with Systems Manager or Lambda.

A company needs to continuously audit IAM policy changes across multiple AWS accounts and evaluate compliance against organizational standards. Which service best addresses this requirement? A. AWS Systems Manager B. AWS Config C. AWS CloudTrail D. AWS Organizations ✅ B. AWS Config 🎯 Trigger mapping: "Continuously audit" + "evaluate compliance" = AWS Config's core functionality of ongoing configuration assessment against rules. CloudTrail logs API calls but doesn't evaluate compliance. Systems Manager focuses on operational tasks. Organizations provides governance but not detailed compliance evaluation.

A solutions architect proposes using service-linked roles for cross-account resource sharing. Why is this problematic? A. Service-linked roles are too expensive B. Service-linked roles are predefined by AWS services and cannot be customized C. Service-linked roles don't support encryption D. Service-linked roles only work within the same account ✅ B. Service-linked roles are predefined by AWS services and cannot be customized Service-linked roles are created and managed by AWS services with predetermined permissions. They cannot be modified to grant custom cross-account access to your resources. 🎯 Better approach: Use standard IAM roles with custom trust policies for cross-account access, or resource-based policies when users need to retain existing permissions.

A company launched a bug bounty program to find security vulnerabilities. As solutions architect, you're focused on checking system vulnerabilities for DDoS attacks on AWS resources. Due to budget constraints , the company cannot afford AWS Shield Advanced for higher-level attack prevention. Which TWO techniques best help mitigate Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks for cloud infrastructure hosted in AWS? A. Use Amazon CloudFront distribution for static and dynamic content. Add CloudWatch alerts for CPUUtilization and NetworkIn metrics to trigger Auto Scaling B. Add multiple Elastic Network Interfaces to each EC2 instance and use Enhanced Networking to increase network bandwidth C. Use Reserved EC2 instances for maximum performance. Use AWS WAF to protect web applications from common exploits D. Use Application Load Balancer (ALB) to distribute traffic across backend instances. Integrate AWS WAF with ALB for web exploit protection ✅ A & D. CloudFront + Auto Scaling and ALB + WAF integration 🎯 Why correct: CloudFront acts as a shield by only accepting well-formed connections and filtering malicious traffic at edge locations before it reaches your origin. ALB distributes attack traffic across multiple instances while auto-scaling provides elastic capacity to absorb large volumes of requests. ⚠️ B. Multiple ENIs + Enhanced Networking Even with increased network bandwidth, the CPU of individual instances will still be saturated by DDoS requests, making the application unresponsive. This doesn't address the core problem of traffic distribution and filtering. ⚠️ C. Reserved EC2 instances Reserved instances are a billing model that doesn't provide any additional computing performance compared to On-Demand instances. They offer cost savings through commitment but no DDoS mitigation capabilities.

When comparing DDoS protection services, when should you choose AWS Shield Standard over AWS Shield Advanced? A. When you need 24/7 access to DDoS Response Team (DRT) and cost protection for scaling charges B. When you have budget constraints and need basic protection against common network and transport layer attacks C. When you require real-time attack notifications and detailed attack diagnostics D. When you need protection against sophisticated application layer attacks targeting specific applications ✅ B. Budget constraints with basic protection needs AWS Shield Standard • Free with all AWS services • Protects against common network/transport layer attacks • Basic CloudWatch metrics • Automatic protection for CloudFront and Route 53 AWS Shield Advanced • $3,000/month fee • 24/7 DDoS Response Team access • Cost protection for scaling charges • Advanced attack diagnostics and notifications • Enhanced protection for EC2, ALB, NLB, CloudFront 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Standard when budget is constrained and you only need basic protection. Choose Advanced when you can afford the cost and need enterprise-grade DDoS response capabilities.

Which statement about Amazon CloudFront's DDoS protection capabilities is correct? A. CloudFront only protects static content and requires Shield Advanced for dynamic content protection B. CloudFront automatically blocks all traffic that doesn't originate from known geographic regions C. CloudFront only accepts well-formed connections, preventing SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks from reaching your origin D. CloudFront protection is only effective when combined with AWS WAF and cannot work independently ✅ C. CloudFront filters malformed connections and prevents common network attacks 🎯 Key insight: CloudFront acts as a protective barrier by validating connections at edge locations before forwarding legitimate traffic to your origin servers. This built-in filtering prevents many common DDoS attack vectors like SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks from ever reaching your infrastructure, regardless of whether you use Shield Advanced or WAF.

A web application is experiencing sudden traffic spikes that overwhelm individual EC2 instances, causing application timeouts and poor user experience during peak periods. Which AWS service best addresses this scaling challenge? A. Amazon CloudWatch with custom metrics B. Application Load Balancer (ALB) with Auto Scaling C. Amazon ElastiCache for session management D. AWS Lambda for serverless processing ✅ B. Application Load Balancer with Auto Scaling 🎯 Perfect match: ALB distributes incoming traffic across multiple healthy instances while Auto Scaling automatically adds/removes instances based on demand. This combination prevents any single instance from being overwhelmed and ensures consistent performance during traffic spikes. CloudWatch provides monitoring but doesn't solve the traffic distribution problem. ElastiCache helps with data access but doesn't address instance overload. Lambda is serverless but may not be suitable for existing web application architecture.

A solutions architect proposes using Reserved EC2 instances to improve DDoS attack resilience because "reserved instances provide guaranteed maximum performance." Why is this approach problematic? A. Reserved instances have the same performance as On-Demand instances and don't provide DDoS protection B. Reserved instances are more expensive during DDoS attacks due to additional charges C. Reserved instances cannot be used with Auto Scaling groups for elastic capacity D. Reserved instances require AWS Shield Advanced to be effective against attacks ✅ A. Reserved instances offer no performance advantage or DDoS protection Reserved instances are simply a billing model that provides cost savings through commitment - they don't enhance compute performance, network capacity, or provide any security features. A single reserved instance will still be overwhelmed by a DDoS attack just like an On-Demand instance. 🎯 Better approach: Use Application Load Balancer with Auto Scaling to distribute attack traffic across multiple instances and automatically scale capacity. Combine with CloudFront for edge-level filtering and AWS WAF for application-layer protection.

A media company with a hybrid architecture has 50+ TB of digital videos stored on on-premises tape library. They want to implement automated facial recognition catalog with minimal disruption to existing MAM system and least management overhead . Eventually migrate to AWS. Which solution provides the least ongoing management overhead with minimal disruption? A. Use Amazon Kinesis Video Streams for ingestion and Amazon Rekognition for facial recognition processing B. Set up tape gateway appliance and process videos directly from tape gateway using Lambda and Rekognition C. Set up file gateway appliance, use MAM to send files to gateway, process with Lambda and Rekognition from S3 D. Use AWS Snowball to migrate files to S3, install open-source facial recognition on EC2 instance ✅ C. File Gateway with Lambda and Rekognition processing 🎯 Why correct: File Gateway provides seamless integration with existing MAM system while automatically backing files to S3. Rekognition can directly process files from S3 with minimal architectural changes. ⚠️ A. Kinesis Video Streams Requires significant changes to MAM solution to stream files into Kinesis. Designed for real-time streaming, not processing pre-existing archived files from tape library. ⚠️ B. Tape Gateway processing Cannot process videos directly from tape gateway in real-time since it's backed by Glacier storage. Files must be retrieved from archive before processing, adding latency. ⚠️ D. Snowball + open-source tools Requires significant management overhead to maintain open-source facial recognition on EC2. Less accurate than managed Rekognition service and requires custom development.

When should you choose AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway over Tape Gateway for media processing workflows? A. When you need the lowest cost long-term archival storage B. When you need real-time access to files for processing by AWS services C. When you want to replace physical tape infrastructure completely D. When you need to maintain tape-based backup workflows ✅ B. When you need real-time access to files for processing by AWS services File Gateway • Files stored in S3 for immediate access • Real-time processing by Lambda, Rekognition, etc. • NFS/SMB protocol support • Good for active file processing workflows Tape Gateway • Archives to Glacier/Deep Archive • Lowest cost for long-term storage • VTL (Virtual Tape Library) interface • Good for backup and compliance archival 🎯 Decision rule: Choose File Gateway when you need AWS services to actively process files. Choose Tape Gateway when you need cost-effective long-term archival with occasional retrieval.

Which statement about Amazon Rekognition face collections is correct? A. Face collections automatically sync across all AWS regions B. You must create a face collection in a specific region before using IndexFaces operation C. Face collections can only store faces from images, not videos D. Face collections are automatically created when you first use SearchFacesByImage ✅ B. You must create a face collection in a specific region before using IndexFaces operation 🎯 Workflow: First use CreateCollection to create a face collection in your chosen region, then use IndexFaces to detect and store facial features. Collections are region-specific and must be explicitly created. You can then search using SearchFacesByImage , StartFaceSearch (videos), or CreateStreamProcessor (streaming).

A company needs to process 50TB of existing video files for facial recognition while maintaining integration with their current Media Asset Management system and minimizing infrastructure changes . Which AWS service combination best addresses this requirement? A. Amazon Kinesis Video Streams + Rekognition B. Storage Gateway File Gateway + Rekognition + Lambda C. EC2 + OpenCV + S3 D. AWS Batch + Rekognition + EFS ✅ B. Storage Gateway File Gateway + Rekognition + Lambda 🎯 Perfect fit: File Gateway seamlessly integrates with existing file systems, automatically syncs to S3, Lambda triggers Rekognition processing, and requires minimal changes to current MAM workflows. ⚠️ A. Kinesis Video Streams requires streaming architecture changes to existing MAM system ⚠️ C. EC2 + OpenCV requires significant management overhead and custom development ⚠️ D. AWS Batch adds unnecessary complexity for this use case

A solutions architect proposes using Storage Gateway Tape Gateway to process videos with Amazon Rekognition in real-time. Why is this problematic? A. Tape Gateway doesn't support video file formats B. Rekognition cannot access files stored in Glacier/Deep Archive directly C. Tape Gateway only works with physical tape drives D. Lambda functions cannot trigger from Tape Gateway events ✅ B. Rekognition cannot access files stored in Glacier/Deep Archive directly Tape Gateway stores data in Glacier or Deep Archive which requires retrieval time (minutes to hours) before access. This makes real-time processing impossible as files must be restored from archive storage first. 🎯 Better approach: Use File Gateway which stores files in S3 Standard for immediate access by Rekognition, enabling real-time processing workflows.

A company runs a Flight Deals web application on-premises with high-resolution photos and third-party payment integration. A global marketing campaign will increase traffic dramatically. Due to tight deadlines , they cannot fully migrate to AWS but need to handle traffic spikes and implement security rules against SQL injection and XSS attacks. Which option will maintain website functionality despite massive incoming traffic? A. Generate AMI, launch EC2 Auto Scaling group, use ALB to balance traffic between on-premises and AWS B. Use CloudFront to cache images/assets, deploy AWS WAF on CloudFront distribution C. Use AWS Application Migration Service to migrate website, create Auto Scaling group, deploy WAF D. Create S3 static website hosting, move domain to Route 53, enable S3 encryption ✅ B. Use CloudFront to cache images/assets, deploy AWS WAF on CloudFront distribution 🎯 Why correct: CloudFront provides immediate scalability by caching static assets at edge locations globally, reducing load on on-premises servers. AWS WAF on CloudFront adds security rules without infrastructure changes. This solution requires minimal time and provides global performance. ⚠️ A. AMI + EC2 Auto Scaling + ALB hybrid Requires AWS Direct Connect or VPN connection between on-premises and AWS for ALB to route traffic properly. The scenario doesn't mention existing connectivity, making this solution incomplete and potentially impossible to implement quickly. ⚠️ C. AWS Application Migration Service Migration takes significant time for planning, testing, and execution, which contradicts the "tight deadline" constraint. While technically sound for long-term scalability, it doesn't address the immediate need to handle traffic spikes. ⚠️ D. S3 static website + Route 53 Flight Deals website accepts payments and bookings, making it a dynamic application that cannot function as a static S3 website. Domain migration to Route 53 also takes time for DNS propagation and testing.

When should you choose CloudFront over Application Load Balancer for handling traffic spikes? A. When you need SSL termination and health checks for backend servers B. When you have static content to cache globally and want to reduce origin server load C. When you need to route traffic based on HTTP headers and paths D. When you need to distribute traffic across multiple AZs within a region ✅ B. When you have static content to cache globally and want to reduce origin server load CloudFront • Global edge locations for content caching • Reduces origin server load • Optimizes static/dynamic content delivery • Integrates with AWS WAF for security • Works with any HTTP origin (on-premises or cloud) Application Load Balancer • Layer 7 load balancing within AWS regions • Advanced routing based on content • SSL termination and health checks • Target groups for EC2, containers, IPs • Requires targets within AWS infrastructure 🎯 Decision rule: Choose CloudFront when you need global content delivery and caching. Choose ALB when you need intelligent routing and load balancing within AWS regions.

Which statement about AWS WAF deployment options is correct? A. WAF can only be deployed on CloudFront distributions, not on load balancers B. WAF requires additional EC2 instances to run the firewall software C. WAF can be deployed on CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway D. WAF rules must be manually updated whenever new attack patterns emerge ✅ C. WAF can be deployed on CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway 🎯 Why correct: AWS WAF is a managed service that integrates with these three services without requiring additional infrastructure. Managed Rules automatically update for new threats, making options A, B, and D incorrect. This flexibility allows security at edge (CloudFront), application tier (ALB), or API layer (API Gateway).

A company needs to quickly handle global traffic spikes for their on-premises website without major infrastructure changes, while adding protection against common web attacks . Which combination of services best addresses this requirement? A. Auto Scaling groups with Elastic Load Balancer B. CloudFront with AWS WAF C. Route 53 with health checks D. AWS Shield with Network Load Balancer ✅ B. CloudFront with AWS WAF 🎯 Key triggers: "Quickly" and "without major infrastructure changes" point to CloudFront's ability to use existing on-premises servers as custom origins. "Global traffic spikes" requires edge caching. "Common web attacks" requires WAF rules for SQL injection/XSS protection. A. Requires migrating to AWS infrastructure C. DNS routing doesn't handle traffic spikes or security D. Shield protects against DDoS, not application-layer attacks

Requirements: Immediate scalability for high-resolution images, no time for migration , global user base , protection against SQL injection , existing on-premises payment processing. Which service combination meets ALL requirements? A. S3 static hosting with CloudFront B. EC2 Auto Scaling with Application Load Balancer C. CloudFront with custom origin and AWS WAF D. AWS Application Migration Service with Auto Scaling ✅ C. CloudFront with custom origin and AWS WAF 🎯 Requirements mapping: Immediate scalability → CloudFront edge caching; No migration time → custom origin points to existing servers; Global users → worldwide edge locations; SQL injection protection → WAF managed rules; Payment processing → dynamic functionality preserved. A. Static hosting can't handle payment processing B. Requires migration to AWS infrastructure D. Migration takes significant time

A company uses AWS Organizations to manage multi-account infrastructure. They're automating daily processes including sharing AWS resources across organizational accounts using AWS RAM . Previously, a separate organization account moderator managed this service and maintained configuration details. What is a simple and effective solution to allow the service to perform tasks on organization accounts on the moderator's behalf? A. Enable cross-account access with AWS Organizations in the Resource Access Manager Console B. Configure a service-linked role for AWS RAM and modify the permissions and trust policies C. Use trusted access by running the enable-sharing-with-aws-organization command in the AWS RAM CLI D. Attach an IAM role on the service and use AWS Systems Manager for automation workflows ✅ C. Use trusted access by running the enable-sharing-with-aws-organization command in the AWS RAM CLI 🎯 Why correct: Trusted access enables AWS RAM to automatically create service-linked roles across all organization accounts, allowing the service to perform resource sharing tasks without manual configuration in each account. This is the simplest approach for organization-wide automation. ⚠️ A. Cross-account access via console This enables cross-account access but not trusted access with AWS Organizations. Trusted access is specifically needed to allow AWS RAM to operate across the entire organization automatically, not just cross-account sharing. ⚠️ B. Configure service-linked role manually Service-linked roles for trusted services are created automatically when trusted access is enabled. Additionally, you cannot modify the trust policy of a service-linked role - only the linked AWS service can assume it. ⚠️ D. IAM role with Systems Manager Systems Manager is designed for EC2 instances and on-premises servers automation, not for AWS RAM resource sharing across Organizations. This adds unnecessary complexity and doesn't address the core requirement of organization-wide resource sharing.

Which statement about AWS RAM service-linked roles in Organizations is correct? A. Service-linked roles must be manually created in each organization account B. Trust policies of service-linked roles can be modified to allow cross-service access C. Service-linked roles are automatically created in all accounts when trusted access is enabled D. Service-linked roles require explicit permission boundaries to function properly ✅ C. Service-linked roles are automatically created in all accounts when trusted access is enabled 🎯 Key insight: When you enable trusted access for AWS RAM with Organizations, it automatically creates the AWSResourceAccessManagerServiceRolePolicy service-linked role in every organization account. This eliminates manual configuration and ensures consistent permissions across all accounts. Trust policies of service-linked roles cannot be modified - only the linked service can assume them.

When should you use AWS RAM trusted access versus cross-account IAM roles for resource sharing? A. Always use cross-account IAM roles for better security control B. Use trusted access for organization-wide automation and cross-account roles for specific sharing C. Use trusted access only for read-only access and cross-account roles for write access D. Both approaches are identical and can be used interchangeably ✅ B. Use trusted access for organization-wide automation and cross-account roles for specific sharing AWS RAM Trusted Access • Automatic service-linked role creation • Organization-wide resource sharing • Simplified management at scale • Built-in integration with Organizations Cross-Account IAM Roles • Manual role configuration required • Account-to-account specific sharing • Fine-grained permission control • Custom trust relationships 🎯 Decision rule: Choose trusted access when you need automated, organization-wide resource sharing with minimal configuration. Choose cross-account roles when you need specific, controlled sharing between particular accounts with custom permissions.

A company needs to automatically share VPC subnets and transit gateways across all accounts in their AWS Organization without manual intervention in each account. Which AWS service configuration best addresses this requirement? A. AWS Config with organization-wide configuration rules B. AWS RAM with trusted access enabled C. AWS CloudFormation StackSets for cross-account deployment D. AWS Control Tower with Service Control Policies ✅ B. AWS RAM with trusted access enabled 🎯 Trigger recognition: The key phrase "automatically share [AWS resources] across all accounts" without manual intervention directly maps to AWS RAM's trusted access capability. This creates service-linked roles automatically and enables seamless resource sharing across the entire organization. ⚠️ A. AWS Config - Monitors compliance, doesn't share resources ⚠️ C. CloudFormation StackSets - Deploys resources but doesn't share existing ones ⚠️ D. Control Tower - Provides governance but not resource sharing automation

A solutions architect proposes manually creating IAM service-linked roles for AWS RAM in each organization account instead of using trusted access. Why is this problematic? A. Service-linked roles cannot be created manually by users B. It creates inconsistent permissions across accounts C. Manual creation violates AWS security best practices D. It prevents AWS RAM from functioning properly ✅ A. Service-linked roles cannot be created manually by users This approach fails because service-linked roles are AWS-managed roles that can only be created by the AWS service itself (in this case, AWS RAM). Users cannot manually create, modify, or delete these roles. They are automatically created when the service needs them and trusted access is enabled. 🎯 Better approach: Use the enable-sharing-with-aws-organization CLI command to enable trusted access, which allows AWS RAM to automatically create the required service-linked roles across all organization accounts with the correct permissions and trust relationships.

An IT consultancy uses AWS Organizations to manage multiple AWS accounts across regional offices. A new account was added to an OU and uses an Amazon ECS Cluster with an attached service-linked role . The solutions architect created a custom SCP to deny certain ECS actions for regulatory purposes, but after applying the policy, the account could still perform the restricted actions. Which of the following is the most likely reason for this problem? A. The default SCP grants all permissions attached to every root, OU, and account. To apply stricter permissions, this policy is required to be modified. B. There is an SCP attached to a higher-level OU that permits the actions of the service-linked role. This permission would therefore be inherited by the current OU, and override the SCP placed by the administrator. C. SCPs do not affect any service-linked role. Service-linked roles enable other AWS services to integrate with AWS Organizations and can't be restricted by SCPs. D. The ECS service is being run outside the jurisdiction of the organization. SCPs affect only the principals that are managed by accounts that are part of the organization. ✅ C. SCPs do not affect any service-linked role 🎯 Why correct: Service-linked roles are special IAM roles that enable AWS services to integrate with Organizations and cannot be restricted by SCPs. This is a fundamental limitation of SCPs - they don't affect service-linked roles regardless of how the SCP is configured. ⚠️ A. Default SCP modification This is incorrect because the scenario already states a custom deny SCP was created. The FullAWSAccess default SCP allows all actions, but explicit deny policies override any allow policies, so modifying the default wouldn't solve this issue with service-linked roles. ⚠️ B. Higher-level OU permissions This misunderstands SCP inheritance. Even if a higher-level OU has an allow policy, a deny SCP at the current level would still block actions for regular IAM users and roles. The issue isn't about inheritance but about service-linked roles being exempt from SCP restrictions entirely. ⚠️ D. ECS outside organization This is technically incorrect because the service-linked role was created within the organization by the root account. The ECS service itself isn't "outside" the organization's jurisdiction - the issue is that service-linked roles have special exemptions from SCP restrictions.

Which statement about Service Control Policies (SCPs) is correct? A. SCPs grant permissions directly to users and roles in member accounts B. SCPs can restrict service-linked roles to prevent unauthorized AWS service integrations C. SCPs act as permission filters that can only deny actions, never grant them D. SCPs only apply to the root account and cannot affect individual member accounts ✅ C. SCPs act as permission filters that can only deny actions, never grant them 🎯 Key concept: SCPs are permission boundaries that filter what actions are allowed, but they don't grant permissions themselves. Users still need IAM policies to grant permissions, and SCPs can only restrict (deny) what those policies allow. SCPs cannot override explicit deny policies in IAM, and they cannot restrict service-linked roles. A is wrong because SCPs filter permissions but don't grant them - IAM policies grant permissions. B is wrong because service-linked roles are explicitly exempt from SCP restrictions. D is wrong because SCPs can be attached to OUs and individual accounts, not just the root.

A company wants to prevent any account in their organization from launching EC2 instances in specific regions while still allowing all other AWS services. They need a solution that applies across all current and future accounts automatically. Which service best addresses this requirement? A. IAM permission boundaries applied to each account B. Service Control Policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations C. AWS Config rules with automatic remediation D. VPC endpoint policies to block regional access ✅ B. Service Control Policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations 🎯 Why SCPs: SCPs provide centralized governance across all accounts in an organization and can deny specific actions (like EC2 launches) in specific regions. They automatically apply to new accounts added to the organization and work as permission filters. A requires manual application to each account and doesn't scale. C can detect violations but can't prevent them proactively. D only affects VPC endpoints, not EC2 launching permissions.

When should you use Service Control Policies (SCPs) versus IAM Permission Boundaries? A. Use SCPs for organization-wide governance, IAM boundaries for individual user/role limits B. Use SCPs to grant permissions, IAM boundaries to deny permissions C. Use SCPs for temporary restrictions, IAM boundaries for permanent ones D. Use SCPs for service-linked roles, IAM boundaries for regular users ✅ A. Use SCPs for organization-wide governance, IAM boundaries for individual user/role limits Service Control Policies • Organization-wide governance • Applied to accounts/OUs • Cannot restrict service-linked roles • Automatic inheritance • Central management IAM Permission Boundaries • Individual entity control • Applied to specific users/roles • Works with all role types • Manual attachment required • Delegated administration 🎯 Decision rule: Choose SCPs when you need organization-wide guardrails that apply automatically. Choose IAM boundaries when you need to limit what specific users or roles can do, especially for delegated administration scenarios.

A solutions architect proposes using SCPs to prevent a service-linked role from accessing sensitive S3 buckets in a member account. Why is this problematic? A. SCPs can only be applied at the OU level, not to individual accounts B. Service-linked roles are exempt from SCP restrictions and cannot be limited by them C. SCPs require explicit allow statements and cannot use deny statements D. S3 bucket policies override SCPs making the restriction ineffective ✅ B. Service-linked roles are exempt from SCP restrictions and cannot be limited by them This approach fails because service-linked roles have a special exemption from SCP restrictions. SCPs are designed not to interfere with AWS service integrations that rely on these roles. 🎯 Better approach: Use S3 bucket policies with condition statements to restrict access based on the requesting principal, or use S3 Access Points with specific access policies to control how the service-linked role can interact with sensitive data.

A print media company wants to migrate their on-premises web application to AWS. The app allows global users to search and retrieve newspaper pages stored as PNG images with OCR-converted text files . Their OCR license expires soon and they need a scalable, durable, highly available AWS architecture. Which is the best option to achieve this requirement? A. Store images in S3, use Amazon Kendra for search, lifecycle policy to Glacier after 3 months with Glacier Select for queries B. CloudFormation with EBS-backed EC2 instances, ALB, NGINX, open source search, EBS volumes with Data Lifecycle Manager C. S3 bucket with CloudFront distribution, Elastic Beanstalk multi-AZ environment, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Textract for OCR D. S3 Intelligent-Tiering, migrate OCR software to Auto Scaling Spot instances with ALB, Amazon Rekognition for text recognition ✅ C. S3 bucket with CloudFront distribution, Elastic Beanstalk multi-AZ environment, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Textract for OCR 🎯 Why correct: This solution replaces the expiring OCR license with managed AWS services (Textract), provides scalable storage (S3), high availability (multi-AZ Beanstalk), and robust search capabilities (OpenSearch Service). CloudFront ensures global content delivery performance. ⚠️ A. Amazon Kendra approach Kendra is an enterprise search service for existing content repositories, not designed for OCR text recognition from scanned documents. Moving frequently accessed images to Glacier would severely impact retrieval performance for a global web application. ⚠️ B. EBS-based solution EBS volumes are neither scalable nor durable compared to S3, requiring manual management and creating single points of failure. This approach lacks the cost-effectiveness and automated scaling of managed services. ⚠️ D. Rekognition with existing OCR This solution still relies on the expiring OCR software that needs replacement. Amazon Rekognition is optimized for general image recognition, while Textract is specifically designed for document text extraction.

When should you choose Amazon Textract over Amazon Rekognition for document processing? A. When you need to detect faces and objects in images B. When you need to extract structured text, forms, and tables from documents C. When you need to identify inappropriate content in images D. When you need to recognize celebrities in photos ✅ B. When you need to extract structured text, forms, and tables from documents Amazon Textract • Specialized for document text extraction • Handles forms, tables, and structured data • OCR replacement for scanned documents • Invoice and receipt processing • ID document analysis Amazon Rekognition • General computer vision service • Face detection and recognition • Object and scene detection • Content moderation • Celebrity recognition • Basic text detection in images 🎯 Decision rule: Choose Textract when you need to extract and understand structured document content. Choose Rekognition when you need general image analysis, face recognition, or content moderation.

Which statement about Amazon OpenSearch Service is correct? A. It can only be deployed in a single Availability Zone for cost optimization B. It automatically provisions resources and deploys highly-tuned search indexes C. It requires manual installation and configuration of the OpenSearch engine D. It only supports basic keyword searching without analytics capabilities ✅ B. It automatically provisions resources and deploys highly-tuned search indexes 🎯 Why correct: OpenSearch Service is a fully managed service that handles provisioning, scaling, and optimization automatically. You simply upload data and it creates optimized search indexes. The other options are incorrect because: A) It supports multi-AZ deployments for high availability, C) It's fully managed requiring no manual installation, D) It provides comprehensive search and analytics capabilities beyond basic keyword search.

A company has thousands of scanned PDF invoices and needs to automatically extract vendor names, amounts, and line items for processing in their accounting system. Which AWS service best addresses this requirement? A. Amazon Rekognition B. Amazon Textract C. Amazon Comprehend D. Amazon Kendra ✅ B. Amazon Textract 🎯 Key trigger: "Extract structured data from scanned documents" maps directly to Textract's AnalyzeExpense API, which is specifically designed for invoice and receipt processing to extract vendor names, amounts, and line items. ⚠️ A. Rekognition - General computer vision, not optimized for structured document data extraction ⚠️ C. Comprehend - Natural language processing for sentiment/entity analysis, not document structure extraction ⚠️ D. Kendra - Enterprise search service, not document data extraction

A media company requires: global content delivery for images, serverless web hosting with auto-scaling, advanced search capabilities across text content, and 99.99% availability . Which combination of services meets ALL requirements? A. S3 + EC2 Auto Scaling + RDS + Route 53 B. S3 + CloudFront + Elastic Beanstalk + OpenSearch Service C. EFS + Application Load Balancer + Lambda + DynamoDB D. S3 + CloudFront + API Gateway + ElastiCache ✅ B. S3 + CloudFront + Elastic Beanstalk + OpenSearch Service 🎯 Requirements mapping: • Global delivery: CloudFront CDN • Serverless hosting: Elastic Beanstalk with auto-scaling • Advanced search: OpenSearch Service • 99.99% availability: Multi-AZ deployment across all services • Durable storage: S3's 11 9's durability ⚠️ A. EC2 Auto Scaling isn't serverless, RDS doesn't provide search capabilities ⚠️ C. Missing global CDN and advanced search functionality ⚠️ D. ElastiCache is for caching, not search; API Gateway alone doesn't provide web hosting

A company hosts a multi-tiered web application on Auto Scaling EC2 instances across two Availability Zones . Application Load Balancer is in public subnets, EC2 instances in private subnets. Users report the "find a nearby store" function (third-party API call) works only 50% of the time when refreshed. EC2 NAT instances handle outbound API calls. What is the MOST likely cause and recommended solution? A. Failed NAT instance in one public subnet. Use NAT Gateways instead of EC2 NAT instances for availability and scalability. B. Failure in third-party provider's availability zone. Contact third-party support to fix it. C. Overloaded NAT instance. Scale EC2 NAT instances to larger-sized instances. D. Misconfigured Network ACL blocking outbound traffic. Update ACL and configure IAM permissions. ✅ A. Failed NAT instance in one public subnet. Use NAT Gateways instead of EC2 NAT instances for availability and scalability. 🎯 Why correct: The 50% failure rate strongly indicates one of two NAT instances has failed. NAT instances are single points of failure per AZ and AWS doesn't automatically recover them. NAT Gateways provide built-in redundancy within an AZ. ⚠️ B. Third-party provider failure Why wrong: If the third-party API was failing, it would affect all requests consistently, not just 50%. The pattern suggests infrastructure failure on the customer side, not the provider. ⚠️ C. Overloaded NAT instance Why wrong: Overload would cause intermittent slowness or timeouts, not a consistent 50% failure pattern. Scaling wouldn't address the underlying single point of failure issue. ⚠️ D. Network ACL misconfiguration Why wrong: Network ACL issues would block traffic consistently (100% failure), not create a 50% failure pattern. The intermittent nature indicates availability, not permission problems.

When should you choose NAT Gateway over NAT Instance for outbound internet connectivity? A. When you need custom firewall rules and deep packet inspection capabilities B. When you require high availability and managed service with automatic scaling C. When you need to minimize costs for low-traffic applications D. When you need to route traffic through specific security appliances ✅ B. When you require high availability and managed service with automatic scaling NAT Gateway • Managed by AWS • Built-in redundancy within AZ • Automatic bandwidth scaling • Higher availability SLA • No instance management NAT Instance • Customer-managed EC2 instance • Single point of failure • Manual scaling required • Custom security configurations • Lower cost for small workloads 🎯 Decision rule: Choose NAT Gateway for production workloads requiring high availability and minimal management. Choose NAT Instance only when you need custom configurations or cost optimization for low-traffic scenarios.

A company experiences intermittent outbound connectivity failures affecting exactly half of their private subnet instances across two AZs. The pattern is consistent - roughly 50% success rate for external API calls. Which infrastructure component is most likely causing this issue? A. Application Load Balancer health checks B. Failed NAT instance in one Availability Zone C. Route table misconfiguration D. Security group blocking outbound traffic ✅ B. Failed NAT instance in one Availability Zone 🎯 Pattern recognition: A consistent 50% failure rate across two AZs strongly indicates that one of two redundant components has failed. NAT instances are deployed per AZ, so one failed instance would affect exactly half the traffic. Route table or security group issues would affect 100% of traffic, not create a 50/50 pattern. ALB health checks don't impact outbound connectivity from private subnets.

Which statement about NAT Gateway redundancy and availability is correct? A. NAT Gateways automatically replicate across multiple AZs for cross-AZ redundancy B. NAT Gateways provide redundancy within a single AZ but require manual deployment across AZs C. NAT Gateways are single points of failure and require multiple instances for redundancy D. NAT Gateways share the same availability characteristics as NAT instances ✅ B. NAT Gateways provide redundancy within a single AZ but require manual deployment across AZs 🎯 Key insight: While NAT Gateways are highly available within their deployed AZ (AWS manages internal redundancy), they don't automatically span multiple AZs. For cross-AZ redundancy, you must deploy separate NAT Gateways in each AZ and configure route tables accordingly. Option A is wrong because NAT Gateways are AZ-specific resources. Option C confuses NAT Gateways with NAT Instances. Option D is incorrect as NAT Gateways have much higher availability than customer-managed NAT instances.

Requirements: Outbound internet access for private instances, 99.99% availability SLA , automatic bandwidth scaling , and minimal operational overhead . Which solution meets ALL requirements? A. NAT Instances with Auto Scaling Groups across multiple AZs B. NAT Gateways deployed in each Availability Zone C. Internet Gateway with custom routing D. VPC Peering to a public subnet ✅ B. NAT Gateways deployed in each Availability Zone 🎯 Why: High availability SLA → NAT Gateway's managed redundancy. Automatic bandwidth scaling → NAT Gateway feature. Minimal operational overhead → AWS-managed service. Multiple AZs → cross-AZ deployment for 99.99% availability. NAT Instances require significant operational overhead for management and scaling. Internet Gateway doesn't provide NAT functionality for private subnets. VPC Peering doesn't solve outbound internet access requirements.

An online media streaming startup has deployed hundreds of containerized microservices using Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate . As new features roll out, the number of running ECS tasks steadily increases. The engineering team needs to be alerted when the number of concurrently running Fargate vCPUs exceeds 75% of the service quota's maximum limit . Which solution most efficiently monitors and alerts when Fargate vCPU usage reaches 75% of the service quota? A. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor service quotas published in the AWS/Usage metric namespace. Set up an alarm when the math expression metricId/SERVICE_QUOTA(metricId)*100 is greater than 75. Configure Amazon SNS to send notifications to the operations team. B. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor the sample count metric for each service in the ECS cluster. Create an alarm based on the math expression sample count/SERVICE_QUOTA(service)*100 when it exceeds 75. Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) to notify the operations team. C. Use AWS Service Quotas to request an increase in the Fargate task limit to 200% of the current limit. Configure AWS Health Dashboard to monitor for quota-related issues and use Amazon EventBridge to trigger an AWS Lambda function that sends notifications via Amazon SNS when the usage reaches 75% of the new limit. D. Use Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights to monitor ECS clusters and tasks. Create a custom CloudWatch dashboard that displays the current Fargate task count and the account limit. Set up a CloudWatch alarm based on a custom metric that calculates the percentage of tasks used. ✅ A. Use Amazon CloudWatch to monitor service quotas published in the AWS/Usage metric namespace with SERVICE_QUOTA() math expression 🎯 Why correct: AWS publishes service quota metrics in the AWS/Usage namespace, and the SERVICE_QUOTA() function retrieves the actual quota limit for calculations. This provides real-time monitoring without custom metrics or complex configurations. ⚠️ B. Sample count metric monitoring Sample count measures the number of requests or invocations, not the actual resource usage against quotas. This metric doesn't directly correlate to vCPU consumption or service quota utilization for Fargate tasks. ⚠️ C. Quota increase with AWS Health Dashboard This approach focuses on increasing quotas rather than monitoring them. AWS Health Dashboard is reactive and designed for service health notifications, not proactive quota monitoring against percentage thresholds. ⚠️ D. Custom metrics with Container Insights While Container Insights provides valuable monitoring, creating custom metrics requires additional development and maintenance effort. This is less operationally efficient than using built-in AWS/Usage namespace metrics.

Which statement about the CloudWatch SERVICE_QUOTA() function is correct? A. It retrieves the current usage percentage of a service quota automatically B. It returns the maximum allowed limit for a specific AWS service quota C. It can only be used with custom CloudWatch metrics, not built-in AWS metrics D. It requires AWS Config to be enabled to function properly ✅ B. It returns the maximum allowed limit for a specific AWS service quota 🎯 Key insight: SERVICE_QUOTA() is a built-in CloudWatch function that retrieves the actual service quota limit value, enabling mathematical expressions like usage/SERVICE_QUOTA(metric)*100 to calculate percentage utilization. It works with AWS/Usage namespace metrics without requiring additional services or custom metrics.

When should you choose AWS/Usage namespace metrics over CloudWatch Container Insights for quota monitoring? A. When you need detailed container-level performance metrics B. When you need to monitor service quotas and limits proactively C. When you need to troubleshoot individual container failures D. When you need to optimize container resource allocation ✅ B. When you need to monitor service quotas and limits proactively AWS/Usage Namespace • Built-in service quota metrics • Direct integration with SERVICE_QUOTA() function • Minimal configuration required • Focused on quota and limit monitoring CloudWatch Container Insights • Detailed container performance metrics • Application-level monitoring • Resource utilization at task/container level • Troubleshooting and optimization focus 🎯 Decision rule: Choose AWS/Usage when monitoring quotas and limits. Choose Container Insights when you need detailed container performance analysis and troubleshooting capabilities.

A company needs to automatically increase AWS service quotas when usage approaches 90% of the current limit to prevent service disruptions. Which AWS service best addresses this automated quota management requirement? A. AWS Service Quotas with automatic quota increase requests B. CloudWatch Alarms with EventBridge triggering Lambda functions C. AWS Config with remediation configurations D. AWS Systems Manager with automation documents ✅ B. CloudWatch Alarms with EventBridge triggering Lambda functions 🎯 Why: AWS Service Quotas doesn't support automatic quota increases - they must be requested manually. The automation requires CloudWatch Alarms to detect the 90% threshold, EventBridge to route the alarm, and Lambda to programmatically submit quota increase requests via the Service Quotas API. A is incorrect because Service Quotas requires manual approval for increases. C and D don't have native integration with quota monitoring and management.

Requirements: Real-time monitoring of Fargate vCPU usage, percentage-based alerting at 75% threshold, minimal operational overhead , and no custom metric development . Which monitoring approach meets ALL requirements? A. Custom CloudWatch dashboard with manual threshold calculations B. AWS/Usage namespace with SERVICE_QUOTA() math expressions C. Third-party monitoring tools with AWS API integration D. AWS Config rules with compliance monitoring ✅ B. AWS/Usage namespace with SERVICE_QUOTA() math expressions 🎯 Why: AWS/Usage provides real-time quota metrics, SERVICE_QUOTA() enables percentage calculations without custom metrics, CloudWatch alarms provide threshold alerting, and the entire solution uses native AWS services with minimal overhead. A requires custom development. C adds external dependencies and complexity. D is designed for compliance, not real-time performance monitoring.

A company has multiple AWS accounts . Account A hosts a private hosted zone in Route 53 with CNAME record db.turotialsdojo.com for centralized DNS. Account B hosts the new VPC with EC2 instances and RDS . The application in Account B cannot resolve the database endpoint db.turotialsdojo.com, though the Route 53 entry is configured correctly. Which TWO actions will resolve this cross-account DNS issue? A. Create VPC peering and configure EC2 instances to use Account A DNS resolver IPs B. Create new private hosted zone in Account B and associate to Account A for replication C. On Account B, associate the VPC to Account A's private hosted zone, then delete authorization D. Create custom AMI with updated /etc/resolv.conf containing RDS endpoint mapping E. On Account A, create authorization to associate its private hosted zone to Account B VPC ✅ C & E. Cross-account Route 53 association with authorization 🎯 Why correct: Route 53 private hosted zones require explicit cross-account authorization before VPC association. Account A must first authorize Account B's VPC, then Account B associates its VPC to Account A's hosted zone. ⚠️ A. VPC peering with custom DNS resolver While VPC peering enables connectivity, Route 53 in Account A has no knowledge of the RDS instance in Account B. The EC2 instances still cannot resolve the endpoint because the DNS record points to Account A's resolver which doesn't know Account B's resources. ⚠️ B. Route 53 zone replication Route 53 private hosted zones cannot replicate between AWS accounts. There's no built-in replication mechanism for hosted zones across account boundaries - you must use the proper cross-account association process instead. ⚠️ D. Static IP mapping in /etc/resolv.conf Hardcoding RDS endpoint to IP mappings is unreliable because RDS private IP addresses can change during maintenance, failover, or other AWS operations. This creates a brittle solution that will break unexpectedly.

Which statement about Route 53 private hosted zones across AWS accounts is correct? A. Private hosted zones automatically replicate DNS records across all accounts in an organization B. You must create authorization before associating a VPC from a different account to a private hosted zone C. Cross-account VPC association can only be done through the AWS Management Console D. Private hosted zones can only be associated with VPCs in the same AWS account ✅ B. Authorization is required before cross-account VPC association 🎯 Cross-account Route 53 process: The account owning the hosted zone must first create authorization using create-vpc-association-authorization , then the VPC owner associates their VPC. This two-step process ensures security and prevents unauthorized access to DNS records. Options A and D are false - no automatic replication exists and cross-account association is supported. Option C is false - console cannot be used for cross-account associations.

A company needs centralized DNS management across multiple AWS accounts with secure cross-account resolution . Teams must resolve internal endpoints from VPCs in different accounts. The solution must prevent unauthorized DNS access and support programmatic management . Which DNS solution meets ALL requirements? A. Public hosted zone with restricted access policies B. Route 53 Resolver with forwarding rules C. Private hosted zone with cross-account VPC associations D. Custom DNS servers on EC2 with VPC peering ✅ C. Private hosted zone with cross-account VPC associations 🎯 Why this meets all requirements: Private hosted zones provide centralized management from one account, secure internal resolution (not internet-accessible), authorization-controlled access preventing unauthorized associations, and full API/CLI support for programmatic management. Cross-account VPC association enables resolution across accounts while maintaining security boundaries. ⚠️ A. Public hosted zone: Exposes internal DNS records to the internet, violating security requirements for internal endpoints. ⚠️ B. Route 53 Resolver: Primarily for hybrid connectivity and conditional forwarding, not centralized internal DNS management across accounts. ⚠️ D. Custom DNS servers: Requires significant operational overhead, lacks AWS integration, and doesn't provide centralized management benefits.

A solutions architect proposes using VPC peering with custom DNS resolver configuration to solve cross-account DNS resolution. Why is this problematic for Route 53 private hosted zones? A. VPC peering doesn't support DNS resolution across accounts B. Route 53 in the source account has no knowledge of resources in the target account C. Custom DNS resolvers cannot query Route 53 private hosted zones D. VPC peering requires identical CIDR blocks which prevents DNS forwarding ✅ B. Route 53 in the source account has no knowledge of resources in the target account The fundamental issue is that a Route 53 private hosted zone in Account A containing DNS records cannot resolve resources that physically exist in Account B, even with network connectivity through VPC peering. The DNS service doesn't have cross-account resource awareness. 🎯 Better approach: Use cross-account VPC association with Route 53 private hosted zones. This properly links the VPC containing the resources with the hosted zone containing the DNS records, enabling correct resolution without complex networking workarounds.

A company has DNS records centrally managed in one AWS account but needs applications in other accounts to resolve these internal endpoints . The solution must be secure and not expose records publicly . Which AWS service best addresses this cross-account DNS requirement? A. AWS Direct Connect with custom DNS B. Route 53 private hosted zones with VPC association C. CloudFront with custom domain names D. Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing ✅ B. Route 53 private hosted zones with VPC association 🎯 Trigger mapping: "Centrally managed DNS" + "cross-account" + "internal endpoints" + "secure/not public" = Route 53 private hosted zones. The cross-account VPC association feature specifically addresses this scenario by allowing VPCs in different accounts to resolve records from a centralized private hosted zone while maintaining security. A. Direct Connect is for hybrid connectivity, not cross-account DNS C. CloudFront is for content delivery, not internal DNS resolution D. ALB provides load balancing, not DNS record management
