[SAW] What is SAW (Support Automation Workflows)? Customer-facing automation runbooks built on AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Automation . Prefixed with AWSSupport- or AWSPremiumSupport- . Customers run them in their own accounts for troubleshooting, maintenance, deployment, and remediation. 🧠 Mnemonic: SAW = Support Automates Workflows (customers self-solve)

[SAW] What schema version do SSM Automation runbooks use? Schema version 0.3 — always. Runbooks are SSM documents of type Automation (not Command, Policy, or Session). They support YAML and JSON formats, but SAW requires JSON .

[SAW] What does the SAW Build and Testing Framework do? A Python-based platform that: 1. Composes different artifacts (scripts, CFN templates, attachments) into a deployable SSM runbook 2. Performs integration tests against real AWS resources You develop artifacts → framework assembles them → generates the final SSM document.

[SAW] What are SAW integration tests? Functional tests that automatically execute an SSM runbook against AWS resources created via CloudFormation . You model test cases with different input parameters and resource configurations. You define both success and failure tests. They are required before promoting changes to production.

[SAW] What is the difference between the Core stack and Test stacks in SAW integration tests? Core stack (CoreInfrastructure.yml): - Shared resources across ALL tests (IAM AutomationAssumeRole, VPC, subnet, S3 bucket, etc.) - Created once, deleted last Test stacks (SuccessExecution.yml, FailedExecution.yml): - Test-specific resources (EC2 instances, specific configs) - Reference Core stack outputs via cross-stack references (Fn::ImportValue) - One per test case

[SAW] What are the two test methods used in SAW InnerTests? 1. make_automation_test — asserts the overall automation execution status (Success/Failed) 2. make_step_test — asserts the status of an individual step (Success/Failed/Pending) You should include one make_step_test for each automation step. A Pending status means the step was not executed (e.g., wrong branch taken).

[SAW] What command runs SAW integration tests? make ARGS="--log_level=debug" test Optional overrides: - --region=us-east-1 - --profile_name=myprofile - --ssm_doc_name=AWSSupport-MyDoc - --cfn_test_template_name=FailedExecution - --sequential_tests (default is parallel)

[SAW] Describe the 10-step SAW integration test execution flow. 1. make test calls run_integration_tests.py 2. Parses arguments (region, profile, doc name, templates) 3. Calls ssm_integration_testing.py + ssm_testing.py 4. Creates Core CloudFormation stack 5. Creates the SSM Automation document in your account 6. Calls test_document.py (test case definitions) 7. Each test case runs setUpClass() → creates Test CFN stack 8. Executes the SSM document with input parameters from stack outputs 9. tearDownClass() deletes Test stacks 10. Core stack deleted, test report generated 🧠 Mnemonic: "PACS-CTE-DR" — Parse, Args, Core, SSMdoc, Call tests, Test stack, Execute, Delete, Report

[SAW] What are the key files in a SAW project root folder? Makefile — automates build/test (change DOCUMENT_NAME variable for new runbooks) run_integration_tests.py — entry point for integration tests, defines SSM_DOC_NAME, CFN templates, region ssm_integration_testing.py + ssm_testing.py — core testing framework (usually don't modify)

[SAW] What is in the Documents folder of a SAW project? The SSM Automation runbook in JSON format (e.g., AWSSupport-HelloWorldWorkshop.json). Contains placeholders (like %PYTHONSCRIPT%, %WINDOWSSCRIPT%) that the build process replaces with actual code. Subfolders: - Scripts/ — Python, Bash, PowerShell scripts - CloudFormationTemplates/ — CFN templates used by steps - Attachments/ — files attached to the document ⚠️ Never edit files in the Output/ folder — they're overwritten on every build.

[SAW] What does the Setup folder contain? 4 files that handle the build process (usually don't modify): 1. create_document.py — parses JSON, inserts scripts into placeholders 2. create_document_readme.py — auto-generates README.md from the runbook 3. create_document_graph.py — creates DOT language representation 4. render_document_graph.py — renders the graph as PNG using Graphviz

[SAW] What are the key Makefile commands in a SAW project? Build and Documentation Commands make documents — This is the main build command that compiles your runbook. It processes your workflow definition and replaces any placeholders with the actual script content, creating the final executable runbook. make readme — Automatically generates a README.md file for your project, providing documentation about your workflow. Visualization Commands make graph — Creates a DOT format representation of your workflow. DOT is a graph description language that shows the structure and dependencies of your workflow steps. make render — Takes the graph representation and renders it as a PNG image, giving you a visual diagram of your workflow's structure and flow. Utility Commands make clean — Removes the Output folder, cleaning up any generated files from previous builds. This is useful when you want a fresh build or need to clear old artifacts. make ARGS="..." test — Runs integration tests for your workflow. You can pass specific arguments through the ARGS parameter to customize which tests run or how they execute.

[SAW] What SSM parameter types are available for runbook inputs? Parameter Types Standard types are basic data types you can use for CloudFormation parameters: String : Text values (e.g., "my-bucket-name") StringList : Comma-separated list of strings (e.g., "subnet-1,subnet-2,subnet-3") Integer : Whole numbers (e.g., 5, 100, 1024) Boolean : True/false values MapList : List of key-value pair maps StringMap : Single map of key-value pairs Auto-populate Types These are AWS-specific parameter types that provide a dropdown in the CloudFormation console showing actual AWS resources from your account: AWS::EC2::Instance::Id : Shows existing EC2 instance IDs AWS::IAM::Role::Arn : Shows existing IAM role ARNs And many others documented in the CloudFormation parameter types reference This makes it easier for users to select existing resources rather than typing IDs manually, reducing errors. Validation You can add constraints to parameters: allowedPattern : Uses regex to validate the format (e.g., ^[a-z0-9-]+$ for lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens) allowedValues : Provides a specific list of acceptable values (e.g., ["dev", "staging", "prod"] )

[SAW] Name 6 key SSM Automation actions used in SAW runbooks. 1. aws:executeAwsApi — call any AWS API (uses Selector for JSONPath output) 2. aws:assertAwsResourceProperty — assert a resource state (e.g., PingStatus == Online) 3. aws:waitForAwsResourceProperty — wait until a resource reaches a state 4. aws:branch — conditional branching based on inputs/outputs 5. aws:runCommand — run scripts on managed instances (via SSM Agent) 6. aws:executeScript — run Python/PowerShell in AWS (no instance needed) 7. aws:sleep — pause automation for a duration 🧠 Mnemonic: "EAAB-RES" — Execute API, Assert, wAit, Branch, Run command, Execute script, Sleep

[SAW] What is the difference between aws:runCommand and aws:executeScript? aws:runCommand : - Runs on a managed instance (needs SSM Agent) - Uses AWS-RunPowerShellScript or AWS-RunShellScript - For on-instance operations aws:executeScript : - Runs in AWS (no instance needed) - Python or PowerShell, inline or via attachments - Max 600 seconds (10 min) per execution - Uses Handler (e.g., function_handler) and InputPayload - Returns values via return {'key': value}

[SAW] How does the SAW build process replace script placeholders? In create_document.py , the process() function maps steps to scripts: insert_executescript_in_document(document, "ExecuteScript", "test_function.py") insert_script_in_document(document, "RunLinuxScript", "test_script.sh") insert_script_in_document(document, "RunWindowsPowerShellScript", "test_powershell.ps1") Placeholders like %PYTHONSCRIPT% and %WINDOWSSCRIPT% in the JSON are replaced with actual file contents during make documents .

[SAW] How do you access Automation system variables in aws:executeScript? Via the context parameter in your handler function: context["automation:EXECUTION_ID"] context["global:ACCOUNT_ID"] context["global:REGION"] context["global:DATE"] context["global:DATE_TIME"] Use these instead of hard-coding account IDs, regions, etc.

[SAW] What are the SAW step naming conventions? - aws:branch steps → name as "BranchOn[...]" (e.g., BranchOnPlatform) - aws:waitForAwsResourceProperty steps → name as "Assert[...]" (e.g., AssertInstanceIsSsmManaged) - Every step needs a name and description - Description starts with a verb (as if writing "This step...") - Step names use PascalCase

[SAW] What are the SAW parameter best practices? Validation Requirements Validate ALL parameters using allowedValues, allowedPattern, and appropriate input types Default values should always be the safest option (e.g., CreateBackup defaults to True) Naming Conventions Use CamelCase naming (InstanceId, AutomationAssumeRole) Required vs Optional Parameters Required Parameters No default value specified in the parameter definition Users must provide a value when executing the automation The description must explicitly state (Required) at the beginning Example: yaml InstanceId : type : String description : (Required) The ID of the Amazon EC2 instance to backup allowedPattern : ^i - [ a - z0 - 9 ] { 8 , 17 } $ Optional Parameters Have a default value specified in the parameter definition Users can omit the parameter, and the default will be used The description must explicitly state (Optional) at the beginning The default should be the safest option (e.g., CreateBackup defaults to True) Example: yaml CreateBackup : type : Boolean description : (Optional) Whether to create a backup before modification default : true Why This Matters This convention ensures that anyone reading the automation document can immediately understand: Which inputs they must provide Which inputs have safe defaults they can rely on What the automation will do if they don't specify optional parameters Description Format Start descriptions as if writing "This parameter is..." Example: "The ID of the Amazon EC2..." (not "This parameter is the ID of the Amazon EC2...") Cost Considerations Highlight if the document will incur considerable costs

[SAW] What is the max SSM document size and how do you work around it? Max runbook size: 64 KB . Workarounds: 1. Use document attachments (.zip files) with aws:executeScript — content is decompressed locally 2. Split into multiple smaller runbooks if individually useful 💡 Pro tip: attachments can contain any file type , not just scripts (e.g., large CFN templates).

[SAW] What are the security best practices for SAW runbooks? - Least privilege : specific IAM permissions, never use "*" or Administrator - No sensitive info in outputs (visible in execution history for 30 days) - Mutating actions: explain to customers, add approval/rollback mechanisms, create backups by default - Use DryRun parameter to test permissions before mutating - Secure temp directories: use /var/lib/amazon/ssm/ (Linux), C:\ProgramData\Amazon\SSM (Windows) — never system temp dirs - No 3rd party libraries without AppSec approval - Include Amazon Software License header in scripts

[SAW] What are the region parity considerations for SAW? - SAW publishes to ALL regions : commercial, opt-in, China, GovCloud, MVP - Never hard-code partitions — use CloudFormation pseudo parameters (AWS::Partition, AWS::Region, AWS::AccountId) - Research if resources/features are available in all regions - Test in opt-in regions and China (if accessible) before release - Document any region limitations in the design document

[SAW] What are the key step-level best practices? - Fail early : check preconditions before acting (e.g., assert instance status before RunCommand) - Add timeoutSeconds to all steps (default timeout can be very long) - Avoid maxAttempts on mutating actions unless safe to retry - Keep actions simple : "Functions should do something, or answer something, but not both" - Specify onFailure , nextStep , isEnd , and onCancel for transparency - Only include outputs that customers need — don't overwhelm with values

[SAW] What was the Exercise goal in the workshop? Add a step to put an object in S3 using the random number from ExecuteScript: 1. Add S3 bucket name as input parameter 2. Pass bucket name from CoreInfrastructure.yml outputs to test templates 3. Create new step using aws:executeScript with boto3 s3.put_object() 4. Add VersionId to step and runbook outputs 5. Add s3:PutObject and kms:GenerateDataKey permissions to AutomationAssumeRole 6. Add make_step_test for the new step in both test templates 7. Fix bug: replace cls.ssm_params with cls.override_parameters in test_document.py

[SAW] How is Amazon Q Developer used in the SAW workshop? Two scenarios: 1. Generate docstrings : write one docstring as context, then prompt Q to generate for other functions. Also works with inline suggestions (press TAB). 2. Write unit tests : prompt Q to generate initial boilerplate unit tests for your code. ⚠️ These are NOT necessarily all the tests you need — supplement manually. Unit test coverage must be at least 80% for Python scripts.
SAW runbooks are built on top of {{c1::AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Automation}} and prefixed with {{c2::AWSSupport-}} or {{c2::AWSPremiumSupport-}}.
SSM Automation runbooks always use schema version {{c1::0.3}} and SAW requires them in {{c2::JSON}} format (not YAML).
In a SAW project, the {{c1::Makefile}} variable {{c2::DOCUMENT_NAME}} must be changed when creating a new runbook.
The command {{c1::make documents}} builds the runbook by replacing placeholders with scripts. The final output goes to the {{c2::Output/}} folder.

In SAW integration tests, the {{c1::Core}} stack (CoreInfrastructure.yml) contains shared resources like the {{c2::AutomationAssumeRole}}, while {{c3::Test}} stacks contain test-specific resources like EC2 instances.
Test stacks reference Core stack outputs using CloudFormation {{c1::cross-stack references}} via {{c2::Fn::ImportValue}}.

In SAW InnerTests, {{c1::make_automation_test}} checks the overall execution status, while {{c2::make_step_test}} checks individual step status. A step status of {{c3::Pending}} means it was not executed.

The action {{c1::aws:executeAwsApi}} calls AWS APIs and uses a {{c2::Selector}} (JSONPath) to extract outputs. The action {{c1::aws:assertAwsResourceProperty}} uses a {{c2::PropertySelector}} instead.
{{c1::aws:runCommand}} runs scripts on a managed instance via SSM Agent, while {{c2::aws:executeScript}} runs Python/PowerShell directly in AWS with a max duration of {{c3::600 seconds}}.
In aws:executeScript, the handler function receives {{c1::events}} (input payload) and {{c2::context}} (system variables like EXECUTION_ID, ACCOUNT_ID, REGION).
Script placeholders like {{c1::%PYTHONSCRIPT%}} in the JSON runbook are replaced by the {{c2::create_document.py}} script during the build process via the {{c3::process()}} function.
SAW step naming: aws:branch steps are named {{c1::BranchOn[...]}} and aws:waitForAwsResourceProperty steps are named {{c2::Assert[...]}}.
The maximum SSM document size is {{c1::64 KB}}. To work around this, use {{c2::document attachments}} (.zip files) with aws:executeScript.
SAW parameters: those without a default value are {{c1::Required}}, those with a default are {{c2::Optional}}. Names must use {{c3::CamelCase}}.
For SAW region parity, never hard-code partitions — use CloudFormation {{c1::pseudo parameters}} like {{c2::AWS::Partition}}, {{c2::AWS::Region}}, and {{c2::AWS::AccountId}}.
In the workshop exercise, the bug fix was replacing {{c1::cls.ssm_params}} with {{c2::cls.override_parameters}} in test_document.py because ssm_params was {{c3::never defined}}.

How do you sort a list in-place vs. creating a new sorted list? lst.sort() # in-place, modifies lst sorted(lst, key=lambda x: -x) # new list, reverse 🧠 S.O.N. — S ort = O riginal mutated, sorted = N ew copy Both O(n log n) — Timsort

How do you safely get a dict value without KeyError? And auto-create missing keys? d.get(key, default) # returns default if missing d.setdefault(key, []).append(val) # creates [] if missing 🧠 GET is polite (asks nicely, returns default). SET is bossy (creates the key if it doesn't exist)

Counter: how to count characters and get the top N most frequent? from collections import Counter c = Counter("abracadabra") # {'a':5,'b':2,'r':2,...} c.most_common(2) # [('a',5),('b',2)] 🧠 Counter Counts, Most Common is the Medal Ceremony — gold, silver, bronze order

deque: how to add/remove from both ends in O(1)? from collections import deque dq = deque() dq.append(x) # right end dq.appendleft(x) # left end dq.pop() # right end dq.popleft() # left end 🧠 Deque = Double-Ended Queue . "left" suffix = left side. No suffix = right side (like a normal list) All operations O(1). List popleft would be O(n)!

How to reverse a list? (two ways) lst[::-1] # new reversed list (ASCII hyphen!) lst.reverse() # in-place 🧠 [::-1] = "step back 1 from end to start". ⚠️ Unicode minus (−) will TypeError — must be ASCII hyphen (-)

defaultdict: how does it differ from a regular dict? from collections import defaultdict dd = defaultdict(list) # missing key → empty [] dd['new_key'].append(1) # no KeyError! 🧠 Default = Don't Error, Factory Auto-creates Underlying List/Type

BFS template: what data structure and pattern? from collections import deque queue = deque([start]) visited = {start} while queue: node = queue.popleft() for nb in neighbors(node): if nb not in visited: visited.add(nb) queue.append(nb) 🧠 BFS = Breadth = Bus Queue — people line up (deque), first in first out (popleft). DFS = Dive = Stack (or recursion)

DFS template: recursive with visited set def dfs(node, visited=None): if visited is None: visited = set() visited.add(node) for nb in neighbors(node): if nb not in visited: dfs(nb, visited) 🧠 DFS = Dive First, Surface later — recursion goes deep before backtracking. Always if visited is None to avoid mutable default arg bug

Binary search template lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1 while lo = hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if arr[mid] == target: return mid elif arr[mid] target: lo = mid + 1 else: hi = mid - 1 return -1 🧠 LO-HI-MID : too small → LO jumps right, too big → HI jumps left. Loop ends when LO passes HI O(log n)

Two pointers pattern left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1 while left right: if condition: left += 1 else: right -= 1 🧠 Two guards walking toward each other — left walks right →, right walks left ←, they stop when they meet

Sliding window pattern left = 0 for right in range(len(arr)): # expand window while window_invalid(): left += 1 # shrink # update result 🧠 Caterpillar — right end stretches forward, left end catches up when the body is too long

Heap: how to use as a min-heap and max-heap? import heapq heapq.heappush(h, val) # min-heap heapq.heappop(h) # smallest heapq.heappush(h, -val) # max-heap trick -heapq.heappop(h) # largest 🧠 Python heaps are always min . For max-heap: negate in, negate out push/pop O(log n), heapify O(n)

String: split, join, strip — the 3 essentials s.split() # split by whitespace → list ' '.join(lst) # list → string with separator s.strip() # remove leading/trailing whitespace 🧠 SJS — S plit breaks apart, J oin glues together, S trip trims the edges. Split and Join are inverses

Complexity cheat sheet: list vs dict vs deque # list: append O(1) | insert O(n) | sort O(n log n) # dict: get/set/del O(1) average # set: add/remove/in O(1) average # deque: append/popleft O(1) # heap: push/pop O(log n) | heapify O(n) 🧠 "Lists insert slow, dicts do it all in O(1), deques own both ends, heaps log-climb"

File I/O: read whole file, iterate lines, write with open('f.txt') as f: content = f.read() # whole file for line in f: ... # iterate lines with open('out.txt','w') as f: f.write('text\n') import json data = json.load(open('d.json')) json.dump(data, open('o.json','w'), indent=2) 🧠 WITH = auto-close . read() = gulp whole thing, for line = sip one at a time. JSON: load/dump (files), loads/dumps (strings)

[SAW] When a customer runs a SAW runbook (like AWSSupport-TroubleshootEC2Connectivity ), what happens behind the scenes from start to finish? Describe the full execution flow. Customer opens AWS Systems Manager → Automation in their AWS console (or uses the CLI) They select the runbook and fill in input parameters (e.g., InstanceId, AutomationAssumeRole) The SSM Automation engine (an AWS-managed service) picks up the request It assumes the IAM role specified in AutomationAssumeRole — from this point, all actions run with that role's permissions, NOT the customer's The engine reads the mainSteps array and executes steps in order (top to bottom) Each step runs an action — e.g., aws:executeAwsApi calls an AWS API, aws:executeScript runs Python code, aws:runCommand runs a script on an EC2 instance Each step can produce outputs . Later steps reference these as {{ StepName.OutputKey }} aws:branch steps act like if/else — they check conditions and jump to different steps If a step fails, onFailure decides: Abort , Continue , or step:GoToStepName Final status: Success , Failed , Cancelled , or TimedOut The customer sees all of this in real-time in the Automation console — each step shows its status, inputs, outputs, and any error messages. 🧠 Think of it like a recipe: Parameters = ingredients, Steps = instructions, Role = the chef's permissions in the kitchen

[SAW] SAW runbooks always require an AutomationAssumeRole parameter. What is this role, why does every runbook need it, and what happens if it's missing or misconfigured? The AutomationAssumeRole is an IAM role that the SSM Automation service "puts on" to do its work — like a badge that says "I'm allowed to do X, Y, Z in this AWS account." Why it exists: SAW runbooks perform actions in the customer's account (describe instances, restart services, etc.) The SSM service needs explicit permission to do these things The role defines exactly which AWS actions the runbook can perform — least privilege How it works technically: The role's trust policy must allow ssm.amazonaws.com to assume it The role's permissions policy lists the specific API calls needed (e.g., ec2:DescribeInstances ) Uses sts:AssumeRole under the hood If missing: The automation runs with the caller's own IAM permissions — bad because customers may have too many or too few permissions. If misconfigured: Steps fail with AccessDenied errors. In SAW integration tests: The role is created in CoreInfrastructure.yml so tests have a consistent, properly-scoped role. 🧠 The runbook does NOT run as the customer — it runs as this role

[SAW] SAW runbooks are JSON files with a specific structure. What are all the top-level sections, what goes in each one, and which are required? { "schemaVersion": "0.3", "description": "Troubleshoots EC2 connectivity issues...", "assumeRole": "{{ AutomationAssumeRole }}", "parameters": { "InstanceId": { "type": "String", "description": "The EC2 instance" }, "AutomationAssumeRole": { "type": "String", "default": "" } }, "mainSteps": [ { "name": "...", "action": "...", ... } ], "outputs": ["StepName.OutputKey"] } Section Required? Purpose schemaVersion ✅ Yes Always "0.3" for Automation documents description ✅ Yes Customer-facing explanation assumeRole No (but always used in SAW) References the IAM role parameter parameters No (but almost always present) Inputs — each has type, description, optionally default/allowedValues. No default = required ; with default = optional mainSteps ✅ Yes Ordered list of actions to execute outputs No Values surfaced to caller after execution (format: "StepName.OutputKey" ) 🧠 The {{ }} syntax is SSM's variable interpolation — replaced at runtime with actual values

[SAW] Inside mainSteps , each step is an object with several fields. What are the key fields in a step, and how do steps pass data to each other? Example step: { "name": "DescribeInstance", "action": "aws:executeAwsApi", "inputs": { "Service": "ec2", "Api": "DescribeInstances", "InstanceIds": ["{{ InstanceId }}"] }, "outputs": [{ "Name": "InstanceState", "Selector": "$.Reservations[0].Instances[0].State.Name", "Type": "String" }], "nextStep": "CheckIfRunning", "onFailure": "Abort", "isCritical": true } Field Purpose name Unique step ID — used to reference its outputs action Which SSM action to run inputs Parameters specific to the action outputs Values extracted from the result. Selector is a JSONPath expression nextStep Which step runs next (if omitted, runs the next in array) isEnd If true, automation stops after this step onFailure Abort, Continue, or step:StepName isCritical If false, failure won't fail the whole automation Data flow: Step A output → referenced as {{ DescribeInstance.InstanceState }} in Step B. Top-level parameters: {{ ParameterName }}

[SAW] CloudFormation (CFN) is used heavily in SAW for creating test infrastructure. If you've never written a CFN template before, what are the core concepts you need to understand? CloudFormation is AWS's Infrastructure as Code service. Instead of clicking around the console, you write a template (YAML/JSON) describing what you want, and CFN creates it. Core concepts: Template — a YAML/JSON file describing AWS resources. This is what you write. Stack — when you deploy a template, CFN creates a "stack" — a group of resources managed together. Delete the stack → all resources deleted. Resource — each AWS thing you want (EC2, IAM role, S3). Only required section. Parameters — inputs at deploy time ("which instance type?"). Makes templates reusable. Outputs — values exported after creation ("here's the role ARN"). Other stacks can import these. Cross-stack references — Stack A exports an output; Stack B uses Fn::ImportValue to read it. This is how SAW's Core stack shares the AutomationAssumeRole ARN with test stacks. Pseudo parameters — built-in variables like AWS::Region , AWS::AccountId , AWS::Partition . SAW uses these instead of hard-coding (for region parity). Resources: MyRole: Type: AWS::IAM::Role Properties: AssumeRolePolicyDocument: Statement: - Effect: Allow Principal: Service: ssm.amazonaws.com Action: sts:AssumeRole Outputs: RoleArn: Value: !GetAtt MyRole.Arn Export: Name: CoreStack-RoleArn

[SAW] In a SAW project, the Setup/ folder contains CloudFormation templates. What templates are typically there, how do they relate to each other, and what's the deployment order during integration tests? The Setup/ folder typically contains: Template Purpose CoreInfrastructure.yml Shared resources for ALL tests — AutomationAssumeRole, VPC, subnet, S3 bucket SuccessExecution.yml Resources for the happy path test — e.g., a properly configured EC2 instance FailedExecution.yml Resources for the failure path test — e.g., an instance with a broken config How they connect: Test stacks reference Core stack outputs using cross-stack references ( Fn::ImportValue ). Deployment order during make test : ☁️ Deploy CoreInfrastructure stack → creates shared resources, exports outputs ☁️ Deploy SuccessExecution stack → imports Core outputs, creates test resources ☁️ Deploy FailedExecution stack → same pattern 🚀 Run the runbook against each stack's resources with different parameters ✅ Assert results (did it succeed? did the right steps run?) 🗑️ Delete test stacks first, then Core stack last (because test stacks depend on Core)

[SAW] You're joining a development team that uses Git and GitHub. What are the essential Git commands you'll use daily, and what's the typical workflow from starting a task to getting your code merged? The daily workflow: git pull origin main — get the latest code from the team git checkout -b my-feature — create your own branch (isolated copy) (make your code changes) git status — see what files you changed git diff — see line-by-line changes git add file1.py file2.py — stage files to commit (or git add . for all) git commit -m "fix: update port validation" — save a snapshot git push origin my-feature — upload your branch to GitHub Open a Pull Request on GitHub → teammates review After approval → merge into main Other commands you'll need: Command When to use git clone url First time — download the repo git log --oneline -10 See last 10 commits git stash / git stash pop Temporarily save uncommitted work git branch -a List all branches git checkout main Switch back to main 🧠 Branches are like parallel universes — you work in yours, teammates in theirs, merging combines them

[SAW] 🖥️ PRACTICE EXERCISE — Your First Merge Conflict Context: Merge conflicts happen when two people edit the same line in the same file. Git can't decide which version to keep, so it pauses and asks you to fix it manually. This is normal on teams. Scenario: You just joined a team. A coworker has been working on feature/new-api . Meanwhile, someone pushed changes to main . You need to update feature/new-api with the latest main before opening a Pull Request. Paste this to set up the repo: cd /tmp && rm -rf git-practice && mkdir git-practice && cd git-practice && git init -b main && git config user.name "You" && git config user.email "you@example.com" && echo -e "# My API Service
port=8080
host=localhost
timeout=30
log_level=info" > config.txt && echo -e "# README
This is the API service.
Version: 1.0" > README.md && git add . && git commit -m "initial project setup" && git checkout -b feature/new-api && sed -i '' 's/port=8080/port=3000/' config.txt && sed -i '' 's/timeout=30/timeout=60/' config.txt && git add . && git commit -m "feat: update port and timeout for new API" && git checkout main && sed -i '' 's/port=8080/port=9090/' config.txt && sed -i '' 's/Version: 1.0/Version: 1.1/' README.md && git add . && git commit -m "ops: update port for production deploy" && git checkout feature/new-api && echo "Ready. You are on: feature/new-api" && echo "YOUR TASK: Run: git merge main" Your task: Run git merge main . You'll hit a conflict — resolve it and complete the merge. What happens when you run git merge main : Git combines main's changes with your branch. README.md merges cleanly (only main changed it). But config.txt conflicts: you changed port to 3000, main changed it to 9090. You'll see: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.txt Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result. Open the file ( cat /tmp/git-practice/config.txt ). You'll see: # My API Service HEAD port=3000 ======= port=9090 main host=localhost timeout=60 log_level=info What the markers mean: Between HEAD and ======= → your branch's version (port=3000) Between ======= and main → main's version (port=9090) timeout=60 has no markers — Git merged that automatically These markers are literally written into the file by Git. If you opened this in VS Code, you'd see them highlighted with buttons to pick a version. To resolve: Edit the file: nano /tmp/git-practice/config.txt Delete ALL marker lines ( , ======= , ), keep the port you want Save, then: cd /tmp/git-practice && git add config.txt && git commit -m "merge main, keep port=3000" Verify: git log --oneline — merge commit at top 🧠 Merge conflicts are normal. The key: read the markers, understand both sides, decide.

[SAW] 🖥️ PRACTICE EXERCISE — Multi-file Conflict via Rebase Context: In real projects, merges can conflict in several files at once. Also, many teams prefer rebase over merge — it replays your commits on top of main for a cleaner linear history (no merge commits). Resolving rebase conflicts works slightly differently. Scenario: You've been working on feature/refactor-handler . Meanwhile, a teammate pushed changes to main . Your tech lead says: "rebase onto main before opening the PR." Paste this: cd /tmp && rm -rf git-practice && mkdir git-practice && cd git-practice && git init -b main && git config user.name "You" && git config user.email "you@example.com" && echo -e "def handler(event):
 return 200" > main.py && echo -e "version=1.0
owner=platform-team" > metadata.txt && echo "# Handler Service" > README.md && git add . && git commit -m "initial commit" && git checkout -b feature/refactor-handler && echo -e "def handler(event, context):
 print('processing')
 return 200" > main.py && echo -e "version=2.0
owner=platform-team
author=you" > metadata.txt && git add . && git commit -m "refactor: add context param and metadata" && git checkout main && echo -e "def handler(event):

[SAW] You've pushed your branch and need to get your code reviewed before it can be merged. What is the code review process, what makes a good Pull Request, and what's expected of you as both author and reviewer? The process (as author): Push your branch: git push origin my-feature Go to GitHub → open a Pull Request (PR) from your branch into main Write a clear title (what changed) and description (why, how, context) Add reviewers (1-2 teammates) Reviewers examine the diff and either: ✅ Approve , 💬 Comment , or ❌ Request changes Address feedback — push new commits to the same branch (PR updates automatically) Once approved → Squash and merge into main Delete the feature branch What makes a good PR: Small and focused — one logical change per PR Self-reviewed first — read your own diff before asking others Descriptive — don't make reviewers guess Tests included — if you changed behavior, show it works As a reviewer: Be constructive — suggest improvements, don't just say "wrong" Distinguish "must fix" (blocking) from "nit" (nice-to-have) If you don't understand something, ask — that means the code needs better comments

[SAW] AWS CDK (Cloud Development Kit) is used in the SAW ecosystem. If you've used CloudFormation templates (YAML/JSON), what problem does CDK solve, how does it work under the hood, and what are its key concepts? The problem: CloudFormation templates are verbose. An IAM role + S3 bucket + Lambda can be hundreds of lines of YAML. CDK lets you write the same in ~10 lines of TypeScript/Python with sensible defaults. How it works: You write infrastructure in a real language (TypeScript, Python, Java) cdk synth → generates a CloudFormation template from your code cdk deploy → submits that template to CloudFormation → CFN creates resources CDK is NOT a replacement for CloudFormation — it's a layer on top. CFN still does the provisioning. Key concepts: Concept What it is App Top-level container. A CDK project is an "app" Stack Maps 1:1 to a CloudFormation stack Construct L1 Raw CFN resources (1:1 mapping, no defaults) Construct L2 Opinionated with sensible defaults (e.g., s3.Bucket() adds encryption by default) Construct L3 Multi-resource patterns (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB in one construct) Example: new s3.Bucket(this, 'MyBucket', { versioned: true }) generates ~40 lines of CFN YAML.

[SAW] How does CDK fit into the SAW ecosystem? SAW runbooks are JSON documents — so where does CDK come in, and what's the relationship between CDK, CloudFormation, and SAW? SAW runbooks themselves are NOT written in CDK. Runbooks are SSM Automation JSON with their own structure ( schemaVersion , parameters , mainSteps ). Where CDK IS used in SAW: SAW platform infrastructure — build systems, CI/CD pipelines, artifact storage Integration test infrastructure — some teams use CDK to generate the CFN templates in Setup/ Internal tooling — dashboards, monitoring, support tools The relationship chain: CDK code (TypeScript/Python) ↓ cdk synth CloudFormation templates (YAML/JSON) ↓ cdk deploy / SAW test framework AWS Resources (IAM roles, EC2, etc.) ↓ used by SAW Runbooks (SSM Automation JSON) Why you should know CDK: As a SAW developer, you'll encounter CDK in pipeline and tooling code even though you write runbooks in JSON. Understanding CDK helps you read and modify the infrastructure that supports your runbooks.

Search recursively in all files find . -name "*.json" Find files by name JSON (critical — runbooks are JSON): Command What it does jq '.' file.json Pretty-print JSON jq '.mainSteps[0]' Extract specific data Piping redirection: cmd1 | cmd2 — pipe output: cat log.txt | grep "ERROR" cmd > file.txt — write to file (overwrites) cmd >> file.txt — append to file cmd 2>&1 — redirect errors to same place as output echo $? — last command's exit code (0=success) Control flow: cmd1 && cmd2 — run cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeds cmd1 || cmd2 — run cmd2 only if cmd1 fails chmod +x script.sh — make script executable
